category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives

original_label: Board approval conditions for Fastow's SPE participation

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Concealment of repurchase transactions from Board
original_label: Concealment of repurchase transactions from Board

context: The indictment describes how management systematically excluded information about LJM repurchase transactions from Board presentations, preventing the Board from understanding the true nature of the arrangement.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Violation of promised restrictions on Fastow's pecuniary interest
original_label: Violation of promised restrictions on Fastow's pecuniary interest
quote: Finally, as described more fully below in connection with a transaction known as Southampton, FASTOW, GLISAN, and others violated their duty to provide honest services to Enron. In addition FASTOW violated his duty to provide honest services when he arranged for the other participants in the transaction to profit personally from the Southampton transaction at the expense of Enron and others, without the knowledge or approval of Enron and in violation of Enron's internal ethics policies.
context: The indictment shows that Fastow's conduct directly violated both the Board's stated conditions and Enron's ethics policies, indicating failures in monitoring and enforcement mechanisms.

label: Inside and outside counsel advice on improper transactions
original_label: Inside and outside counsel advice on improper transactions

original_label: Fastow's simultaneous control over SPEs and Enron operations

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives

original_label: Enron management secretly agreed to prop up LJM

original_label: Earnings recognition as dominant organizational goal

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings

original_label: Undisclosed oral side deal to guarantee LJM repurchase

original_label: Delayed asset repurchase to hide Fastow's LJM exit

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings

original_label: Oral promises to Merrill Lynch outside documentation

original_label: False representations to outside auditors

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Hedging to protect portfolio value against market risk
original_label: Hedging to protect portfolio value against market risk
quote: Following an IPO, Enron was at risk for market price fluctuations in the shares, many of which were extremely volatile. category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Secret side agreement guaranteeing LJM payment before hedging
original_label: Secret side agreement guaranteeing LJM payment before hedging
quote: As FASTOW, GLISAN, and others knew, however, Talon was not properly off balance sheet. First, as FASTOW, GLISAN, and others knew, Enron and FASTOW entered into a secret side agreement whereby Enron guaranteed that it would pay $41 million to LJM before Talon would engage in the hedging transactions for which it was created. In exchange, FASTOW allowed Enron to use Talon to manipulate Enron's financial statements. As a result of this secret side deal, LJM's investment was never truly at risk.
context: The indictment describes the core mechanism of Talon fraud: a secret side agreement that violated accounting requirements and prevented the 3% outside equity from being genuinely at risk, hidden from auditors and the Board.

label: Manufactured put transaction to justify hidden payment
original_label: Manufactured put transaction to justify hidden payment
quote: In order to mask the side deal, FASTOW, GLISAN and others devised a scheme to manufacture an ostensible reason for a $41 million payment from Enron to LJM. To do so, Enron and Talon entered into a "put," that is, a transaction that purportedly served to hedge Enron against a decline in its own stock value. Although there was no true business purpose, the "put" option was purchased by Enron for $41 million. The price was designed by FASTOW, GLISAN, and others to ensure that LJM would receive its prearranged $41 million prior to Talon engaging in any other business.
context: The indictment describes how management created fake transaction documentation to conceal the true nature of a payment from LJM, creating a fraudulent paper trail for auditors.

label: Back-dating hedge documents to inflate asset values
original_label: Back-dating hedge documents to inflate asset values
quote: For example, Enron used a back-dated hedge to fraudulently inflate the value of its investment in 1.09 million shares of AVICI stock. Specifically, FASTOW and others caused documents related to the hedge to be backdated to August 3, 2000, when the price of AVICI reached an all time high of $163.50. In fact, the share price by the actual date of the hedge had declined significantly. By backdating the hedge transaction to August 3, 2000, Enron was able to falsely record the value of its AVICI shares at a significantly inflated price.
context: The indictment describes deliberate document falsification by Fastow and others to manipulate financial statements, showing active management tampering with the accounting record.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: NatWest bankers induced to sell equity interest below value
original_label: NatWest bankers induced to sell equity interest below value

Indeed, on or about March 22, 2000, FASTOW finalized an agreement with Enron to pay Swap Sub $30 million to unwind Enron's transactions with Swap Sub. FASTOW represented to Enron that CSFB would receive $10 million, and falsely represented that NatWest would receive $20 million. In fact, as FASTOW, GLISAN, and others knew, NatWest received only $1 million.
context: The indictment describes deliberate misrepresentation of payment amounts to Enron's own management to conceal the fraud scheme targeting the external bank partner.

label: Fastow-Kopper-bankers conspiracy to fraudulently undervalue equity
original_label: Fastow-Kopper-bankers conspiracy to fraudulently undervalue equity
quote: By early 2000, Enron's and Rhythms Net's share prices had increased; consequently, so had the value of Swap Sub. Even though FASTOW was prohibited by Enron's Board from having any direct pecuniary interest in Enron's stock held by LJM, FASTOW, Kopper, and three bankers employed by NatWest devised a scheme to defraud Enron and NatWest by capturing a substantial portion of the increased value of Swap Sub's Enron shares for themselves and others, including GLISAN.
context: The indictment describes how Fastow recruited external bankers to help him circumvent the Board's restriction on his personal interest in LJM holdings, showing how structural position enabled recruitment of third-party conspirators.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Business skill and success appearance as organizational goal
original_label: Business skill and success appearance as organizational goal
quote: The goals of the schemes included: (a) fraudulent manipulation of Enron's reported financial results so that Enron would appear more successful than it was; (b) artificial manipulation of the share price of Enron stock; (c) circumvention of federal regulations so that Enron could obtain benefits to which it was not entitled; (d) appearance of business skill and success on the part of FASTOW, GLISAN, BOYLE and others; and (e) personal enrichment of FASTOW, GLISAN, BOYLE, and others at the expense of Enron, its shareholders, and others to whom they owed a duty of honest services.
context: The indictment identifies both organizational-level goals (appearing successful to the market) and individual-level goals (personal enrichment), showing how these were intertwined in Enron's culture.

label: Board approval process for CFO SPE participation
original_label: Board approval process for CFO SPE participation
quote: By 1999, Enron was increasingly dependent on transactions with SPEs to close the gap between its actual business performance and its financial reporting goals. By June 1999, in order to have an off-balance-sheet SPE to which Enron regularly could turn, Enron's Board of Directors (the "Board") agreed to permit FASTOW to create and serve as the managing partner of a new SPE known as LJM Cayman.
context: The indictment describes the formal Board approval process for Fastow's LJM role, showing the governance channel through which the arrangement was supposed to be overseen.

label: Treasurer GLISAN shared responsibility for financial wellbeing
original_label: Treasurer GLISAN shared responsibility for financial wellbeing
quote: The defendant BEN F. GLISAN, JR., a resident of Houston, Texas, was a former Arthur Andersen accountant who joined Enron in 1996. GLISAN held various positions at Enron, rising to the position of Treasurer in the spring of 2000, until his termination for cause in November 2001. As Treasurer, GLISAN along with FASTOW and other senior Enron management had responsibility for overseeing the financial well-being of the company.
context: The indictment identifies Glisan's structural position as Treasurer with shared responsibility for financial oversight, showing his position in the chain of financial decision-making.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas

original_label: Enron management focused on closing quarterly earnings gap

The Cuiaba project had caused Enron to incur significant costs and by 2001 was approximately over $200 million over budget. When no true third-party buyer could be found, FASTOW and others arranged on September 30, 1999 to "sell" a portion of Enron's interest in the Cuiaba project to LJM for $11.3 million. This purported sale enabled Enron to recognize a total of approximately $65 million of income in the third and fourth quarter of 1999, when it was struggling to meet its projected financial results.
context: The indictment shows that management's dominant agenda was meeting quarterly earnings targets, which drove the decision to use LJM parking transactions rather than address the underlying project problems.

label: False audit representations about Merrill Lynch barge transaction
original_label: False audit representations about Merrill Lynch barge transaction

original_label: Fastow's LJM interest sale to exit disclosure requirements

context: The indictment describes a deliberate organizational move to avoid regulatory disclosure requirements while maintaining access to LJM's financial benefits, showing management's focus on disclosure avoidance.

original_label: Boyle as lead employee on Nigerian barge transactions

original_label: Management arranged LJM purchase of Merrill Lynch barges

context: The indictment describes the formal governance procedures promised to the Board to oversee LJM transactions, showing the design of internal controls that were then undermined.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Undisclosed fee paid to LJM for assuming barge interest
original_label: Undisclosed fee paid to LJM for assuming barge interest

original_label: Fastow received kickbacks from arrangement fee to Chewco

FASTOW and his wife did not report those kickbacks to their tax accountants or as income on their 1998 and 1999 federal income tax returns to the IRS.
context: The indictment describes a payment structure used to secretly compensate Fastow for approving a transaction contrary to Enron's interests, showing active management of hidden compensation channels.

original_label: Obstruction by Fastow persuading Kopper to destroy evidence

original_label: Enron CFO reported directly to Chief Executive Officer

original_label: Enron funded 97 percent of RADR purchase price

original_label: Adverse publicity about Fastow's LJM role triggered disclosure concerns

original_label: Offer to purchase Swap Sub communicated via fax

context: The indictment lists communication channels through which Southampton transaction documents were transmitted, showing how the scheme used formal business communication methods.

label: Analyst discovers Raptor losses backstopped by Enron stock
original_label: Analyst discovers Raptor losses backstopped by Enron stock
quote: While working for Mr. Fastow in 2001, I was charged with reviewing all assets that Enron considered for sale and determining the likely economic impact of sale. As part of the sale analysis, I reviewed the estimated book values and market values of each asset. A number of assets were hedged with an entity called Raptor. Any asset that was hedged should, for the most part, have a locked-in sales value for Enron, meaning that despite current market prices Enron should realize the hedged price with Raptor. It was my understanding that the Raptor special purpose entities were owned by LJM, the partnership run by Mr. Fastow. In completing my work, certain Enron business units provided me with analyses that showed certain of the hedged losses that had been incurred by Raptor were actually coming back to Enron. The general explanation was that the Enron stock backstopping the Raptor hedge had declined in value such that Raptor would have a shortfall and would be unable to fully cover the hedge price that it owed to Enron.
context: Watkins describes her initial discovery as Vice President of Corporate Development in June-August 2001 that Raptor SPEs had negative economic implications for Enron.

label: Employee recognizes stock cannot generate income without violating accounting principles
original_label: Employee recognizes stock cannot generate income without violating accounting principles
quote: I was highly alarmed by the information I was receiving. My understanding as an accountant is that a company could never use its own stock to generate a gain or avoid a loss on its income statement. I continued to ask questions and seek answers, primarily from former co-workers in the global finance group, or in the business units that had hedged assets with Raptor. I never heard reassuring explanations.
context: Watkins explains her accounting-based concerns as she investigated the Raptor structure in summer 2001.

label: Raptor losses widespread knowledge among finance and business unit staff
original_label: Raptor losses widespread knowledge among finance and business unit staff
quote: As I was doing my work and looking at these assets hedged by Raptor, my concern was that it seemed to be just common knowledge that the Raptor losses were backstopped by Enron stock. And an analysis was always looked at, what's the value of Enron stock compared to the money Raptor owes us? And I was shocked that people could explain this to me with no concern in their voice, like there was some magic structure that Enron and Andersen had come up with to make this work.
context: Watkins testifies about how widespread awareness of the problematic Raptor structure was among Enron staff in summer 2001.

label: Anonymous letter to CEO warns of wave of accounting scandals
original_label: Anonymous letter to CEO warns of wave of accounting scandals
quote: On August 14, 2001, I was informed of Mr. Skilling's sudden resignation and felt compelled to inform Mr. Lay of the accounting problems that faced Enron. I sent Mr. Lay an anonymous letter on August 14, 2001, in response to a request for questions for an upcoming all-employee meeting to be held August 16 to address Mr. Skilling's departure.
context: Watkins describes sending the first warning signal to Ken Lay immediately after Skilling's unexpected resignation.

label: Five memos documenting Raptor oddities and $700 million risk
original_label: Five memos documenting Raptor oddities and $700 million risk
quote: I met with Mr. Lay on the afternoon of Wednesday, August 22, 2001. The meeting lasted just over one half hour. I provided him with five memos I had drafted to help explain the problems facing the company. These five memos constitute the seven pages this committee discovered and subsequently disclosed on January 14, 2002. Additionally, I provided Mr. Lay an analysis of the Raptor entity economics and a presentation prepared by Enron's risk assessment and control group. I primarily used the memo titled "Summary of Raptor Oddities" as talking points with Mr. Lay. My main point to Mr. Lay was that by this time Raptor owed Enron in excess of $700 million under certain hedging agreements.
context: Watkins describes delivering detailed written and documentary evidence of accounting problems to the CEO on August 22, 2001.

label: Analyst reports $500 million unhedged loss from Raptor in 2000
original_label: Analyst reports $500 million unhedged loss from Raptor in 2000

They had dropped significantly in value, and in the related party footnote in 2000 it mentions that Enron had recognized $500 million of revenue from the special entities' offsetting of corresponding writedown in the equity investment portfolio of Enron. I think that tended to make readers think that it was a $500 million gain offset by a $500 million loss. Therefore, zero impact on the income statement. However, without the Raptor transactions, Enron would have had a $500 million loss not covered by any gains running through the 2000 income statement.
context: Watkins explains to Chairman Greenwood how the Raptor hedges masked real losses in financial statements.

label: CFO's former partner complains to COO about LJM conflict of interest
original_label: CFO's former partner complains to COO about LJM conflict of interest

Mr. McMahon did not characterize it as a bonus discussion with me. He characterized it as more of an ultimatum that he was giving Mr. Skilling; Make these changes or I can't stay as Treasurer. And as I recall Mr. McMahon telling me, he felt like that was a strong statement to Mr. Skilling.
context: Watkins recounts McMahon's prior warning to Skilling in August 2001 about LJM partnership conflicts.

label: Risk officer documents Raptor structure permanently underwater
original_label: Risk officer documents Raptor structure permanently underwater

label: Survey of Labor Day weekend revealed dozen employees with accounting concerns
original_label: Survey of Labor Day weekend revealed dozen employees with accounting concerns

label: Employee meets with HR VP about concerns, directed to CEO
original_label: Employee meets with HR VP about concerns, directed to CEO

label: Employee vets concerns with former Andersen mentor and former colleague
original_label: Employee vets concerns with former Andersen mentor and former colleague

context: Watkins describes informal communication channels used to validate her concerns before escalating to the CEO.

label: Associate General Counsel told of Raptor concerns two days before CEO meeting
original_label: Associate General Counsel told of Raptor concerns two days before CEO meeting

label: Lay initiates investigation after August 22 meeting

original_label: MCAS Review meeting concludes no redesign needed for AOA failures

context: Committee quoting June 22, 2016 Boeing MCAS Review meeting minutes showing how concerns about faulty AOA data were dismissed.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing determines pilot can manage repetitive MCAS without redesign
original_label: Boeing determines pilot can manage repetitive MCAS without redesign
quote: The technical discussions of MCAS also included the possibility of a faulty angle of attack sensor potentially leading to repeated MCAS activation. After evaluating the issue, the group of technical experts and pilots involved in this discussion determined, based on their collective expertise, that there was no need to redesign MCAS to address this possibility because the flight crew would be able to manage the condition using ... well-understood piloting techniques and procedures.
context: Boeing's written response to Committee describing internal decision-making that dismissed engineer concerns about repetitive activation.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Single AOA sensor concern resolved without addressing vulnerability
original_label: Single AOA sensor concern resolved without addressing vulnerability
quote: In 2015, a Boeing AR raised the question of whether MCAS was "vulnerable to single AOA sensor failures...." Despite this, the aircraft was delivered with MCAS dependent on a single AOA sensor.
context: Committee's executive summary showing AR raised concern but design was not changed before certification.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing removes MCAS references from pilot training same day as redesign approval
original_label: Boeing removes MCAS references from pilot training same day as redesign approval
quote: Just hours after the approval for MCAS's redesign was granted, Boeing sought, and the FAA approved, the removal of references to MCAS from Boeing's Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM) — a document that provides procedures, performance, and systems information to flight crews to enable their safe and efficient operation of the airplane. As a result, 737 MAX pilots were precluded from knowing of the existence of MCAS and its potential effect on aircraft handling without pilot command.
context: Committee investigation finding removal of MCAS from pilot training materials coincided with expanded operational authority for system.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing test data on catastrophic reaction time never shared with FAA
original_label: Boeing test data on catastrophic reaction time never shared with FAA
quote: In 2012, at the start of the 737 MAX program, it took a Boeing test pilot more than 10 seconds to respond to uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator, which the pilot found to be "catastrophic[.]" Boeing never shared this information with the FAA, its MAX customers, or MAX pilots.
context: Committee executive summary documenting that Boeing possessed and internally documented critical test data but withheld it from regulators.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing documented catastrophic reaction time in six coordination sheets but not disclosed
original_label: Boeing documented catastrophic reaction time in six coordination sheets but not disclosed
quote: From 2015 to 2018, the information regarding the fact that Boeing's own test pilot took more than 10 seconds to respond to uncommanded MCAS activation in a flight simulator leading to potentially "catastrophic" consequences was included in at least six separate internal Boeing Coordination Sheets on MCAS's requirements. This indicates Boeing's keen awareness of the importance of this information. The Committee has found no evidence that Boeing shared this information with the FAA, its customers, or 737 MAX pilots.
context: Committee investigation showing Boeing repeatedly documented critical safety finding internally while withholding from external parties.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing AR raises MCAS concerns internally but does not report to FAA
original_label: Boeing AR raises MCAS concerns internally but does not report to FAA
quote: In June 2016, a Boeing AR raised concerns following a test flight of the 737 MAX during which MCAS countered the pilot's attempts to trim the airplane, including concerns related to the vulnerability caused by faulty AOA readings. These concerns were discounted by the AR's Boeing colleagues, particularly Boeing's test pilots. However, faulty AOA data that resulted in uncommanded MCAS activation was a significant contributing factor in the crashes of both the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines flights.
context: Committee finding showing AR raised concerns internally that aligned with actual crash causes but concerns were not transmitted to FAA.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing AR fails to inform FAA of AOA Disagree alert inoperability
original_label: Boeing AR fails to inform FAA of AOA Disagree alert inoperability
quote: In 2017, a Boeing AR failed to inform the FAA that the AOA Disagree Alert feature on a majority of the 737 MAX fleet were inoperative and that Boeing was aware of this condition. Moreover, Boeing continued to manufacture and deliver airplanes with the nonfunctioning alert to customers without informing them or the FAA that the alert was not operating.
context: Committee identifying specific instance where Boeing AR with knowledge of non-compliance failed to report to FAA.

label: Boeing OMB and FAA AD omit MCAS reference after Lion Air crash
original_label: Boeing OMB and FAA AD omit MCAS reference after Lion Air crash
quote: In November 2018, days after the Lion Air crash, both Boeing and the FAA issued advisories for 737 MAX pilots that failed to even mention the existence of MCAS by name. Only after receiving inquiries about MCAS from airlines did Boeing describe MCAS in a Multi Operator Message (MOM), on November 10, 2018, that went to Boeing's MAX customers but was not otherwise made public.
context: Committee investigation of post-crash response showing critical information about MCAS initially withheld from pilots.

label: Boeing and FAA fail to ground MAX based on post-Lion Air risk assessment
original_label: Boeing and FAA fail to ground MAX based on post-Lion Air risk assessment
quote: In December 2018, the FAA conducted a risk assessment based on its Transport Aircraft Risk Assessment Methodology (TARAM) and estimated that without a fix to MCAS, during the lifetime of the 737 MAX fleet, there could potentially be 15 additional fatal crashes resulting in over 2,900 deaths. Despite that assessment, the FAA permitted the 737 MAX to continue flying while Boeing and the FAA worked on designing and validating, respectively, a fix to the MCAS software.
context: Committee documenting FAA's December 2018 quantitative risk assessment predicting catastrophic consequences but permitting continued flight operations.

label: Boeing continues production amid reported safety concerns
original_label: Boeing continues production amid reported safety concerns
quote: Rather than heeding Mr. Pierson's dire warnings and thoroughly evaluating his safety concerns, Boeing continued to ramp up production on the 737 MAX and rehired retired Boeing employees to keep the production lines moving at the Renton plant. Lion Air flight 610 crashed three months later in October 2018.
context: Committee documenting Boeing's response to senior plant supervisor's June 2018 safety concerns was to accelerate production.

label: Boeing does not update certification plans after MCAS redesign
original_label: Boeing does not update certification plans after MCAS redesign
quote: When responding to a question from committee staff about whose job it would be at Boeing to inform the FAA about a change to MCAS, Mr. Teal noted, "...the certification plans would have to be updated..." However, "[T]he JATR team found that the certification plans and some certification deliverables (e.g., the preliminary system safety assessment (PSSA)) were not updated to describe the expansion of the MCAS function for the low Mach portion of the flight envelope and for compliance with stall-related requirements."
context: Committee investigation finding Boeing failed to formally update FAA certification documentation after March 2016 MCAS redesign.

label: Lion Air crash identified MCAS as major factor
original_label: Lion Air crash identified MCAS as major factor
quote: Lion Air flight 610 crashes 13 minutes after takeoff killing 189 people. MCAS is quickly determined to be a major factor in the crash. Faulty AOA data erroneously caused MCAS to repetitively activate more than 20 times as the pilots battled MCAS for control of the aircraft.
context: Committee's MCAS timeline marking first fatal crash and immediate identification of MCAS involvement.

label: Ethiopian Airlines crash prompts FAA to finally ground MAX
original_label: Ethiopian Airlines crash prompts FAA to finally ground MAX
quote: Ethiopian Airlines flight 302 crashes six minutes after takeoff killing all 157 passengers and crew. The FAA is the last civil aviation authority to ground the 737 MAX on March 13, 2020, three days after the Ethiopian crash. The 737 MAX aircraft has been grounded worldwide ever since.
context: Committee's MCAS timeline documenting second crash and resulting worldwide grounding of aircraft.

label: Engineer questions MCAS pilot response time adequacy
original_label: Engineer questions MCAS pilot response time adequacy
quote: Do you think that with pilot training/knowledge of the [MCAS] system there will be a sufficiently quick response to the stab runaway during the windup turn/recovery and that it is appropriate to deem it hazardous and have the MCAS system designed to meet this? Or should we step up to catastrophic with the assumption that not all pilots will recognize it quickly enough?
context: In November 2012, a Boeing engineer emails two Boeing test pilots asking critical questions about pilot response time to MCAS activation, raising the possibility that the system poses catastrophic risk if pilots cannot react quickly enough.

label: Boeing test pilot fails to respond to MCAS in simulator
original_label: Boeing test pilot fails to respond to MCAS in simulator
quote: A typical reaction time was observed to be approximately 4 seconds. A slow reaction time scenario (>10 seconds) found the failure to be catastrophic due to the inability to arrest the airplane overspeed.
context: Boeing's own coordination sheets document that during testing, a slow pilot response time greater than 10 seconds to MCAS activation resulted in a catastrophic failure outcome.

label: Chief Project Engineer unaware of basic MCAS facts
original_label: Chief Project Engineer unaware of basic MCAS facts
quote: At the time that you approved MCAS, you were not aware that it operated from a single AOA sensor, you were not aware that it could activate repeatedly, and you were not aware that Boeing was aware that if a pilot didn't react in 10 seconds to an MCAS activation the result could be catastrophic. At the time you signed -- this was all information that you were not aware of when you signed off on MCAS. Mr. Teal: That is correct.
context: During a Committee staff interview in May 2020, Michael Teal, the former Chief Project Engineer and Deputy Program Manager of the 737 MAX program, acknowledges he approved MCAS without understanding critical design parameters including single-sensor reliance, repetitive activation capability, and catastrophic pilot response time implications.

label: Program leadership lacks direct engineering reports
original_label: Program leadership lacks direct engineering reports
quote: no employees actually report[ed] to me. …. no engineers directly report[ed] to me. They all are functionally aligned to the engineering leaders of the company... But from a daily direction and overseeing of the program, you know, you could say that none of them worked for me but all of them worked for me, is what I like to say.
context: Michael Teal describes to Committee staff the organizational structure where the Chief Project Engineer had formal responsibility for the MAX program but no direct authority over the engineers working on it, creating ambiguity in accountability.

label: MCAS references removed from pilot training materials
original_label: MCAS references removed from pilot training materials
quote: In a March 30, 2016, email, Mr. Forkner assured an FAA official that references to MCAS could be deleted from the official FCOM and other 737 MAX training documents because MCAS is 'completely transparent to the flight crew and only operates WAY outside of the normal operating envelope.'
context: Boeing's 737 Chief Technical Pilot Mark Forkner requests and obtains FAA permission to remove MCAS references from flight crew training materials, justifying the deletion on the grounds that the system is invisible to pilots and operates outside normal envelope.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Level B training as design objective for MAX program
original_label: Level B training as design objective for MAX program
quote: Guaranteeing that the 737 MAX did not require simulator training for pilots transitioning from the 737 NG to the 737 MAX was a key Boeing objective of the 737 MAX program. This goal demanded that pilot differences training be kept to 16 hours or less of Level B (non-simulator) training requirements.
context: The Committee's investigation identifies that avoiding simulator training requirements was established as a core design objective of the MAX program from the beginning, creating a powerful incentive that influenced technical decisions.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Southwest Airlines contract financially penalizes simulator training
original_label: Southwest Airlines contract financially penalizes simulator training
quote: In December 2011, Boeing agreed to pay Southwest Airlines $1 million per MAX airplane that Boeing delivered to Southwest if its pilots were unable to operate the 737 NG and 737 MAX interchangeably due to any reason. In addition, if the FAA required more than 10 hours of pilot training and/or required flight simulator training, Boeing would reimburse SWA for any direct training expense that exceeded 10 hours.
context: Boeing's contract with Southwest Airlines explicitly penalizes the company financially if simulator training becomes necessary, creating a powerful economic incentive to avoid it even at the expense of safety.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Countdown clocks emphasize schedule pressure
original_label: Countdown clocks emphasize schedule pressure
quote: To remind Boeing employees of how critical sticking to the program's schedule was, Boeing's management introduced 'countdown clocks' into the MAX program, and they made certain that they were easy to spot... The 'countdown clocks' were located in the conference room where the 737 MAX program's senior-most management held 'business performance reviews,' 'technical review boards,' and other meetings.
context: Boeing management installed physical countdown clocks in senior leadership meeting rooms to emphasize the importance of adhering to the MAX development schedule, making schedule pressure a visible and constant aspect of the environment.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Boeing Chief Technical Pilot dismisses simulator training concerns
original_label: Boeing Chief Technical Pilot dismisses simulator training concerns
quote: In response to a March 2017 request from Boeing's Africa & Caribbean Sales Director related to an inquiry from a customer airline about costs to provide training to its flight crews, Mr. Forkner wrote: 'I want to stress the importance of holding firm that there will not be any type of simulator training required to transition from the NG to the MAX. Boeing will not allow that to happen. We'll go face to face with any regulator who tries to make that a requirement.'
context: Mark Forkner, Boeing's 737 Chief Technical Pilot, resists airline inquiries about simulator training requirements with aggressive language, stating Boeing will not permit such training regardless of regulator positions.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Engineer pressured on trim technique checklist design
original_label: Engineer pressured on trim technique checklist design
quote: In July 2014, for example, the Level B training goal overshadowed discussions Mr. Forkner had with a colleague concerning the development of pilot checklists for the Flight Crew Training Manual. As related to the specific checklists they were developing, Mr. Forkner advised that they follow 'the path with the least risk to Level B' and 'sell' an action pertaining to trim technique as a 'very intuitive basic pilot skill.' Mr. Forkner's colleague cautioned: 'I fear that skill is not very intuitive any more with the younger pilots and those who have become too reliant on automation.' Mr. Forkner responded: 'Probably true, but it's the box we're painted into with the Level B training requirements.'
context: In 2014 email exchanges about checklist development, Boeing's Chief Technical Pilot prioritizes maintaining Level B training requirements over pilot skill concerns, acknowledging that the training constraint dictates checklist design choices.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing dismisses repetitive MCAS activation concern
original_label: Boeing dismisses repetitive MCAS activation concern
quote: Boeing had assumed that repetitive MCAS activations would not adversely impact the ability of the MAX pilots to maintain control of the aircraft despite the fact that a Boeing AR raised this question. Boeing 'Engineering and Test pilots discussed scenario of repeated unintended MCAS activation during MAX development,' according to a December 2018 Boeing presentation to the FAA, 'and deemed [it] no worse than single unintended MCAS activation.' Those assumptions were proven tragically wrong.
context: An Authorized Representative raised concerns about repetitive MCAS activation, but Boeing engineers and test pilots dismissed the concern by deeming it equivalent to single activation, an assumption later proven catastrophically incorrect.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing rejects synthetic airspeed on cost and training grounds
original_label: Boeing rejects synthetic airspeed on cost and training grounds
quote: A synthetic airspeed system addresses that risk by creating a redundancy to the mechanical pitot-static system... However, because the system relies on AOA data as one datapoint, the system can also be used to assess the reliability of AOA sensors... Unfortunately, the request to install synthetic airspeed on the 737 MAX was rejected by Boeing management because its introduction would have been too costly and may have resulted in the FAA requiring simulator training on the MAX – something that would have jeopardized the 737 MAX program's clear and consistent goal to avoid simulator training requirements.
context: Boeing engineers proposed synthetic airspeed as a safety redundancy that could have helped detect AOA sensor failures, but Boeing management rejected it citing cost and the risk it would trigger simulator training requirements.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Level B training goal blocks synthetic airspeed implementation
original_label: Level B training goal blocks synthetic airspeed implementation
quote: As I pointed out in the telecom today, an introduction of synthetic airspeed to the MAX would drastically alter [the Airspeed Unreliable] Critical Action, Memory Item Non-Normal Checklist. If synthetic airspeed is standard as opposed to an option, it would likely jeopardize the Program directive to maintain Level B training for our customers.
context: A Boeing technical pilot explains in 2013 email that implementing synthetic airspeed would interfere with maintaining Level B training requirements, illustrating how the training constraint shaped technical design decisions.

label: Boeing postpones AOA Disagree alert fix for three years
original_label: Boeing postpones AOA Disagree alert fix for three years
quote: Rather than immediately informing the FAA about the inoperable AOA Disagree alert and advising Boeing to fix the problem as soon as possible, a Boeing Authorized Representative consented to Boeing's plan to postpone a software update to fix the problem until 2020, nearly three years later, so it could be done in conjunction with the planned rollout of the MAX-10 aircraft. This decision to defer the fix to 2020 was made in September 2017.
context: Boeing's Authorized Representative agreed to defer fixing the non-functioning AOA Disagree alert on more than 80 percent of the MAX fleet until 2020, despite knowing since August 2017 that the alert was inoperative.

label: Boeing continues MAX production despite Pierson safety warnings
original_label: Boeing continues MAX production despite Pierson safety warnings
quote: Rather than heeding Mr. Pierson's dire warnings and thoroughly evaluating his safety concerns, Boeing continued to ramp up production on the 737 MAX. Lion Air flight 610 crashed three months later.
context: After Ed Pierson, a senior Boeing manager, raised serious safety concerns about worker fatigue and production quality in June and July 2018, Boeing management did not halt production but instead continued to increase production rates.

label: Authorized Representatives experience undue pressure survey
original_label: Authorized Representatives experience undue pressure survey
quote: In November 2016, at the height of the 737 MAX's certification activities, and provided to the Committee from a whistleblower, highlighted a number of findings related to undue influence at Boeing. The survey focused on Boeing's Authorized Representatives (ARs), part of the ODA program, who although they are Boeing employees, are supposed to represent the interests of the FAA. Over 520 Boeing ODA members participated in the survey. Alarmingly, the survey found that 39 percent of the Boeing ARs that responded believed they had experienced undue pressure... In addition, of those 39 percent, 80 percent had encountered more than one situation where they perceived potential undue pressure.
context: A Boeing internal survey in November 2016 found that 39 percent of Authorized Representatives believed they had experienced undue pressure, and 80 percent of those reported multiple instances of such pressure.

label: Pierson warns Campbell of exhausted workforce and safety hazards
original_label: Pierson warns Campbell of exhausted workforce and safety hazards
quote: Scott, I have some safety concerns that I need to share with you as the leader of the 737 Program. Today we have 38 unfinished airplanes located outside the factory. The following concerns are based on my own observations and 30 years of aviation safety experience. My first concern is that our workforce is exhausted. …. Fatigued employees make mistakes. My second concern is schedule pressure (combined with fatigue) is creating a culture where employees are either deliberately or unconsciously circumventing established processes.
context: In June 2018, Ed Pierson, a senior Boeing manager at the Renton MAX final assembly plant, emails Scott Campbell, the 737 General Manager, with detailed safety concerns about workforce exhaustion and process circumvention driven by schedule pressure.

label: Pierson recommends temporary production line shutdown
original_label: Pierson recommends temporary production line shutdown
quote: Mr. Pierson recommended temporarily shutting down the production line 'to allow our team time to regroup so we can safely finish the planes outside and then shift our attention to the planes inside. I don't make this recommendation lightly,' he wrote. 'I know this would take a lot of planning, but the alternative of rushing the build is far riskier. Nothing we do is as important that it is worth hurting someone,' Mr. Pierson declared.
context: In his June 2018 email to Campbell, Pierson recommends a temporary production halt to address quality and safety issues, stating that no production goal justifies risking worker or passenger safety.

label: Campbell acknowledges safety concerns but no halt occurs
original_label: Campbell acknowledges safety concerns but no halt occurs
quote: Mr. Campbell responded to Mr. Pierson at 6:48 a.m. the following morning, Sunday, June 10, 2018. His reply suggested he clearly understood Mr. Pierson's concerns. Mr. Campbell wrote: 'We need and will remind everyone constantly that quality is number one and schedule come [sic] after that. We are trying to make sure people take time off so the [sic] can recharge…because your [sic] right we don't want people coming to work tired.'
context: Campbell responds to Pierson's safety email acknowledging that quality should come before schedule and addressing fatigue concerns, but despite this acknowledgment no production halt occurs.

label: Campbell meeting with Pierson yields no action
original_label: Campbell meeting with Pierson yields no action
quote: According to Mr. Pierson's testimony to the Committee, he told Mr. Campbell that in the military they would temporarily halt production if they had the kinds of safety problems that Mr. Pierson was seeing on the MAX factory floor. According to Mr. Pierson, Mr. Campbell responded: ''The military isn't a profit-making organization.''
context: In July 2018 meeting with Campbell, Pierson references military safety practices of halting operations when safety problems emerge, and Campbell's response implicitly prioritizes profit over safety.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Production pressure overrides quality concerns at Renton
original_label: Production pressure overrides quality concerns at Renton
quote: The Seattle Times also reported that some work groups at the plant had 'asked their managers about perhaps stopping the production lines in order to catch up' on all of the half-finished airplanes that were accumulating at the Boeing factory. 'Managers have responded categorically that a pause cannot happen because of the severe impact it would have on suppliers, on airline customers and on the company's stock price,' wrote the Seattle Times.
context: In September 2018, the Seattle Times reports that Renton plant workers requested production halts to address quality issues, but management categorically refused citing impacts on suppliers, customers, and stock price.

label: Multiple Boeing engineers raise MCAS and pilot response time concerns
original_label: Multiple Boeing engineers raise MCAS and pilot response time concerns
quote: In June 2016, more than two years prior to the October 2018 crash of the Lion Air flight, Boeing engineers had predicted some of the key issues that led to the Lion Air crash, including the potential adverse consequences of erroneous AOA sensor data on MCAS, and they questioned whether or not pilots would have trouble combatting repetitive MCAS activation. These concerns, however, were either not adequately addressed or largely dismissed by their Boeing colleagues.
context: Boeing engineers raised concerns in June 2016 about erroneous AOA data effects on MCAS and pilot difficulty with repetitive activation, but these warnings were not adequately addressed.

label: Boeing employee predicts faulty AOA could cause stall
original_label: Boeing employee predicts faulty AOA could cause stall
quote: What happens when we have faulty AOA or Mach number? His colleague, a Boeing engineer, quickly assured him that this was not something to worry about. 'As for faulty AOA and/or Mach number,' his colleague responded, '… if they are faulty then MCAS shuts down immediately.' That may have been the intent, but that did not happen on Lion Air flight 610.
context: On June 15, 2016, a Boeing AR asks about faulty AOA consequences and receives reassurance that MCAS shuts down, but the actual behavior contradicts this assumption.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing dismisses repetitive MCAS response concern as certification non-issue
original_label: Boeing dismisses repetitive MCAS response concern as certification non-issue
quote: A different Boeing engineer who was aware of a Boeing test pilot having trouble countering repetitive MCAS activations during a test flight asked his colleague if the difficulties the Boeing test pilot had countering repetitive MCAS activation was a safety or a certification issue. His Boeing colleague responded: 'I don't think this is safety other then (sic) the pilot could fight the MCAS input and over time find themselves in a large mistrim.'
context: In June 2016 email exchange, when a Boeing engineer raises concerns about test pilot difficulty with repetitive MCAS activation, a colleague minimizes it as potentially only a mistrim issue rather than a safety concern.

label: Boeing and FAA omit MCAS from post-Lion Air emergency guidance
original_label: Boeing and FAA omit MCAS from post-Lion Air emergency guidance
quote: On November 6, 2018, eight days after the Lion Air crash, Boeing issued an Operations Manual Bulletin (OMB) that directed airline operators and flight crews to various flight crew procedures to address erroneous angle-of-attack (AOA) sensor data... Noticeably absent from the Boeing bulletin was any reference to the 'Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System' or 'MCAS.'
context: Boeing issues an Operations Manual Bulletin about erroneous AOA data effects just after the Lion Air crash but conspicuously omits any mention of MCAS, the system causing the problem.

label: FAA removes MCAS reference from draft Emergency Airworthiness Directive
original_label: FAA removes MCAS reference from draft Emergency Airworthiness Directive
quote: At the last minute, an F.A.A. manager told agency engineers to remove the only mention of the system, according to internal agency documents and two people with knowledge of the matter... The FAA therefore decided to remove the MCAS reference from the draft AD so that flight crews would focus on runaway stabilizer recognition instead of attempting to troubleshoot MCAS.
context: According to internal FAA documents and sources, an FAA manager directed engineers to delete MCAS references from the Emergency Airworthiness Directive, reasoning that pilots should focus on runaway stabilizer procedures rather than understanding MCAS.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing proposes Level A training despite MCAS redesign
original_label: Boeing proposes Level A training despite MCAS redesign
quote: In January 2019, in the wake of the Lion Air accident, Boeing proposed MAX pilots should only receive Level A training regarding MCAS, the lowest training level available, that encompasses simply reviewing written material... Boeing only seemed to concede that some training may be necessary simply to placate inquiries from MAX 'operators' and 'customers.' Boeing proposed Level A training requirements on MCAS for pilots transitioning from the 737 NG to the 737 MAX.
context: Three months after the Lion Air crash and while MCAS was being redesigned, Boeing proposes only Level A (written material review) training for pilots, suggesting minimal safety concern despite known design flaws.

label: Boeing issues Multi Operator Message after pilot media pressure
original_label: Boeing issues Multi Operator Message after pilot media pressure
quote: Three days after the FAA issued its Emergency AD, Boeing issued a Multi Operator Message (MOM) on November 10, 2018... However, it was also clear that Boeing only did this under intense pressure from its 737 MAX customers who wanted more information about the Lion Air crash. According to the MOM, 'Boeing has received many requests for the same information from 737 fleet operators' and the MOM provided a technical description of MCAS while never specifically mentioning the Lion Air crash.
context: Boeing releases a Multi Operator Message with MCAS technical description only after receiving numerous customer requests and media reports, revealing that Boeing withheld the information until pressure forced disclosure.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Boeing officials minimize MCAS as routine control law
original_label: Boeing officials minimize MCAS as routine control law
quote: One of the Boeing officials attempted to explain away MCAS to the American Airlines pilots: 'MCAS is a control law, which it's–it's in the flight control system. So it's just a little bit of software in the flight control system that is designed to change the handling characteristics of the airplane at high angles of attack.'
context: In November 2018 meeting with Allied Pilots Association officials, a Boeing representative characterizes MCAS as merely 'a little bit of software' rather than a critical flight control system, understating its significance.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing defends single-point-of-failure design using pilot backup
original_label: Boeing defends single-point-of-failure design using pilot backup
quote: At the meeting with American Airline pilots, one of the Boeing officials said that despite the reports that MCAS was a 'single-point failure' system, that was not true because they believed the pilots were part of the 'system' and essentially served as a backup to any technical failure of MCAS. 'So the [MCAS] function and trained pilot are part of the system,' said one of the Boeing officials. 'So rightly or wrongly, that was the design criteria, and that's how they're being certified with the – the – the system and the pilot working together,' he said.
context: Boeing officials defend MCAS's single-sensor design by arguing that pilots serve as a redundant safety layer, claiming this was the design criterion accepted during certification.

label: FAA conducts TARAM risk analysis predicting 15 fatal crashes
original_label: FAA conducts TARAM risk analysis predicting 15 fatal crashes
quote: Despite the TARAM analysis, the FAA permitted the 737 MAX aircraft to continue flying. In addition, Boeing continued to expand the MAX fleet in between the time of the Lion Air crash in October 2018 and the Ethiopian Airlines crash in March 2019. In those five months, Boeing delivered nearly 150 more aircraft to its customers, increasing the global 737 MAX fleet to 387 aircraft. Each new aircraft deployed without a fix to MCAS increased the risk to the public. The FAA and Boeing were gambling on the fact that issuance of the Boeing OMB and the FAA's Emergency AD would be enough to save MAX pilots and the flying public from the potentially devastating and deadly effect of MCAS.
context: The FAA's quantitative risk assessment predicts over 15 fatal MAX crashes over the fleet's lifetime if MCAS is not fixed, yet the FAA permits continued operations and Boeing continues deliveries, effectively betting on interim procedures.

label: FAA safety officer unaware of TARAM analysis details
original_label: FAA safety officer unaware of TARAM analysis details
quote: Although Mr. Bahrami said he was unfamiliar with the details of the TARAM analysis that predicted 15 more fatal MAX crashes over the lifetime of the MAX fleet, he said he believed FAA officials 'used the [TARAM] process the right way.' He also acknowledged that the Emergency AD and the focus on pilot responses was only an interim fix.
context: Ali Bahrami, FAA's Associate Administrator for Aviation Safety, states he is unfamiliar with details of the internal TARAM analysis predicting 15 fatal crashes, despite it being conducted by his own agency.

label: FAA permits MAX operations despite pilot-dependent safety
original_label: FAA permits MAX operations despite pilot-dependent safety
quote: Committee staff: But you made a decision that those changes could wait - Ali Bahrami: Yes, we did. Committee staff: -- and still the plane could fly, and you were relying on the pilots to prevent a catastrophic failure. Ali Bahrami: There are a lot of other scenarios out there that we -- again, it gets back to the cockpit design philosophy. Pilots are part of the system, and we rely on the pilots to do certain things.
context: Ali Bahrami, FAA's Associate Administrator for Aviation Safety, confirms in December 2019 interview that the FAA made a conscious decision to permit continued MAX operations while relying on pilot intervention to prevent catastrophic failure.

label: Beth Pasztor emails Bahrami requesting Lion Air discussion
original_label: Beth Pasztor emails Bahrami requesting Lion Air discussion
quote: In her email to Mr. Bahrami, she wrote: 'I would appreciate a few minutes of your time, the topic is on Lion Air. Would it be possible to connect today or tomorrow? Please let me know, thanks for your time.' Mr. Bahrami responded: 'Let's plan for tomorrow. Let me know what works fo[r] you.' The two scheduled a call for 11:30 a.m. on January 25, 2019.
context: On January 24, 2019, Boeing's Vice President of Safety, Security and Compliance reaches out to FAA's Associate Administrator for Aviation Safety to discuss Lion Air, and they schedule a call for the following day.

label: FAA issues only interim measures despite known MCAS risks
original_label: FAA issues only interim measures despite known MCAS risks
quote: The FAA issued an emergency AD reminding pilots how to deal with runaway speed trim eight days after the Lion Air accident and before the TARAM analysis was complete. When the AD was issued, the FAA determined the permanent action was to require a design change to address MCAS. So, despite his testimony that FAA was unaware of the root cause of the Lion Air accident, it is clear that the FAA was fully aware that MCAS was a primary cause of the Lion Air accident at the time it conducted the TARAM analysis in late 2018. Despite that, the FAA chose to let the 737 MAX keep flying with the uncorrected and dangerously defective MCAS software operating on the airplanes.
context: FAA Administrator Dickson acknowledges in written response that the FAA was fully aware MCAS was the primary cause of Lion Air crash when it issued only an interim Emergency AD and allowed continued operations.

label: Ethiopian Airlines crash prompts immediate FAA grounding
original_label: Ethiopian Airlines crash prompts immediate FAA grounding
quote: On March 11, 2019, the day after the Ethiopian Airlines crash, the FAA issued a Continued Airworthiness Certification to the International Community permitting the 737 MAX to keep flying. In part, the document said: 'External reports are drawing similarities between this accident and the Lion Air Flight 610 accident on October 29, 2018. However, this investigation has just begun and to date we have not been provided data to draw any conclusions or take any actions.'... I saw that and I said, thank you, anything else? And they said, well, what are you going to do? I said, we need to ground the fleet. At 3:00 p.m. on March 13, 2019, the FAA grounded the 737 MAX fleet.
context: After the second fatal MAX crash, and following Boeing's presentation of evidence showing similarities between Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines accidents, FAA's Ali Bahrami immediately recommends grounding, resulting in the FAA's emergency grounding order that same day.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: FAA finds no MCAS noncompliance despite design flaws
original_label: FAA finds no MCAS noncompliance despite design flaws
quote: Although the Boeing presentation highlighted many areas where a more robust review should have been conducted, it still asserted that none of these failures, either singularly or in combination with each other, amounted to a violation of FAA regulations. In its own examination of MCAS after the Lion Air crash, in early 2019, the FAA reached the same conclusion. The FAA did not identify any 'noncompliances' by Boeing despite the litany of incomplete test results on MCAS, the lack of transparency by Boeing with the FAA on critically important data regarding potential pilot reactions to uncommanded MCAS activation, or the disjointed communications by Boeing with the FAA regarding the redesign of MCAS.
context: Despite identifying incomplete testing, lack of transparency, and disjointed communications about MCAS, both Boeing and the FAA concluded that no regulatory violations or noncompliances had occurred.

label: Bahrami unaware of Boeing test pilot catastrophic response
original_label: Bahrami unaware of Boeing test pilot catastrophic response
quote: He was unaware of the FAA's TARAM analysis. He also said he was unaware that Boeing had internal test data showing that it took of Boeing's own test pilots more than 10-seconds to respond to uncommanded MCAS activation, which the pilot described as 'catastrophic.' This was despite the fact the Committee held a hearing in October 2019 where this information was released and it was widely covered by the media.
context: Ali Bahrami, FAA's lead safety officer, states he is unaware of Boeing's internal test data showing a test pilot taking over 10 seconds to respond to MCAS and calling it catastrophic, information that was widely publicized at a Congressional hearing.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Bahrami deflects responsibility to cockpit design philosophy
original_label: Bahrami deflects responsibility to cockpit design philosophy
quote: While both Boeing and the FAA have pointed to pilot performance as a factor in the MAX crashes and while pilot performance is often a contributing factor in any aircraft accident, neither Boeing nor the FAA can shirk their responsibility for developing and certifying an aircraft that was not safe to fly for all pilots. What makes Boeing's decision to stick to its goal of no simulator training most troubling is the fact that Boeing had information from its own test data suggesting that some pilots, even U.S.-trained Boeing test pilots, would need more training on the MAX, particularly to respond to an erroneous activation of MCAS effectively. However, Boeing appears to have discounted this test data and ignored this evidence, assuming that all pilots would respond quickly and effectively to uncommanded MCAS activation.
context: The Committee notes that while Boeing and FAA attributed crashes to pilot performance, both ignored Boeing's own test data showing even trained test pilots struggled to respond to MCAS activation within safe timeframes.

label: Boeing engineer raised concerns about MCAS repetitive activation
original_label: Boeing engineer raised concerns about MCAS repetitive activation
quote: It failed to build in essential redundancies by permitting MCAS to rely on a single AOA sensor. It allowed MCAS to activate repetitively, although at least one Boeing engineer had raised concerns about that capability.
context: House Committee report summarizing Boeing's design failures on MCAS, including identification of an internal warning from a Boeing engineer about repeated activation risk.

label: Test pilot found MCAS activation response time catastrophic
original_label: Test pilot found MCAS activation response time catastrophic
quote: it was not right for Boeing to fail to share with the FAA Boeing's own test data showing that it had taken a test pilot more than 10 seconds to respond to uncommanded MCAS activation, and the test pilot believed the condition was catastrophic.
context: House Committee report identifying Boeing's internal test results showing dangerous pilot response times to MCAS activation that were not disclosed to regulators.

label: AOA Disagree alert nonfunctional on 80 percent of fleet
original_label: AOA Disagree alert nonfunctional on 80 percent of fleet
quote: Nor did Boeing do the right thing when it became aware that the AOA Disagree alert was not functioning on more than 80 percent of the 737 MAX fleet and then failed to alert the FAA, its customers, and MAX pilots while it continued to both manufacture and deliver an estimated 200 airplanes with this known nonfunctional component.
context: House Committee report detailing Boeing's discovery of a critical safety alert malfunction across the majority of delivered aircraft that was not disclosed.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing claimed no process violation after Lion Air crash
original_label: Boeing claimed no process violation after Lion Air crash
quote: In the weeks after the Lion Air crash, Boeing defended its development and certification of MCAS to the FAA, writing that there was no process violation or non-compliance regarding the inconsistencies in the system's development and Boeing's actions, including (1) removing reference to MCAS from the FCOM, (2) determining repeated unintended MCAS activation to be no worse than a single unintended activation, (3) determining the loss of one AOA sensor followed by erroneous readings from the other AOA sensor to be extremely remote and not analyzing this scenario in its failure assessments, and (4) not reassessing failure analyses following the MCAS design change.
context: House Committee report quoting Boeing's post-crash response to FAA, showing the company's reframing of serious design defects as compliant with regulations.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: FAA found no non-compliances despite design missteps
original_label: FAA found no non-compliances despite design missteps
quote: The FAA's own draft review of MCAS in the wake of the Lion Air crash also found no non-compliances with FAA regulations on the part of Boeing. The fact that multiple technical design missteps or certification blunders were deemed compliant by the FAA points to a critical need for legislative and regulatory reforms.
context: House Committee report analyzing FAA's post-crash review, showing how serious defects were categorized as compliant with existing rules.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Safety sacrificed to production pressures
original_label: Safety sacrificed to production pressures
quote: Boeing has gone from being a great engineering company to being a big business focused on financial success. Continuing on the same path it followed with the 737 MAX, where safety was sacrificed to production pressures, exposes the company to potentially repeating those mistakes and to additional reputational damage and financial losses.
context: House Committee's concluding analysis of Boeing's organizational transformation and how production incentives overrode safety considerations in the 737 MAX program.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Culture change required: reprioritizing safety over production and cost
original_label: Culture change required: reprioritizing safety over production and cost
quote: the importance of really following up on those actions of taking safety issues very seriously, of reprioritizing safety with regard to production and cost in schedule, those changes are going to require a lot of continued interaction by management
context: Dr. Mica Endsley, human factors expert and former Chief Scientist of the U.S. Air Force, testifying to House Committee about the need to change organizational incentives and management priorities at Boeing.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Stonecipher changed Boeing culture to run like business not engineering firm
original_label: Stonecipher changed Boeing culture to run like business not engineering firm
quote: When people say I changed the culture of Boeing, that was the intent, so it's run like a business rather than a great engineering firm.
context: House Committee quoting McDonnell Douglas CEO Harry Stonecipher (who became Boeing COO) in 2004 Chicago Tribune interview, describing his intentional shift in organizational priorities away from engineering excellence.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Current Boeing employees recognize shift from engineering to business focus
original_label: Current Boeing employees recognize shift from engineering to business focus
quote: It is unfortunate that many current and former Boeing employees the Committee has spoken to during this investigation believe Boeing has succeeded in meeting that goal. They understand they once worked for a great engineering firm, and many hope that they will again in the future.
context: House Committee reporting on interviews with Boeing staff who witnessed organizational cultural transformation away from engineering emphasis.

label: Leverkuhn held senior-most position on 737 MAX program
original_label: Leverkuhn held senior-most position on 737 MAX program
quote: Keith Leverkuhn, the former senior-most official on Boeing's 737 MAX program, who is now Vice President of Supply Chain Propulsion for Boeing Commercial Airplanes
context: House Committee identifying Leverkuhn's role and current position, establishing his authority and responsibility for the MAX program.

label: Leverkuhn refused to acknowledge any problems on MAX program
original_label: Leverkuhn refused to acknowledge any problems on MAX program
quote: In a transcribed interview with Committee staff, Keith Leverkuhn, the former senior-most official on Boeing's 737 MAX program, who is now Vice President of Supply Chain Propulsion for Boeing Commercial Airplanes, appeared unable or unwilling to either take responsibility for any of the problems that occurred on the MAX program or to even acknowledge that any problems existed at all.
context: House Committee reporting on Leverkuhn's response to investigators, showing leadership's refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing despite fatal crashes.

label: Leverkuhn called MAX development a success despite two fatal crashes
original_label: Leverkuhn called MAX development a success despite two fatal crashes
quote: T&I Committee staff: In light of the two crashes and the fact that the MAX has been grounded for more than a year, would you consider the development of the MAX a success? Mr. Leverkuhn: Yes, I would. …. …. I do challenge the suggestion that the development [of the 737 MAX] was a failure.
context: House Committee transcribing Leverkuhn's interview responses, where the senior 737 MAX official refused to acknowledge program failure despite two fatal accidents and 346 deaths.

label: Two crashes within two years triggered regulatory and investigative attention
original_label: Two crashes within two years triggered regulatory and investigative attention
quote: The fact that Boeing was able to show that its new transport category commercial aircraft met the FAA's certification criteria, yet was involved in two fatal crashes within the span of just two years and two days after the FAA granted certification, is disconcerting. The FAA's aviation oversight system failed in dramatic fashion.
context: House Committee analyzing the immediate juxtaposition of certification and crashes as evidence of systemic regulatory failure.

label: Boeing attempted rebranding as response to fatal accident publicity
original_label: Boeing attempted rebranding as response to fatal accident publicity
quote: Several weeks before this report was finalized, multiple news stories suggested that Boeing was endeavoring to change the name of the 737 MAX to the 737-8 in an effort to combat the indelible image problems now surrounding the aircraft.
context: House Committee documenting Boeing's post-crash response of attempting to rebrand the aircraft, showing management's focus on public relations rather than safety reform.

label: Cultural issues at both Boeing and FAA prevented proper oversight
original_label: Cultural issues at both Boeing and FAA prevented proper oversight
quote: Both must learn critical lessons from these tragic accidents to improve the certification process, and the FAA must dramatically amplify and improve its oversight of Boeing. While the changes that the FAA and Boeing have proposed will be the start of a long process, changing the fundamental cultural issues that led to an environment that permitted Boeing to build, and FAA to certify, a technologically faulty aircraft will take much longer.
context: House Committee's opening finding in its final observations, identifying cultural barriers in both organizations' oversight systems.

label: Boeing engineer assumed MCAS would shut down but it did not
original_label: Boeing engineer assumed MCAS would shut down but it did not
quote: It did not appropriately address the question of faulty AOA data and the negative implications for MCAS because a Boeing engineer falsely assumed that MCAS would not allow that to happen and shut down. That did not happen in either of the MAX crashes.
context: House Committee summarizing a critical internal engineering assumption about MCAS behavior that proved incorrect and contributed to both accidents.

label: Boeing removed MCAS references from pilot operations manual
original_label: Boeing removed MCAS references from pilot operations manual
quote: Furthermore, Boeing did not do the right thing when it removed references to MCAS from the pilot's Flight Crew Operations Manual (FCOM).
context: House Committee identifying Boeing's decision to omit critical information about MCAS from pilot training and reference materials.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Name change proposed instead of addressing root cultural issues
original_label: Name change proposed instead of addressing root cultural issues
quote: If the Committee's investigation offers any lessons for Boeing, it is that a name change and a public relations effort will not address the cultural issues at Boeing that hampered the safety of the 737 MAX in the first place and ultimately led to two fatal accidents and the death of 346 people. A name change may help confront a public relations problem, but only a genuine, holistic, and assertive commitment to changing the cultural issues unearthed in the Committee's investigation at both Boeing and the FAA can enhance aviation safety and truly help both Boeing and the FAA learn from the dire lessons of the 737 MAX tragedies.
context: House Committee's final assessment, contrasting Boeing's superficial branding response with the need for genuine organizational and cultural reform.

label: West Virginia University study signals emissions non-compliance
original_label: West Virginia University study signals emissions non-compliance
quote: In the spring of 2014 when the West Virginia University study was published, I was told that there was a possible emissions non-compliance that could be remedied.
context: Michael Horn, CEO of VW Group of America, recounts to Congress the initial warning signal about diesel vehicle emissions that reached him in 2014.

label: EPA regulations and defeat device testing procedures known
original_label: EPA regulations and defeat device testing procedures known
quote: I was informed that EPA regulations included various penalties for non-compliance with the emissions standards and that the agencies can conduct engineering tests which could include "defeat device" testing or analysis.
context: Horn describes the procedural knowledge communicated to him about how EPA could detect and test for defeat devices in emissions compliance processes.

label: Engineers engaged with agencies on remedies
original_label: Engineers engaged with agencies on remedies
quote: I was also informed that the company engineers would work with the agencies to resolve the issue. Later in 2014, I was informed that the technical teams had a specific plan for remedies to bring the vehicles into compliance and that they were engaged with the agencies about the process.
context: Horn explains the communication channel and process through which technical teams were supposed to coordinate with regulators on compliance solutions.

label: September 2015 disclosure of defeat device to regulators
original_label: September 2015 disclosure of defeat device to regulators
quote: On September 3, 2015, Volkswagen AG disclosed at a meeting with the California Air Resources Board ("CARB") and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency ("EPA") that emissions software in four cylinder diesel vehicles from model years 2009-2015 contained a "defeat device" in the form of hidden software that could recognize whether a vehicle was being operated in a test laboratory or on the road.
context: Horn testifies before Congress about the public disclosure event in September 2015 that marked the shift from internal knowledge to external regulatory admission.

label: Vehicles emit higher nitrogen oxides in road use than in tests
original_label: Vehicles emit higher nitrogen oxides in road use than in tests
quote: The software made those emit higher levels of nitrogen oxides when the vehicles were driven in actual road use than during laboratory testing.
context: Horn describes the technical anomaly that the defeat device created: a discrepancy between laboratory and real-world emissions performance.

label: AECD disclosure and certification process with regulators
original_label: AECD disclosure and certification process with regulators
quote: In Volkswagen's recent ongoing discussions with the regulators, we described to the EPA and CARB that our emissions control strategy also included a software feature that should be disclosed to and approved by them as an auxiliary emissions control device ("AECD") in connection with the certification process. As a result, we have withdrawn the application for certification of our model year 2016 vehicles.
context: Horn describes the procedural channel of model certification and how VW attempted to work with agencies on the software feature in question.

label: Horn as President and CEO receiving information about emissions issue
original_label: Horn as President and CEO receiving information about emissions issue
quote: In the spring of 2014 when the West Virginia University study was published, I was told that there was a possible emissions non-compliance that could be remedied.
context: Horn, in his position as President and CEO, testifies about his role in receiving information about the emissions problem from subordinates.

label: Worldwide investigations to identify responsible parties
original_label: Worldwide investigations to identify responsible parties
quote: First, we are conducting investigations on a world-wide scale into how these matters happened. Responsible parties will be identified and held accountable. Thorough investigations have already begun, but any information developed at this stage is preliminary.
context: Horn outlines VW's organizational response after the September 2015 disclosure, committing to investigate and hold people accountable.

label: Remedy development for affected vehicle groups
original_label: Remedy development for affected vehicle groups
quote: Third, technical teams are working tirelessly to develop remedies for each of the affected groups of vehicles. These solutions will be tested and validated, and then shared with the responsible authorities for approval. There are three groups of vehicles involved, each containing one of the three generations of the 2.0L diesel engine. Each will require a different remedy, but these remedies can only be our first step for our customers.
context: Horn describes VW's organizational response of developing and seeking approval for technical remedies to address the defeat device.

label: Compliance processes and standards examination
original_label: Compliance processes and standards examination
quote: Fourth, we will examine our compliance, processes, and standards at Volkswagen and adopt measures to make certain that something like this cannot happen again.
context: Horn outlines VW's commitment to review internal organizational structures and processes to prevent recurrence.

label: Customer communication channels established
original_label: Customer communication channels established
