context: The SEC complaint describes how management knowingly violated rules at interim close with a plan to fix the violations before reporting.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Borrowed equity disguised as outside investment through pledged collateral
original_label: Borrowed equity disguised as outside investment through pledged collateral
quote: Chewco's structure at year-end 1997 again failed to meet SPE non-consolidation requirements. Its purported outside 'equity' investment consisted of approximately $11.49 million from Chewco's general and limited partners. However, Enron structured the transaction so that $11.36 million of the supposed outside equity was actually borrowed from Barclays by various entities set up and controlled by Kopper. The Barclays loans were secured by approximately $6.58 million in cash that was generated by JEDI's November 1997 sale of an asset. Those funds were held in accounts that were fully pledged to Barclays, meaning that Barclays was partly protected against risk of loss.
context: The SEC complaint describes how the structure made borrowed funds appear as at-risk equity through layered entities and pledging arrangements.

label: Kopper as conduit for CFO's profit-sharing demands from SPE
original_label: Kopper as conduit for CFO's profit-sharing demands from SPE
quote: Fastow's undisclosed control of Chewco and Kopper permitted him to demand a share of Chewco's profits and other Chewco related funds. From December 1997 through December 2000, Fastow directed Kopper to secretly share with him various payments received by Kopper relating to Chewco. Kopper received a total of approximately $1.5 million in 'management fees' relating to Chewco, which he shared with Fastow at his direction mainly through checks payable to members of Fastow's family.
context: The SEC complaint describes how Kopper served as an intermediary for transferring profits from the SPE to Fastow's family members.

label: Enron CEO approval delegated to CFO for undisclosed side payments
original_label: Enron CEO approval delegated to CFO for undisclosed side payments
quote: In December 1998, Fastow caused Enron to pay a $400,000 'nuisance fee' to Chewco as compensation for agreeing to amend JEDI's partnership agreement, even though the amendment benefitted Chewco, not Enron. At Fastow's direction, Kopper transferred approximately $67,224 of the nuisance fee back to Fastow, again through checks written to Fastow or members of his family.
context: The SEC complaint describes how Fastow used his authority to approve payments that were structured to generate funds he could subsequently redirect.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Asset deconsolidation enabling mark-to-market earnings recognition opportunity
original_label: Asset deconsolidation enabling mark-to-market earnings recognition opportunity
quote: Enron did not want to consolidate the Cuiaba project's debt on its balance sheet, and attempted to sell its interest. Deconsolidating would also permit Enron to mark to market a related power supply contract, thereby recognizing earnings. However, the Cuiaba project was so problematic that no independent third-party would purchase an interest in the project.
context: The SEC complaint describes the earnings opportunity that made Cuiaba deconsolidation a priority despite the project's fundamental problems.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Problematic asset sold to Fastow-controlled entity to achieve accounting goal
original_label: Problematic asset sold to Fastow-controlled entity to achieve accounting goal
quote: Enron and Fastow solved their Cuiaba project problem by 'selling' an interest in the project to Fastow-controlled LJM1. On September 30, 1999, Enron sold LJM1 a 13% interest in the project for $11.3 million. The sale of this interest (and the board seat that went with it) was purportedly sufficient for Enron to conclude that it did not control the Cuiaba project. The 'sale' enabled Enron to keep the Cuiaba project's substantial debt off its balance sheet. Furthermore, this purported sale enabled Enron to recognize a total of approximately $65 million of income in the third and fourth quarters of 1999, when it was struggling to meet its projected financial results.
context: The SEC complaint describes how a troubled asset was sold to an entity under Fastow's control to achieve deconsolidation and create $65 million in earnings.

label: Secret repurchase guarantee understanding replacing written buyback clause
original_label: Secret repurchase guarantee understanding replacing written buyback clause
quote: LJM1, through Fastow, agreed to 'buy' Enron's interest in the Cuiaba project because Enron agreed in an undisclosed side deal to repurchase the interest if necessary and guarantee LJM1 a profit. Enron agreed to repurchase LJM1's interest at a higher price regardless of the actual performance of the Cuiba project.
context: The SEC complaint describes how the buyback guarantee was converted from a written agreement into an oral understanding to avoid audit objections.

label: Buyback priced to provide profit despite project value deterioration
original_label: Buyback priced to provide profit despite project value deterioration
quote: After LJM1's purchase, the Cuiaba project continued to suffer serious cost overruns, technical, and environmental problems. Despite the ongoing problems with the Cuiaba project affecting its value, on or about March 2001, Fastow and Enron agreed upon the buyback price of LJM1's interest. For various reasons (including the fact that Fastow did not sell his interest in LJM1 to Kopper until July 2001), Fastow delayed the closing until August 15, 2001. Enron bought back LJM1's interest for $13,752,000. This purchase price was calculated to provide LJM1 a significant profit even though the market value for Cuiaba had decreased.
context: The SEC complaint describes how the repurchase was executed at a price that guaranteed LJM1 a profit despite the project's deteriorated condition.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Quarterly earnings pressure driving fraudulent asset sale structure
original_label: Quarterly earnings pressure driving fraudulent asset sale structure
quote: In 1999, Fastow caused Enron to engage in a fraudulent 'sale' of assets to permit Enron to record approximately $12 million of earnings in the fourth quarter of 1999.
context: The SEC complaint identifies the quarterly earnings target as the motivating agenda for the fraudulent Nigerian Barges transaction.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Earnings booking without true economic substance or business purpose
original_label: Earnings booking without true economic substance or business purpose
quote: Enron falsely recorded the transaction with the Financial Institution as a sale and improperly recorded approximately $12 million of fictitious earnings in the fourth quarter of 1999.
context: The SEC complaint describes how Enron recorded earnings from a transaction that lacked true economic substance.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Lock-up restrictions on stock sales creating hedging pressure
original_label: Lock-up restrictions on stock sales creating hedging pressure
quote: Enron invested in other companies, including start-up ventures that later did initial public offerings ('IPO') of their shares. At the time of an IPO, Enron often owned millions of shares of the newly public company. Following the IPO, Enron was at risk for market price fluctuations in the shares. The value of such stock was required to be recorded in Enron's financial statements at the end of each quarter. Because Enron was restricted by 'lock up' agreements from selling its shares until some future date, it sought to reduce the impact on its financial results of a possible dramatic decline in the share price.
context: The SEC complaint describes the market risk and regulatory restrictions that motivated the design of the Raptor hedging structures.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Undisclosed side agreement promising return of capital before hedging risk transfer
original_label: Undisclosed side agreement promising return of capital before hedging risk transfer
quote: Pursuant to the side deal, Enron agreed that, prior to conducting any hedging activity with Talon, Enron would return to LJM2 its full investment in Talon plus a guaranteed return. This undisclosed side deal would have 'broken' the SPE, that is, it would have required Talon to be consolidated on Enron's financial statements because the supposed outside three percent equity was not at risk. Further, with the return of LJM2's capital by Talon, there was no outside equity at risk to justify Talon not being consolidated. Yet, Enron did not consolidate Talon on its financial statements filed with the Commission.
context: The SEC complaint describes how an undisclosed side agreement eliminated the at-risk capital requirement for SPE status while Talon remained unconsolidated.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Manipulating portfolio value through put option on company's own stock
original_label: Manipulating portfolio value through put option on company's own stock
quote: Talon was funded mainly by Enron through a promissory note and Enron's own stock. The remainder of Talon's funding, $30 million, was from LJM2, representing the purported three percent outside equity required for Talon to be off Enron's balance sheet.
context: The SEC complaint describes how Enron structured Talon funding to create a minimum three-percent appearance while relying on LJM2's capital.

label: Put option on Enron stock manufactured to disguise side deal payment
original_label: Put option on Enron stock manufactured to disguise side deal payment
quote: To conceal the side deal, Fastow and others devised a scheme to manufacture a $41 million payment to LJM2. Fastow and others made it appear that the payment represented the premium paid on a 'put option' on Enron shares that Enron purchased from Talon. Enron purchased the put option, set to expire on October 18, 2000, for a premium of $41 million. Enron settled the put option early and Talon then distributed the $41 million to LJM2. The transaction was unusual for several reasons, including the fact that the put option was a bet by Enron that its own stock price would decline. There was no true business purpose for the put option other than to generate funds to pay LJM2 under the undisclosed side deal.
context: The SEC complaint describes how a put option structure was created as a vehicle to transfer cash to LJM2 while disguising the true nature of the payment.

label: Backdating transaction documents to lock in advantageous valuation date
original_label: Backdating transaction documents to lock in advantageous valuation date
quote: Fastow caused the AVICI hedge to be backdated to August 3, 2000. Fastow chose this date because he knew it was the date AVICI traded at an all time high price of $163.50. By back-dating the AVICI hedge in this manner, Fastow and Enron fraudulently locked in the recognition of a substantial gain and booked $75 million in additional mark to market gains that they otherwise would not have recognized.
context: The SEC complaint describes how Fastow manipulated transaction dating to recognize gains at stock prices significantly higher than the actual transaction date.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Risk reduction on IPO stock holdings driving derivative transaction design
original_label: Risk reduction on IPO stock holdings driving derivative transaction design
quote: Enron had an investment in an Internet company called Rhythms NetConnections, Inc. ('Rhythms'). Enron owned approximately 5.4 million shares of Rhythms stock, and following an IPO in April 1999, Enron was at risk for market price fluctuations in the stock. Because Enron was restricted from selling its shares until November 1999, it sought to reduce the impact on its financial results of a possible dramatic decline in the share price of Rhythms stock.
context: The SEC complaint describes the risk management need that motivated the Southampton derivative transaction structure.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Swap Sub ownership manipulated to capture value increase for insiders
original_label: Swap Sub ownership manipulated to capture value increase for insiders
quote: In January-February 2000, both Enron and Rhythms shares increased in price, making Swap Sub's main asset (its Enron shares) more valuable while decreasing its potential liability on the Rhythms put option. Thus, Swap Sub had significantly more value than previously. Fastow was prohibited from having any direct pecuniary interest in Enron's stock held by LJM1. Nevertheless, in approximately February 2000, Fastow, Kopper, and three NatWest bankers devised and later executed a scheme to capture the increase in Swap Sub's value for themselves and others and defraud Enron, NatWest, and others by: (i) causing Enron to pay $30 million to buy out, or 'unwind,' the banks' interests in Swap Sub; (ii) causing NatWest to accept only $1 million for its interest in Swap Sub, while representing to Enron that NatWest was getting $20 million, and (iii) splitting the $19 million balance among themselves and certain Enron and LJM employees.
context: The SEC complaint describes how Fastow and others devised a scheme to convert unrealized gains in Swap Sub into personal proceeds through misrepresentation to Enron.

label: False value representation to Enron about bank buyout price allocation
original_label: False value representation to Enron about bank buyout price allocation
quote: To carry out the scheme, Fastow, Kopper and others, on or about March 22, 2000, caused Enron to agree to pay $30 million (purportedly allocated $20 million to NatWest and $10 million to CSFB) to unwind Swap Sub. That purchase price was based on Fastow's false representation to Enron that NatWest and CSFB had agreed to sell their interests in Swap Sub for $20 million and $10 million, respectively. In fact, NatWest received only $1 million and had agreed to receive this sum based on misrepresentations and fraudulent conduct of its own employees, who sought to skim profits that should have gone to NatWest.
context: The SEC complaint describes how Fastow misrepresented the allocation of the $30 million payment to induce Enron's agreement, while the banks' own employees were complicit in understating their own bank's share.

label: Insider investment vehicles capturing proceeds from fraudulent transaction
original_label: Insider investment vehicles capturing proceeds from fraudulent transaction
quote: As a result, the three NatWest bankers who participated in the scheme received approximately $7.3 million. The balance of the funds went to Fastow, Kopper and other investors in an entity called Southampton Place LP ('Southampton'), which Kopper created. The Southampton 'investors' were a purported charitable foundation set up by Fastow for the purpose of receiving Southampton proceeds, which contributed $25,000 and received approximately $4.5 million; Kopper, who contributed $25,000 and caused Chewco to loan another $680,000, and received approximately $4.5 million; and five Enron and LJM employees chosen by Kopper and Fastow, who contributed a total of less than $20,000 and received a total of approximately $3.3 million.
context: The SEC complaint describes how the $30 million payment was distributed to insiders through a structure that magnified their return on minimal investments.

label: Form 8-K consolidation announcement revealing massive prior misstatements
original_label: Form 8-K consolidation announcement revealing massive prior misstatements
quote: In November 2001, in a Form 8-K filed with the Commission, Enron announced that it would consolidate Chewco and JEDI retroactive to 1997. This resulted in a massive reduction in Enron's reported net income and a massive increase in its reported debt. The consolidation revealed the following effect, according to Enron: reduction of net income in the amounts of $45 million (1997), $107 million (1998), $153 million (1999), and $91 million (2000), and debt increased in the amounts of $711 million (1997), $561 million (1998), $685 million (1999), and $628 million (2000).
context: The SEC complaint describes the public disclosure that revealed the magnitude of prior financial statement falsifications.

label: Swap Sub consolidation retroactively reducing reported income and increasing debt
original_label: Swap Sub consolidation retroactively reducing reported income and increasing debt
quote: In November 2001, in a Form 8-K filed with the Commission, Enron announced that it would consolidate Swap Sub retroactive to 1999. Enron concluded that Swap Sub did not qualify for nonconsolidation treatment because of inadequate capitalization. The consolidation had the effect of reducing Enron's reported net income by $95 million in 1999, and by $8 million in 2000.
context: The SEC complaint describes the public disclosure that revealed additional retroactive misstatements related to the Southampton transaction.

label: Media reports of OxyContin abuse emerge
original_label: Media reports of OxyContin abuse emerge
quote: In early 2000, media reports began to surface in several states that OxyContin was being abused—that is, used for nontherapeutic purposes or for purposes other than those for which it was prescribed—and illegally diverted. According to FDA and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the abuse of OxyContin is associated with serious consequences, including addiction, overdose, and death.
context: The GAO report documents the earliest public warning signals about OxyContin abuse and diversion that emerged in 2000.

label: Congressional hearings document growing abuse problem
original_label: Congressional hearings document growing abuse problem
quote: During a December 2001 congressional hearing, witnesses from DEA and other law enforcement officials from Kentucky, Virginia, and West Virginia described the growing problem of abuse and diversion of OxyContin. Questions were raised about what factors may have caused the abuse and diversion, including whether Purdue's efforts to market the drug may have contributed to the problem.
context: GAO describes formal warning signals delivered to Congress in 2001 about OxyContin abuse and questions about Purdue's marketing role.

label: Rural communities devastated by OxyContin addiction and deaths
original_label: Rural communities devastated by OxyContin addiction and deaths
quote: Rural communities in Maine, Kentucky, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia were reportedly being devastated by the abuse and diversion of OxyContin. For example, media reports told of persons and communities that had been adversely affected by the rise of addiction and deaths related to OxyContin. One report noted that drug treatment centers and emergency rooms in a particular area were receiving new patients who were addicted to OxyContin as early as 1999. Pain patients, teens, and recreational drug users who had abused OxyContin reportedly entered drug treatment centers sweating and vomiting from withdrawal. In West Virginia, as many as one-half of the approximately 300 patients admitted to a drug treatment clinic in 2000 were treated for OxyContin addiction. The media also reported on deaths due to OxyContin. For example, a newspaper's investigation of autopsy reports involving oxycodone-related deaths found that OxyContin had been involved in over 200 overdose deaths in Florida since 2000.
context: GAO documents media reports from 1999-2000 showing widespread warning signals about OxyContin abuse, addiction, and deaths in specific geographic regions.

label: DEA verifies OxyContin-related deaths
original_label: DEA verifies OxyContin-related deaths
quote: In response to the abuse and diversion reports, DEA analyzed data collected from medical examiner autopsy reports and crime scene investigation reports. The most recent data available from DEA show that as of February 2002, the agency had verified 146 deaths nationally involving OxyContin in 2000 and 2001.
context: GAO describes DEA's formal documentation of OxyContin-related deaths as a warning signal in response to abuse reports.

label: Over 300 lawsuits filed alleging improper marketing and inadequate abuse prevention
original_label: Over 300 lawsuits filed alleging improper marketing and inadequate abuse prevention
quote: According to Purdue, as of early October 2003, over 300 lawsuits concerning OxyContin were pending against Purdue, and 50 additional lawsuits had been dismissed. The cases involve many allegations, including, for example, that Purdue used improper sales tactics and overpromoted OxyContin causing the drug to be inappropriately prescribed by physicians, and that Purdue took inadequate actions to prevent addiction, abuse, and diversion of the drug.
context: GAO documents the volume of litigation against Purdue as evidence of warning signals about the company's marketing practices and failure to prevent abuse.

label: Purdue forms response team after Maine abuse reports
original_label: Purdue forms response team after Maine abuse reports
quote: After learning about the initial reports of abuse and diversion of OxyContin in Maine in 2000, Purdue formed a response team made up of its top executives and physicians to initiate meetings with federal and state officials in Maine to gain an understanding of the scope of the problem and to devise strategies for preventing abuse and diversion.
context: GAO documents Purdue's institutional response structure in January 2000, showing that top executives and physicians were positioned to receive and respond to warning signals about abuse.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Purdue marketing focused on expanding OxyContin prescribers
original_label: Purdue marketing focused on expanding OxyContin prescribers
quote: Purdue conducted an extensive campaign to market and promote OxyContin using an expanded sales force and multiple promotional approaches to encourage physicians, including primary care specialists, to prescribe OxyContin as an initial opioid treatment for noncancer pain. OxyContin sales and prescriptions grew rapidly following its market introduction in 1996, with the growth in prescriptions for noncancer pain outpacing the growth in prescriptions for cancer pain from 1997 through 2002. By 2003, nearly half of all OxyContin prescribers were primary care physicians.
context: GAO summarizes Purdue's dominant strategic agenda from 1996-2003, which was expanding OxyContin market penetration through primary care physicians.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Sales force expansion tied to prescription growth targets
original_label: Sales force expansion tied to prescription growth targets
quote: In 1996, Purdue began promoting OxyContin with a sales force of approximately 300 representatives in its Prescription Sales Division. Through a 1996 copromotion agreement, Abbott Laboratories provided at least another 300 representatives, doubling the total OxyContin sales force. By 2000, Purdue had more than doubled its own internal sales force to 671. The expanded sales force included sales representatives from the Hospital Specialty Division, which was created in 2000 to increase promotional visits on physicians located in hospitals.
context: GAO documents how Purdue's organizational structure and resource allocation were focused on expanding OxyContin market penetration throughout 1996-2002.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Sales compensation structured to incentivize OxyContin growth
original_label: Sales compensation structured to incentivize OxyContin growth
quote: Purdue stated it offered a 'better than industry average' salary and sales bonuses to attract top sales representatives and provide incentives to boost OxyContin sales as it had done for MS Contin. Although the sales representatives were primarily focused on OxyContin promotion, the amount of the bonus depended on whether a representative met the sales quotas in his or her sales territory for all company products. As OxyContin's sales increased, Purdue's growth-based portion of the bonus formula increased the OxyContin sales quotas necessary to earn the same base sales bonus amounts. The amount of total bonuses that Purdue estimated were tied to OxyContin sales increased significantly from about $1 million in 1996, when OxyContin was first marketed, to about $40 million in 2001. In 2001, the average annual salary for a Purdue sales representative was $55,000, and the average annual bonus was $71,500.
context: GAO documents the financial incentive structure that directed Purdue sales representatives' attention to maximizing OxyContin sales from 1996-2001.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Promotional spending on OxyContin far exceeded competitor spending
original_label: Promotional spending on OxyContin far exceeded competitor spending
quote: According to DEA's analysis of IMS Health data, Purdue spent approximately 6 to 12 times more on promotional efforts during OxyContin's first 6 years on the market than it had spent on its older product, MS Contin, during its first 6 years, or than had been spent by Janssen Pharmaceutical Products, L.P., for one of OxyContin's drug competitors, Duragesic.
context: GAO presents DEA analysis showing Purdue's exceptional focus on OxyContin promotion compared to its own prior product and competitors' products.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Sales representatives directed to target high opioid prescribers
original_label: Sales representatives directed to target high opioid prescribers
quote: Purdue directed its sales representatives to focus on the physicians in their sales territories who were high opioid prescribers. This group included cancer and pain specialists, primary care physicians, and physicians who were high prescribers of Purdue's older product, MS Contin. One of Purdue's goals was to identify primary care physicians who would expand the company's OxyContin prescribing base.
context: GAO documents the targeting rules that shaped sales representatives' attention and priorities from the launch of OxyContin.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Physician call lists and call frequency as attention metrics
original_label: Physician call lists and call frequency as attention metrics
quote: Each Purdue sales representative has a specific sales territory and is responsible for developing a list of about 105 to 140 physicians to call on who already prescribe opioids or who are candidates for prescribing opioids. In 1996, the 300-plus Purdue sales representatives had a total physician call list of approximately 33,400 to 44,500. By 2000, the nearly 700 representatives had a total call list of approximately 70,500 to 94,000 physicians. Each Purdue sales representative is expected to make about 35 physician calls per week and typically calls on each physician every 3 to 4 weeks.
context: GAO documents the formal metrics and rules that structured sales representatives' activities and attention to maximizing physician contact.

label: Promotional materials submitted to FDA only after dissemination
original_label: Promotional materials submitted to FDA only after dissemination
quote: FDA regulations require that promotional labeling and advertisements be submitted to FDA at the time of initial dissemination (for labeling) and initial publication (for advertisements). The FD&C Act defines labeling to include all labels and other written, printed, or graphic matter accompanying an article. However, the FD&C Act and its implementing regulations require that all promotional materials for prescription drugs be submitted to FDA at the time the materials are first disseminated or used, but it generally is not required that these materials be approved by FDA before their use. As a result, FDA's actions to address violations occur after the materials have already appeared in public.
context: GAO describes the regulatory procedural channel for FDA oversight of promotional materials, showing that the system was designed for post-hoc rather than prior review.

label: FDA lack of resources for reviewing promotional materials
original_label: FDA lack of resources for reviewing promotional materials
quote: FDA said that it receives numerous marketing and promotional materials for promoted prescription drugs and that while every effort is made to review the materials, it cannot guarantee that all materials are reviewed because of limited resources and competing priorities. FDA officials also stated that pharmaceutical companies do not always submit promotional materials as required by regulations and that in such instances FDA would not have a record of the promotional pieces.
context: GAO documents the procedural breakdown in FDA's oversight channel, showing how lack of resources prevented detection of promotional violations.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: OxyContin promotional video not submitted to FDA for three years
original_label: OxyContin promotional video not submitted to FDA for three years
quote: Beginning in 1998, Purdue, as part of its marketing and promotion of OxyContin, distributed 15,000 copies of an OxyContin video to physicians without submitting it to FDA for review. This video, entitled I Got My Life Back: Patients in Pain Tell Their Story, presented the pain relief experiences of various patients and the pain medications, including OxyContin, they had been prescribed. FDA regulations require pharmaceutical manufacturers to submit all promotional materials for approved prescription drug products to the agency at the time of their initial use. Because Purdue did not comply with this regulation, FDA did not have an opportunity to review the video to ensure that the information it contained was truthful, balanced, and accurately communicated. Purdue has acknowledged the oversight of not submitting the video to FDA for review.
context: GAO documents how Purdue bypassed the procedural channel for FDA review of promotional materials from 1998-2001.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: FDA did not review second OxyContin video until inquiry from GAO
original_label: FDA did not review second OxyContin video until inquiry from GAO
quote: In February 2001, Purdue submitted a second version of the video to FDA, which included information about the 160-milligram OxyContin tablet. FDA did not review this second version until October 2002, after we inquired about its content. FDA told us it found that the second version of the video appeared to make unsubstantiated claims regarding OxyContin's effect on patients' quality of life and ability to perform daily activities and minimized the risks associated with the drug. Distribution of all four Purdue videos was discontinued by July 2001, in response to OxyContin's labeling changes, which required the company to modify all of its promotional materials, but copies of the videos that had already been distributed were not retrieved and destroyed.
context: GAO documents how FDA did not review the video until external pressure from GAO investigation, and how already-distributed materials were not retrieved.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: FDA original label language minimized OxyContin abuse potential
original_label: FDA original label language minimized OxyContin abuse potential
quote: The OxyContin label originally approved by FDA indicated that the controlled-release characteristics of OxyContin were believed to reduce its potential for abuse. FDA officials said when OxyContin was approved the agency believed that the controlled-release formulation would result in less abuse potential because, when taken properly, the drug would be absorbed slowly, without an immediate rush or high. FDA officials acknowledged that the initial wording of OxyContin's label was 'unfortunate' but was based on what was known about the product at that time. FDA officials told us that abusers typically seek a drug that is intense and fast-acting. When OxyContin was approved, FDA did not recognize that if the drug is dissolved in water and injected its controlled-release characteristics could be disrupted, creating an immediate rush or high and thereby increasing the potential for misuse and abuse.
context: GAO documents how FDA's original framing of OxyContin as low-abuse-potential filtered out recognition of actual abuse risks.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Safety warning inadvertently alerted abusers to crushing method
original_label: Safety warning inadvertently alerted abusers to crushing method
quote: The safety warning on the OxyContin label may also have contributed to the drug's potential for abuse and diversion, by inadvertently providing abusers with information on how the drug could be misused. The label included the warning that the tablets should not be broken, chewed, or crushed because such action could result in the rapid release and absorption of a potentially toxic dose of oxycodone. FDA places similar safety warnings on other drugs to ensure that they are used properly. FDA officials stated that neither they nor other experts anticipated that crushing the controlled-release tablet and intravenously injecting or snorting the drug would become widespread and lead to a high level of abuse.
context: GAO documents how a standard safety warning, designed to prevent misuse, instead provided abusers with knowledge of methods to defeat the drug's controlled-release mechanism.

label: Purdue initiated educational programs and brochures after Maine reports
original_label: Purdue initiated educational programs and brochures after Maine reports
quote: After these meetings, Purdue distributed brochures to health care professionals that described several steps that could be taken to prevent prescription drug abuse and diversion.
context: GAO documents Purdue's initial response action to the 2000 Maine abuse reports, which was to distribute educational materials.

label: FDA issued untitled letter for OxyContin advertisement violations
original_label: FDA issued untitled letter for OxyContin advertisement violations
quote: In May 2000, FDA issued an untitled letter to Purdue regarding a professional medical journal advertisement for OxyContin. FDA noted that among other problems, the advertisement implied that OxyContin had been studied for all types of arthritis pain when it had been studied only in patients with moderate-to-severe osteoarthritis pain, the advertisement suggested OxyContin could be used as an initial therapy for the treatment of osteoarthritis pain without substantial evidence to support this claim, and the advertisement promoted OxyContin in a selected class of patients—the elderly—without presenting risk information applicable to that class of patients. Purdue agreed to stop dissemination of the advertisement.
context: GAO documents FDA's enforcement action in May 2000 against Purdue for misleading OxyContin advertisements.

label: FDA issued warning letter for OxyContin advertisements minimizing risks
original_label: FDA issued warning letter for OxyContin advertisements minimizing risks
quote: In January 2003, FDA issued a warning letter to Purdue regarding two professional medical journal advertisements for OxyContin that minimized its risks and overstated its efficacy, by failing to prominently present information from the boxed warning on the potentially fatal risks associated with OxyContin and its abuse liability, along with omitting important information about the limitations on the indicated use of OxyContin. The FDA requested that Purdue cease disseminating these advertisements and any similar violative materials and provide a plan of corrective action. In response, Purdue issued a corrected advertisement, which called attention to the warning letter and the cited violations and directed the reader to the prominently featured boxed warning and indication information for OxyContin.
context: GAO documents FDA's more serious warning letter enforcement action in January 2003 against Purdue for OxyContin advertisements.

label: FDA revised OxyContin label with black box warning
original_label: FDA revised OxyContin label with black box warning
quote: In July 2001, FDA reevaluated OxyContin's label and made several changes in an effort to strengthen the 'Warnings' section of the label. FDA added a subsection—'Misuse, Abuse, and Diversion of Opioids'—to stress that physicians and pharmacists should be alert to the risk of misuse, abuse, and diversion when prescribing or dispensing OxyContin. FDA also added a black box warning—the highest level of warning FDA can place on an approved drug product.
context: GAO documents FDA's major organizational response to OxyContin abuse reports in July 2001.

label: FDA and Purdue collaborated to develop risk management plan
original_label: FDA and Purdue collaborated to develop risk management plan
quote: Beginning in early 2001, FDA collaborated with Purdue to develop and implement a risk management plan to help identify and prevent abuse and diversion of OxyContin. As a part of the risk management plan in connection with the labeling changes, Purdue was asked by FDA to revise all of its promotional materials for OxyContin to reflect the labeling changes. In August 2001, FDA sent a letter to Purdue stating that all future promotional materials for OxyContin should prominently disclose the information contained in the boxed warning; the new warnings that address misuse, abuse, diversion, and addiction; and the new precautions and revised indication for OxyContin.
context: GAO documents the collaborative risk management approach FDA and Purdue implemented in 2001 in response to abuse reports.

label: DEA developed national action plan targeting OxyContin
original_label: DEA developed national action plan targeting OxyContin
quote: In April 2001, DEA developed a national action plan to deter abuse and diversion of OxyContin. According to DEA officials, this marked the first time the agency had targeted a specific brand-name product for monitoring because of the level and frequency of abuse and diversion associated with the drug. Key components of the action plan include coordinating enforcement and intelligence operations with other law enforcement agencies to target people and organizations involved in abuse and diversion of OxyContin, pursuing regulatory and administrative action to limit abusers' access to OxyContin, and building national outreach efforts to educate the public on the dangers related to the abuse and diversion of OxyContin.
context: GAO documents DEA's organizational response in April 2001, which was unprecedented for targeting a specific brand-name drug.

label: DEA enforcement investigations and arrests for OxyContin
original_label: DEA enforcement investigations and arrests for OxyContin
quote: DEA has increased enforcement efforts to prevent abuse and diversion of OxyContin. From fiscal year 1996 through fiscal year 2002, DEA initiated 313 investigations involving OxyContin, resulting in 401 arrests. Most of the investigations and arrests occurred after the initiation of the action plan. Since the plan was enacted, DEA initiated 257 investigations and made 302 arrests in fiscal years 2001 and 2002. Among those arrested were several physicians and pharmacists.
context: GAO documents DEA's enforcement actions in response to OxyContin abuse, with most activity occurring after the April 2001 action plan.

label: Purdue trained sales force on revised OxyContin label
original_label: Purdue trained sales force on revised OxyContin label
quote: Purdue trained its sales force on the specifics of the revised label and provided sales representatives with updated information on the appropriate use of opioid analgesics, legal guidelines associated with promotion of its products, and their responsibility and role in reporting adverse events. Purdue also reiterated to its sales representatives that failure to promote products according to the approved label, promotional materials, and applicable FDA standards would result in disciplinary action by the company.
context: GAO documents Purdue's organizational response to the July 2001 label changes through sales force training.

label: Purdue disciplined sales representatives for improper promotion
original_label: Purdue disciplined sales representatives for improper promotion
quote: According to Purdue, from April 2001 through May 2003 at least 10 Purdue employees were disciplined for using unapproved materials in promoting OxyContin. Disciplinary actions included warning letters, suspension without pay, and termination.
context: GAO documents Purdue's disciplinary response to sales representatives promoting OxyContin improperly.

label: Initial reports of OxyContin abuse in Maine in 2000
original_label: Initial reports of OxyContin abuse in Maine in 2000
quote: After learning about the initial reports of abuse and diversion of OxyContin in Maine in 2000, Purdue formed a response team made up of its top executives and physicians to initiate meetings with federal and state officials in Maine to gain an understanding of the scope of the problem and to devise strategies for preventing abuse and diversion.
context: GAO identifies the Maine reports in 2000 as a triggering event that shifted Purdue's attention and led to formation of a response team.

label: December 2001 congressional hearing on OxyContin abuse
original_label: December 2001 congressional hearing on OxyContin abuse
quote: During a December 2001 congressional hearing, witnesses from DEA and other law enforcement officials from Kentucky, Virginia, and West Virginia described the growing problem of abuse and diversion of OxyContin.
context: GAO identifies the December 2001 congressional hearing as a triggering event that elevated attention to OxyContin abuse issues.

label: FDA issued untitled letter in May 2000 for advertisement violations
original_label: FDA issued untitled letter in May 2000 for advertisement violations
quote: In May 2000, FDA issued an untitled letter to Purdue regarding a professional medical journal advertisement for OxyContin.
context: GAO identifies FDA's May 2000 untitled letter as an enforcement action that signaled regulatory attention to Purdue's promotional practices.

label: July 2001 OxyContin label revision with black box warning
original_label: July 2001 OxyContin label revision with black box warning
quote: In July 2001, FDA reevaluated OxyContin's label and made several changes in an effort to strengthen the 'Warnings' section of the label. FDA added a subsection—'Misuse, Abuse, and Diversion of Opioids'—to stress that physicians and pharmacists should be alert to the risk of misuse, abuse, and diversion when prescribing or dispensing OxyContin. FDA also added a black box warning—the highest level of warning FDA can place on an approved drug product.
context: GAO identifies the July 2001 label revision as a major triggering event that shifted organizational attention and prompted risk management planning.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Purdue did not analyze prescribing data for abuse patterns until fall 2002
original_label: Purdue did not analyze prescribing data for abuse patterns until fall 2002
quote: Although Purdue has used very specific information on physician prescribing practices to market and promote OxyContin since its approval, it was not until October 2002 that Purdue began to use this information and other indicators to identify patterns of prescribing that could point to possible improper sales representative promotion or physician abuse and diversion of OxyContin.
context: GAO documents how Purdue had access to physician prescribing data for marketing purposes from 1996 but did not use it to detect abuse patterns until October 2002, nearly two years after abuse reports became public.

label: Purdue developed 11 indicators to identify possible abuse and diversion
original_label: Purdue developed 11 indicators to identify possible abuse and diversion
quote: Although this information has always been available for use by Purdue and its sales representatives, it was not until fall 2002 that Purdue directed its sales representatives to begin using 11 indicators to identify possible abuse and diversion and to report the incidents to Purdue's General Counsel's Office for investigation. Among the possible indicators are a sudden unexplained change in a physician's prescribing patterns that is not accounted for by changes in patient numbers, information from credible sources such as a pharmacist that a physician or his or her patients are diverting medications, or a physician who writes a large number of prescriptions for patients who pay with cash. As of September 2003, Purdue—through its own investigations—had identified 39 physicians and other health care professionals who were referred to legal, medical, or regulatory authorities for further action.
context: GAO documents Purdue's October 2002 implementation of a formal screening process for abuse and diversion indicators, resulting in 39 referrals by September 2003.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Sales bonus structure modified due to U.S. Attorney meeting
original_label: Sales bonus structure modified due to U.S. Attorney meeting
quote: In 2001, Purdue decided to limit the sales bonus a representative could earn based on the growth in prescribing of a single physician after a meeting with the U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Virginia at which the company was informed of the possibility that a bonus could be based on the prescribing of one physician.
context: GAO documents how external pressure from law enforcement led Purdue to modify the incentive rules that had previously structured sales representatives' attention.

label: DEA expressed concern about Purdue's aggressive marketing
original_label: DEA expressed concern about Purdue's aggressive marketing
quote: DEA has expressed concern that Purdue's aggressive marketing of OxyContin focused on promoting the drug to treat a wide range of conditions to physicians who may not have been adequately trained in pain management.
context: GAO documents DEA's position as a federal regulator that lacked the authority to prevent Purdue's marketing practices despite expressing concerns.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: OxyContin became Purdue's main product by 2001
original_label: OxyContin became Purdue's main product by 2001
quote: The drug became Purdue's main product, accounting for 90 percent of the company's total prescription sales by 2001.
context: GAO documents OxyContin's dominance in Purdue's business model by 2001, showing the company's strategic focus on this single product.

label: Purdue discontinued 160-milligram OxyContin tablet
original_label: Purdue discontinued 160-milligram OxyContin tablet
quote: Other actions included in the plan that were taken by Purdue prior to submission of its risk management plan include discontinuance of the 160-milligram tablet of OxyContin to reduce the risk of overdose from this dosage strength.
context: GAO documents Purdue's product modification action in response to overdose risk, which was included in the risk management plan.

label: Purdue developed RADARS system to study abuse and diversion
original_label: Purdue developed RADARS system to study abuse and diversion
quote: Because reliable data on the abuse and diversion of controlled substance drugs are not available, Purdue developed the Researched Abuse, Diversion, and Addiction-Related Surveillance (RADARS) System, as part of its risk management plan, to study the nature and extent of abuse of OxyContin and other schedule II and III prescription medications and to implement interventions to reduce abuse and diversion.
context: GAO documents Purdue's development of a surveillance system as part of its risk management plan to track abuse and diversion.

label: State Medicaid fraud units investigated OxyContin cases
original_label: State Medicaid fraud units investigated OxyContin cases
quote: State Medicaid fraud control units have conducted investigations of abuse and diversion of OxyContin, but generally do not maintain precise data on the number of investigations and enforcement actions completed. Although complete information was not available from directors of state Medicaid fraud control units in Kentucky, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia with whom we spoke, each of those directors told us that abuse and diversion of OxyContin is a problem in his or her state. The directors told us that they had investigated cases that involved physicians or individuals who had either been indicted or prosecuted for writing medically unnecessary OxyContin prescriptions in exchange for cash or sexual relationships.
context: GAO documents state-level enforcement actions by Medicaid fraud units in response to OxyContin abuse reports.

label: FDA risk management plan guidance not yet issued when OxyContin approved
original_label: FDA risk management plan guidance not yet issued when OxyContin approved
quote: FDA plans to provide guidance to the pharmaceutical industry by September 2004 on risk management plans, which are an optional feature of new drug applications. FDA defines a risk management program as a strategic safety program that is designed to decrease product risks by using one or more interventions or tools beyond the approved product labeling.
context: GAO documents the procedural gap: risk management plans did not exist as a formal FDA procedure when OxyContin was approved in 1995.

label: Purdue promotional video made unsubstantiated addiction claims
original_label: Purdue promotional video made unsubstantiated addiction claims
quote: Purdue stated that the video was to be used 'in physician waiting rooms, as a 'check out' item for an office's patient education library, or as an educational tool for office or hospital staff to utilize with patients and their families.' The video did not need to be submitted to FDA for its review because it did not contain any information about OxyContin. However, the video included a statement that opioid analgesics have been shown to cause addiction in less than 1 percent of patients. According to FDA, this statement has not been substantiated.
context: GAO documents how Purdue's 1999 promotional video made unsubstantiated claims about addiction rates, which was not detected until FDA reviewed it in 2002.

label: Independent researchers identify higher on-road NOx emissions
original_label: Independent researchers identify higher on-road NOx emissions
quote: May 2014: A study conducted by independent researchers at West Virginia University (WVU) on behalf of the International Council for Clean Transportation (ICCT) identified significantly higher on-road NOx emissions from two VW vehicles — a 2012 Jetta and a 2013 Passat. The results of this study were brought to the attention of the EPA, CARB, and VW.
context: The hearing memo describes the initial warning signal that triggered regulatory attention to VW's emissions behavior.

label: Regulatory agencies and manufacturer testing and investigation procedures
original_label: Regulatory agencies and manufacturer testing and investigation procedures
quote: May 2014 to December 2014: CARB and EPA launched investigations into the higher emissions in VW vehicles. VW initiated testing to replicate the ICCT/WVU research and identify technical causes for the higher on-road emissions observed by the researchers.
context: The memo describes the formal procedural channels through which warning signals were communicated and investigated between regulators and the manufacturer.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: VW attributes higher emissions to technical issues and unexpected conditions
original_label: VW attributes higher emissions to technical issues and unexpected conditions
quote: VW asserted to EPA and CARB that increased emissions from these vehicles could be attributed to various technical issues and unexpected in-use conditions.
context: The memo shows how VW reframed and narrowed the interpretation of the warning signal, attributing it to benign technical factors rather than deliberate design.

label: VW proposes recalibration fix and initiates voluntary recall
original_label: VW proposes recalibration fix and initiates voluntary recall
quote: December 2, 2014: VW shared testing results with EPA and CARB and proposed a recalibration fix for the Gen1 (Lean NOx Trap technology) and Gen2 (Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) Technology). December 2014: VW initiated a voluntary recall of approximately 500,000 vehicles in the United States. The recall included MY2009 to MY2014 diesel vehicles equipped with Gen1 and Gen2 technology.
context: The memo documents VW's initial response to the warning signal through proposed technical fixes and a voluntary recall.

label: CARB testing shows limited improvement from VW's recall solution
original_label: CARB testing shows limited improvement from VW's recall solution
quote: May 6, 2015 to July 2015: CARB conducted laboratory and on-road testing to confirm the efficacy of the recall. The testing showed limited improvement, prompting CARB to expand its investigation.
context: The memo describes a subsequent warning signal when regulatory testing revealed that VW's proposed fix did not adequately address the emissions problem.

label: VW discloses second calibration during technical meetings
original_label: VW discloses second calibration during technical meetings
quote: July 8, 2015: CARB shared test results with VW and the EPA, prompting a series of technical meetings. According to CARB, in the course of those meetings, VW disclosed that Gen1, Gen2, and the 2015 model-year improved SCR vehicle (known as Gen3) had a second calibration intended to run only during confirmatory testing.
context: The memo describes a critical procedural moment when VW disclosed to regulators through formal technical meetings the existence of a second calibration mode, revealing the defeat device.

label: Regulators announce they will not certify 2016 vehicles
original_label: Regulators announce they will not certify 2016 vehicles
quote: August 2015: EPA and CARB informed VW that they would not issue certificates of conformity for 2016 vehicles until VW could explain the higher emissions and provide assurance that they would not occur in 2016 vehicles.
context: The memo shows how regulatory pressure in response to test results and the undisclosed calibration became an escalating signal that forced VW's eventual admission.

label: VW admits to designing and installing defeat device
original_label: VW admits to designing and installing defeat device
quote: September 3, 2015: VW admitted to EPA and CARB that it had designed and installed what was effectively a defeat device into these vehicles.
context: The memo documents VW's formal admission to regulators, marking a shift from earlier explanations of technical issues.

label: EPA issues Notice of Violation and CARB sends compliance letter
original_label: EPA issues Notice of Violation and CARB sends compliance letter
quote: September 18, 2015: EPA sent VW a Notice of Violation. CARB sent VW an in-use compliance letter.
context: The memo identifies the formal regulatory action that marked the official recognition and public disclosure of the wrongdoing.

label: CEO resignation and leadership restructuring
original_label: CEO resignation and leadership restructuring
quote: September 23, 2015: Dr. Winterkorn resigned from VW. September 25, 2015: VW suspended the leaders of the VW, Audi, and Porsche research and development divisions and announced a restructuring of its North American business unit.
context: The memo documents major leadership changes and organizational restructuring that occurred immediately after public disclosure, indicating a dramatic shift in attention and priorities.

label: EPA OTAQ and CARB investigate emissions compliance across vehicle lifecycle
original_label: EPA OTAQ and CARB investigate emissions compliance across vehicle lifecycle
quote: EPA's Office of Transportation and Air Quality (OTAQ) oversees a broad set of compliance activities to ensure that vehicles manufacturers satisfy regulatory requirements. These include the review of COC applications and a variety of testing and other requirements that occur over the life a vehicle. In addition to review of manufacturer supplied testing data, EPA's own testing may include so-called confirmatory testing, both random and targeted, and in use compliance testing.
context: The memo describes the formal structural positions and procedures through which regulatory agencies were designed to monitor compliance and detect anomalies throughout a vehicle's life.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Manufacturer must list and justify auxiliary emission control devices
original_label: Manufacturer must list and justify auxiliary emission control devices
quote: In the COC application submitted to the EPA, the manufacturer must list all auxiliary emission control devices (AECDs) installed on the vehicle. An AECD is defined as any element of design which senses temperature, vehicle speed, engine RPM, transmission gear, manifold vacuum, or any other parameter for the purpose of activating, modulating, delaying or deactivating the operation of any part of the emission control system. The manufacturer must also justify each AECD and explain why it is not a defeat device.
context: The memo describes the formal regulatory rules and documentation requirements designed to make manufacturers attend to and disclose whether their software constitutes a defeat device.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Definition and legal prohibition of defeat devices
original_label: Definition and legal prohibition of defeat devices
quote: An AECD is considered a defeat device if it: . . . reduces the effectiveness of the emission control system under conditions which may reasonably be expected to be encountered in normal vehicle operation and use, unless: (1) Such conditions are substantially included in the Federal emission test procedure; (2) The need for the AECD is justified in terms of protecting the vehicle against damage or accident; (3) The AECD does not go beyond the requirements of engine starting; or (4) The AECD applies only to emergency vehicles. It is a violation of the CAA to manufacture or sell any part or component if it will: . . . bypass, defeat, or render inoperative any device or element of design installed on or in a motor vehicle or motor vehicle engine in compliance with regulations under this subchapter, and where the person knows or should know that such part or component is being offered for sale or installed for such use or put to such use.
context: The memo presents the legal rules that were supposed to direct manufacturer attention to what constitutes prohibited conduct and when to disclose such conduct in regulatory submissions.

label: Crash tests reveal fuel tank vulnerability
original_label: Crash tests reveal fuel tank vulnerability
quote: The crash tests revealed that the Pinto's fuel system as designed could not meet the 20-mile-per-hour proposed standard. Mechanical prototypes struck from the rear with a moving barrier at 21 miles per hour caused the fuel tank to be driven forward and to be punctured, causing fuel leakage in excess of the standard prescribed by the proposed regulation. A production Pinto crash tested at 21 miles per hour into a fixed barrier caused the fuel neck to be torn from the gas tank and the tank to be punctured by a bolt head on the differential housing.
context: The trial court's opinion summarizes results of Ford's own crash tests conducted during development of the Pinto, which showed critical safety defects.

label: Seam separation and fuel entry into passenger compartment
original_label: Seam separation and fuel entry into passenger compartment
quote: In at least one test, spilled fuel entered the driver's compartment through gaps resulting from the separation of the seams joining the rear wheel wells to the floor pan. The seam separation was occasioned by the lack of reinforcement in the rear structure and insufficient welds of the wheel wells to the floor pan.
context: The trial court describes additional findings from crash tests showing how fuel could enter the passenger cabin during rear-end collisions.

label: Alternative designs proved safe at higher speeds
original_label: Alternative designs proved safe at higher speeds
quote: Tests conducted by Ford on other vehicles, including modified or reinforced mechanical Pinto prototypes, proved safe at speeds at which the Pinto failed. Where rubber bladders had been installed in the tank, crash tests into fixed barriers at 21 miles per hour withstood leakage from punctures in the gas tank. Vehicles with fuel tanks installed above rather than behind the rear axle passed the fuel system integrity test at 31-miles-per-hour fixed barrier. A Pinto with two longitudinal hat sections added to firm up the rear structure passed a 20-mile-per-hour rear impact fixed barrier test with no fuel leakage.
context: The trial court documents Ford's own comparative testing showing that relatively simple design modifications would have solved the fuel tank vulnerability.

label: Inexpensive fixes available to remedy defects
original_label: Inexpensive fixes available to remedy defects
quote: The vulnerability of the production Pinto's fuel tank at speeds of 20 and 30-miles-per-hour fixed barrier tests could have been remedied by inexpensive "fixes," but Ford produced and sold the Pinto to the public without doing anything to remedy the defects. Design changes that would have enhanced the integrity of the fuel tank system at relatively little cost per car included the following: Longitudinal side members and cross members at $2.40 and $1.80, respectively; a single shock absorbant "flak suit" to protect the tank at $4; a tank within a tank and placement of the tank over the axle at $5.08 to $5.79; a nylon bladder within the tank at $5.25 to $8; placement of the tank over the axle surrounded with a protective barrier at a cost of $9.95 per car; substitution of a rear axle with a smooth differential housing at a cost of $2.10; imposition of a protective shield between the differential housing and the tank at $2.35; improvement and reenforcement of the bumper at $2.60; addition of eight inches of crush space a cost of $6.40.
context: The trial court documents the availability and cost of design modifications that Ford knew could make the Pinto safe, presented as evidence at trial.

label: Crash test results forwarded up chain of command
original_label: Crash test results forwarded up chain of command
quote: The Pinto crash tests results had been forwarded up the chain of command to the ultimate decision-makers and were known to the Ford officials who decided to go forward with production.
context: The trial court's factual finding about the mechanism by which crash test data reached senior management at Ford.

label: Product review meetings chaired by management
original_label: Product review meetings chaired by management
quote: During the course of the project, regular product review meetings were held which were chaired by Mr. MacDonald and attended by Mr. Alexander. As the project approached actual production, the engineers responsible for the components of the project "signed off" to their immediate supervisors who in turn "signed off" to their superiors and so on up the chain of command until the entire project was approved for public release by Vice Presidents Alexander and MacDonald and ultimately by Mr. Iacocca.
context: The trial court describes Ford's formal approval process and decision-making hierarchy for the Pinto project.

label: Iacocca conceived project; Alexander supervised engineering; MacDonald chaired reviews
original_label: Iacocca conceived project; Alexander supervised engineering; MacDonald chaired reviews
quote: In 1968, Ford began designing a new subcompact automobile which ultimately became the Pinto. Mr. Iacocca, then a Ford vice president, conceived the project and was its moving force. The feasibility study was conducted under the supervision of Mr. Robert Alexander, vice president of car engineering. Ford's Product Planning Committee, whose members included Mr. Iacocca, Mr. Robert Alexander, and Mr. Harold MacDonald, Ford's group vice president of car engineering, approved the Pinto's concept and made the decision to go forward with the project.
context: The trial court identifies the senior executives responsible for the Pinto project and its approval, establishing the relevant decision-making hierarchy.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Project driven by cost and weight targets
original_label: Project driven by cost and weight targets
quote: In 1968, Ford began designing a new subcompact automobile which ultimately became the Pinto. Mr. Iacocca, then a Ford vice president, conceived the project and was its moving force. Ford's objective was to build a car at or below 2,000 pounds to sell for no more than $2,000.
context: The trial court explains Ford's primary design objectives for the Pinto, which constrained engineering decisions and directed attention toward cost minimization.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Styling dictated engineering design decisions
original_label: Styling dictated engineering design decisions
quote: Ordinarily marketing surveys and preliminary engineering studies precede the styling of a new automobile line. Pinto, however, was a rush project, so that styling preceded engineering and dictated engineering design to a greater degree than usual.
context: The trial court describes the unusual process used for Pinto development, in which aesthetic and cost goals drove engineering rather than the reverse.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Management decision based on cost savings from deferring fixes
original_label: Management decision based on cost savings from deferring fixes
quote: Harley Copp, a former Ford engineer and executive in charge of the crash testing program, testified that the highest level of Ford's management made the decision to go forward with the production of the Pinto, knowing that the gas tank was vulnerable to puncture and rupture at low rear impact speeds creating a significant risk of death or injury from fire and knowing that "fixes" were feasible at nominal cost. He testified that management's decision was based on the cost savings which would inure from omitting or delaying the "fixes."
context: Key witness Copp testifies about Ford management's stated rationale for proceeding without safety fixes, establishing what senior managers prioritized.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Cost-benefit analysis balancing lives against savings
original_label: Cost-benefit analysis balancing lives against savings
quote: Mr. Copp testified to conversations in late 1968 or early 1969 with the chief assistant research engineer in charge of cost-weight evaluation of the Pinto, and to a later conversation with the chief chassis engineer who was then in charge of crash testing the early prototype. In these conversations, both men expressed concern about the integrity of the Pinto's fuel system and complained about management's unwillingness to deviate from the design if the change would cost money.
context: Copp's testimony about conversations with engineers reveals management's cost-focused orientation and resistance to design changes regardless of safety implications.

label: April 1971 report on financial impact of safety standards
original_label: April 1971 report on financial impact of safety standards
quote: At an April 1971 product review meeting chaired by Mr. MacDonald, those present received and discussed a report (exhibit 125) prepared by Ford engineers pertaining to the financial impact of a proposed federal standard on fuel system integrity and the cost savings which would accrue from deferring even minimal "fixes." The report refers to crash tests of the integrity of the fuel system of Ford vehicles and design changes needed to meet anticipated federal standards.
context: The trial court identifies a specific product review meeting where senior management discussed and received documentation about crash test results and the financial consequences of deferring safety fixes.

label: 1970 report on fuel tank repackaging requirements
original_label: 1970 report on fuel tank repackaging requirements
quote: Also in evidence was a September 23, 1970, report (exhibit 124) by Ford's "Chassis Design Office" concerning a program "to establish a corporate [Ford] position and reply to the government" on the proposed federal fuel system integrity stand ard which included zero fuel spillage at 20 miles per hour fixed barrier crash by January 1, 1972, and 30 miles per hour by January 1, 1973. The report states in part: "The 20 and 30 mph rear fixed barrier crashes will probably require repackaging the fuel tanks in a protected area such as above the rear axle. This is based on moving barrier crash tests of a Chevelle and a Ford at 30 mph and other Ford products at 20 mph. [¶] Currently there are no plans for forward models to repackage the fuel tanks. Tests must be conducted to prove that repackaged tanks will live without significantly strengthening rear structure for added protection." The report also notes that the Pinto was the "[smallest] car line with most difficulty in achieving compliance."
context: Ford's own engineering report, dated before production, identified the Pinto's fuel tank vulnerability and the need for redesign to meet anticipated federal standards.

label: Crash tests requested to demonstrate fuel tank relocation feasibility
original_label: Crash tests requested to demonstrate fuel tank relocation feasibility
quote: The fact that two of the crash tests were run at the request of the Ford chassis and vehicle engineering department for the specific purpose of demonstrating the advisability of moving the fuel tank over the axle as a possible "fix" further corroborated Mr. Copp's testimony that management knew the results of the crash tests. Mr. Kennedy, who succeeded Mr. Copp as the engineer in charge of Ford's crash testing program, admitted that the test results had been forwarded up the chain of command to his superiors.
context: Evidence that Ford engineers deliberately conducted tests to evaluate a design fix, and that results were formally communicated up the management hierarchy.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Engineers complained management unwilling to spend on safety
original_label: Engineers complained management unwilling to spend on safety
quote: In these conversations, both men expressed concern about the integrity of the Pinto's fuel system and complained about management's unwillingness to deviate from the design if the change would cost money.
context: Copp's testimony reveals that Ford engineers raised safety concerns internally but found management resistant to expenditures regardless of the safety implications.

label: Production proceeded without implementing safety fixes
original_label: Production proceeded without implementing safety fixes
quote: The vulnerability of the production Pinto's fuel tank at speeds of 20 and 30-miles-per-hour fixed barrier tests could have been remedied by inexpensive "fixes," but Ford produced and sold the Pinto to the public without doing anything to remedy the defects.
context: The trial court's factual conclusion that despite knowledge of defects and availability of low-cost solutions, Ford proceeded with the unsafe design.

label: Fuel tank placement left only 9-10 inches crush space
original_label: Fuel tank placement left only 9-10 inches crush space
quote: Among the engineering decisions dictated by styling was the placement of the fuel tank. It was then the preferred practice in Europe and Japan to locate the gas tank over the rear axle in subcompacts because a small vehicle has less "crush space" between the rear axle and the bumper than larger cars. The Pinto's styling, however, required the tank to be placed behind the rear axle leaving only 9 or 10 inches of "crush space"--far less than in any other American automobile or Ford overseas subcompact.
context: The trial court identifies the unsafe fuel tank placement that resulted from the Pinto's styling-driven design process, establishing the core design defect.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Report inference that management aware of test results
original_label: Report inference that management aware of test results
quote: It is reasonable to infer that the report was prepared for and known to Ford officials in policy-making positions.
context: The trial court's reasoning about the routing and intended audience of the September 1970 report on fuel tank vulnerability, establishing that the warning reached decision-makers.

label: Vice presidents Alexander and MacDonald in decision chain
original_label: Vice presidents Alexander and MacDonald in decision chain
quote: As the project approached actual production, the engineers responsible for the components of the project "signed off" to their immediate supervisors who in turn "signed off" to their superiors and so on up the chain of command until the entire project was approved for public release by Vice Presidents Alexander and MacDonald and ultimately by Mr. Iacocca. The Pinto crash tests results had been forwarded up the chain of command to the ultimate decision-makers and were known to the Ford officials who decided to go forward with production.
context: The trial court describes how the formal approval chain placed crash test results before Vice Presidents Alexander and MacDonald before final production approval.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Report recommends deferring safety fixes to save money
original_label: Report recommends deferring safety fixes to save money
quote: Exhibit No. 125 was a report presented at a Ford production review meeting in April 1971, recommending action to be taken in anticipation of the promulgation of federal standards on fuel system integrity. The report recommended, inter alia, deferral from 1974 to 1976 of the adoption of "flak suits" or "bladders" in all Ford cars, including the Pinto, in order to realize a savings of $20.9 million. The report stated that the cost of the flak suit or bladder would be $4 to $8 per car.
context: The trial court describes the specific cost-benefit recommendation presented to Ford management at a senior product review meeting.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Rush project with styling preceding engineering
original_label: Rush project with styling preceding engineering
quote: Pinto, however, was a rush project, so that styling preceded engineering and dictated engineering design to a greater degree than usual.
context: The trial court explains how schedule pressure (rush project) and design process (styling first) oriented the project away from engineering-led safety analysis.

label: No corrective action taken despite knowledge of defects
original_label: No corrective action taken despite knowledge of defects
quote: Through the results of the crash tests Ford knew that the Pinto's fuel tank and rear structure would expose consumers to serious injury or death in a 20- to 30-mile-per-hour collision. There was evidence that Ford could have corrected the hazardous design defects at minimal cost but decided to defer correction of the shortcomings by engaging in a cost-benefit analysis balancing human lives and limbs against corporate profits.
context: The trial court's summary of findings establishing that Ford had knowledge of defects, knew of feasible fixes, but chose not to implement them based on cost considerations.

label: MacDonald attended April 1971 meeting where report discussed
original_label: MacDonald attended April 1971 meeting where report discussed
quote: At an April 1971 product review meeting chaired by Mr. MacDonald, those present received and discussed a report (exhibit 125) prepared by Ford engineers pertaining to the financial impact of a proposed federal standard on fuel system integrity and the cost savings which would accrue from deferring even minimal "fixes."
context: The trial court establishes that Vice President MacDonald was present when the specific cost-benefit report on deferring safety fixes was discussed.

label: Alexander admitted awareness of crash test results
original_label: Alexander admitted awareness of crash test results
quote: There is substantial evidence that management was aware of the crash tests showing the vulnerability of the Pinto's fuel tank to rupture at low speed rear impacts with consequent significant risk of injury or death of the occupants by fire. There was testimony from several sources that the test results were forwarded up the chain of command; vice president Robert Alexander admitted to Mr. Copp that he was aware of the test results; vice president Harold MacDonald, who chaired the product review meetings, was present at one of those meetings at which a report on the crash tests was considered and a decision was made to defer corrective action
context: The trial court cites evidence establishing that Vice Presidents Alexander and MacDonald had direct knowledge of crash test results and the decision to defer fixes.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Decision made to defer corrective action
original_label: Decision made to defer corrective action
quote: vice president Harold MacDonald, who chaired the product review meetings, was present at one of those meetings at which a report on the crash tests was considered and a decision was made to defer corrective action
context: The trial court's finding that after crash test results were reviewed at the senior management level, the explicit decision was to defer rather than implement fixes.

label: Recommendation to defer safety fixes until 1976
original_label: Recommendation to defer safety fixes until 1976
quote: The report recommended, inter alia, deferral from 1974 to 1976 of the adoption of "flak suits" or "bladders" in all Ford cars, including the Pinto, in order to realize a savings of $20.9 million.
context: The trial court describes the specific timing and rationale of Ford's decision to delay safety improvements for financial reasons.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Cost savings materialized through deferring design improvements
original_label: Cost savings materialized through deferring design improvements
