context: The complaint documents the circulation of the master software files containing the defeat device among Porsche and VW employees.

label: Audi engineers develop and calibrate 3.0L dual-mode strategy
original_label: Audi engineers develop and calibrate 3.0L dual-mode strategy
quote: Between approximately 2007 and 2015, engineers at Audi AG developed, calibrated, and refined the dual-mode strategy software functions described in Paragraphs 102–103, including the temperature conditioning mode.
context: The complaint establishes that Audi engineers had direct responsibility for developing the defeat device used in 3.0L vehicles.

label: Audi admits temperature conditioning mode is defeat device
original_label: Audi admits temperature conditioning mode is defeat device
quote: On November 23, 2015, Audi AG admitted in a press release that one of the undisclosed AECDs - the temperature conditioning mode – is regarded as a defeat device under the Act and implementing regulations.
context: The complaint describes Audi's public acknowledgment of the defeat device for 3.0L vehicles after EPA and CARB's investigation.

label: Internal Audi discussions about disclosure after EPA Notice
original_label: Internal Audi discussions about disclosure after EPA Notice
quote: In fact, in the days following EPA's issuance of a Notice of Violation for the 2.0L Subject Vehicles, engineers at Audi AG continued to communicate internally about what to tell CARB about the 3.0L Subject Vehicles, including whether or not they should disclose a software function related to emission control systems in order to build trust with regulators.
context: The complaint describes internal discussions at Audi about whether to disclose the defeat device, framed as a trust-building exercise.

label: EPA testing of 3.0L vehicle reveals test-dependent behavior
original_label: EPA testing of 3.0L vehicle reveals test-dependent behavior
quote: Following EPA's issuance of a Notice of Violation for the 2.0L Subject Vehicles, EPA OTAQ's NVFEL in Ann Arbor acquired a 3L Subject Vehicle (a Model Year 2014 Volkswagen Touareg) and ran emission tests on it using a number of different methods including the same off-cycle dynamometer test procedures that CARB ran on the 2.0L Subject Vehicle. EPA discovered that emission results from the 2014 Volkswagen Touareg were significantly higher in nearly every form of testing other than when the vehicle precisely followed the FTP procedures. The testing at NVFEL documented that even miniscule variations in the first few minutes of the test procedure caused emissions to increase dramatically for all subsequent testing.
context: The complaint describes how EPA's own testing methodology revealed the test-detection capability of the 3.0L software.

label: Porsche employees aware of defeat device investigation
original_label: Porsche employees aware of defeat device investigation
quote: At least as early as October 7, 2015, Porsche Cars North America employees and Porsche AG employees in the Certification and Emission Legislation, Regulatory Affairs group were aware that EPA and Environment Canada were conducting a "defeat device investigation" and in-use testing of the 3.0L Subject Vehicles.
context: The complaint establishes that Porsche personnel knew an official defeat device investigation was underway.

label: Porsche employees acknowledged possibility of defeat devices
original_label: Porsche employees acknowledged possibility of defeat devices
quote: As early as October 7, 2015, employees of Porsche Cars North America acknowledged in internal emails that there was a possibility that the Porsche 3.0L Subject Vehicles could include defeat devices.
context: The complaint quotes internal Porsche communications acknowledging the possibility of defeat devices in their vehicles.

label: EPA issues Notice of Violation for 3.0L vehicles
original_label: EPA issues Notice of Violation for 3.0L vehicles
quote: On November 2, 2015, EPA issued a Notice of Violation to Volkswagen AG, VWoA, Audi AG, Porsche AG, and Porsche Cars North America, Inc., citing violations of the Act related to the dual-mode strategy involving the "temperature conditioning mode" and the "normal mode," and the resultant excess emissions in certain 3.0L diesel vehicles.
context: The complaint describes EPA's formal notification of violations in the 3.0L vehicles.

label: VW denies 3.0L defeat devices after EPA Notice
original_label: VW denies 3.0L defeat devices after EPA Notice
quote: On that same day, November 2, 2015, Volkswagen AG issued a statement denying that software had been installed in 3.0L diesel vehicles to alter emissions in a prohibited manner.
context: The complaint shows that VW made a public denial of defeat devices in 3.0L vehicles on the same day EPA issued the Notice of Violation.

label: Audi admits to three undisclosed AECDs in 3.0L vehicles
original_label: Audi admits to three undisclosed AECDs in 3.0L vehicles
quote: On or about November 19, 2015, representatives of Audi AG, Volkswagen AG, and VWoA, attended a meeting at EPA OTAQ offices in Ann Arbor, Michigan. At that meeting, representatives of Audi AG presented to regulators and admitted that the 3.0L Subject Vehicles contain three undisclosed AECDs.
context: The complaint describes Audi's reversal from denying defeat devices to admitting the existence of undisclosed AECDs.

label: Porsche states Audi developed 3.0L ECM software
original_label: Porsche states Audi developed 3.0L ECM software
quote: At the Porsche November 19, 2015 meeting, Porsche AG stated that it installed and integrated the engines, including the EDC17 ECM, into the Porsche 3.0L Subject Vehicles. Porsche also stated that Audi AG developed and calibrated the EDC17 ECM software for the Porsche 3.0L Subject Vehicles.
context: The complaint describes Porsche's allocation of responsibility for the defeat device software to Audi.

label: Hidden dual-mode software detects test parameters
original_label: Hidden dual-mode software detects test parameters
quote: The EDC17 ECM of the 2.0L Subject Vehicles contains software functions and/or calibrations that sense when the vehicle is being tested for compliance with applicable emission standards, based on various inputs including the position of the steering wheel, vehicle speed, the duration of the engine's operation, and barometric pressure. These inputs precisely track the parameters of the federal test procedure ("FTP") and other test cycles used for emission testing required to obtain a COC. During FTP emission testing, the 2.0L Subject Vehicles' EDC17 ECMs run software functions and/or calibrations that produce compliant emission results, which VW has referred to as the "dyno mode" (referring to the equipment used in emissions testing, called a dynamometer). At all other times during normal vehicle operation, the 2.0L Subject Vehicles' EDC17 ECM software functions and/or calibrations run a separate "road mode" that reduces the effectiveness of the emission control systems in the vehicles, including engine control systems and after-treatment control systems.
context: The complaint describes the technical architecture of the defeat device, showing how it detects the test cycle and switches operating modes.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Certification requirement to attest to absence of defeat devices
original_label: Certification requirement to attest to absence of defeat devices
quote: At all times relevant to this Complaint, at the time that a manufacturer submits an initial COC application for a test group of vehicles on EPA's online database, the manufacturer must certify that the vehicles covered by that test group are free of defeat devices and strategies before the application can be submitted.
context: The complaint describes the regulatory requirement that made certification of compliance a necessary procedural step for market entry.

label: MCAS active at lower speed than designed
original_label: MCAS active at lower speed than designed
quote: On or about November 15, 2016, during a test flight of the 737 MAX in a simulator, Boeing Employee-1 experienced what Boeing Employee-1 recognized as MCAS operating at lower speed. Later that day, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 discussed MCAS in an electronic chat (the "November 15, 2016 Chat") which contained the following exchange: Boeing Employee-1: Oh shocker alerT! / MCAS is now active down to M[ach] .2 / It's running rampant in the sim[ulator] on me… / so I basically lied to the regulators (unknowingly) Boeing Employee-2: [I]t wasn't a lie, no one told us that was the case
context: Boeing employees discovered during simulator testing that MCAS was operating outside its original design parameters, in a conversation that explicitly acknowledged misrepresentation to regulators.

label: Documentation gaps in MCAS certification
original_label: Documentation gaps in MCAS certification
quote: The MCAS Certification Compliance Review ultimately concluded that the certification process with respect to MCAS was compliant with FAA regulations. However, the written report identified several documentation gaps and inconsistencies relating to MCAS and the certification process, including a lack of adequate supporting documentation for the assumption, used by Boeing engineers and test pilots throughout the design and testing process, that repeated unintended MCAS activations (as the crew of Lion Air Flight 610 experienced) would be no more hazardous than a single unintended MCAS activation – an assumption that was later called into doubt by the SRB.
context: Boeing's internal MCAS Certification Compliance Review, completed in December 2018, identified significant gaps in documentation supporting critical safety assumptions about MCAS behavior.

label: Rationale for MCAS omission from training not documented
original_label: Rationale for MCAS omission from training not documented
quote: The MCAS Certification Compliance Review report also noted that the supporting rationale for the decision to remove MCAS from the differences training and flight manuals was not properly documented and had been made contemporaneously with the MCAS Expansion. These findings raised questions as to whether the FAA-AEG had been made aware of, and had an opportunity to evaluate, the MCAS Expansion when it agreed to Boeing's proposal to remove MCAS from the differences training and manuals.
context: Boeing's internal compliance review discovered that the decision to exclude MCAS from pilot training was made at the same time MCAS was being expanded in scope, raising questions about FAA awareness.

label: SRB identifies MCAS as airplane safety issue
original_label: SRB identifies MCAS as airplane safety issue
quote: The SRB determined that the high crew workload required to counter repeated unintended MCAS activation triggered by erroneous AoA data, and the limited amount of time a crew might have to do so before the airplane became unrecoverable (as happened on the Lion Air Crash flight), posed an "airplane safety issue" that required remediation. The crew workload issue was compounded by the presence of other distracting visual, auditory, and tactile alerts and warnings associated with a damaged or malfunctioning AoA sensor on the 737 MAX.
context: Boeing's Safety Review Board meetings in November 2018 formally concluded that MCAS posed an active safety issue requiring corrective action, shortly after the Lion Air crash.

label: FAA-AEG tasked with training and manuals approval
original_label: FAA-AEG tasked with training and manuals approval
quote: In connection with the overall evaluation, approval and certification process for a derivative airplane, the FAA-AEG is responsible for determining the required level of differences training for U.S.-based airline pilots – and, relatedly, the extent to which new or updated functions must be described in the flight manuals – based on information provided, and recommendations made, by manufacturers such as Boeing. At the end of this process, the FAA-AEG publishes a Flight Standardization Board Report (the "FSB Report") which contains, among other things, the FAA-AEG's determination on the level and scope of differences training and the contents of the flight manuals.
context: The regulatory structure assigned FAA-AEG responsibility for reviewing Boeing's recommendations on pilot training and manuals for derivative aircraft, with formal publication of determinations.

label: Boeing employees presented MCAS as high-speed only scenario
original_label: Boeing employees presented MCAS as high-speed only scenario
quote: In advocating for CBT only, Boeing employees responsible for communicating with the FAA-AEG as to differences training and manuals certification – including Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2, senior members of the 737 MAX Flight Technical Group – presented MCAS to the FAA-AEG as a feature that could only activate in a very specific, high-speed scenario that was outside the normal flight envelope and therefore unlikely to ever be encountered by a commercial pilot. They made these representations to FAA-AEG personnel beginning in or around June 2015.
context: Boeing's designated representatives to the FAA's training and manuals review body characterized MCAS in restrictive terms that became the basis for excluding it from pilot training materials.

label: FAA-AEG provisional approval contingent on no system changes
original_label: FAA-AEG provisional approval contingent on no system changes
quote: Boeing employees responsible for communicating with the FAA-AEG understood, as evidenced by internal emails, that this provisional determination was contingent on there being "no significant systems changes to the airplane," and that the subsequent disclosure of additional differences to the FAA-AEG "would be a huge threat to that differences training determination."
context: Boeing communications staff recognized that the FAA-AEG's August 2016 provisional approval of computer-based training only was conditional, and understood that revealing MCAS changes would jeopardize that approval.

label: Boeing instructed FAA to delete MCAS from flight manuals
original_label: Boeing instructed FAA to delete MCAS from flight manuals
quote: Following this exchange, Boeing employees responsible for communicating with the FAA-AEG did not inform the FAA-AEG about the MCAS Expansion. And in a January 17, 2017 email to the FAA-AEG, Boeing Employee-1 reminded the FAA-AEG to delete any references to MCAS from the FSB Report, saying "Flight Controls: Delete MCAS, recall we decided we weren't going to cover it in the [manuals] or the CBT … since it's way outside the normal operating envelope."
context: After discovering in November 2016 that MCAS was operating outside its design parameters, Boeing Employee-1 sent a directive to the FAA requesting deletion of MCAS from certification documents, using language that concealed the scope expansion.

label: Muilenburg directed drafting and approved press release
original_label: Muilenburg directed drafting and approved press release
quote: Muilenburg directed the drafting of the Press Release and approved it before it was issued. In that Press Release, Boeing highlighted certain aspects of the preliminary accident report while downplaying others, and also offered the public its "assurance" that the 737 MAX "is as safe as any airplane that has ever flown the skies." However, by that point, Boeing had determined that MCAS posed an ongoing safety issue that required remediation; indeed, Boeing had already begun work on a redesign of the MCAS software to address the safety issue. However, the Press Release made no mention of the MCAS safety issue or planned software redesign. At the time he authorized the Press Release, Muilenburg was aware that Boeing was redesigning the MCAS software to remediate the safety issue.
context: CEO Dennis Muilenburg exercised direct control over Boeing's November 2018 public reassurance about 737 MAX safety while possessing knowledge of active safety remediation work.

label: Muilenburg briefed on MCAS safety issue and software redesign
original_label: Muilenburg briefed on MCAS safety issue and software redesign
quote: On or about November 15, 2018, senior executives at Boeing, including Muilenburg, were informed that the SRB had identified the crew workload issue associated with unintended MCAS activation due to erroneous AoA data as an "airplane safety issue" that required remediation, and that Boeing engineers were working on redesigning the MCAS software to address the issue.
context: Muilenburg received formal notification that Boeing's Safety Review Board had identified MCAS as an active safety problem requiring software redesign.

label: Muilenburg instructed deletion of MCAS redesign from draft
original_label: Muilenburg instructed deletion of MCAS redesign from draft
quote: Later that day, the Communications team sent Muilenburg and other executives an updated version of the Draft Press Release. After reviewing the draft, Muilenburg directed that the Draft Press Release be modified to incorporate a discussion of facts drawn from the Lion Air Preliminary Report, and also suggested removing discussion of the planned MCAS software redesign from the Draft Press Release.
context: Muilenburg edited the press release to include preliminary accident report facts while instructing removal of the MCAS software redesign that was underway.

label: In-house counsel informed Muilenburg of November 15 chat
original_label: In-house counsel informed Muilenburg of November 15 chat
quote: In or around January 2019, Boeing's in-house counsel informed Muilenburg and other senior executives about the existence of the November 15, 2016 Chat. Following that communication, Muilenburg understood the November 15, 2016 Chat to be "concerning." Muilenburg did not take any steps to learn additional details about the November 15, 2016 Chat.
context: When Boeing's Legal Department discovered the chat in which Employee-1 stated he had lied to regulators, in-house counsel reported it to Muilenburg, who characterized it as concerning but took no further action to investigate.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Stock price declining and negative media coverage
original_label: Stock price declining and negative media coverage
quote: During this time period, Boeing was the subject of extensive negative media coverage over allegations that Boeing had withheld information from pilots, airlines, regulators and the general public regarding MCAS. Other articles raised concerns about MCAS being too powerful and/or relying on a single sensor, and about the integrity of the certification process for the 737 MAX. Boeing's stock price was also dropping during this time. By November 20, 2018, Boeing's stock price had fallen by 11.6% since the Lion Air Crash.
context: As Boeing faced mounting criticism and financial pressure following the Lion Air crash, negative media coverage and stock decline dominated attention in the period before the November 2018 press release.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Muilenburg expressed need to play offense not defense
original_label: Muilenburg expressed need to play offense not defense
quote: On November 20, 2018, Muilenburg expressed disappointment in Boeing's response to the negative post-crash media coverage, stating in an email that "[w]e are spending too much time playing defense… [we] need to start playing some offense."
context: Muilenburg's communication reveals his focus on public relations messaging strategy in response to media criticism, one week before approving the November 2018 press release.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: MCAS Expansion not disclosed to FAA-AEG
original_label: MCAS Expansion not disclosed to FAA-AEG
quote: In or around March 2016, Boeing introduced the MCAS Expansion, significantly broadening MCAS's operational scope. No longer limited to a specific, rare high-speed scenario, MCAS could now activate at abnormally high AoA throughout the entire speed range of the 737 MAX, including during the initial climb and the final descent, and its command authority was significantly increased to allow it to function effectively at lower speeds. In or around August 2016, the FAA-AEG made a provisional determination to accept Boeing's proposal of CBT-only and to omit MCAS from the differences training and flight manuals. At that time, the FAA-AEG was not aware of the MCAS Expansion.
context: Boeing made a major expansion of MCAS's operational parameters in March 2016, but when the FAA-AEG decided in August 2016 to exclude MCAS from training and manuals, it was not informed of this expansion.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: MCAS Certification Compliance Review did not discover November 15 chat
original_label: MCAS Certification Compliance Review did not discover November 15 chat
quote: The MCAS Certification Compliance Review team was not aware of the November 15, 2016 Chat. Consequently, the November 15, 2016 Chat was not referenced in the MCAS Certification Compliance Review report and did not factor into its findings and conclusions.
context: Boeing's internal compliance review of MCAS certification, completed in December 2018, did not discover the November 2016 communication in which an engineer acknowledged lying to regulators, so this warning signal was excluded from the review's findings.

label: SRB convened meetings to assess MCAS safety
original_label: SRB convened meetings to assess MCAS safety
quote: In the weeks following the Lion Air Crash, Boeing convened a series of meetings of its Safety Review Board ("SRB") – an internal body comprised of Boeing personnel that evaluate in-service aircraft safety issues – on November 4, 2018, November 6, 2018, and November 15, 2018, to assess the ongoing safety of the 737 MAX in light of the Lion Air Crash.
context: Boeing's Safety Review Board held multiple meetings between November 4-15, 2018 to evaluate MCAS safety following the Lion Air crash.

label: Boeing issued bulletin and FAA issued emergency directive
original_label: Boeing issued bulletin and FAA issued emergency directive
quote: On November 6, 2018, Boeing issued a bulletin to operators of 737 MAX aircraft informing them that erroneous AoA data could cause uncommanded nose-down movements of the aircraft (without mentioning MCAS by name). The bulletin instructed pilots to follow the procedures in the flight manuals for a "runaway stabilizer" – a type of malfunction that could present as similar to repeated unintended MCAS activations on the 737 MAX – in the event of uncommanded nose-down movement. On November 7, 2018, the FAA issued a public emergency airworthiness directive to airlines operating the 737 MAX, informing them of the potential for repeated nose-down movements of the aircraft which, "if not addressed, could cause the flight crew to have difficulty controlling the airplane … and [could result in] possible impact with terrain."
context: Boeing and the FAA issued regulatory notices about the nose-down movement problem following the Lion Air crash, directing pilots to existing procedures without explicitly naming MCAS.

label: Boeing engineers concluded MCAS software must be redesigned
original_label: Boeing engineers concluded MCAS software must be redesigned
quote: On or about November 15, 2018, Boeing safety engineers concluded that, in light of the SRB's findings, the MCAS software should be redesigned and re-installed on the 737 MAX fleet to remediate the high crew workload "airplane safety issue." They determined that the software redesign had to be completed within approximately 27 months, but that the 737 MAX fleet could continue to operate in the interim in light of Boeing's bulletin and the FAA emergency airworthiness directive.
context: Boeing's safety engineering organization formally concluded that MCAS required a software redesign, with a 27-month timeline, while allowing continued operations under interim procedures.

label: Communications team began drafting press release
original_label: Communications team began drafting press release
quote: Also, on or about November 15, 2018, Boeing's Communications team began working with senior Boeing engineers and lawyers, among others, to draft a press release to update the public following the Lion Air Crash (the "Draft Press Release"), which would evolve to become the November 2018 Press Release.
context: Boeing's Communications department initiated drafting of a public statement on November 15, 2018, the same day engineers concluded MCAS required remediation.

label: Lion Air crash on October 29, 2018
original_label: Lion Air crash on October 29, 2018
quote: The Lion Air Crash occurred on October 29, 2018. Soon after the crash, investigators identified repeated unintended activations of MCAS triggered by erroneous AoA data as a cause of the accident.
context: The crash of Lion Air Flight 610 on October 29, 2018 became the event that triggered investigation into MCAS and identification of its unintended activations as the cause.

label: Ethiopian Airlines crash on March 10, 2019
original_label: Ethiopian Airlines crash on March 10, 2019
quote: The Ethiopian Airlines Crash occurred on March 10, 2019. Once again, accident investigators determined that the accident involved repeated unintended activations of MCAS triggered by erroneous data from an AoA sensor.
context: A second identical crash on March 10, 2019 again involved MCAS unintended activations, triggering major consequences including fleet grounding.

label: FAA grounded 737 MAX fleet
original_label: FAA grounded 737 MAX fleet
quote: On March 13, 2019, three days after the Ethiopian Airlines Crash, the FAA issued an order grounding the entire 737 MAX fleet due to ongoing safety concerns; similar grounding orders were issued by regulators around the world. Ultimately, more than 20 months would elapse before the 737 MAX was once again permitted to fly.
context: The second crash triggered a global fleet grounding on March 13, 2019, the most severe regulatory action.

label: DOJ investigation began into 737 MAX certification
original_label: DOJ investigation began into 737 MAX certification
quote: In the wake of the Lion Air Crash, the DOJ began an investigation into the 737 MAX certification process. In January 2019, while collecting documents in connection with the DOJ's investigation, members of Boeing's Legal Department uncovered a series of communications that raised questions about the disclosures made to the FAA-AEG concerning the differences training and manuals certification, including the November 15, 2016 Chat in which Boeing Employee-1 wrote that he had "lied to regulators (unknowingly)" about MCAS.
context: A Department of Justice criminal investigation into 737 MAX certification prompted Boeing's Legal Department to discover the November 15, 2016 chat in January 2019.

label: House Committee obtained emails and scheduled Muilenburg testimony
original_label: House Committee obtained emails and scheduled Muilenburg testimony
quote: On October 18, 2019, it was widely reported that the U.S. House of Representatives Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which was conducting hearings relating to the 737 MAX, had obtained a series of documents concerning Boeing Employee-1's communications with the FAA-AEG, including the November 15, 2016 Chat, and would be questioning Muilenburg about those documents and related issues during his scheduled congressional testimony later that month. On October 18, 2019, Boeing's stock price dropped by 6.8%, compared to a 0.4% decline for the S&P 500.
context: Public disclosure that Congress would question Muilenburg about the November 2016 email exchange immediately triggered a 6.8% stock price decline.

label: Accidents revealed MCAS not in flight manuals or training
original_label: Accidents revealed MCAS not in flight manuals or training
quote: Accident investigations revealed that both crashes involved the erroneous activation of the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System ("MCAS"), a new Boeing flight control law (not described in the 737 MAX flight manuals or pilot training materials) that was designed to help avert stalls by pushing the nose of the airplane downward without input from the crew whenever a sensor on the outside of the fuselage indicated the aircraft was approaching an angle at which a stall may occur.
context: The Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crash investigations discovered that MCAS, the system that caused both crashes, had been excluded from pilot training and flight manuals.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Boeing contractually guaranteed CBT-only training
original_label: Boeing contractually guaranteed CBT-only training
quote: Here, Boeing took the view that pilots transitioning from the 737 NG to the 737 MAX should be required to undergo only a short computer-based training ("CBT") course, as opposed to more extensive, simulator-based training. Indeed, even before certification, Boeing advertised, and, in some cases, contractually guaranteed, to its airline customers that only CBT would be required for 737 NG pilots to operate the 737 MAX. For instance, one purchase agreement with a major airline required Boeing to refund up to $1 million per plane in the event the FAA required more than CBT for 737 MAX pilots.
context: Boeing created strong contractual and financial incentives favoring minimal pilot training by guaranteeing CBT-only and risking $1 million refunds per plane if more extensive training was required.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Similarity to predecessor plane reduced training requirements
original_label: Similarity to predecessor plane reduced training requirements
quote: When a derivative of an existing aircraft model enters service, pilots certified to fly the previous model can become certified to fly the new model by undergoing "differences training," a training course focused on those aspects of the new model (here, the 737 MAX) that are meaningfully different from the previous model (here, the 737 NG). As a general matter, the greater the similarity between the two models, the less differences training is required, reducing training costs incurred by operators of the aircraft.
context: Regulatory structure created an incentive to minimize differences between aircraft models to reduce training costs, directing Boeing's efforts toward making 737 MAX appear similar to its predecessor.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: November 2018 press release omitted MCAS safety issue
original_label: November 2018 press release omitted MCAS safety issue
quote: The November 2018 Press Release highlighted certain facts from the Lion Air Preliminary Report suggesting that pilot error and poor airplane maintenance by Lion Air had contributed to the crash. The November 2018 Press Release did not mention that the SRB had identified an ongoing "airplane safety issue" associated with MCAS or the planned software redesign – indeed, it did not mention MCAS at all. The final November 2018 Press Release also contained the statement: "As our customers and their passengers continue to fly the 737 MAX to hundreds of destinations around the world every day, they have our assurance that the 737 MAX is as safe as any airplane that has ever flown the skies."
context: Boeing's public statement selectively highlighted accident report findings suggesting pilot error while completely omitting the Safety Review Board's identification of MCAS as an active safety problem requiring remediation.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: April 2019 statements claimed no gaps in certification
original_label: April 2019 statements claimed no gaps in certification
quote: While speaking to investors and analysts during Boeing's first quarter 2019 earnings call on April 24, 2019, and in comments to reporters following Boeing's annual shareholders' meeting on April 29, 2019, Muilenburg stated on behalf of Boeing that "there was no surprise or gap or unknown … that somehow slipped through [the] certification process" for the 737 MAX, and that Boeing had "gone back and confirmed … that we followed exactly the steps in our design and certification processes that consistently produce safe airplanes."
context: In April 2019, after discovering documentation gaps and the November 2016 chat, Muilenburg made public statements asserting no gaps existed in the certification process.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Documentation questions about FAA-AEG disclosure not disclosed
original_label: Documentation questions about FAA-AEG disclosure not disclosed
quote: Prior to the April 2019 Statements, Boeing had, in responding to a subpoena issued by the U.S. Department of Justice ("DOJ") in a criminal investigation into the 737 MAX certification process, uncovered documents that suggested that key facts about MCAS's operational scope had not been disclosed to the FAA's Aircraft Evaluation Group ("FAA-AEG"), the section of the FAA responsible for the review and approval of pilot training requirements and flight manuals for the 737 MAX. In addition, an internal compliance review had separately identified certain documentation gaps and inconsistencies relating to MCAS and the certification process. Muilenburg had been briefed on the existence of those documents, as well as on the core findings of the internal compliance review. However, those facts were not disclosed or otherwise known to the public when Muilenburg made his April 2019 statements.
context: Boeing and Muilenburg possessed knowledge of documents suggesting MCAS information had not been disclosed to the FAA, plus internal compliance findings about certification gaps, but withheld this information from public statements and investors.

label: NTSB official complained about selective press release
original_label: NTSB official complained about selective press release
quote: Prior to the issuance of the November 2018 Press Release, Boeing provided drafts to the FAA and NTSB for informational purposes, and those drafts contained the "as safe as any airplane that has ever flown the skies" language. After the November 2018 Press Release was published, a senior official at the NTSB complained to Boeing, via email, that the November 2018 Press Release was not appropriate given Boeing's involvement in the crash investigation, and that "the omission of certain facts and the highlighting of other facts [in the November 2018 Press Release] leads the reader to Boeing's analytical conclusion."
context: An NTSB official raised concerns that Boeing's press release selectively presented accident facts to support Boeing's preferred conclusions rather than presenting a balanced account.

label: Boeing communications team coordinated with engineers and lawyers
original_label: Boeing communications team coordinated with engineers and lawyers
quote: Also, on or about November 15, 2018, Boeing's Communications team began working with senior Boeing engineers and lawyers, among others, to draft a press release to update the public following the Lion Air Crash (the "Draft Press Release"), which would evolve to become the November 2018 Press Release.
context: Boeing established a coordinated process involving communications, engineering, and legal functions to draft the post-crash press release, with all three functions aware of the message being developed.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Early drafts mentioned MCAS software update
original_label: Early drafts mentioned MCAS software update
quote: Early versions of the Draft Press Release generally confirmed the plane's safety, stating that the 737 MAX was either a "safe airplane" or that it "continue[d] to be safe to fly." Certain versions also noted that Boeing was working with the FAA to "expedite the development and certification of a flight control software update" for MCAS.
context: Initial draft versions of the press release included acknowledgment of the MCAS software update project before Muilenburg directed its removal.

label: Boeing convened MCAS Certification Compliance Review
original_label: Boeing convened MCAS Certification Compliance Review
quote: On or about November 21, 2018, Boeing senior management assembled a team to review the 737 MAX certification process with a particular focus on MCAS (the "MCAS Certification Compliance Review"), led by a senior Boeing engineer who was familiar with the 737 MAX design, but who had not been directly involved in the certification process. The MCAS Certification Compliance Review team was specifically directed to include in its review aspects of the certification process relating to differences training and flight manuals.
context: Boeing senior management initiated an internal review of MCAS certification in November 2018, specifically directing investigation of how training and manuals were handled.

label: Stock price recovered after November 2018 press release
original_label: Stock price recovered after November 2018 press release
quote: On November 28, 2018, the first trading day following the public release of the Lion Air Preliminary Report and Boeing's after-hours publication of the November 2018 Press Release, Boeing's stock closed at $333.5, up 4.8% from the prior day's close (compared to a 2% gain for the S&P 500).
context: The market responded positively to Boeing's November 2018 reassurance statement, with Boeing stock gaining 4.8% compared to 2% for the S&P 500, reversing earlier declines.

label: Negative media coverage intensified after Ethiopian crash
original_label: Negative media coverage intensified after Ethiopian crash
quote: The extensive negative media coverage of Boeing that followed the Lion Air Crash intensified after the Ethiopian Airlines Crash and the subsequent grounding, as did the downward pressure on Boeing's stock price.
context: The March 10, 2019 Ethiopian Airlines crash and March 13 grounding amplified negative media coverage and stock price pressure beyond what followed the initial Lion Air crash.

label: Boeing Employee-1 and Employee-2 communicated with FAA-AEG
original_label: Boeing Employee-1 and Employee-2 communicated with FAA-AEG
quote: In advocating for CBT only, Boeing employees responsible for communicating with the FAA-AEG as to differences training and manuals certification – including Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2, senior members of the 737 MAX Flight Technical Group – presented MCAS to the FAA-AEG as a feature that could only activate in a very specific, high-speed scenario that was outside the normal flight envelope and therefore unlikely to ever be encountered by a commercial pilot. They made these representations to FAA-AEG personnel beginning in or around June 2015.
context: Two senior Boeing engineers held designated positions as the company's communicators to the FAA group responsible for training and manuals decisions, starting in June 2015.

label: Employee warns Skilling of conflict pressure
original_label: Employee warns Skilling of conflict pressure
quote: Skilling met in March 2000 with Jeffrey McMahon, Enron's Treasurer (who reported to Fastow). McMahon told us that he approached Skilling with serious concerns about Enron's dealings with the LJM partnerships. McMahon and Skilling disagree on some important elements of what was said. However, if McMahon's account (which is reflected in what he describes as contemporaneous talking points for the discussion) is correct, it appears that Skilling did not take action (nor did McMahon approach Lay or the Board) after being put on notice that Fastow was pressuring Enron employees who were negotiating with LJM--clear evidence that the controls were not effective.
context: The Powers Report recounts McMahon's warning to Skilling about Fastow's pressure on negotiators, a signal that controls designed by the Board were failing.

label: ENA attorney documents asset selection for Raptor
original_label: ENA attorney documents asset selection for Raptor
quote: There is some evidence of a concern within Enron North America ("ENA"), which held almost all of the assets that were subject to Raptor derivative transactions, that ENA selected only assets that were expected to decline substantially in value. On September 1, 2000, an ENA attorney, Stuart Zisman, wrote (emphasis added): "Our original understanding of this transaction was that all types of assets/securities would be introduced into this structure (including both those that are viewed favorably and those that are viewed as being poor investments). As it turns out, we have discovered that a majority of the investments being introduced into the Raptor Structure are bad ones. This is disconcerting [because] ... it might lead one to believe that the financial books at Enron are being "cooked" in order to eliminate a drag on earnings that would otherwise occur under fair value accounting . . . ."
context: Zisman raised concerns in a memorandum to ENA leadership that Raptors were being used to hide bad investments, suggesting potential manipulation of financial results.

label: Andersen raises concerns at internal meeting
original_label: Andersen raises concerns at internal meeting
quote: Recent public disclosures show that Andersen held an internal meeting on February 5, 2001, to address serious concerns about Enron's accounting for and oversight of the LJM relationship. The people attending that meeting reportedly decided to suggest that Enron establish a special committee of the Board of Directors to review the fairness of LJM transactions or to provide for other procedures or controls, such as competitive bidding.
context: The report documents that Andersen's internal team identified material concerns about LJM governance one week before their audit committee presentation, indicating the firm recognized risks internally.

label: Watkins sends letter identifying Raptor problems
original_label: Watkins sends letter identifying Raptor problems
quote: Shortly after Enron announced Skilling's unexpected resignation on August 14, 2001, Watkins sent a one-page anonymous letter to Lay. The letter stated that "Enron has been very aggressive in its accounting--most notably the Raptor transactions." The letter raised serious questions concerning the accounting treatment and economic substance of the Raptor transactions (and transactions between Enron and Condor Trust, a subsidiary of Whitewing Associates), identifying several of the matters discussed in this Report. It concluded that "I am incredibly nervous that we will implode in a wave of accounting scandals."
context: Watkins, a former Andersen employee, provided written warning to the CEO in August 2001 documenting concerns about Raptor accounting and economic substance, serving as a formal whistleblower signal.

label: Kaminski calculates default probability on Rhythms structure
original_label: Kaminski calculates default probability on Rhythms structure
quote: In late February or early March of 2000, the accounting group asked him to analyze the credit capacity of the Rhythms structure. Kaminski and his analysts reviewed the structure and determined there was a 68% probability that the structure would default and would not be able to meet its obligations to Enron on the Rhythms put. Kaminski says that, when he relayed this conclusion to the accounting group, they said they had suspected that would be the result.
context: Kaminski's quantitative analysis detected a high-probability failure of the Rhythms hedge structure, which accounting personnel acknowledged they suspected but did not escalate or reserve for.

label: Board approves LJM2 with stated controls
original_label: Board approves LJM2 with stated controls
quote: Over time, the Board required, and Management told the Board it was implementing, an ever-increasing set of procedures and controls over the related-party transactions. These included, most importantly, review and approval of all LJM transactions by Richard Causey, the Chief Accounting Officer; and Richard Buy, the Chief Risk Officer; and, later during the period, Jeffrey Skilling, the President and COO (and later CEO). The Board also directed its Audit and Compliance Committee to conduct annual reviews of all LJM transactions.
context: The Powers Report describes the formal control structure that the Board established, including named officers responsible for review and an annual audit committee oversight procedure.

label: Audit Committee annual LJM reviews
original_label: Audit Committee annual LJM reviews
quote: The Audit and Compliance Committee, and later the Finance Committee, took on a specific role in the control structure by carrying out periodic reviews of the LJM transactions. This was an opportunity to probe the transactions thoroughly, and to seek outside advice as to any issues outside the Board members' expertise. Instead, these reviews appear to have been too brief, too limited in scope, and too superficial to serve their intended function.
context: The report documents the formal procedure of annual committee reviews and their inadequate implementation despite Board expectations of rigorous scrutiny.

label: V&E investigation scope excludes accounting review
original_label: V&E investigation scope excludes accounting review
quote: Derrick and V&E agreed that V&E's review would not include questioning the accounting treatment and advice from Andersen, or a detailed review of individual LJM transactions. Instead, V&E would conduct a "preliminary investigation," which was defined as determining whether the facts raised by Watkins warranted further independent legal or accounting review.
context: The General Counsel and outside counsel explicitly agreed to limit their investigation of whistleblower allegations by excluding accounting and detailed transaction review, creating a procedural barrier to discovering problems.

label: Disclosure process controlled by Global Finance
original_label: Disclosure process controlled by Global Finance
quote: It appears that no one outside of Enron Global Finance, the entity principally responsible for the related-party transactions, exercised significant supervision or control over the disclosure process concerning these transactions. The Financial Reporting Group collected comments from the various reviewers, made changes, and distributed revised versions. This process was repeated until all outstanding issues had been resolved. We were told that Causey, Enron's Chief Accounting Officer, was the final arbiter of unresolved differences among the various contributors to the financial reporting process.
context: The report identifies a structural problem in the disclosure process: the unit responsible for the transactions (Global Finance) dominated the process for disclosing them, and other reviewers deferred.

label: Fastow controls both sides of LJM transactions
original_label: Fastow controls both sides of LJM transactions
quote: Fastow was Enron's Chief Financial Officer and was involved on both sides of the related-party transactions. What he presented as an arrangement intended to benefit Enron became, over time, a means of both enriching himself personally and facilitating manipulation of Enron's financial statements. Both of these objectives were inconsistent with Fastow's fiduciary duties to Enron and anything the Board authorized.
context: The Committee concludes that Fastow's dual role as CFO and LJM manager created an inherent conflict of interest that undermined all controls designed by the Board.

label: Kopper occupies position between Fastow and transactions
original_label: Kopper occupies position between Fastow and transactions
quote: Michael Kopper, who worked for Fastow in the Finance area, enriched himself substantially at Enron's expense by virtue of his roles in Chewco, Southampton Place, and possibly LJM2. In a transaction he negotiated with Fastow, Kopper, and his co-investor in Chewco received more than $10 million from Enron for a $125,000 investment.
context: The Committee describes Kopper's structural role as Fastow's subordinate with financial interests in partnerships that also transacted with Enron, exemplifying the problem of multiple simultaneous roles.

label: Glisan involved in multiple Raptor transactions while invested in Southampton
original_label: Glisan involved in multiple Raptor transactions while invested in Southampton
quote: In 2000, Glisan was involved on behalf of Enron in several significant transactions with LJM2. Most notably, he was a major participant in the Raptor transactions. He presented the Raptor I transaction to the Board, and was intimately involved in designing its structure. Enron approval documents show Glisan as the "business unit originator" and "person negotiating for Enron" in the Raptor I, II, and IV transactions. Glisan told us that Fastow never asked him for any favors or other consideration in return for the Southampton investment.
context: The report documents that Glisan held a conflicted position: negotiating the Raptors for Enron while simultaneously an undisclosed investor in Southampton Place, receiving $1 million from a $5,800 investment.

label: Employees negotiating with LJM report to Fastow
original_label: Employees negotiating with LJM report to Fastow
quote: In many cases, the safeguard requiring that a transaction could be negotiated on behalf of Enron only by employees who did not report to Fastow was ignored. We have identified at least 13 transactions between Enron and LJM2 in which the individuals negotiating on behalf of Enron reported directly or indirectly to Fastow.
context: The report identifies a structural flaw: the control procedure designed to separate negotiators from Fastow was frequently bypassed, with 13+ transactions involving Fastow's direct reports as Enron's negotiators.

label: Skilling claims minimal involvement despite assigned oversight role
original_label: Skilling claims minimal involvement despite assigned oversight role
quote: With respect to the LJM partnerships, Skilling personally supported the Board's decision to permit Fastow to proceed with LJM, notwithstanding Fastow's conflict of interest. Skilling had direct responsibility for ensuring that those reporting to him performed their oversight duties properly. He likewise had substantial responsibility to make sure that the internal controls that the Board put in place--particularly those involving related-party transactions with the Company's CFO--functioned properly. He has described the detail of his expressly-assigned oversight role as minimal. That answer, however, misses the point.
context: The Committee documents a major disconnect: Skilling held direct responsibility for LJM oversight as COO and later CEO, but claims to have had minimal involvement, undermining the control structure the Board believed was in place.

label: Lay absent from LJM operational oversight
original_label: Lay absent from LJM operational oversight
quote: It does not appear that Lay had, or was intended to have, any managerial role in connection with LJM once the entities became operational. His involvement was principally on the same basis as other Directors. By the accounts of both Lay and Skilling, the division of labor between them was that Skilling, as President and COO (later CEO) had full responsibility for domestic operational activities such as these. Skilling said he would keep Lay apprised of major issues, but does not recall discussing LJM matters with him.
context: The report identifies a structural gap: while the CEO retained ultimate responsibility, he delegated LJM matters to Skilling, who in turn claimed minimal involvement, leaving no clear locus of executive accountability.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Business units incentivized to sell assets to LJM
original_label: Business units incentivized to sell assets to LJM
quote: The Board apparently believed that the conflict, and the substantial risks associated with it, could be mitigated through certain controls (involving oversight by both the Board and Senior Management) to ensure that transactions were done on terms fair to Enron. The principal reason advanced by Management in favor of the relationship, in the case of LJM2, was that it would permit Enron to accomplish a particular transaction it could not otherwise accomplish. In the case of LJM2, Management advocated that it would provide Enron with an additional potential buyer of assets that Enron wanted to sell, and that Fastow's familiarity with the Company and the assets to be sold would permit Enron to move more quickly and incur fewer transaction costs.
context: The Committee describes the Board's understanding that LJM would benefit Enron by providing a ready buyer, creating an implicit incentive for business units to use LJM, especially under time pressure.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Enron's financial metrics depend on earnings from LJM
original_label: Enron's financial metrics depend on earnings from LJM
quote: Enron's reported earnings for that period were $570 million (pre-tax) and $549 million (after-tax). The Raptors made an extremely significant contribution to Enron's reported financial results over the last five quarters before Enron sought bankruptcy protection--i.e., from the third quarter of 2000 through the third quarter of 2001. Transactions with the Raptors during that period allowed Enron to avoid reflecting on its income statement almost $1 billion in losses on its merchant investments. Not including the $710 million pre-tax charge Enron recorded in the third quarter of 2001 related to the termination of the Raptors, Enron's reported pre-tax earnings during that five-quarter period were $1.5 billion.
context: The report shows that LJM and Raptor earnings constituted 72% of reported earnings ($1.1B of $1.5B) over five quarters, making these transactions critical to reported results and thus focal to management attention and incentives.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Code of Conduct prohibits related-party investments without approval
original_label: Code of Conduct prohibits related-party investments without approval
quote: Enron's Code of Conduct required Kopper to obtain approval for his participation in Chewco from the Chairman and CEO. Lay, who held both positions at this time, said he does not know Kopper and is confident that he was neither informed of Kopper's participation nor asked to approve it under the Code. We have seen no evidence that Kopper obtained the permission required by Enron's Code of Conduct to own interests in the partnerships.
context: The report documents a rule (Code of Conduct requirement for CEO approval) that was never applied to multiple employees investing in LJM partnerships, creating a procedural control that was not enforced.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: LJM Approval Sheet process designed but not rigorously followed
original_label: LJM Approval Sheet process designed but not rigorously followed
quote: Still other controls were not properly implemented. The LJM Deal Approval Sheet process was not well-designed, and it was not consistently followed. We have been unable to locate Approval Sheets for some transactions. Other Approval Sheets do not have all the required signatures. The Approval Sheet form contained pre-printed check marks in boxes signifying compliance with a number of controls and disclosure concerns, with the intention that a signature would be added to certify the accuracy of the pre-printed check-marks. Some transactions closed before the Approval Sheets were completed. The Approval Sheets did not require any documentation of efforts to find third party, unrelated buyers for Enron assets other than LJM1 or LJM2, and it does not appear that such efforts were systematically pursued.
context: The report describes a formal control procedure designed by management but not rigorously implemented, with missing documentation, pre-closed transactions, and routinized checkboxes that did not ensure substantive review.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Board agenda dominated by earnings and market confidence
original_label: Board agenda dominated by earnings and market confidence
quote: Much of this growth involved large initial capital investments that were not expected to generate significant earnings or cash flow in the short term. While Enron believed these investments would be beneficial over a period of time, they placed immediate pressure on Enron's balance sheet. Enron already had a substantial debt load. Funding the new investments by issuing additional debt was unattractive because cash flow in the early years would be insufficient to service that debt and would place pressure on Enron's credit ratings. Maintaining Enron's credit ratings at investment grade was vital to the conduct of its energy trading business.
context: The Committee identifies the foundational business problem that drove LJM creation: maintaining investment-grade credit ratings and reporting attractive near-term earnings were critical to Enron's business model and thus dominated management attention.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Board focused on transaction approval rather than ongoing oversight
original_label: Board focused on transaction approval rather than ongoing oversight
quote: The Board believed it was addressing a specific, already-negotiated transaction, rather than a series of future transactions. This was the Rhythms "hedge." It was presented as a transaction that would benefit Enron by reducing income statement volatility resulting from a large investment that could not be sold. The Board understood that (1) the terms were already fixed, (2) Enron would receive an opinion by PricewaterhouseCoopers as to the fairness of the consideration received by Enron, and (3) Fastow would not benefit from changes in the value of Enron stock that Enron contributed to the transaction. The Board saw little need to address controls over already-completed negotiations.
context: The Committee documents that when approving LJM1, the Board focused on specific transaction terms already negotiated rather than systemic controls, reducing attention to the broader structure and risks of an ongoing relationship.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Committee reviews limited in scope and time
original_label: Committee reviews limited in scope and time
quote: In fact, the reviews were brief, reportedly lasting ten to fifteen minutes. More to the point, the specific economic terms, and the benefits to LJM1 or LJM2 (or to Fastow), were not discussed. There does not appear to have been much, if any, probing with respect to the underlying basis for Causey's representation that the transactions were at arm's-length and that "the process was working effectively."
context: The report documents that the annual Audit Committee reviews of LJM transactions, which were designed as a key control, lasted only 10-15 minutes with no substantive questioning of the terms or process.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Board minutes record lack of scrutiny of Raptor risks
original_label: Board minutes record lack of scrutiny of Raptor risks
quote: The Finance Committee was also given information strongly suggesting, if not making perfectly clear, that the Raptor vehicle was not a true economic hedge. Notes on the presentation materials, apparently taken at the meeting by Enron's Corporate Secretary to assist her in preparing the minutes, state: "Does not transfer economic risk but transfers P&L volatility." According to the minutes, Causey informed the Finance Committee that Andersen "had spent considerable time analyzing the Talon structure and the governance structure of LJM2 and was comfortable with the proposed transaction."
context: The Board minutes record both that Raptors do not transfer economic risk (a red flag) and that Andersen was comfortable with the transaction, but there is no evidence of Board questioning this apparent contradiction.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Zisman raises concerns but recipients do not escalate
original_label: Zisman raises concerns but recipients do not escalate
quote: Zisman met with the senior ENA attorneys. He told them that, contrary to what the memorandum implied, he did not know whether only "bad" assets had in fact been selected for Raptor, but that he was concerned Raptor could be misused in that way. The senior ENA attorneys and the senior ENA business people who received Zisman's memorandum--for varying reasons and with varying levels of direct knowledge--believed the assertion in Zisman's memo to be untrue, so they did not take any further action.
context: Senior ENA personnel received a warning about potential misuse of Raptors to hide bad assets; they disagreed with the concern and took no further action, filtering out the signal.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: McMahon raises conflict concern; Skilling takes no action
original_label: McMahon raises conflict concern; Skilling takes no action
quote: Skilling took no action of which we are aware, and shortly thereafter McMahon accepted a transfer within Enron that removed him from contact with LJM. Neither Skilling nor McMahon raised the issue with Lay or the Board.
context: After McMahon warned Skilling of conflict pressure in March 2000, neither executive acted on or escalated the concern; McMahon was transferred away from the issue, effectively removing the whistleblower from the problem.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Andersen partners do not raise February concerns to Audit Committee
original_label: Andersen partners do not raise February concerns to Audit Committee
quote: There is no evidence of any discussion by either Andersen representative about the problems or concerns they apparently had discussed internally just one week earlier. None of the Committee members we interviewed recalls that such concerns were raised, and the minutes make no mention of any discussion of the subject. Rather, according to the minutes and to written presentation materials, Duncan reported that "no material weaknesses had been identified" in Andersen's audit and that Andersen's "[o]pinion regarding internal control ... [w]ill be unqualified."
context: Andersen partners who had raised serious concerns in an internal meeting on February 5, 2001, reported no concerns to the Audit Committee one week later, instead affirming unqualified audit opinions.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: V&E investigation predetermined by narrow scope
original_label: V&E investigation predetermined by narrow scope
quote: We identified the most serious problems in the Raptor transactions only after a detailed examination of the relevant transactions and, most importantly, discussions with our accounting advisors--both steps that Enron determined (and V&E accepted) would not be part of V&E's investigation. With the exception of Watkins, V&E spoke only with very senior people at Enron and Andersen. Those people, with few exceptions, had substantial professional and personal stakes in the matters under review. The scope and process of the investigation appear to have been structured with less skepticism than was needed to see through these particularly complex transactions.
context: The external investigation of whistleblower Watkins's allegations was structured with built-in constraints (no accounting review, only senior interviews) that made it unlikely to find problems, effectively filtering out her concerns.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Causey presents incomplete transaction lists to Audit Committee
original_label: Causey presents incomplete transaction lists to Audit Committee
quote: First, in each of the two years in which the February annual review occurred, Causey presented to the Committees a list of transactions with LJM1 and LJM2 in the preceding year. The lists were incomplete (though Causey says he did not know this, and in any event a more complete presentation may not have affected the Committee's review): the 1999 list identified eight transactions, when in fact there were ten, and the 2000 list of transactions omitted the "buyback" transactions described earlier. Knowledge of these "buyback" transactions would have raised substantial questions about the nature and purpose of the earlier sales.
context: The Chief Accounting Officer's annual presentation to the Audit Committee omitted transactions (buybacks) that would have triggered substantive questions about the nature of LJM sales, filtering information from the Committee.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Fastow withholds LJM compensation details from Board
original_label: Fastow withholds LJM compensation details from Board
quote: We have seen only very limited information concerning Fastow's compensation from the LJM partnerships. The Board's review apparently never occurred until October 2001, after newspaper reports focused attention on Fastow's involvement in LJM1 and LJM2. The only references we have found to procedures for checking whether Fastow's compensation was modest, as the Board had expected, are in the minutes of the October 6, 2000 meeting of the Finance Committee. There, Fastow told the Committee (in Skilling's presence) that Skilling received "a review of [Fastow's] economic interest in [Enron] and the LJM funds," and the Committee then unanimously agreed that the Compensation Committee should review Fastow's compensation from LJM1 and LJM2.
context: The Board delegated review of Fastow's compensation to the Compensation Committee; no review was conducted; the Board did not learn the actual amounts ($30+ million) until October 2001 after media exposure.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Causey views role narrowly, not reviewing all transactions
original_label: Causey views role narrowly, not reviewing all transactions
quote: Causey was also charged by the Board of Directors with a substantial role in the oversight of Enron's relationship with the LJM partnerships. He was to review and approve all transactions between Enron and the LJM partnerships, and he was to review those transactions with the Audit and Compliance Committee annually. The evidence we have examined suggests that he did not implement a procedure for identifying all LJM1 or LJM2 transactions and did not give those transactions the level of scrutiny the Board had reason to believe he would.
context: The Chief Accounting Officer, a key control person, did not implement a comprehensive procedure for identifying all LJM transactions, undermining the Board's belief that he was reviewing all such transactions.

label: Chewco consolidation deferred for four years
original_label: Chewco consolidation deferred for four years
quote: Enron assisted Kopper (whom Fastow identified for the role) in forming Chewco to purchase CalPERS' interest. Kopper was the manager and owner of Chewco's general partner. Under the SPE rules summarized above, Enron could only avoid consolidating JEDI onto Enron's financial statements if Chewco had some independent ownership with a minimum of 3% of equity capital at risk. Enron and Kopper, however, were unable to locate any such outside investor, and instead financed Chewco's purchase of the JEDI interest almost entirely with debt, not equity. This was done hurriedly and in apparent disregard of the accounting requirements for non-consolidation. Notwithstanding the shortfall in required equity capital, Enron did not consolidate Chewco (or JEDI) into its consolidated financial statements.
context: Enron knew Chewco lacked required outside equity at formation in 1997; despite failing to meet non-consolidation criteria, Enron kept it off its balance sheet for four years without corrective action.

label: Raptor restructuring defers $500 million loss to Q1 2001
original_label: Raptor restructuring defers $500 million loss to Q1 2001
quote: Rather than take that loss, Enron "restructured" the Raptor vehicles by, among other things, transferring more than $800 million of contracts to receive its own stock to them just before quarter-end. This transaction apparently was not disclosed to or authorized by the Board, involved a transfer of very substantial value for insufficient consideration, and appears inconsistent with governing accounting rules. It continued the concealment of the substantial losses in Enron's merchant investments.
context: In late March 2001, facing a $500 million impairment charge on Raptors I and III, Enron management restructured the vehicles without Board authorization to defer recognition of the loss, transferring $800 million in stock contracts.

label: Cross-guarantee among Raptors avoids year-end 2000 reserve
original_label: Cross-guarantee among Raptors avoids year-end 2000 reserve
quote: In an effort to avoid having to record a loss for Raptors I and III on its 2000 financial statements, Enron's accountants, working with Andersen, decided to use the "excess" credit capacity in Raptors II and IV to shore up the credit capacity in Raptors I and III. A 45-day cross-guarantee agreement, dated December 22, 2000, essentially merged the credit capacity of all four Raptors. The effect was that Enron would not, for year end, record a credit reserve loss unless there was negative credit capacity on a combined basis. Enron paid LJM2 $50,000 to enter into this agreement, even though the cross-guarantee had no effect on LJM2's economic interests. We have seen no evidence that Enron's Board was informed of either the credit capacity problem or the solution selected to resolve that problem.

label: Flight test identified stall characteristics problem
original_label: Flight test identified stall characteristics problem

label: Design assumptions not validated during development
original_label: Design assumptions not validated during development

label: MCAS information fragmented across documents
original_label: MCAS information fragmented across documents

As a result, the MCAS description, including architecture, interfaces, logics, etc., is fragmented among several documents.

label: FAA lacks procedural visibility of design details
original_label: FAA lacks procedural visibility of design details

label: FAA awareness incomplete and fragmented
original_label: FAA awareness incomplete and fragmented
quote: FAA's visibility into important system safety information was therefore incomplete and fragmented.
context: JATR finding (F4.3-A) about the consequence of late FHA/PSSA submission.

label: Procedural layers hinder direct engineer-FAA contact
original_label: Procedural layers hinder direct engineer-FAA contact
quote: There are a number of Boeing internal procedural layers that hinder the E-UMs from directly communicating with the BASOO/FAA engineers. If an E-UM has questions or has difficulties with a subject, the E-UM is required to first try to solve the issue within the ODA instead of directly involving the BASOO experts. Although Boeing's internal guidelines documented in D685963, Guidelines for Communicating Certification Related Issues, allow E-UMs to directly contact the FAA, this contact is for technical-only communication and only to better understand a documented FAA method of compliance. Even though the communication is allowed between the E-UM and FAA, the E-UM would have to submit a summary of the conversation to the ODA. These procedural layers may prevent "free" communication of issues/concerns to the FAA.
context: JATR finding (F5.5-A) about the ODA communication structure that blocked escalation of concerns.

label: AOA system excluded from certification review
original_label: AOA system excluded from certification review
quote: The AOA sensing system of the B737 MAX was not changed from the B737 NG and was not affected by any of the changes, including the MCAS. Based on preliminary accident information, both B737-8 MAX accidents appear to have involved an interaction between the AOA system and MCAS.
context: JATR observations (O1.2-A and O1.2-B) showing how the certification process structure missed a critical interaction.

label: FAA staffing imbalance versus Boeing resources
original_label: FAA staffing imbalance versus Boeing resources
quote: The Boeing ODA organization is staffed by approximately 1,500 people, whereas the FAA's BASOO is staffed by 45 people.
context: JATR observation (O5.2-B) documenting the resource disparity that constrained FAA oversight capacity.

label: FAA engineers lack depth and experience
original_label: FAA engineers lack depth and experience
quote: Out of 45 BASOO personnel, there are 18 working-level engineers and 6 senior engineers (24 engineers total). The JATR team was unable to conclusively determine the levels of experience of the working-level engineers and understands at least some of them may be entry-level engineers. Depending on the number of entry-level engineers in the BASOO, there could be an imbalance of working-level engineers in relation to the number of senior engineers reasonably expected to be required given the complexity of work by Boeing.
context: JATR finding (F5.2-A) about the capability gap within the FAA oversight office.

label: Insufficient BASOO capacity for retained items
original_label: Insufficient BASOO capacity for retained items
quote: The allocated staffing levels of 24 BASOO engineers may not be sufficient to carry out the work associated with retained items and with the conduct of oversight duties. BASOO engineers are required to review and find compliance for retained items as well as conduct on-site and desk audits of the Boeing ODA. The BASOO may not be sufficiently staffed to review all the Boeing programs (737, 747, 767, 777, and 787). There are two technical staff assigned per Boeing program. Some of the technical staff are new engineers with limited airworthiness experience.
context: JATR finding (F5.2-B) about the structural constraint on FAA capacity to retain safety-critical oversight.

label: BASOO personnel lack technical insight from limited involvement
original_label: BASOO personnel lack technical insight from limited involvement
quote: BASOO engineers may not have had the technical insight, due to lack of involvement, to assess compliance.
context: JATR finding (F5.2-C) about how organizational structure prevented technical expertise from developing.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Certification process focused on discrete changes only
original_label: Certification process focused on discrete changes only
quote: The JATR team determined that the Changed Product Rule process was followed and that the process was effective for addressing discrete changes. However, the team determined that the process did not adequately address cumulative effects, system integration, and human factors issues.
context: JATR summary of findings about how the certification process rules directed attention to parts instead of wholes.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Compliance orientation overrides safety considerations
original_label: Compliance orientation overrides safety considerations
quote: Other broader recommendations raise the foundational issue of whether a process that has historically served the industry well for decades based largely upon compliance needs to be revisited to address not only compliance but also safety. As systems become more complex and may interact in unforeseeable ways, the likelihood increases that regulations and standards will not address every conceivable scenario. To the extent they do not address every scenario, compliance with every applicable regulation and standard does not necessarily ensure safety.
context: JATR overview noting how the regulatory framework rules directed focus toward meeting specific requirements rather than safety outcomes.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Changed Product Rule allows bottom-up approach
original_label: Changed Product Rule allows bottom-up approach
quote: Section 21.101 was designed to lead to a top-down approach to the certification of changed products whereby the whole aircraft is assumed to be affected by changes, and compliance with current amendments must be found at the level of the aircraft, unless otherwise noted.
context: JATR observation (O1.1-B) about the stated intent of the regulation versus its application.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Boeing compliance submissions used bottom-up approach
original_label: Boeing compliance submissions used bottom-up approach
quote: Boeing's compliance submissions to the FAA followed a bottom-up approach whereby each change and areas affected by a change were presented separately, showing compliance at the level of the specific regulation and its application to a given change.
context: JATR finding (F1.1-C) about how Boeing's organizational procedures directed attention to compliance by compartment.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Engineers emphasize meeting individual requirements
original_label: Engineers emphasize meeting individual requirements
quote: Some of the Boeing engineers the JATR team spoke with described the Boeing process in a manner that reflected an emphasis on meeting individual certification requirements, without necessarily having an appreciation for the overall safety-based reasons for those requirements.
context: JATR finding (F1.1-E) about how organizational norms shaped what engineers attended to during development.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Pilot recognition time standards assumed without validation
original_label: Pilot recognition time standards assumed without validation
quote: Often, recognition time is assumed to be 1 second, and reaction time is assumed to be 3 seconds. Thus, test pilots are told that "Recovery action should not be initiated until 3 seconds after the recognition point"
context: JATR observation (O2.8-A) about the rules that guided what engineers and test pilots did during design validation.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: HQRM guidance allows reduced envelope evaluation
original_label: HQRM guidance allows reduced envelope evaluation
quote: Boeing's application of HQRM allowed for a reduced envelope in the evaluation of SPEED TRIM FAIL, which may not meet the intent of guidance within AC 25-7C and AC 25-1309-1A.
context: JATR finding (F3.11-C) showing how guidance rules were interpreted to reduce required testing scope.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Certification focused on large number of small details
original_label: Certification focused on large number of small details
quote: The certification process is focused on a large number of small details which may minimize the opportunity for a "big picture" view.
