context: JATR finding (F1.3-A) describing what actually occupied the certification process's attention.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: FHA not used to drive design mitigations
original_label: FHA not used to drive design mitigations
quote: There is a perception that the FHA reports are not used to drive the design; rather, they are used to document the design as already defined. The STS and flight control computer (FCC) FHAs were updated reports from the B737 NG, and in the JATR team's assessment, they did not appear to be used as tools to identify new hazards related to MCAS and drive design mitigations. As an example, in the hierarchy of safety solutions, mitigation by design should be prioritized over warnings and training/procedures. By documenting the as-is configuration, Boeing concluded that pilot training and procedures were sufficient to ensure safety.
context: JATR finding (F6.6-A) about how the safety analysis process was subordinated to design documentation rather than guiding design.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Design consideration limited to worst-case AOA scenario
original_label: Design consideration limited to worst-case AOA scenario
quote: As far as AOA failures are concerned, the JATR team observed that the S&MF analysis was limited to a single worst-case scenario: loss of AOA on one side plus erroneous AOA on the other side. Other AOA failures were not evaluated because the worst-case failure modes were analyzed and the hazard analyses in the S&MF was limited to only those combined worst-case failures.
context: JATR observation (O6.9-A) about how the analysis scope was artificially narrowed.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: MCAS described as not novel because it existed on B767
original_label: MCAS described as not novel because it existed on B767
quote: Boeing engineers did not see MCAS as "new or novel," partly because it was already operational on the military tanker version of the B767.
context: JATR observation (O6.9-B) about how prior existence on a different aircraft model was used to discount the novelty of B737 MAX implementation.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: SSA not updated after MCAS software expansion
original_label: SSA not updated after MCAS software expansion
quote: The SSA was not updated beyond Revision C of the STS requirements for MCAS. The JATR team observed no documented risk, failure, or safety analyses conducted on the MCAS software beyond Revision C. Boeing determined the high-speed regime to be the critical aspect of MCAS, and thus no revision to the SSA was necessary when the low speeds were added to the software's lookup table.
context: JATR observations (O6.9-F and O6.9-G) about how the logic of 'already analyzed the critical part' led to skipping re-analysis.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Pilot assumptions not validated despite being central to safety
original_label: Pilot assumptions not validated despite being central to safety
quote: Basic assumptions about trained and qualified flight crew response to malfunctions used in the design and certification of the B737-8 MAX did not appear to hold in the two accident cases, based on preliminary information.
context: JATR finding (F6.12-B) showing that unvalidated assumptions underpinned the entire design.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: MCAS activation not assessed for human factors
original_label: MCAS activation not assessed for human factors
quote: MCAS, although a significant functional change, was never highlighted as an area requiring additional scrutiny from a human factors perspective. As a result, no human factors test cases were designed to investigate the adequacy of the design.
context: JATR observation (O2.1-A) showing how a major design addition was not flagged for review by relevant specialists.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Information about MCAS removed from pilot manual
original_label: Information about MCAS removed from pilot manual
quote: During the certification process, a decision was made to remove information relating to MCAS functionality from the draft Flight Crew Operating Manual (FCOM). This decision meant that the FAA Flight Standardization Board (FSB) was not fully aware of the MCAS function and was not in a position to adequately assess training needs.
context: JATR finding about how critical system information was deliberately excluded from crew documentation without multi-disciplinary approval.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Cumulative changes not assessed for crew training impact
original_label: Cumulative changes not assessed for crew training impact
quote: Boeing's response to this concern was that there was no precedent in prior Boeing amended type certification projects and that AC 120-53B did not require the cumulative effects on system changes to be considered. The FAA accepted Boeing's response on 26 January 2016.
context: JATR observation (O9.1-B) showing how FAA's concern about cumulative effects was dismissed by citing absence of precedent.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Erroneous MCAS activation not adequately evaluated
original_label: Erroneous MCAS activation not adequately evaluated
quote: When all flight deck effects are considered, the introduction of the MCAS function invalidated aircraft-level assumptions for flight crew responses related to erroneous AOA failures under certain conditions. A complete workload assessment was not performed for validation of the erroneous AOA effects with the added MCAS functionality. The same assumptions for flight crew responses to erroneous AOA were carried over from previous programs without formal validation.
context: JATR finding (F6.4-A) showing how old assumptions were not re-examined despite new system interactions.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Pilot failure to follow assumptions blamed on training
original_label: Pilot failure to follow assumptions blamed on training
quote: By documenting the as-is configuration, Boeing concluded that pilot training and procedures were sufficient to ensure safety.
context: JATR finding (F6.6-A) showing how design was rationalized by assuming pilot adherence to procedures.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: No independent safety review of MCAS design
original_label: No independent safety review of MCAS design
quote: The JATR team could not identify whether Boeing has an independent safety group coordinating the systems safety analysis and their role within a development program. Each system team conducts both the design and related safety assessments.
context: JATR observation (O6.7-A) showing the organizational structure lacked independent review to challenge design choices.

label: FAA delegated MCAS compliance to Boeing ODA
original_label: FAA delegated MCAS compliance to Boeing ODA
quote: Safety critical areas, including system safety documents related to MCAS, were initially retained by the FAA and then delegated to the Boeing ODA.
context: JATR finding (F5.1-A) about the FAA's decision to delegate oversight of the system that caused the accidents.

label: FAA involvement would likely have changed MCAS design
original_label: FAA involvement would likely have changed MCAS design
quote: The JATR team's belief is that FAA involvement in the certification of MCAS would likely have resulted in design changes that would have improved safety.
context: JATR finding (F5.1-B) showing the counterfactual: what FAA action might have prevented the accidents.

label: BASOO conducted oversight interviews finding undue pressure
original_label: BASOO conducted oversight interviews finding undue pressure
quote: The BASOO conducted oversight interviews of the E-UMs, resulting in a finding and associated corrective action pertaining to undue pressure.
context: JATR observation (O5.3-B) showing that FAA found, but did not adequately remedy, structural pressure on delegated engineers.

label: Issue papers contain inconsistencies and errors
original_label: Issue papers contain inconsistencies and errors
quote: Some closed B737-8 MAX issue papers contain inconsistencies. For instance, in Issue Paper O-1, MDR and ODR stand for different definitions between Boeing's position and the FAA's response. Some B737-8 MAX issue papers contain typographical and grammatical errors which could indicate a hurried process.
context: JATR findings (F2.5-A and F2.5-B) showing how the agreement process between applicant and FAA was executed hurriedly.

label: Two fatal accidents trigger comprehensive technical review
original_label: Two fatal accidents trigger comprehensive technical review
quote: On October 29, 2018, Lion AIR Flight JT610 (JT610), a B737-8 MAX, crashed shortly after takeoff in Jakarta, Indonesia. On November 7, 2018, the FAA issued Emergency Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2018-23-51 to require revising certificate limitations and operating procedures of the Airplane Flight Manual (AFM) for the B737 MAX to provide the flight crew with runaway horizontal stabilizer trim procedures to follow under certain conditions. On March 10, 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 (ET302), also a B737-8 MAX, crashed shortly after takeoff in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. On March 13, 2019, the FAA issued an emergency order prohibiting operation of the B737 MAX in the United States. Because of apparent similarities in factors that may have contributed to these accidents, the FAA Associate Administrator for Aviation Safety established a Joint Authorities Technical Review (JATR) to review the type certification of the flight control system on the B737 MAX.
context: JATR background describing how two fatal accidents redirected organizational attention to the certification process.

label: Post-accident rapid response procedures were inadequate
original_label: Post-accident rapid response procedures were inadequate
quote: After a catastrophic fatal accident, an interim corrective action is often issued to prevent a second accident. Sometimes flight crew procedural changes are used, and the interim action AD requires a revision to the AFM.
context: JATR observation (O12.2-A) reflecting on the FAA's response to the first crash and its insufficiency to prevent the second.

label: Safety Risk Management identifies out-of-sequence work as unairworthiness risk
original_label: Safety Risk Management identifies out-of-sequence work as unairworthiness risk
quote: Between 2021 and 2023, Boeing conducted several Safety Risk Management assessments that identified out-of-sequence work as a risk factor that could cause the delivery of an "unairworthy" or non-conforming aircraft to Boeing's customers.
context: The DOJ Factual Basis for Breach document identifies known risks that Boeing's own assessments flagged but the company failed to adequately address during the DPA term.

label: Boeing receives hundreds of stamping non-compliance reports
original_label: Boeing receives hundreds of stamping non-compliance reports
quote: Boeing received hundreds of reports of stamping non-compliance through its internal reporting channels. Boeing Compliance identified this anti-fraud risk during the DPA term and issued training and communications throughout the Company in response to the risk.
context: The DOJ identifies internal warnings about false stamping in manufacturing records that persisted despite compliance awareness and training efforts.

label: FAA issues numerous formal or informal actions on removal records policy
original_label: FAA issues numerous formal or informal actions on removal records policy
quote: In addition, since 2019, the FAA has issued numerous formal or informal actions to Boeing related to Boeing's policy governing removals.
context: The DOJ breach determination notes that external regulators repeatedly signaled concerns about Boeing's recordkeeping procedures for part removals throughout the DPA term.

label: Boeing receives numerous reports of removal record non-compliance
original_label: Boeing receives numerous reports of removal record non-compliance
quote: Boeing received numerous reports of incidents of non-compliance with its policy governing removals throughout the DPA term.
context: The DOJ's breach finding documents internal warnings about a recordkeeping failure that could undermine airworthiness certifications.

label: MCAS expanded to operate at low speeds, different from FAA briefing
original_label: MCAS expanded to operate at low speeds, different from FAA briefing
quote: On or about November 15, 2016, during a test flight of the 737 MAX in a simulator, Boeing Employee-1 experienced what Boeing Employee-1 recognized as MCAS operating at lower speed. Boeing Employee-1 further recognized that this lower-speed operation was different from what Boeing had briefed and described to the FAA AEG.
context: Boeing's chief technical pilot discovered during simulator testing that MCAS had been expanded beyond the scope described to the FAA, a critical anomaly in the system's design.

label: Chat reveals MCAS operating at Mach 0.2, different from representations
original_label: Chat reveals MCAS operating at Mach 0.2, different from representations
quote: Boeing Employee-1: Oh shocker alerT! [sic] / MCAS is now active down to [Mach] .2 / It's running rampant in the sim on me / at least that's what [a Boeing simulator engineer] thinks is happening
context: Internal Boeing communication shows employee recognition that MCAS's expanded operational scope contradicted what had been told to regulators.

label: Boeing Employee-1 acknowledges lying to regulators about MCAS
original_label: Boeing Employee-1 acknowledges lying to regulators about MCAS
quote: Boeing Employee-1: so I basically lied to the regulators (unknowingly)
context: Boeing's chief technical pilot explicitly recognizes in internal chat that the information provided to the FAA about MCAS's operational scope was false.

label: Senior engineer confirms MCAS activates beyond high-speed turns
original_label: Senior engineer confirms MCAS activates beyond high-speed turns
quote: Around the time that Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 discussed MCAS's expanded operational scope, Boeing Employee-1 asked a Boeing senior engineer assigned to the 737 MAX program about MCAS's operational scope. The senior engineer confirmed to Boeing Employee-1 that MCAS could activate beyond the limited operational scope of a high-speed, wind-up turn.
context: Boeing's engineering staff provided confirmation to the chief technical pilot that MCAS's operational scope exceeded what had been represented to the FAA.

label: FAA AEG requests Boeing review draft FSB Report for issues
original_label: FAA AEG requests Boeing review draft FSB Report for issues
quote: On or about November 17, 2016, the FAA AEG emailed three Boeing employees, including Boeing Employee-1, Boeing Employee-2, and another Boeing employee, a draft of the forthcoming 737 MAX FSB Report. That same day, Boeing Employee-1 asked Boeing Employee-2 and the other Boeing employee to review the draft 737 MAX FSB Report "for any glaring issues."
context: The formal regulatory process for finalizing the Flight Standardization Board Report involved Boeing employees reviewing draft materials, creating a channel where MCAS information could have been disclosed but was not.

label: Compliance not involved in Safety Risk Assessments
original_label: Compliance not involved in Safety Risk Assessments
quote: Moreover, although fraud is an inherent risk in production and quality compliance activities, Boeing's Safety Risk Management assessments also failed to identify out-of-sequence risk as a fraud risk or consider enhanced production procedures, or preventive or detective controls, to mitigate the risk. Boeing's Global Compliance function, which is responsible for Boeing's anti-fraud ethics and compliance program, was not involved in the Safety Risk Assessments. Compliance therefore did not evaluate fraud risks associated with out-of-sequence work, including the risk of incomplete, inaccurate, false, and/or fraudulent statements to the FAA.
context: The DOJ's breach finding shows that safety and compliance functions were structurally separated, preventing integration of anti-fraud oversight with manufacturing and quality risk assessment.

label: Compliance not sufficiently involved in removals root cause analysis
original_label: Compliance not sufficiently involved in removals root cause analysis
quote: Compliance was not sufficiently involved in root cause analysis, remediation, or risk mitigation related to this process, notwithstanding the (1) impact non-compliance with Boeing's policy governing removals could have on Boeing's representations regarding its aircraft, and (2) recordkeeping consequences.
context: The DOJ identifies a structural gap where the compliance function did not participate in investigating and fixing a recordkeeping problem that created fraud risks in airworthiness certifications.

label: Flight Technical Team responsible for FAA AEG communications on MCAS
original_label: Flight Technical Team responsible for FAA AEG communications on MCAS
quote: Boeing's 737 MAX Flight Technical Team was principally responsible for identifying and providing to the FAA AEG all information that was relevant to the FAA AEG in connection with the FAA AEG's publication of the 737 MAX FSB Report. The 737 MAX Flight Technical Team was separate and distinct from another group within Boeing that was responsible for providing information to the FAA for certification of whether the airplane met U.S. federal airworthiness standards.
context: The organizational structure placed responsibility for FAA disclosures about MCAS in the hands of the Flight Technical Team (Boeing Employee-1 and Employee-2), separate from airworthiness certification personnel.

label: Boeing Employee-1 and Employee-2 understood role to disclose relevant MCAS information
original_label: Boeing Employee-1 and Employee-2 understood role to disclose relevant MCAS information
quote: Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 understood that the FAA AEG relied on them, as members of Boeing's 737 MAX Flight Technical Team, to identify and provide to the FAA AEG all information that was relevant to the FAA AEG in connection with the FAA AEG's publication of the 737 MAX FSB Report, including information that could impact the FAA AEG's differences-training determination.
context: The technical pilots held explicit responsibility to disclose information relevant to the FAA's training determination, establishing their awareness of the disclosure obligation before the concealment began.

label: Boeing Employee-1 led Flight Technical Team, later Boeing Employee-2 assumed role
original_label: Boeing Employee-1 led Flight Technical Team, later Boeing Employee-2 assumed role
quote: From in or around early 2012 until in or around early 2014, Boeing Employee-1 was a Technical Pilot for Boeing's 737 MAX Flight Technical Team. In or around early 2014, Boeing Employee-1 became Boeing's 737 MAX Chief Technical Pilot. In that role, Boeing Employee-1 led the 737 MAX Flight Technical Team. In or around July 2018, Boeing Employee-1 left Boeing to work for a major U.S.-based airline. From in or around mid-2014 until in or around July 2018, Boeing Employee-2 was a Technical Pilot for Boeing's 737 MAX Flight Technical Team. In or around July 2018, after Boeing Employee-1 left Boeing, Boeing Employee-2 became Boeing's 737 MAX Chief Technical Pilot. In that role, Boeing Employee-2 led the 737 MAX Flight Technical Team.
context: The two employees who discovered and concealed MCAS's expanded scope held the chief technical pilot positions responsible for FAA communications throughout the period of concealment.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Boeing's objective to secure no greater than Level B differences training
original_label: Boeing's objective to secure no greater than Level B differences training
quote: Principally for this reason, Boeing's stated objectives in designing the 737 MAX included securing the FAA AEG's determination to require no greater than "Level B" differences training in the 737 MAX FSB Report. Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 understood as much.
context: The organization's stated strategic objective was to minimize pilot training requirements, creating an incentive for the technical pilots to avoid disclosures that might require higher training levels.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Level B training significantly less expensive than Level D for airlines
original_label: Level B training significantly less expensive than Level D for airlines
quote: As Boeing knew, "Level B" differences training was significantly less expensive for airlines to complete than "Level D." For example, a pilot could complete "Level B" differences training from anywhere in the world in a matter of hours using a computer or tablet. In contrast, a pilot could complete "Level D" differences training only by appearing in person wherever the pilot's airline operated a full-flight simulator. Apart from the cost of acquiring one or more multimillion-dollar simulators and other related expenses, airlines that were required by the FAA AEG to train pilots on a full-flight simulator could also lose revenue that the pilot might otherwise have generated from flying airline passengers during that time.
context: The document establishes the financial incentive structure: Level B training meant significantly lower costs for customers and therefore greater sales appeal, creating pressure to avoid disclosures that would trigger higher training requirements.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Boeing Employee-2 warns nothing can jeopardize Level B status
original_label: Boeing Employee-2 warns nothing can jeopardize Level B status
quote: For example, in or around November 2014, Boeing Employee-2 wrote in an internal Boeing electronic chat communication to Boeing Employee-1 that "nothing can jepordize [sic] level b[.]"
context: Internal communications show that employees understood Level B status as a paramount objective that could not be compromised, establishing the decision rule that guided their subsequent conduct.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Boeing Employee-1 warns Level B loss would be his personal responsibility
original_label: Boeing Employee-1 warns Level B loss would be his personal responsibility
quote: In or around December 2014, Boeing Employee-1 wrote in an email to another Boeing employee that "if we lose Level B [it] will be thrown squarely on my shoulders. It was [Boeing Employee-1], yes [Boeing Employee-1]! Who cost Boeing tens of millions of dollars!"
context: The chief technical pilot explicitly understood that he would be held personally accountable for loss of Level B status, creating strong individual incentive to avoid disclosures that would trigger training level changes.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: FAA AEG provisional Level B based on understanding of MCAS scope
original_label: FAA AEG provisional Level B based on understanding of MCAS scope
quote: As Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 knew, the FAA AEG based its provisional "Level B" differences training for the 737 MAX in part on its understanding that MCAS could only activate during the limited operational scope of a high-speed, wind up turn.
context: The technical pilots understood that the FAA's decision rule for training level was linked to MCAS's operational scope, meaning disclosure of the expanded scope would trigger reconsideration and higher requirements.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Boeing prioritized aircraft movement over reducing out-of-sequence work
original_label: Boeing prioritized aircraft movement over reducing out-of-sequence work
quote: Boeing senior executives prioritized the movement of aircraft through Boeing's factories over reducing out-of-sequence work to ensure production quality.
context: The DOJ's breach finding shows that organizational priorities during the DPA term favored production throughput over quality and compliance objectives, directing attention away from manufacturing risks.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing Employee-1 conceals MCAS expansion from FAA AEG in conversation
original_label: Boeing Employee-1 conceals MCAS expansion from FAA AEG in conversation
quote: For example, shortly after the simulated test flight described in paragraph 30, Boeing Employee-1 talked with FAA AEG Employee-1, who asked Boeing Employee-1 about the simulated test flight. Boeing Employee-1 intentionally withheld and concealed from FAA AEG Employee-1 the fact that MCAS's operational scope had been expanded beyond what the FAA AEG relied upon when it issued its provisional "Level B" differences-training determination for the 737 MAX.
context: When directly asked about test results by the FAA, Boeing's chief technical pilot actively concealed rather than disclosed the critical finding about MCAS's expanded operational scope.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing proposes deletion of MCAS from FSB Report without disclosing expansion
original_label: Boeing proposes deletion of MCAS from FSB Report without disclosing expansion
quote: On or about November 22, 2016, the other Boeing employee emailed the draft 737 MAX FSB Report back to the FAA AEG with proposed edits. Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 were included on this email. Boeing Employee-1 included a proposed edit to delete a reference to MCAS, and wrote, "We agreed not to reference MCAS since it's outside normal operating envelope." Neither Boeing Employee-1 nor Boeing Employee-2 shared the fact of MCAS's expanded operational scope with the FAA AEG or otherwise corrected the FAA AEG's misimpression that MCAS's operational scope was limited to high-speed, wind-up turns.
context: When reviewing the FAA's draft report, Boeing employees actively moved to delete MCAS information while concealing knowledge that the basis for deletion (limited operational scope) no longer applied.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing Employee-1 reiterates MCAS deletion to FAA based on outdated assumption
original_label: Boeing Employee-1 reiterates MCAS deletion to FAA based on outdated assumption
quote: On or about January 17, 2017, Boeing Employee-1 again reminded the FAA AEG in an email to delete any reference to MCAS from the forthcoming 737 MAX FSB Report, and wrote, "Flight Controls: Delete MCAS, recall we decided we weren't going to cover it [. . .] since it's way outside the normal operating envelope." Again, Boeing Employee-1 deceived the FAA AEG into believing that the basis upon which the FAA AEG had initially "decided" to remove any information about MCAS from the 737 MAX FSB Report—that MCAS could only activate during the limited operational scope of a high-speed, wind-up turn—remained the same.
context: Nearly two months after discovering MCAS's expanded scope, Boeing's chief technical pilot continued to reinforce the deletion decision to the FAA without revealing that the factual predicate for that decision had changed.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing failed to design sufficient controls for out-of-sequence work risks
original_label: Boeing failed to design sufficient controls for out-of-sequence work risks
quote: Despite the acknowledgement of this risk, the Safety Risk Management assessments did not sufficiently consider measures to reduce out-of-sequence work. Boeing senior executives prioritized the movement of aircraft through Boeing's factories over reducing out-of-sequence work to ensure production quality. Boeing did not implement sufficient policies or procedures to mitigate the risk posed by out-of-sequence work.
context: Even though Boeing's own risk assessments identified out-of-sequence work as a threat to aircraft airworthiness, the organization chose not to implement mitigating controls, filtering out the warning.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing failed to test effectiveness of stamping training despite violations
original_label: Boeing failed to test effectiveness of stamping training despite violations
quote: Despite awareness of stamping non-compliance reports, Boeing did not conduct sufficient testing to evaluate whether its stamping integrity communications and training efforts were effective in practice and stamping issues persisted.
context: Boeing's compliance function was aware of repeated stamping violations but did not implement adequate monitoring to determine whether remedial training was working, allowing problems to continue.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing failed to implement controls for incomplete, inaccurate airworthiness certifications
original_label: Boeing failed to implement controls for incomplete, inaccurate airworthiness certifications
quote: Although Boeing knew about manufacturing, quality, safety, and anti-fraud risks capable of undermining the completeness, accuracy, and truthfulness of those records, Boeing did not implement additional or sufficient controls concerning the risk that its certifications of airworthiness to the FAA could be incomplete, inaccurate, false and/or fraudulent and that aircraft delivered to its customers "conforms to its type design and is in a condition for safe operation."
context: Boeing's leadership acknowledged manufacturing and quality risks but did not strengthen anti-fraud controls to protect the airworthiness certification process, despite the criticality of that certification.

label: Boeing withheld MCAS expansion from FAA AEG, concealed from regulators
original_label: Boeing withheld MCAS expansion from FAA AEG, concealed from regulators
quote: Despite knowing that the FAA AEG had issued its provisional "Level B" determination without any awareness that MCAS's operational scope had been expanded to include high angle of attack conditions in nearly the entire speed range of ordinary commercial flight, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 did not correct the FAA AEG's understanding of MCAS's operational scope or otherwise ensure that the FAA AEG's "Level B" determination was based on an accurate understanding of MCAS's operation. Instead, Boeing—through Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2—intentionally withheld and concealed from the FAA AEG their knowledge of MCAS's expanded operational scope.
context: Upon discovering that MCAS's scope had been expanded, Boeing's technical pilots made the deliberate choice to withhold this information from the FAA rather than update their disclosure.

label: Boeing sent FSB Report drafts without MCAS information to airline customers
original_label: Boeing sent FSB Report drafts without MCAS information to airline customers
quote: From in or around January 2017 through in or around July 2017 (when the 737 MAX FSB Report was published), Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 sent and caused to be sent emails to representatives of various Boeing airline customers that had agreed to purchase the 737 MAX, including major U.S.-based airlines. In these emails, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 or members of their 737 MAX Flight Technical Team referenced and included drafts of the forthcoming 737 MAX FSB Report and airplane manuals and pilot-training materials for Boeing's 737 MAX airline customers. None of these items contained any information about MCAS, consistent with Boeing Employee-1's and Boeing Employee-2's efforts to deceive the FAA AEG into deleting information about MCAS.
context: Boeing systematically distributed FSB Report and training materials to customers that excluded MCAS information, propagating the deception to the airlines that would operate the aircraft.

label: Boeing Compliance identified stamping anti-fraud risk but did not ensure effectiveness
original_label: Boeing Compliance identified stamping anti-fraud risk but did not ensure effectiveness
quote: Boeing Compliance identified this anti-fraud risk during the DPA term and issued training and communications throughout the Company in response to the risk. Despite awareness of stamping non-compliance reports, Boeing did not conduct sufficient testing to evaluate whether its stamping integrity communications and training efforts were effective in practice and stamping issues persisted.
context: Boeing's compliance function took some corrective actions (training, communications) in response to discovered stamping violations, but failed to implement rigorous testing to verify that the remediation worked.

label: Lion Air Flight 610 crash exposed MCAS's expanded operational scope
original_label: Lion Air Flight 610 crash exposed MCAS's expanded operational scope
quote: On October 29, 2018, Lion Air Flight 610, a Boeing 737 MAX, crashed shortly after takeoff into the Java Sea near Indonesia. All 189 passengers and crew on board died. Following the Lion Air crash, the FAA AEG learned that MCAS activated during the flight and may have played a role in the crash. The FAA AEG also learned for the first time about MCAS's expanded operational scope.
context: The first crash outside the regular regulatory process forced the FAA to discover MCAS's actual operational scope for the first time, shifting attention to the concealed design change.

label: Boeing Employee-2 misled FAA about prior knowledge of MCAS after Lion Air crash
original_label: Boeing Employee-2 misled FAA about prior knowledge of MCAS after Lion Air crash
quote: In and around the same time, Boeing employees, including Boeing Employee-2, met with personnel from the FAA AEG to discuss, among other things, MCAS's operational scope. After that meeting, Boeing Employee-2 told FAA AEG Employee-1 that he was previously unaware of MCAS's expanded operational scope and otherwise misled FAA AEG Employee-1 about Boeing Employee-2's prior knowledge of MCAS.
context: After the crash revealed MCAS's role, Boeing's chief technical pilot actively misrepresented his prior knowledge of the expanded scope to the FAA, rather than disclosing the concealment.

label: Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crash and fleet grounding
original_label: Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crash and fleet grounding
quote: On March 10, 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, a Boeing 737 MAX, crashed shortly after takeoff near Ejere, Ethiopia. All 157 passengers and crew on board died. Following the Ethiopian Airlines crash, the FAA AEG learned that MCAS activated during the flight and may have played a role in the crash. On March 13, 2019, the 737 MAX was officially grounded in the United States, indefinitely halting further flights of this airplane by any U.S.-based airline.
context: A second crash and the resulting fleet grounding forced organizational attention and regulatory action, ending the concealment strategy and forcing redesign of MCAS.

label: False stamping discovered at Boeing 787 manufacturing facility in April 2024
original_label: False stamping discovered at Boeing 787 manufacturing facility in April 2024
quote: In or around April 2024, Boeing disclosed to the Fraud Section false stamping during the DPA term at the Boeing 787 manufacturing facility in Charleston, South Carolina. The false stamps caused Boeing's quality management systems to reflect that all required steps were complete, when they were not. Employees involved in the false stamping did not understand Boeing's stamping policy, were not familiar with its requirements, and were not effectively trained on it.
context: During the DPA term, Boeing discovered that employees were making false stamps in build records, indicating that training and compliance efforts had not prevented the fraud risk that compliance had identified.

label: Independent Compliance Consultant to report to DOJ on compliance progress
original_label: Independent Compliance Consultant to report to DOJ on compliance progress
quote: In addition, the Company agrees that it will engage an Independent Compliance Consultant to assess the Company's progress regarding remediation and implementation of the compliance measures described in Attachment C ('Independent Compliance Consultant'). The Company and the Independent Compliance Consultant will report to the Offices during the Term (as defined in Paragraph 5 below), in accordance with Attachment D to this Agreement.
context: The NPA establishes a new reporting channel through the Independent Compliance Consultant to ensure ongoing monitoring of Boeing's compliance program implementation after the prior DPA's breaches.

label: Multiple stamping policy weaknesses identified in assessment
original_label: Multiple stamping policy weaknesses identified in assessment
quote: These reported stamping issues highlighted several shortcomings in Boeing's anti-fraud compliance program with respect to stamping integrity, including the following weaknesses: Boeing did not effectively evaluate its stamping policy to ensure it was effective. Specifically, Boeing failed to measure employee understanding of the policy, including whether employees understood that stamping, build, and quality records were the basis for Boeing's certification to the FAA of airworthiness. Boeing did not effectively ensure compliance with its stamping policy. Boeing did not implement enhanced or remedial controls to prevent or detect stamping policy violations.
context: Post-discovery analysis of the false stamping incident revealed systemic weaknesses in how Boeing had designed and enforced its stamping integrity controls.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Provisional Level B approval presumed no significant systems changes
original_label: Provisional Level B approval presumed no significant systems changes
quote: Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 also understood, as Boeing Employee-1 acknowledged in his email on or about August 16, 2016, that the FAA AEG's "Level B" differences determination for the 737 MAX was only a "provisional approval [. . .] assuming no significant systems changes to the airplane."
context: The provisional approval contained an explicit condition that would be violated if MCAS's scope changes were disclosed, establishing a decision rule that discouraged disclosure.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Directive not to create differences that would threaten Level B
original_label: Directive not to create differences that would threaten Level B
quote: For example, in an email to Boeing employees including Boeing Employee-2 discussing a potential change to another part of the 737 MAX's flight controls on or about November 10, 2016, Boeing Employee-1 emphasized that "[o]ne of the Program Directives we were given was to not create any differences [. . .]. This is what we sold to the regulators who have already granted us the Level B differences determination. To go back to them now, and tell them there is in fact a difference [. . .] would be a huge threat to that differences training determination."
context: Boeing's leadership explicitly directed technical staff not to disclose differences in the aircraft systems, framing disclosure as a threat to the program objective.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Boeing employee celebrates achievement of Level B provisional approval
original_label: Boeing employee celebrates achievement of Level B provisional approval
quote: On or about August 16, 2016, before the FAA AEG published the 737 MAX FSB Report, the FAA AEG issued a provisional "Level B" differences-training determination for the 737 MAX. At the time of this provisional determination, the FAA AEG was unaware that Boeing had expanded MCAS's operational scope. On or about the same day, Boeing Employee-1 recognized Boeing's achievement in an email to Boeing employees, including Boeing Employee-2, and wrote that the FAA AEG's provisional determination "culminates more than 3 years of tireless and collaborative efforts across many business units" and that the 737 MAX program management "is VERY happy."
context: The chief technical pilot's celebratory email shows that securing Level B was a dominant organizational objective that had received extensive cross-functional investment and executive attention.

label: Boeing appointed first Global Chief Compliance Officer in May 2020
original_label: Boeing appointed first Global Chief Compliance Officer in May 2020
quote: At the time of the conduct described in Attachment A-2, Boeing did not have a centralized compliance function. Boeing appointed its first Global Chief Compliance Officer ('CCO') and established its Global Compliance function ('Global Compliance' or 'Compliance') in May of 2020.
context: The DOJ breach determination notes that Boeing lacked centralized compliance oversight during the period when MCAS was concealed (2016-2018), establishing a structural gap in anti-fraud controls.

label: Grounding order issued after crashes
original_label: Grounding order issued after crashes
quote: The FAA issued an Emergency Order or Prohibition grounding the Boeing 737 MAX on March 13, 2019.
context: FAA regulatory document describing the trigger event that initiated the certification review process.

label: Crashes trigger systematic safety investigation
original_label: Crashes trigger systematic safety investigation
quote: The FAA engaged with Boeing, operators, international civil aviation regulators, and independent review panels investigating the crashes of Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302. This work resulted in the identification of seven safety issues that played a role in the two accidents.
context: FAA timeline document describing the organizational response to crash investigations that redirected attention to systemic safety issues.

label: Seven safety issues identified from accident investigations
original_label: Seven safety issues identified from accident investigations
quote: This work resulted in the identification of seven safety issues that played a role in the two accidents.
context: FAA document reporting the outcome of interim work following the crashes that revealed previously undetected safety problems.

label: Independent review panels established to assess safety issues
original_label: Independent review panels established to assess safety issues
quote: The FAA engaged with Boeing, operators, international civil aviation regulators, and independent review panels investigating the crashes of Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302.
context: FAA procedural response establishing formal channels involving multiple stakeholders to investigate and resolve identified safety issues.

label: FAA administrator personally conducts certification flight test
original_label: FAA administrator personally conducts certification flight test
quote: FAA Administrator Steve Dickson took the recommended pilot training, including academic and simulator training on September 29, 2020. He followed that training with a familiarization flight on September 30, 2020, during which he piloted the aircraft for two hours to evaluate its handling qualities and the functionality of the flight control system.
context: FAA timeline document showing the positioning of the top regulatory authority directly in the evaluation process to assess aircraft safety.

label: Joint international authority review board established
original_label: Joint international authority review board established
quote: To support the review of proposed training for the Boeing 737 MAX and carry out the functions of the FSB, a JOEB was established. The JOEB was comprised of the FAA, and the civil aviation authorities of Brazil (ANAC), Canada (TCCA), and Europe (EASA). The JOEB conducted training sessions with global pilots (with varied experience in the 737 MAX) to validate proposed training requirements.
context: FAA procedural documentation showing the creation of a multi-national channel to collectively validate training and safety requirements.

label: Independent Technical Advisory Board reviews corrective actions
original_label: Independent Technical Advisory Board reviews corrective actions
quote: The FAA commissioned a TAB to independently review Boeing's proposed corrective actions. The TAB is made up of experts with no involvement in the initial certification of the 737 MAX, including members from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the United States Air Force, the Volpe National Transportation Systems Center, and the FAA. The TAB originally met in Spring 2019 and reviewed proposed MCAS changes at that time. Since that time, they reviewed all proposed modifications and made recommendations throughout the process. The FAA addressed all return to service recommendations prior to rescinding the grounding order.
context: FAA document describing the establishment of an independent procedural channel to review corrective actions, explicitly designed to avoid bias from initial certification personnel.

label: Multi-national Joint Authorities Technical Review conducted
original_label: Multi-national Joint Authorities Technical Review conducted
quote: The FAA established the JATR to conduct a review of the FAA's certification of the automated flight control system of the 737 MAX, determine compliance with all applicable regulations, and identify any future enhancements that may be necessary. The JATR was chaired by former NTSB Chairman Christopher Hart and included technical experts in a variety of disciplines from the FAA, NASA, and the civil aviation authorities of Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, Singapore, and the United Arab Emirates. The JATR concluded its work and submitted its recommendations on October 11, 2019. The FAA addressed all recommendations that applied to the 737 MAX prior to approving the aircraft for return to service.
context: FAA document establishing an independent, multi-national procedural review mechanism to assess the adequacy of original certification and compliance with regulations.

label: Special Committee reviews FAA certification process
original_label: Special Committee reviews FAA certification process
quote: On March 25, 2019, Secretary Elaine L. Chao established a Special Committee to review the FAA's Aircraft Certification Process. It was co-chaired by Air Force General (Ret.) Darren McDew, former head of the U.S. Transportation Command, and Captain Lee Moak, former President of the Air Line Pilots Association. The Official Report of the Special Committee to Review the Federal Aviation Administration's Aircraft Certification Process was delivered to the Secretary on January 16, 2020.
context: FAA document describing the creation of a high-level procedural review channel to examine the certification process itself in response to the crashes.

label: DOT Office of Inspector General audit of certification activities
original_label: DOT Office of Inspector General audit of certification activities
quote: On March 19, 2019, Secretary Chao directed the DOT OIG to conduct an audit to compile an objective and detailed factual history of the activities that resulted in the certification of the Boeing 737 MAX. The OIG's initial timeline of certification of the Boeing 737 MAX was published on June 29, 2020.
context: FAA document describing the establishment of an independent oversight procedural channel by the Department of Transportation to examine certification history.

label: Software architecture redesigned with dual computer requirement
original_label: Software architecture redesigned with dual computer requirement
quote: Multiple tests of software for failure conditions were conducted after Boeing submitted a new software architecture that relied on the simultaneous use of two Flight Control Computers. Initial testing was completed in November 2019, and the final evaluation was completed on August 13, 2020.
context: FAA timeline documenting Boeing's redesign response and the testing conducted to validate the corrective action.

label: Crew workload and human factors testing conducted
original_label: Crew workload and human factors testing conducted
quote: Crew Workload/Human Factors 1302 testing with flight crews from Southwest Airlines, American Airlines, United Airlines, and Aeromexico was conducted during the week of December 2, 2019.
context: FAA timeline showing testing protocols established to validate safety-critical human factors after the crashes were identified.

label: Software development process audited for safety compliance
original_label: Software development process audited for safety compliance
quote: Audit of the software development process was completed to verify safety requirements were appropriately coded into the software. The FAA completed an initial audit during the week of June 15, 2020, and the final audit on September 14, 2020.
context: FAA document describing corrective action to verify that safety requirements were properly implemented in the original design process.

label: FAA certification flight test evaluates proposed changes
original_label: FAA certification flight test evaluates proposed changes
quote: The FAA and Boeing conducted the certification flight test to evaluate Boeing's proposed changes to the automated flight control system on the 737 MAX during the week of June 29, 2020. All conditions flown were satisfactory.
context: FAA timeline documenting the agency's direct testing of Boeing's corrective modifications before return to service approval.

label: Airworthiness Directive issued mandating corrective actions
original_label: Airworthiness Directive issued mandating corrective actions
quote: The FAA issued an Airworthiness Directive on November 18, 2020, which applies to 737 MAX airplanes that received FAA airworthiness certificates and export certificates of airworthiness prior to the date of issuance of the Rescission of Emergency Order of Prohibition (November 18, 2020). The AD mandates actions to correct the unsafe condition.
context: FAA regulatory document formalizing mandatory corrective actions to be implemented by aircraft operators.

label: Grounding order rescinded after comprehensive review
original_label: Grounding order rescinded after comprehensive review
quote: On November 18, 2020, FAA Administrator Steve Dickson signed a rescission of the grounding order issued in March 2019. This marks the FAA's official ungrounding of the aircraft, pending operators' completion of the work specified in the AD, along with any required training.
context: FAA document describing the final approval action after completing extensive testing and review procedures.

label: Public notice and comment period established for design changes
original_label: Public notice and comment period established for design changes
quote: The FAA issued the NPRM for an Airworthiness Directive to collect public comments on the design changes to the 737 MAX flight control computer. The comment period closed on September 21, 2020.
context: FAA procedural process establishing a formal channel for public stakeholder input on proposed design modifications.

label: Draft pilot training requirements posted for public review
original_label: Draft pilot training requirements posted for public review
quote: The FAA posted the draft FSB Report to collect public comments on the changes to minimum pilot training requirements. The comment period closed on November 2, 2020.
context: FAA procedural process establishing a formal public comment channel on training requirements modifications.

label: Final design documentation submitted and approved
original_label: Final design documentation submitted and approved
quote: Boeing submitted its final design documentation to the FAA on October 16, 2020. The FAA reviewed the documentation, made a finding of compliance with the applicable regulations, and issued the design approval to Boeing on November 17, 2020.
context: FAA timeline documenting the formal submission and regulatory approval of Boeing's final corrective design.

label: Service Bulletin approved for aircraft operators
original_label: Service Bulletin approved for aircraft operators
quote: Boeing proposed a Service Bulletin with instructions for operators to modify their aircraft. The FAA approved it for issuance on November 17, 2020.
context: FAA timeline showing approval of Boeing's operator implementation guidance for aircraft modifications.

label: Accident investigations reviewed for recommendations
original_label: Accident investigations reviewed for recommendations
quote: The FAA has also reviewed recommendations from the September 19, 2019 National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) report, October 29, 2019 Republic of Indonesia Komite Nasional Keselamatan Transportasi (KNKT) Lion Air accident investigation report, and March 9, 2020 Ethiopia Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (EAIB) Ethiopian Airlines interim accident investigation report.
context: FAA timeline documenting the agency's incorporation of independent accident investigation findings into the recertification process.

label: FDR data showed AOA anomalies and stabilizer movement
original_label: FDR data showed AOA anomalies and stabilizer movement
quote: The FDR data analysis showed Angle of Attack (AOA) data input anomalies sent to the flight control computer (FCC), unusual movement of the horizontal stabilizer trim system, and multiple flight deck effects.
context: FAA describes the Flight Data Recorder analysis from JT610 crash on November 4, 2018, which revealed sensor failures and erratic stabilizer behavior.

label: Previous flight showed same AOA anomalies and stabilizer movement
original_label: Previous flight showed same AOA anomalies and stabilizer movement
quote: The review by the FAA and Boeing of the FDR data showed that the flight immediately prior to the accident flight also experienced anomalous AOA vane behavior and corresponding stabilizer movement.
context: FAA documents that the same aircraft experienced the failure mode on a flight before the fatal accident, demonstrating a repeated anomaly that should have triggered attention.

label: JT610 maintenance records show mis-calibrated AOA sensor
original_label: JT610 maintenance records show mis-calibrated AOA sensor
quote: The replacement AOA sensor that was installed on the accident aircraft had been mis-calibrated during an earlier repair. This mis-calibration was not detected during the repair. The investigation could not determine that the installation test of the AOA sensor was performed properly. The mis-calibration was not detected.
context: KNKT final accident investigation report identifies a root cause: improper calibration of a replaced AOA sensor that went undetected through maintenance procedures.

label: First accident prompted preliminary risk assessment
original_label: First accident prompted preliminary risk assessment
quote: On October 29, 2018, JT610 crashed shortly after takeoff in Jakarta, Indonesia. The KNKT (the accident investigation board in Indonesia) recovered the Flight Data Recorder (FDR). With assistance from Australia and Singapore, the KNKT conducted a preliminary FDR data analysis and shared it with the FAA on November 4, 2018. On November 5, 2018, after evidence emerged of a potential contributor to the accident, the FAA conducted a preliminary risk assessment using the continued operation safety process established in FAA Order 8110.107A, Monitor Safety/Analyze Data (MSAD). Based on this risk assessment, the FAA determined urgent mandatory action was needed.
context: FAA describes its immediate response to the first accident, showing how the crash redirected organizational attention to the MCAS system.

label: Second accident established causal link between crashes
original_label: Second accident established causal link between crashes
quote: On March 10, 2019, ET302 crashed shortly after takeoff in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Partial data (e.g., altitude, airspeed and vertical speed) was available from a land-based Automatic Dependent Surveillance—Broadcast (ADS-B) system. On March 11, 2019, the FAA issued another CANIC (see Appendix D) indicating the FAA was actively involved in supporting the investigations. On March 11, the FAA received additional ADS-B data. The data was analyzed and reviewed on March 12 and through the early hours of March 13. Also on March 13, physical evidence from the crash site indicated that the aircraft was in a configuration that would have armed MCAS. The satellite ADS-B data from ET302, when compared with the Lion Air Flight Data Recorder (FDR) and physical data, indicated a potential causal link between the accidents. On March 13, with the potential relationship established between the two accidents, the FAA issued an Emergency Order of Prohibition (see Appendix A) grounding 737 MAX aircraft.
context: FAA documents the second crash and the data analysis that proved MCAS was a common factor, triggering an emergency grounding order.

label: FAA issued Emergency AD after first accident
original_label: FAA issued Emergency AD after first accident
quote: On November 6, 2018, the FAA issued a CANIC (see Appendix D) which notified Civil Aviation Authorities (CAA) around the world that the FAA intended to issue an Emergency AD to correct an unsafe condition on the 737 MAX. On November 7, 2018, the FAA issued Emergency AD 2018-23-51. The AD was an interim action. The FAA planned further terminating action based on what the agency and Boeing learned from further investigating the JT610 accident cause.
context: FAA documents its immediate regulatory action following the first accident, establishing an interim fix while a broader investigation proceeded.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: AOA DISAGREE alert was not functional unless airline selected option
original_label: AOA DISAGREE alert was not functional unless airline selected option
quote: Safety Item #5: AOA DISAGREE: The AOA DISAGREE alert message on the Primary Flight Display is not functional unless the AOA indicator option was chosen by the airline. This alert message is intended to be standard on all 737 MAX airplanes.
context: FAA identifies a design defect where a critical alerting feature that should warn pilots of sensor disagreement was disabled by default and required an optional purchase, preventing its use.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Original MCAS design prioritized matching 737 NG handling feel
original_label: Original MCAS design prioritized matching 737 NG handling feel
quote: The 737 MAX was designed to handle and feel the same to the pilot as the 737 NG. Without the MCAS function, in some small areas of the flight envelope — such as approaching a stall and during higher g-force maneuvering — the new engines contribute to the control column feeling lighter in the 737 MAX than the regulations allow. These are not areas of the flight envelope in which the airplane normally operates. However, FAA regulations - specifically 14 CFR 25.143, 25.201, 25.203, 25.251, and 25.255 - still require the control column to have a higher pull-force feel in these flight regimes than would exist on the 737 MAX without the added stability from the STS and MCAS function.
context: FAA explains the original design rationale for MCAS, revealing that the system's primary purpose was to maintain pilot handling characteristics rather than to address a fundamental safety issue.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Original design assumed immediate and appropriate pilot corrective actions
original_label: Original design assumed immediate and appropriate pilot corrective actions
quote: Recommendation A-19-010: Require that Boeing (1) ensure that system safety assessments for the 737 MAX in which it assumed immediate and appropriate pilot corrective actions in response to uncommanded flight control inputs, from systems such as the MCAS, consider the effect of all possible flight deck alerts and indications on pilot recognition and response; and (2) incorporate design enhancements (including flight deck alerts and indications), pilot procedures, and/or training requirements, where needed, to minimize the potential for and safety impact of pilot actions that are inconsistent with manufacturer assumptions.
context: NTSB safety recommendation reveals that Boeing's original safety analysis assumed pilots would respond correctly and immediately to MCAS malfunctions, without considering how multiple alerts and workload might affect actual pilot behavior.

label: KNKT investigation found lack of equivalency assessment at maintenance organization
original_label: KNKT investigation found lack of equivalency assessment at maintenance organization
quote: The absence of equivalency assessment required by Xtra Aerospace procedure and unavailability of procedure was not detected by the FAA. This indicated inadequacy of FAA oversight.
context: KNKT final report documents that the maintenance organization that repaired the AOA sensor lacked proper procedures and that FAA oversight failed to detect this deficiency.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Crews correctly executed runaway stabilizer checklist but FAA dismissed significance
original_label: Crews correctly executed runaway stabilizer checklist but FAA dismissed significance
quote: The data indicated the flightcrew correctly executed the horizontal stabilizer runaway checklist and used the stab cut-out switches to shut down the horizontal Stabilizer Trim Motor (STM) and therefore disable MCAS. This action enabled the crew to continue safe flight and landing to their planned destination airport. The FAA conclusion from this analysis indicated that an average crew with no prior awareness could sort out the failure scenario and could correctly mitigate the failure using existing procedures.
context: FAA initially downplayed the significance of the pre-accident flight's MCAS activation, concluding that average crews could handle the failure with existing procedures, which proved incorrect during the actual accident.

label: Technical Advisory Board comprised experts independent from original certification
original_label: Technical Advisory Board comprised experts independent from original certification
quote: The FAA also commissioned a Technical Advisory Board (TAB) to independently review Boeing's proposed corrective actions. The TAB consisted of a number of technical experts with no involvement in the initial certification of the 737 MAX. Several of these experts were from other U.S. government agencies.
context: FAA describes the institutional step of creating an independent expert panel to review the post-accident redesign, implicitly acknowledging limitations in the original certification team's perspective.

label: FAA delegated no compliance findings to Boeing ODA during redesign
original_label: FAA delegated no compliance findings to Boeing ODA during redesign
quote: In relation to the FAA's approval of the 737 MAX current design changes, the FAA delegated no compliance findings to the Boeing ODA. In addition, the FAA supplemented BASOO resources with staff from other offices within the FAA.
context: FAA explains its post-accident change in oversight approach, retaining direct control over all compliance decisions rather than delegating to Boeing's internal certification authority.

label: Multiple MCAS commands resulted in stabilizer mistrim pilots could not counter
original_label: Multiple MCAS commands resulted in stabilizer mistrim pilots could not counter
quote: Safety Item #3: MCAS TRIM AUTHORITY: All MCAS commands were incremental commands, which moved the horizontal stabilizer a fixed amount, regardless of the current position of the stabilizer. Therefore, multiple MCAS commands resulted in a significant horizontal stabilizer mistrim condition, which the flightcrew could not counter using only elevator control.
context: FAA identifies a critical design flaw discovered during post-accident analysis: the original MCAS could accumulate enough stabilizer movement to make the aircraft uncontrollable by normal means.

label: MCAS would reset and command repeated movements after pilot trim input
original_label: MCAS would reset and command repeated movements after pilot trim input
quote: Safety Item #2: MCAS RESET GENERATES REPETITIVE MCAS COMMANDS: When a continuous erroneous high AOA sensor value exists, the MCAS control law uses pilot release of the electric trim switch to reset MCAS activation. Once reset, the MCAS system will make another airplane nose-down stabilizer trim command after five seconds. This scenario repeats each time MCAS makes a command and the pilot makes an electric trim command of any duration and releases the trim switch.
context: FAA identifies a second critical design flaw: the original MCAS logic could enter a cycle of repeated activations when pilots attempted to correct the initial erroneous command.

label: MCAS relied on single AOA sensor without cross-check
original_label: MCAS relied on single AOA sensor without cross-check
quote: Safety Item #1: USE OF SINGLE ANGLE OF ATTACK (AOA) SENSOR: Erroneous data from a single AOA sensor activated MCAS and subsequently caused airplane nose-down trim of the horizontal stabilizer.
context: FAA identifies the root cause of both accidents: the original system lacked redundancy and could be controlled by one failed sensor.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: FDR data showed flightcrews unable to manage multiple effects
original_label: FDR data showed flightcrews unable to manage multiple effects
quote: Safety Item #4: FLIGHTCREW RECOGNITION AND RESPONSE: FDR data from both accidents show that the flightcrews were unable to effectively manage the stabilizer movement and multiple flight deck effects that resulted from the single AOA sensor failure.
context: FAA recognizes that the original system created overwhelming demands on pilots during the failure, compounded by multiple confusing alerts and warnings.

label: FAA retained all compliance findings and delegated none to Boeing ODA
original_label: FAA retained all compliance findings and delegated none to Boeing ODA
quote: During its evaluation of Boeing's proposed modifications, the FAA retained all compliance findings and approvals associated with the design changes related to MCAS. This unprecedented level of review has taken more than 22 months and included the full-time work of more than 40 engineers, inspectors, pilots and technical support staff. The effort represents more than 60,000 FAA hours of review, certification testing and on-site evaluation of pertinent documents.
context: FAA documents its intensive post-accident oversight approach, in sharp contrast to the pre-accident certification process where some authority was delegated to Boeing.

label: Multiple independent reviews requested by FAA and stakeholders
original_label: Multiple independent reviews requested by FAA and stakeholders
quote: The FAA and other U.S. bodies commissioned a number of studies to evaluate the initial certification of the 737 MAX, as well as the certification process itself. The FAA invited nine other CAAs to be a part of the Joint Authorities Technical Review (JATR), which assessed the certification of the 737 MAX flight control system. The FAA took into consideration all relevant findings of the JATR, as well as those of the U.S. Department of Transportation Special Committee, the U.S. Department of Transportation Office of the Inspector General (OIG), and other expert reviews.
context: FAA describes post-accident procedural changes: multiple external and internal reviews were commissioned to examine both the product and the certification process itself.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Original design assumed average flightcrew could handle failure scenario
original_label: Original design assumed average flightcrew could handle failure scenario
quote: The FAA conclusion from this analysis indicated that an average crew with no prior awareness could sort out the failure scenario and could correctly mitigate the failure using existing procedures.
context: FAA's initial assessment of the pre-accident flight's MCAS activation reveals an assumption about pilot capability that turned out to be incorrect during actual high-stress accident conditions.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Split vane monitor threshold allows wide AOA disagreement
original_label: Split vane monitor threshold allows wide AOA disagreement
quote: The AOA split-vane monitor threshold is large enough to allow for expected variations in AOA sensors but small enough to prevent MCAS activation due to erroneous AOA data.
context: FAA describes the redesigned safety monitor, indicating that the original system lacked adequate cross-sensor validation despite the availability of dual sensors.

label: Joint Operations Evaluation Board included pilots and authorities from four countries
original_label: Joint Operations Evaluation Board included pilots and authorities from four countries
quote: The 737 MAX Joint Operations Evaluation Board (JOEB) concluded evaluation activities at London's Gatwick Airport on September 22, 2020. The JOEB included civil aviation authorities and airline flightcrews from the United States, Canada, Brazil and the European Union. The civil aviation authorities and industry pilots selected for participation completed all scheduled tasks as planned.
context: FAA describes the post-accident training evaluation process, involving international authorities and line pilots to validate that redesigned systems were operationally suitable.

label: Stabilizer trim wheel forces may exceed pilot capability at high speeds
original_label: Stabilizer trim wheel forces may exceed pilot capability at high speeds
quote: The FAA is aware of concerns over the potential role of stabilizer trim wheel forces during the accidents and therefore required an analysis and test of these forces. Boeing used the results of the analysis and test to show that the system is compliant with FAA and EASA requirements up to maximum operating speeds.
context: FAA identifies a concern about manual control capability that emerged during the post-accident analysis, requiring specific testing and validation.

label: Eight non-normal checklists revised or added for MCAS procedures
original_label: Eight non-normal checklists revised or added for MCAS procedures
quote: To reflect the various updates, Boeing proposed eight new or changed procedures in the Airplane Flight Manual (AFM): SPEED TRIM FAIL, Airspeed Unreliable, AOA DISAGREE, ALTITUDE (ALT) DISAGREE, Runaway Stabilizer, Indicated Airspeed (IAS) DISAGREE, Stabilizer Trim Inoperative, and STAB OUT OF TRIM.
context: FAA documents the redesign of pilot procedures in response to the accident findings, showing systematic revision of checklists.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Original MCAS had no requirement for dual-sensor validation
original_label: Original MCAS had no requirement for dual-sensor validation
quote: In the new design, Boeing eliminated MCAS reliance on a single AOA sensor signal by using both AOA sensor inputs and changing flight control laws to safeguard against MCAS activation due to a failed or erroneous AOA sensor. The updated FCC software with revised flight-control laws uses inputs from both AOA sensors to activate MCAS. This is in contrast to the original MCAS design, which relied on data from only one sensor at a time, and allowed repeated MCAS activation as a result of input from a single AOA sensor.
context: FAA explains that the original design relied on only one of two available sensors, representing a missed opportunity for redundancy that was only implemented post-accident.

label: KNKT investigation showed maintenance procedures did not detect bias
original_label: KNKT investigation showed maintenance procedures did not detect bias
quote: On 15 November 2018, with approval from KNKT and under direction and supervision of the NTSB, Boeing and the NTSB conducted an installation test of an AOA sensor on an exemplar the 737 MAX located at the Boeing Field Flight Line. This test was intended to demonstrate if the AMM installation test, task 34-21-05-400-801, was robust enough to ensure that a bias in an AOA sensor could be identified/detected using the installation and alternate test procedure. The tests were conducted on a production 737 MAX aircraft in serviceable condition inside a hangar with adequate lighting. The first test consisted of installing a known serviceable AOA sensor in the left position of the aircraft on the production aircraft. The second test consisted of installing an AOA sensor with an induced or known bias of approximately 33° (modified to have 33° bias) in the left position of the aircraft. The tests were done with and without entering good weight data into the flight management computer.
context: KNKT conducted a specific test to determine whether the maintenance procedures could catch a mis-calibrated sensor, revealing the maintenance vulnerability that contributed to the accident.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Existing AMM procedures deemed satisfactory despite earlier failure
original_label: Existing AMM procedures deemed satisfactory despite earlier failure
quote: The FAA reviewed the results of this test of the adequacy of the AOA Sensor installation instructions and determined the existing AMM instructions are satisfactory and require no change.
context: FAA initially concluded that existing maintenance procedures were adequate even though they had failed to catch the mis-calibrated sensor that caused the JT610 accident.

label: Collins CMM for AOA sensor revised to add independent check
original_label: Collins CMM for AOA sensor revised to add independent check
quote: The Collins Component Maintenance Manual (CMM) for the AOA sensor was revised to include a final independent check to ensure the repair has not introduced a bias.
context: FAA documents post-accident correction to the component maintenance manual to add a verification step that would have caught the JT610 sensor failure.

label: All 737 MAX aircraft must perform AOA sensor system tests before return to service
original_label: All 737 MAX aircraft must perform AOA sensor system tests before return to service
quote: To ensure that each airplane's two AOA sensors are functioning properly upon return to service, operators must perform AOA Sensor System Tests on each airplane prior to its return to service. This test uses a fixture to position the AOA vane and verify that the reading provided by each AOA sensor is accurate.
context: FAA mandates a specific inspection for all 737 MAX aircraft, reflecting the maintenance failure that contributed to the accidents.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: KNKT recommends larger tolerance for wider pilot population
original_label: KNKT recommends larger tolerance for wider pilot population
quote: Recommendation 04.R-2018-35.12 Boeing: During certification phase, flight test pilots, who normally have exceptional skill and experience, are used to demonstrate compliance. Flight test pilots generally have more knowledge about the aircraft design characteristics than normal pilots do. Flight test pilots however, are trained to replicate the average flightcrew. The Aircraft Evaluation Group pilots, who have an operational flying background, also evaluate the aircraft during the certification phase. These pilots establish the pilot type rating, training, checking and currency requirements as part of the Flight Standardization Board (FSB) process. The FSB process also utilizes airline line pilots to help ensure the requirements are operationally representative. The FAA and OEMs should re-evaluate their assumptions for what constitutes an average flightcrew's basic skill and what level of systems knowledge a 'properly trained average flightcrew' has when encountering failures. Therefore, KNKT recommends that Boeing include a larger tolerance in the design is required to allow operability by a larger population of flight-rated pilots.
context: KNKT accident investigation recommends that design assumptions about pilot capability should be more conservative, acknowledging that the original design relied on above-average pilot performance.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Excessive crew workload from multiple flight deck effects during failure
original_label: Excessive crew workload from multiple flight deck effects during failure
quote: Recommendation 04.R-2018-35.11 Boeing: During flight JT610, multiple alerts and indications occurred which increased flightcrew's workload. This obscured the problem and the flightcrew could not arrive at a solution during the initial or subsequent automatic AND stabilizer trim input, such as performing the runaway stabilizer procedure or continuing to use electric trim to reduce column forces and maintain level flight. Therefore, KNKT recommends that the aircraft manufacture consider the effect of all possible flight deck alerts and indications on flightcrew recognition and response; and incorporate design, flightcrew procedures, and/or training requirements where needed to minimize the potential for flightcrew actions that are inconsistent with manufacturer assumptions.
context: KNKT analysis shows that during the JT610 accident, multiple conflicting alerts overwhelmed the pilots and prevented them from implementing the runaway stabilizer procedure, a critical failure of the alerting system design.

label: Cross-FCC monitoring detected postulated FCC failures not caught by previous design
original_label: Cross-FCC monitoring detected postulated FCC failures not caught by previous design
quote: Safety Item #6: OTHER POSSIBLE FCC STABILIZER RUNAWAY FAILURES: A comprehensive review of the integrated System Safety Analysis (SSA) of MCAS by Boeing and the FAA identified an extremely remote FCC failure condition that required timely pilot intervention to ensure continued safe flight and landing.
context: Post-accident analysis identified an additional failure mode in the Flight Control Computer that the original safety analysis had not adequately addressed.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Pilot assumption that MCAS reliance on single sensor was not critical
original_label: Pilot assumption that MCAS reliance on single sensor was not critical
quote: During the original certification of the 737 MAX and again after the accidents, the FAA required Boeing to assess potential failures of the flight control system, as well as potential flightcrew responses to those failures. The FAA evaluated Boeing's assessment of flightcrew alerting and found that it complies with regulatory requirements.
