context: FAA indicates that the original certification included assessment of single-sensor failures, yet the resulting system design still allowed MCAS to activate on data from one sensor alone.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Erroneous high-AOA event assessed as Major rather than Hazardous
original_label: Erroneous high-AOA event assessed as Major rather than Hazardous
quote: The TAB therefore set out to answer a fundamental question: Does this [737 MAX] false stick-shaker activation interfere with the flightcrew's ability to safely operate the airplane? The FAA essentially answered this fundamental question as 'no' by concluding that the effect on the airplane and crew of the failure is 'Major' in the context of § 25.1309 System Safety Analysis and associated Functional Hazard Assessment. That is, safety margins are reduced, and crew workload is increased, however the failure does not excessively impair the crew's ability to perform their duties.
context: FAA documents its pre-accident safety classification of erroneous AOA events as Major rather than Hazardous, a determination that proved inconsistent with actual accident outcomes.

label: Human factors specialists assigned to TAB from outside FAA
original_label: Human factors specialists assigned to TAB from outside FAA
quote: The FAA assigned human factors specialists to the TAB from outside the agency to help evaluate human factors of the design change.
context: FAA brought in external human factors experts for the post-accident review, suggesting the original certification team lacked adequate human factors expertise.

label: JATR recommended top-down systems perspective on all design changes
original_label: JATR recommended top-down systems perspective on all design changes
quote: Recommendation 1: Based on the JATR team's observations and findings related to the application of the Changed Product Rules to the certification of the flight control system of the 737 MAX, JATR team members recommend that the FAA work with other civil aviation authorities to revise the harmonized approach to the certification of changed products. Changed Product Rules (e.g., 14 CFR §§ 21.19 and 21.101) and associated guidance (e.g., AC 21.101-1B and FAA Orders 8110.4C and 8110.48A) should be revised to require a top-down approach, whereby every change is evaluated from an integrated whole-aircraft system perspective.
context: JATR investigation recommends fundamental changes to the certification process, revealing that the original approach to changed products lacked systemic integration.

label: Original design did not detect oscillatory AOA signals
original_label: Original design did not detect oscillatory AOA signals
quote: The MVS algorithm is effective at minimizing the effect of a low amplitude oscillatory input value. The output of the MVS is used by the MCAS function within the FCC.
context: FAA describes the post-accident addition of a Middle Value Select algorithm to filter out oscillatory sensor signals that the original system could not detect.

label: MCAS maximum command limit prevents loss of pilot control
original_label: MCAS maximum command limit prevents loss of pilot control
quote: This change limits the total amount of airplane nose-down stabilizer movement MCAS can command if there are repeated MCAS activations. This ensures that the flightcrew will always have maneuver capability through control column inputs alone, enabling the flightcrew to maintain level flight without requiring use of the electric trim switches or the stabilizer trim cutout switches.
context: FAA documents the post-accident redesign feature that preserves pilot control authority, addressing a critical failure mode from the original design.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Original certification used flight test pilots to demonstrate compliance
original_label: Original certification used flight test pilots to demonstrate compliance
quote: During certification phase, flight test pilots, who normally have exceptional skill and experience, are used to demonstrate compliance. Flight test pilots generally have more knowledge about the aircraft design characteristics than normal pilots do. Flight test pilots however, are trained to replicate the average flightcrew.
context: KNKT identifies a structural issue in the certification process: highly skilled flight test pilots demonstrated compliance with regulations, potentially masking issues that average pilots would encounter.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Original MCAS design allowed pilot trim input to reset activation
original_label: Original MCAS design allowed pilot trim input to reset activation
quote: Since MCAS no longer resets after pilot activation of the electric trim switch, the five-second wait time following MCAS flight-control-law reset has been eliminated.
context: FAA describes a change to the control law logic, revealing that the original design treated pilot trim inputs as a reset signal for MCAS activation, creating a problematic feedback loop.

label: WIRING SEPARATION VIOLATION DISCOVERED DURING COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW
original_label: WIRING SEPARATION VIOLATION DISCOVERED DURING COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW
quote: As part of the FAA's review of these design changes, the agency re-reviewed the entirety of the 737 MAX horizontal stabilizer control system. This review revealed that the physical separation of the horizontal stabilizer trim-arm wiring and the horizontal stabilizer trim-control wiring does not meet the criteria specified in 14 CFR 25.1707.
context: FAA's comprehensive post-accident review uncovered a wiring compliance violation that had not been identified during the original certification process.

label: New AD removed MMEL allowances for single FCC operation
original_label: New AD removed MMEL allowances for single FCC operation
quote: MMEL Item 22-11-01 Speed Trim Function – the FAA will no longer allow dispatch with this item inoperative (Item Removed)
context: FAA strengthened operational requirements post-accident by no longer permitting aircraft to operate with degraded flight control systems.

label: Internal study showed 68% extraction rate
original_label: Internal study showed 68% extraction rate
quote: Trained PURDUE sales representatives and told some health care providers that it was more difficult to extract the oxycodone from an OxyContin tablet for the purpose of intravenous abuse, although PURDUE's own study showed that a drug abuser could extract approximately 68% of the oxycodone from a single 10mg OxyContin tablet by crushing the tablet, stirring it in water, and drawing the solution through cotton into a syringe
context: The Information describes misrepresentations to health care providers about OxyContin's extractability, despite Purdue's own internal study demonstrating high extraction rates.

label: Sales training misrepresented addiction potential
original_label: Sales training misrepresented addiction potential
quote: Told PURDUE sales representatives they could tell health care providers that OxyContin potentially creates less chance for addiction than immediate-release opioids; Sponsored training that taught PURDUE sales supervisors that OxyContin had fewer peak and trough blood level effects than immediate-release opioids resulting in less euphoria and less potential for abuse than short-acting opioids
context: The Information documents formal training programs within Purdue that conveyed false claims about addiction and abuse potential to sales representatives.

label: Misrepresentations about withdrawal and tolerance
original_label: Misrepresentations about withdrawal and tolerance
quote: Told certain health care providers that patients could stop therapy abruptly without experiencing withdrawal symptoms and that patients who took OxyContin would not develop tolerance to the drug
context: The Information identifies specific false claims about withdrawal and tolerance communicated to health care providers by Purdue personnel.

label: Multiple false claims about euphoria and abuse potential
original_label: Multiple false claims about euphoria and abuse potential
quote: Told certain health care providers that OxyContin did not cause a buzz or euphoria, caused less euphoria, had less addiction potential, had less abuse potential, was less likely to be diverted than immediate-release opioids, and could be used to weed out addicts and drug seekers
context: The Information details numerous interconnected false representations made by Purdue personnel to prescribing physicians.

label: Senior executives responsible for misbranding
original_label: Senior executives responsible for misbranding
quote: Friedman is the former president and CEO of Purdue, Udell is the executive vice president and chief legal officer, and Goldenheim is the former chief scientific officer
context: The court identifies the three individual defendants and their executive positions within Purdue, establishing the hierarchy and roles relevant to the misbranding offense.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Marketing and promotion as central activity
original_label: Marketing and promotion as central activity
quote: Beginning on or about December 12, 1995, and continuing until on or about June 30, 2001, certain PURDUE supervisors and employees, with the intent to defraud or mislead, marketed and promoted OxyContin as less addictive, less subject to abuse and diversion, and less likely to cause tolerance and withdrawal than other pain medications
context: The Information describes the sustained organizational focus on marketing OxyContin with specific false claims over a five-and-a-half year period.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Individual defendants disclaim knowledge despite guilty plea
original_label: Individual defendants disclaim knowledge despite guilty plea
quote: The individual defendants, Michael Friedman, Howard R. Udell, and Paul D. Goldenheim, have pleaded guilty to the misdemeanor charge of misbranding, solely as responsible corporate officers. The individual defendants are not charged with personal knowledge of the misbranding or with any personal intent to defraud. Purdue has agreed that these facts are true, and the individual defendants, while they do not agree that they had knowledge of these things, have agreed that the court may accept these facts in support of their guilty pleas
context: The court documents the executives' plea strategy in which they accept guilty pleas while denying personal knowledge, indicating how warnings may have been filtered at the executive level.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Purdue requires stringent causation proof for restitution
original_label: Purdue requires stringent causation proof for restitution
quote: Purdue argues that third-party payors cannot show that they were directly and proximately harmed by Purdue's misbranding, unless they can prove the following: That a Purdue sales representative misstated to a specific prescribing physician that OxyContin was less addictive, less subject to abuse and diversion, or less likely to cause tolerance or withdrawal than other pain medications; That specific prescribing physician relied upon that misstatement by that Purdue sales representative and, in reliance on that misstatement, prescribed OxyContin rather than an alternative pain medication (e.g. Percocet) for one of the private third-party payor's insured individuals; That the physician prescribed OxyContin for the insured because of the misstatement and not because of the other attributes of OxyContin (e.g., twelve-hour dosing or the absence of acetaminophen, which risks liver toxicity); That the private third-party payor paid for that prescription of OxyContin; and That the private third-party payor paid more for the OxyContin prescription than the particular alternative pain medication that the prescribing physician would have prescribed if he or she had not relied on the misstatement and prescribed OxyContin
context: Purdue's legal defense argument demonstrates how the company filters acknowledgment of harm by imposing elaborate causation requirements that place burden on third-party victims.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Courts consistently found no proximate causation
original_label: Courts consistently found no proximate causation
quote: Courts have consistently found that despite extensive discovery, plaintiffs were unable to show that Purdue's misbranding proximately caused their injuries. See, e.g., Bodie v. Purdue Pharma Co., No. 05-13834, 2007 WL 1577964, at *3 (11th Cir. June 1, 2007) (affirming the district court's conclusion that the plaintiff's claims failed because he could not show that he was proximately harmed by Purdue's allegedly inadequate warnings); Koenig v. Purdue Pharma Co., 435 F. Supp. 2d 551, 556 (N.D. Tex. 2006) (Because plaintiffs have failed to show that an adequate warning would have changed [the physician]'s decision to prescribe OxyContin, and because [the physician] testified that he would not have changed his decision, the Court finds that Plaintiffs have failed to raise a genuine fact issue.); Timmons v. Purdue Pharma Co., No. 8:04-CV-1479-T-26MAP, 2006 WL 263602, at *4 (M.D. Fla. Feb. 2, 2006) (Even if OxyContin were considered unreasonably dangerous, which it has not been deemed so, Plaintiff has failed to show any evidence of causation.); McCauley, 331 F. Supp. 2d at 465 (granting Purdue's motion for summary judgment and stating The plaintiffs' burden is greater than merely showing a temporal link between their use of OxyContin and any injuries they sustained. Instead, it is evidence of the causal link between OxyContin and their injuries that the plaintiffs lack.); Foister v. Purdue Pharma, L.P., No. 01-268-JBC, 2001 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 23765, at *27 (E.D. Ky. Dec. 27, 2001) (denying the plaintiffs' motion for injunctive relief and noting that the plaintiffs have failed to produce any evidence showing that the defendant's marketing, promotional, or distribution practices have ever caused even one table of OxyContin to be inappropriately prescribed or diverted.)
context: The court catalogs multiple civil litigation outcomes where plaintiffs failed to establish proximate causation between Purdue's misbranding and injury, demonstrating systematic filtering of harm recognition.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Class certification denied due to causation complexity
original_label: Class certification denied due to causation complexity
quote: It is argued that restitution might be handled in this case as with a civil class action claim, but class certification has been generally denied in OxyContin claims because of the variety of causation issues. See, e.g., Hurtado v. Purdue Pharma Co., No. 12648/03, 2005 WL 192351, at *1(N.Y. Sup. Ct. Jan. 24, 2005) (denying class certification because of the different reasons and methods by which the drug was prescribed and used.)
context: The court notes structural barriers to collective harm recognition, as courts have refused to certify classes in OxyContin cases due to causation complexity.

label: Plea agreement precludes restitution to private victims
original_label: Plea agreement precludes restitution to private victims
quote: The plea agreements preclude restitution other than as set forth in the agreements and a number of alleged victims object to this provision, contending that the amounts allocated to private parties are insufficient, compared to the recovery by governmental victims
context: The court describes the terms negotiated between Purdue and the government that limit financial accountability to private victims of OxyContin misbranding.

label: Substantial monetary settlement package agreed
original_label: Substantial monetary settlement package agreed
quote: Under the law, Purdue is subject to a penalty of five years probation and a fine of up to $500,000. In its plea agreement, Purdue has agreed to substantial additional monetary sanctions totaling $600 million, reported to be one of the largest in the history of the pharmaceutical industry. The amount includes the following: $100,615,797.25 payable to federal government health care agencies under a Civil Settlement Agreement; $59,384,202.75 in escrow for those states that elect to settle their claims against Purdue. These civil settlements to the federal and state government total $160 million, of which the federal government is receiving sixty percent; $3,471,220.68 to Medicaid programs for improperly calculated rebates; $500,000 fine to the United States; $20 million in trust to the Commonwealth of Virginia for operating the Virginia Prescription Monitoring Program; $5.3 million to the Virginia Medicaid Fraud Control Unit's Program Income Fund; $276.1 million forfeiture to the United States; $130 million to settle private civil claims related to OxyContin; and $4,628,779.32 to be expended by Purdue for monitoring costs in connection with a Corporate Integrity Agreement with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
context: The court details the comprehensive financial settlement and remedial measures negotiated as part of Purdue's organizational response to the misbranding charges.

label: Individual defendants pay millions but avoid imprisonment
original_label: Individual defendants pay millions but avoid imprisonment
quote: The individual defendants are subject to a punishment of twelve months imprisonment and a fine of up to $100,000. In their plea agreements, they have agreed to pay a total of $34.5 million to the Virginia Medicaid Fraud Unit's Program Income Fund. In return, the government has agreed to sentences for them without any imprisonment
context: The court describes the negotiated sentence for individual executives that trades substantial personal financial penalties for complete avoidance of prison time.

label: Restitution statute allows court to decline based on complexity
original_label: Restitution statute allows court to decline based on complexity
quote: To the extent that the court determines that the complication and prolongation of the sentencing process resulting from the fashioning of an order of restitution under this section outweighs the need to provide restitution to any victims, the court may decline to make such an order
context: The court cites the Victim and Witness Protection Act provision that enables procedural avoidance of restitution determinations when causation complexity would extend sentencing.

label: Court allowed victim participation in sentencing
original_label: Court allowed victim participation in sentencing
quote: Notice of the sentencing and of the right of victims to attend and speak was published on the court's Web site, and all of the pleadings and other documents filed in the case have been available for viewing without charge on that site. The court received numerous letters and e-mails from interested members of the public concening the scheduled sentencing. Any person known to be a possible victim was given individual notice of the hearing and of the right to speak, and over twenty people accepted this opportunity. The main courtroom was full, and a second courtroom equipped with an audio and video feed was used for the overflow
context: The court documents the procedures established to give victims notice and opportunity to be heard, though this did not result in restitution orders.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Judge forbidden from participating in plea negotiations
original_label: Judge forbidden from participating in plea negotiations
quote: On the other hand, I am forbidden by law to participate in plea discussions, Fed. R. Crim. P. 11(c)(1), and I will not reject these agreements simply because they do not contain provisions that I would have preferred
context: The judge explains the formal rule that separates judicial review of plea agreements from participation in their negotiation, constraining judicial attention to post-hoc evaluation.

label: Criminal information filed as formal triggering event
original_label: Criminal information filed as formal triggering event
quote: The Information in this case charges, among other things, that Beginning on or about December 12, 1995, and continuing until on or about June 30, 2001, certain PURDUE supervisors and employees, with the intent to defraud or mislead, marketed and promoted OxyContin as less addictive, less subject to abuse and diversion, and less likely to cause tolerance and withdrawal than other pain medications
context: The formal criminal Information filed by the U.S. Attorney charges Purdue with misbranding spanning over five years, representing the official triggering event for this proceeding.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Purdue emphasizes intervening conduct breaks causation chain
original_label: Purdue emphasizes intervening conduct breaks causation chain
quote: Purdue further argues that the chain of causation between the harm alleged and the misbranding offense could have been broken by any intervening act on behalf of the insured patient or the prescribing health care professional. For example, if patients obtained OxyContin improperly by deceiving their physicians or by altering an otherwise proper prescription, the third-party payors would not be entitled to restitution for those prescriptions since the misbranding did not directly and proximately caused any financial loss to the third-party payor. Or if a physician negligently prescribed OxyContin, the third-party payor that paid for that prescription is also not entitled to restitution because the misbranding once again did not directly and proximately cause the third-party payor's financial loss
context: Purdue's legal strategy deflects responsibility by emphasizing contingencies and intervening actors that break any causal chain from misbranding to victim harm.

label: Judge expresses concern but declines to mandate drug treatment funding
original_label: Judge expresses concern but declines to mandate drug treatment funding
quote: I would have preferred that the plea agreements had allocated some amount of the money for the education of those at risk from the improper use of prescription drugs, and the treatment of those who have succumbed to such use. Prescription drug abuse is rampant in all areas of our country, particularly among young people, causing untold misery and harm. The White House drug policy office estimates that such abuse rose seventeen percent from 2001 to 2005. That office reports that currently there are more new abusers of prescription drugs than new users of any illicit drugs. As recently reported, Young people mistakenly believe prescription drugs are safer than street drugs . . . but accidental prescription drug deaths are rising and students who abuse pills are more likely to drive fast, binge-drink and engage in other dangerous behaviors. It has been estimated that there are more than 6.4 million prescription drug abusers in the United States. On the other hand, I am forbidden by law to participate in plea discussions, Fed. R. Crim. P. 11(c)(1), and I will not reject these agreements simply because they do not contain provisions that I would have preferred. The government has represented that it did not demand inclusion of a treatment provision in the plea agreements because national drug policy has been placed by Congress in the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Service Administration, an agency of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. The government prosecutors were reluctant to direct treatment funds in a manner beyond their expertise and possibly contrary to national policy
context: The judge documents public health concerns about prescription drug abuse but accepts prosecutorial rationale for not mandating treatment funding in the plea agreement.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Judge accepts lack of incarceration despite substantial public harm
original_label: Judge accepts lack of incarceration despite substantial public harm
quote: The plea agreements provide for no incarceration for the individual defendants. The government points out that a sentence of incarceration under the federal sentencing guidelines would be unusual based on the facts of the case. The government is also convinced that the nature of the convictions of the individual defendants— based on strict liability for misbranding—will send a strong deterrent message to the pharmaceutical industry. The defendants point to their lack of prior criminal record, their strong commitment to civic and charitable endeavors, as well as their other positive personal attributes. On the other hand, the potential damage by the misbranding disclosed in this case was substantial and I do not minimize the danger to the public from this crime. The defendants voluntarily accepted responsibility over this business enterprise, for which they were generously rewarded. category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Dissent explains bankruptcy court factors for non-debtor releases
original_label: Dissent explains bankruptcy court factors for non-debtor releases
quote: First, and critically, the court must determine whether the released party is closely related to the debtor—for example, through an indemnification agreement—where a suit against the non-debtor is, in essence, a suit against the debtor or will deplete the assets of the estate. Second, the court must determine if the claims against the non-debtor are factually and legally intertwined with claims against the debtor. Third, the court must ensure that the scope of the releases is tailored to only the claims that must be released to protect the plan. Fourth, even then, the court should approve the release only if it is truly essential to the plan's success and the reorganization would fail without it. Fifth, the court must consider whether, as part of the settlement, the non-debtor party has paid substantial assets to the estate. Sixth, the court should determine if the plan provides fair payment to creditors for their released claims. Seventh, the court must ensure that the creditors overwhelmingly approve of the release, which the Second Circuit defined as a 75 percent bare minimum.
context: Justice Kavanaugh's dissent catalogs the developed multi-factor test from Second Circuit precedent for evaluating appropriateness of nonconsensual releases.

original_label: Purdue filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2019

original_label: Bankruptcy court identified potential race to courthouse problem

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas

original_label: Dissent claims Court ignored victim preference for settlement

original_label: Payment plan offered $3,500 to $48,000 per victim in installments

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Dissent argues bankruptcy purpose is collective fair recovery
original_label: Dissent argues bankruptcy purpose is collective fair recovery
quote: The purpose of bankruptcy law is to address the collective-action problem that a bankruptcy poses. When a company's liabilities exceed its ability to pay creditors, every creditor has an incentive to maximize its own recovery before other creditors deplete the pot. Without a mandatory collective system, the creditors would race to the courthouse to recover first. One or a few successful creditors could then recover substantial funds, deplete the assets, and drive the company under—leaving other creditors with nothing.
context: Justice Kavanaugh's dissent articulates the foundational principle that bankruptcy law is designed to solve collective-action problems, which shapes attention priorities.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Majority rejects dissent's reliance on bankruptcy purpose
original_label: Majority rejects dissent's reliance on bankruptcy purpose

So, yes, bankruptcy law may serve to address some collective-action problems, but no one (save perhaps the dissent) thinks it provides a bankruptcy court with a roving commission to resolve all such problems that happen its way, blind to the role other mechanisms (legislation, class actions, multi-district litigation, consensual settlements, among others) play in addressing them.

label: Settlement reached through arms-length negotiation after extensive discovery
original_label: Settlement reached through arms-length negotiation after extensive discovery

original_label: Asbestos bankruptcies provided precedent for non-debtor releases

Robins declared bankruptcy in 1985 in the face of massive tort liability for injuries from its defective intrauterine device, the Dalkon Shield, nearly 200,000 victims filed proof of claims. A plan provision releasing the company's directors and insurance company ensured that the estate would not be depleted through indemnity or contribution claims, or claims brought directly against the directors or insurer. Preventing the victims from engaging in piecemeal litigation against the non-debtor directors and insurance company was the only way to ensure equality of treatment of similarly situated creditors.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas

original_label: Majority focused on statutory text and ejusdem generis canon
quote: When faced with a catchall phrase like paragraph (6), courts do not necessarily afford it the broadest possible construction it can bear. Instead, we generally appreciate that the catchall must be interpreted in light of its surrounding context and read to embrace only objects similar in nature to the specific examples preceding it. Here, each of the preceding paragraphs concerns the rights and responsibilities of the debtor; and they authorize a bankruptcy court to adjust claims without consent only to the extent such claims concern the debtor.
context: The majority's statutory interpretation agenda centered on textual analysis and the ejusdem generis canon rather than bankruptcy policy.

label: Research institute detects off-cycle NOx exceedance
original_label: Research institute detects off-cycle NOx exceedance
quote: Researchers at the Joint Research Centre (JRC) in Europe have identified off-cycle oxides of nitrogen (NOx) emissions from light-duty diesel vehicles (LDV) to substantially exceed the Euro 3-5 emissions standards on average by a factor of 4 to 7 over specific test routes [1]. Hence, the study concluded that the introduction of tighter emissions limits for the purpose of vehicle/engine certification has not necessarily translated into effective on-road NOx reductions of the same magnitude [1].

original_label: Thermodynamic constraints limit SCR conversion efficiency

original_label: On-road testing reveals NOx far exceeds standards

This was speculated to be due to an extended duration of lean exhaust conditions and a lack of frequent enrichment of the exhaust gas (λ < 1) while DPF regeneration was ongoing, leading to an inhibition of necessary LNT regeneration (DeNOx), and thus, causing the NOx storage catalyst to become saturated with NOx emissions that ultimately started to break through.
context: Executive summary describes an observed anomaly: Vehicle A's NOx emissions increased substantially during a specific operational condition (DPF regeneration), suggesting a control system conflict.

original_label: Particulate emissions exceed standard during regeneration

original_label: Mechanical accounting standards motivate financial engineering to circumvent rules
quote: Many U.S. accounting standards tend to be mechanical and inflexible. Clearcut rules have some advantages, but the downside is that this approach motivates financial engineering designed specifically to circumvent these knife-edge rules, as is well understood in the tax literature.
context: Analysis of accounting rule structure showing how mechanical standards created incentives to engineer transactions specifically designed to evade attention mechanisms.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Andersen develops mechanical audit procedures reducing business judgment
original_label: Andersen develops mechanical audit procedures reducing business judgment
quote: They lobbied for mechanical accounting and auditing standards and developed standard operating procedures to reduce the variability in audits. This approach reduced the cost of audits and provided a defense in the case of litigation. But it also meant that auditors were more likely to view their job narrowly, rather than as matters of broader business judgment.
context: Analysis of auditor industry evolution showing how procedural changes created filtering mechanism that reduced attention to broader business context of accounting decisions.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Audit firm partner compensation tied to client retention
original_label: Audit firm partner compensation tied to client retention
quote: One way was by aggressively pursuing a high-volume strategy, and so audit partner compensation and promotion became more closely linked to a cordial relationship with top management that attracted new audit clients and retained existing clients. This made it difficult for partners to be effective watchdogs.
context: Analysis of audit firm compensation structure showing how incentives directed partner attention to client relationship rather than warning signal detection.

label: Auditor consulting business diverts talent and attention from audit
original_label: Auditor consulting business diverts talent and attention from audit
quote: The large audit firms also responded to challenges to their core business by developing new higher-margin, higher-growth consulting services. This diversification strategy deflected top management energy and partner talent from the audit side of the business to the more profitable consulting part.
context: Analysis of audit firm structure showing how business model divided attention and talent away from core audit function where warning signals should have been detected.

label: Chewco structured to avoid consolidation despite substance violations
original_label: Chewco structured to avoid consolidation despite substance violations
quote: However, several controversial special purpose entities were designed primarily to achieve financial reporting objectives. For example, in 1997, Enron wanted to buy out a partner's stake in one of its many joint ventures. However, Enron did not want to show any debt from financing the acquisition or from the joint venture on its balance sheet. Chewco, a special purpose entity that was controlled by an Enron executive and raised debt that was guaranteed by Enron, acquired the joint venture stake for $383 million. The transaction was structured in such a way that Enron did not have to consolidate Chewco or the joint venture into its financials, enabling it effectively to acquire the partnership interest without recognizing any additional debt on its books.
context: Analysis documenting specific transaction anomaly showing structure designed explicitly to circumvent accounting disclosure requirements.

label: Minimal disclosure on special purpose entity relationships
original_label: Minimal disclosure on special purpose entity relationships
quote: In addition to the accounting failures, Enron provided only minimal disclosure on its relations with the special purpose entities. The company represented to investors that it had hedged downside risk in its own illiquid investments through transactions with special purpose entities. Yet investors were unaware that the special purpose entities were actually using Enron's own stock and financial guarantees to carry out these hedges, so that Enron was not actually protected from downside risk.
context: Analysis of information channel failure showing how disclosure procedures were designed to prevent investors from receiving critical information about risk structure.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Accounting rules allow independent equity interpretation dispute
original_label: Accounting rules allow independent equity interpretation dispute
quote: Enron had used hundreds of special purpose entities by 2001. Many of these were used to fund the purchase of forward contracts with gas producers to supply gas to utilities under long-term fixed contracts. However, several controversial special purpose entities were designed primarily to achieve financial reporting objectives. For financial reporting purposes, a series of rules is used to determine whether a special purpose entity is a separate entity from the sponsor. These require that an independent third-party owner have a substantive equity stake that is 'at risk' in the special purpose entity, which has been interpreted as at least 3 percent of the special purpose entity's total debt and equity.
context: Analysis of accounting rule structure showing how specific percentage threshold created discrete interpretation rule that entities could be designed to just meet or evade.

label: Blockbuster video deal with extreme revenue growth assumptions
original_label: Blockbuster video deal with extreme revenue growth assumptions
quote: To assess the embedded expectations in Enron's stock price, begin by assuming that Enron's cost of equity was 12 percent, shown as a horizontal line in Exhibit 4. These assumptions are highly aggressive. For example, Enron's actual return on equity was 18 percent in 1996, 2.5 percent in 1997, 12.5 percent in 1998 and 12 percent in 1999. Thus, the firm would have had to achieve a dramatic increase in return on equity and sustain it forever. The revenue growth needed to justify Enron's peak stock price would have required a dramatic extension of its business model to new areas.
context: Analysis showing valuation anomaly between required assumptions and historical performance that should have generated warning signals for investors.

label: Enron defers asset write-downs under auditor pressure
original_label: Enron defers asset write-downs under auditor pressure
quote: When the credit risks at the special purpose entities became clear, requiring Enron to take a write-down, the auditors apparently succumbed to pressure from Enron's management and permitted the company to defer recognizing the charges.
context: Evidence of organizational response showing deferral of required disclosure in response to management pressure, representing failure to act on warning signal.

original_label: October 2001 Enron charge announcement triggered SEC inquiry

original_label: November 2001 restatement revealed multibillion dollar losses

original_label: Alaska Airlines door plug incident triggers heightened oversight

original_label: Government selected monitor, Boeing has veto power

original_label: Monitor selected by and reports to Government, not Court

original_label: Compliance with monitor recommendations not required as probation condition

original_label: Government monitoring for three years produced no visible compliance improvements

original_label: Boeing's role in strike of monitor candidates raises discrimination concerns

original_label: Boeing tied executive compensation to DEI goals

original_label: Boeing aspirational DEI targets included racial quotas

context: Judge O'Connor documenting Boeing's formally stated DEI targets that included explicit racial representation goals.

original_label: Government admits lack of awareness of specific policy leading to diversity requirement

label: Government's monitor-selection guidance evolved to emphasize diversity and inclusion over merit
original_label: Government's monitor-selection guidance evolved to emphasize diversity and inclusion over merit

context: Judge O'Connor tracing the historical shift in DOJ policy from merit-based monitor selection (2008, 2018) to incorporation of diversity-and-inclusion language (2018 DPA, 2023 guidance).

original_label: 2023 DOJ Justice Manual explicitly requires diversity and inclusion in monitor selection

original_label: Executive Order 14035 defines diversity to include race

original_label: Court skeptical Government will exclude race from monitor selection despite claims

original_label: Plea agreement marginalizes Court from monitor selection and probation oversight

The Government has monitored Boeing for three years now. It is not clear what all Boeing has done to breach the Deferred Prosecution Agreement ("DPA"). The victims assert the "Government was forced to find that Boeing violated [the DPA] after the door fell off the Alaska airplane." Boeing hints that it may have legitimate arguments in opposition to the Government's determination of breach. Regardless, taken as true that Boeing breached the DPA, it is fair to say the Government's attempt to ensure compliance has failed.
context: Judge O'Connor explaining why structural exclusion of the Court from oversight mechanisms is problematic given prior Government monitoring failures.

label: Court rejects plea agreement due to marginalization and diversity provisions
original_label: Court rejects plea agreement due to marginalization and diversity provisions
quote: Accordingly, the diversity-and-inclusion provision renders the plea agreement against the public interest. At this point, the public interest requires the Court to step in. Marginalizing the Court in the selection and monitoring of the independent monitor as the plea agreement does undermines public confidence in Boeing's probation, fails to promote respect for the law, and is therefore not in the public interest. Accordingly, the Court cannot accept the plea agreement.
context: Judge O'Connor announcing rejection of the plea agreement on grounds of both the diversity provision and Court marginalization.

label: Door fell off Alaska Airlines aircraft, triggering discovery of DPA breach
original_label: Door fell off Alaska Airlines aircraft, triggering discovery of DPA breach
quote: The victims assert the "Government was forced to find that Boeing violated [the DPA] after the door fell off the Alaska airplane."
context: Judge O'Connor describing an anomalous event that surfaced evidence of Boeing's non-compliance with a prior enforcement agreement.

label: Crash deaths and victims' families' objections trigger judicial reassessment
original_label: Crash deaths and victims' families' objections trigger judicial reassessment
quote: Years after the catastrophic Lion Air Flight JT610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight ET302 crashes and resulting 346 deaths, the United States and The Boeing Company ("Boeing") have now reached a plea agreement, which they urge the Court to accept. Among the Court's priorities at this point is to ensure Boeing adheres to an ethics and anti-fraud compliance program overseen by an independent monitor during Boeing's probation. A number of victims' families have objected to the plea agreement and argue it should be rejected for several reasons.
context: Judge O'Connor framing the case context: the underlying deaths and the subsequent victims' families' intervention redirecting judicial attention to adequacy of compliance mechanisms.

label: Pre-production crash tests reveal fuel tank rupture
original_label: Pre-production crash tests reveal fuel tank rupture
quote: Ford engineers discovered in pre-production crash tests that rear-end collisions would rupture the Pinto's fuel system extremely easily.
context: Dowie (1977) summarizes Ford's internal discovery of the defect during the Pinto's development phase.

label: Forty crash tests show consistent fuel tank failure
original_label: Forty crash tests show consistent fuel tank failure
quote: Internal company documents in our possession show that Ford has crash-tested the Pinto at a top-secret site more than 40 times and that every test made at over 25 mph without special structural alteration of the car has resulted in a ruptured fuel tank.
context: Dowie presents Ford's own test data showing systematic failures across numerous rear-end crash tests.

label: Eleven pre-production tests confirm fuel tank vulnerability
original_label: Eleven pre-production tests confirm fuel tank vulnerability
quote: Eleven of these tests, averaging a 31-mph impact speed, came before Pintos started rolling out of the factories. Only three cars passed the test with unbroken fuel tanks.
context: Dowie details the pre-production testing history that demonstrated the fuel tank defect before mass production began.

label: Plastic baffle, rubber bladder, and steel alternatives passed crash tests
original_label: Plastic baffle, rubber bladder, and steel alternatives passed crash tests
quote: In one of them an inexpensive light-weight plastic baffle was placed between the front of the gas tank and the differential housing, so those four bolts would not perforate the tank. In another successful test, a piece of steel was placed between the tank and the bumper. In the third test car the gas tank was lined with a rubber bladder. But none of these protective alterations was used in the mass-produced Pinto.
context: Dowie documents that Ford engineers tested and found viable safety solutions during pre-production but chose not to implement them in the final design.

label: Capri gas tank design proved safe in 50+ crash tests
original_label: Capri gas tank design proved safe in 50+ crash tests
quote: In pre-production planning, engineers seriously considered using in the Pinto the same kind of gas tank Ford uses in the Capri. The Capri tank rides over the rear axle and differential housing. It has been so successful in over 50 crash tests that Ford used it in its Experimental Safety Vehicle, which withstood rear-end impacts of 60 mph.
context: Dowie reveals that Ford possessed a proven safer alternative design available from its own existing product line.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Accelerated production schedule compressed development time
original_label: Accelerated production schedule compressed development time
quote: The normal time span from conception to production of a new car model is about 43 months. The Pinto schedule was set at just under 25.
context: Dowie explains the structural constraint that accelerated timelines created, showing how schedule pressure was embedded in the organization's planning process.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Tooling proceeded before crash test completion
original_label: Tooling proceeded before crash test completion
quote: Normally, an auto company doesn't begin tooling until the other processes are almost over: you don't want to make the machines that stamp and press and grind metal into the shape of car parts until you know all those parts will work well together. But Iacocca's speed-up meant Pinto tooling went on at the same time as product development. So when crash tests revealed a serious defect in the gas tank, it was too late. The tooling was well under way.
context: Dowie describes how the compressed schedule created a procedural lock-in that prevented design correction even after defects were discovered.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Product objectives excluded safety from explicit priorities
original_label: Product objectives excluded safety from explicit priorities
quote: The product objectives are clearly stated in the Pinto "green book." This is a thick, top-secret manual in green covers containing a step-by-step production plan for the model, detailing the metallurgy, weight, strength and quality of every part in the car. The product objectives for the Pinto are repeated in an article by Ford executive F.G. Olsen published by the Society of Automotive Engineers. He lists these product objectives as follows: 1. TRUE SUBCOMPACT... 2. LOW COST OF OWNERSHIP... 3. CLEAR PRODUCT SUPERIORITY... Safety, you will notice, is not there. It is not mentioned in the entire article.
context: Dowie analyzes the formal planning documents to show that safety was structurally absent from the organization's stated priorities and attention-directing framework.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Weight and cost limits enforced iron-fisted discipline
original_label: Weight and cost limits enforced iron-fisted discipline
quote: Heightening the anti-safety pressure on Pinto engineers was an important goal set by Iacocca known as "the limits of 2,000." The Pinto was not to weigh an ounce over 2,000 pounds and not to cost a cent over $2,000. "Iacocca enforced these limits with an iron hand," recalls the engineer quoted earlier. So, even when a crash test showed that that one-pound, one-dollar piece of plastic stopped the puncture of the gas tank, it was thrown out as extra cost and extra weight.
context: Dowie documents specific cost and weight constraints that were rigidly enforced and that directly screened out safety improvements even when tested and proven.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Safety was taboo; schedule and cost were sacred
original_label: Safety was taboo; schedule and cost were sacred
quote: "Hell no," replied an engineer who worked on the Pinto, a high company official for many years, who, unlike several others at Ford, maintains a necessarily clandestine concern for safety. "That person would have been fired. Safety wasn't a popular subject around Ford in those days. With Lee it was taboo. Whenever a problem was raised that meant a delay on the Pinto, Lee would chomp on his cigar, look out the window and say 'Read the product objectives and get back to work.'"
context: An anonymous Ford engineer describes the informal rules and norms that made safety concerns unwelcome and punishable.

label: Lee Iacocca drove schedule and cost-first priorities
original_label: Lee Iacocca drove schedule and cost-first priorities
quote: Like the Mustang, the Pinto became known in the company as "Lee's car." Lee Iococca wanted that little car in the showrooms of America with the 1971 models. So he ordered his engineering vice president, Bob Alexander, to oversee what was probably the shortest production planning period in modern automotive history.
context: Dowie establishes Iacocca's position and authority in directing the Pinto program with schedule and market imperatives.

label: Engineers knew of defect but feared speaking to leadership
original_label: Engineers knew of defect but feared speaking to leadership
quote: When it was discovered the gas tank was unsafe, did anyone go to Iacocca and tell him? "Hell no," replied an engineer who worked on the Pinto, a high company official for many years, who, unlike several others at Ford, maintains a necessarily clandestine concern for safety. "That person would have been fired."
context: An anonymous Ford engineer reveals the hierarchical barrier and fear that prevented upward communication of safety concerns to the decision-maker.

label: Lou Tubben's safety presentation met with no attendance
original_label: Lou Tubben's safety presentation met with no attendance
quote: Lou Tubben is one of the most popular engineers at Ford. He's a friendly, outgoing guy with a genuine concern for safety. By 1971 he had grown so concerned about gas-tank integrity that he asked his boss if he could prepare a presentation on safer tank design. Tubben and his boss had both worked on the Pinto and shared a concern for its safety. His boss gave him the go-ahead, scheduled a date for the presentation and invited all company engineers and key production planning personnel. When time came for the meeting, a grand total of two people showed up—Lou Tubben and his boss.
context: Dowie recounts an episode where the formal procedural channel for raising safety concerns (scheduled presentation to engineers and planners) failed due to structural neglect of the topic.

label: Safety Research Center served anti-regulatory lobbying, not consumer protection
original_label: Safety Research Center served anti-regulatory lobbying, not consumer protection
quote: Says John Versace, executive safety engineer at Ford's Safety Research Center, "Ulcers are running pretty high among the engineers who worked on the Pinto. Every lawyer in the country seems to want to take their depositions." (The Safety Research Center is an impressive glass and concrete building standing by itself about a mile from Ford World Headquarters in Dearborn. Looking at it, one imagines its large staff protects consumers from burned and broken limbs. Not so. The Center is the technical support arm of Jack Echold's 14-person anti-regulatory lobbying team in World Headquarters.)
context: Dowie reveals that Ford's ostensible safety research organization was actually structured to support regulatory opposition, not internal safety improvements.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Market competition and schedule drove decision-making
original_label: Market competition and schedule drove decision-making
quote: Fighting strong competition from Volkswagen for the lucrative small-car market, the Ford Motor Company rushed the Pinto into production in much less than the usual time. Iacocca argued forcefully that Volkswagen and the Japanese were going to capture the entire American subcompact market unless Ford put out its own alternative to the VW Beetle.
context: Dowie identifies the competitive market agenda that took precedence over engineering concerns during the Pinto program's launch.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Profitability dominated decisions over safety redesign
original_label: Profitability dominated decisions over safety redesign
quote: Until recently, it was clear that, whatever the cost of these settlements, it was not enough to seriously cut into the Pinto's enormous profits. The cost of retooling Pinto assembly lines and of equipping each car with a safety gadget like that $5.08 Goodyear bladder was, company accountants calculated, greater than that of paying out millions to survivors like Robbie Carlton or to widows and widowers of victims like Sandra Gillespie. The bottom line ruled, and inflammable Pintos kept rolling out of the factories.
context: Dowie documents that Ford's decision-making centered on profit maximization and cost comparison, with safety improvements explicitly ranked below settlement payouts.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Advertising dropped safety messaging that contradicted image
original_label: Advertising dropped safety messaging that contradicted image
quote: Burning Pintos have become such an embarrassment to Ford that its advertising agency, J. Walter Thompson, dropped a line from the end of a radio spot that read "Pinto leaves you with that warm feeling."
context: Dowie notes how Ford's marketing attention reacted to the fire risk by avoiding any warmth-related messaging, showing awareness of the danger.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Ford officials denied crash tests under oath despite evidence
original_label: Ford officials denied crash tests under oath despite evidence
quote: Internal company documents in our possession show that Ford has crash-tested the Pinto at a top-secret site more than 40 times and that every test made at over 25 mph without special structural alteration of the car has resulted in a ruptured fuel tank. Despite this, Ford officials denied under oath having crash-tested the Pinto.
context: Dowie presents evidence of Ford's deliberate misrepresentation to external parties (presumably legal proceedings) about the existence and findings of internal crash tests.

label: Cost-benefit analysis valued human life at $200,000
original_label: Cost-benefit analysis valued human life at $200,000
quote: Rather than be so uncouth as to come up with such a price tag itself, the auto industry pressured the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to do so. And in a 1972 report the agency decided a human life was worth $200,725. Inflationary forces have recently pushed the figure up to $278,000. Furnished with this useful tool, Ford immediately went to work using it to prove why various safety improvements were too expensive to make.
context: Dowie explains Ford's systematic organizational response: using external cost-benefit valuations to justify deferring safety improvements.

label: Ford memo calculates that $11 improvement unprofitable against $200k per-life value
original_label: Ford memo calculates that $11 improvement unprofitable against $200k per-life value
quote: Not long after the government arrived at the $200,725-per-life figure, it surfaced, rounded off to a cleaner $200,000, in an internal Ford memorandum. This cost-benefit analysis argued that Ford should not make an $11-per-car improvement that would prevent 180 fiery deaths a year. (This minor change would have prevented gas tanks from breaking so easily both in rear-end collisions, like Sandra Gillespie's, and in rollover accidents, where the same thing tends to happen.)
context: Dowie presents Ford's specific cost-benefit calculation showing the company chose not to implement a proven low-cost safety improvement based on the government's life valuation.

label: Ford underestimated burn injuries and overstated improvement cost
original_label: Ford underestimated burn injuries and overstated improvement cost
quote: First, note that Ford's table shows an equal number of burn deaths and burn injuries. This is false. All independent experts estimate that for each person who dies by an auto fire, many more are left with charred hands, faces and limbs. Andrew McGuire of the Northern California Burn Center estimates the ratio of burn injuries to deaths at ten to one instead of the one to one Ford shows here. The other side of the equation, the alleged $11 cost of a fire-prevention device, is also a misleading estimation. One document that was not sent to Washington by Ford was a "Confidential" cost analysis Mother Jones has managed to obtain, showing that crash fires could be largely prevented for considerably less than $11 a car. The cheapest method involves placing a heavy rubber bladder inside the gas tank to keep the fuel from spilling if the tank ruptures.
context: Dowie analyzes Ford's memorandum and reveals systematic understatement of benefits and overstatement of costs in the cost-benefit calculation submitted to regulators.

label: Goodyear bladder cost only $5.08 but Ford reported $11 cost
original_label: Goodyear bladder cost only $5.08 but Ford reported $11 cost
quote: We have in our possession crash-test reports showing that the Goodyear bladder worked well. On December 2, 1970 (two years before Echold sent his cost-benefit memo to Washington), Ford Motor Company ran a rear-end crash test on a car with the rubber bladder in the gas tank. The tank ruptured, but no fuel leaked. On January 15, 1971, Ford again tested the bladder and again it worked. The total purchase and installation cost of the bladder would have been $5.08 per car. That $5.08 could have saved the lives of Sandra Gillespie and several hundred others.
context: Dowie documents Ford's knowledge of a proven solution costing $5.08 per car, establishing that the $11 figure used in the cost-benefit memo was inflated.

label: Ford lobbied against safety standard for eight years
original_label: Ford lobbied against safety standard for eight years
quote: For more than eight years afterwards, Ford successfully lobbied, with extraordinary vigor and some blatant lies, against a key government safety standard that would have forced the company to change the Pinto's fire-prone gas tank.
context: Dowie summarizes Ford's sustained organizational response to regulatory pressure: systematic lobbying to delay or block safety standards.

label: Ford settled lawsuits rather than fix defect or go to jury
original_label: Ford settled lawsuits rather than fix defect or go to jury
quote: When the Pinto liability suits began, Ford strategy was to go to a jury. Confident it could hide the Pinto crash tests, Ford thought that juries of solid American registered voters would buy the industry doctrine that drivers, not cars, cause accidents. It didn't work. It seems that juries are much quicker to see the truth than bureaucracies, a fact that gives one confidence in democracy. Juries began ruling against the company, granting million-dollar awards to plaintiffs. "We'll never go to a jury again," says Al Stechter in Ford's Washington office. "Not in a fire case. Juries are just too sentimental. They see those charred remains and forget the evidence. No sir, we'll settle."
context: Dowie documents Ford's shift in litigation strategy from jury trial to out-of-court settlement once adverse verdicts revealed the weakness of the company's factual defense.

label: Settlements treated as profit calculation rather than safety signal
original_label: Settlements treated as profit calculation rather than safety signal
quote: Settlement involves less cash, smaller legal fees and less publicity, but it is an indication of the weakness of their case. Nevertheless, Ford has been settling when it is clear that the company can't pin the blame on the driver of the other car. But, since the company carries $2 million deductible product-liability insurance, these settlements have a direct impact on the bottom line. They must therefore be considered a factor in determining the net operating profit on the Pinto.
context: Dowie explains that Ford treated damage settlements as a business expense factored into profitability calculations rather than as feedback warranting design correction.

label: Rear-end collisions and burn deaths created stream of lawsuits
original_label: Rear-end collisions and burn deaths created stream of lawsuits
quote: While government bureaucrats dragged their feet on lifesaving Standard 301, a different kind of expert was taking a close look at the Pinto—the "recon man." "Recon" stands for reconstruction; recon men reconstruct accidents for police departments, insurance companies and lawyers who want to know exactly who or what caused an accident. It didn't take many rear-end Pinto accidents to demonstrate the weakness of the car. Recon men began encouraging lawyers to look beyond one driver or another to the manufacturer in their search for fault, particularly in the growing number of accidents where passengers were uninjured by collision but were badly burned by fire. Pinto lawsuits began mounting fast against Ford.
context: Dowie describes how field evidence from actual crashes (reconstructed by expert witnesses) created an external triggering event that shifted attention to Ford's liability and led to litigation.

label: Arjay Miller's near-death crash prompted safety advocacy in 1965
original_label: Arjay Miller's near-death crash prompted safety advocacy in 1965
quote: One evening in the mid-1960s, Arjay Miller was driving home from his office in Dearborn, Michigan, in the four-door Lincoln Continental that went with his job as president of the Ford Motor Company. On a crowded highway, another car struck his from the rear. The Continental spun around and burst into flames. Because he was wearing a shoulder-strap seat belt, Miller was unharmed by the crash, and because his doors didn't jam he escaped the gasoline-drenched, flaming wreck. But the accident made a vivid impression on him. Several months later, on July 15, 1965, he recounted it to a U.S. Senate subcommittee that was hearing testimony on auto safety legislation. "I still have burning in my mind the image of that gas tank on fire," Miller said. He went on to express an almost passionate interest in controlling fuel-fed fires in cars that crash or roll over. He spoke with excitement about the fabric gas tank Ford was testing at that very moment. "If it proves out," he promised the senators, it will be a feature you will see in our standard cars."
context: Dowie opens with a precedent: Ford's president experienced a fuel-fed fire hazard in 1965 and publicly committed to addressing it, yet the Pinto program seven years later ignored this institutional memory.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Engineering concern suppressed by informal norm against safety discourse
original_label: Engineering concern suppressed by informal norm against safety discourse
quote: A Ford engineer, who doesn't want his name used, comments: "This company is run by salesmen, not engineers; so the priority is styling, not safety." He goes on to tell a story about gas-tank safety at Ford: Lou Tubben is one of the most popular engineers at Ford. He's a friendly, outgoing guy with a genuine concern for safety. By 1971 he had grown so concerned about gas-tank integrity that he asked his boss if he could prepare a presentation on safer tank design. Tubben and his boss had both worked on the Pinto and shared a concern for its safety. His boss gave him the go-ahead, scheduled a date for the presentation and invited all company engineers and key production planning personnel. When time came for the meeting, a grand total of two people showed up—Lou Tubben and his boss. "So you see," continued the anonymous Ford engineer ironically, "there are a few of us here at Ford who are concerned about fire safety." He adds: "They are mostly engineers who have to study a lot of accident reports and look at pictures of burned people. But we don't talk about it much. It isn't a popular subject."
context: Dowie quotes an anonymous Ford engineer explaining how safety concerns were filtered and neglected through informal organizational norms that discouraged their discussion and visibility.

label: Jack Echold led anti-regulatory lobbying masquerading as safety research
original_label: Jack Echold led anti-regulatory lobbying masquerading as safety research
quote: The Center is the technical support arm of Jack Echold's 14-person anti-regulatory lobbying team in World Headquarters.
context: Dowie identifies Echold's structural position as director of an anti-safety regulatory effort, revealing how the organization centralized opposition to safety standards.

label: Ford lobbied regulators with multi-year technical objections to delay standard
original_label: Ford lobbied regulators with multi-year technical objections to delay standard
quote: Ford picked portions of Standard 301 for strong opposition way back in 1968 when the Pinto was still in the blueprint stage. The intent of 301, and the 300 series that followed it, was to protect drivers and passengers after a crash occurs. Without question the worst post-crash hazard is fire. So Standard 301 originally proposed that all cars should be able to withstand a fixed barrier impact of 20 mph (that is, running into a wall at that speed) without losing fuel. When the standard was proposed, Ford engineers pulled their crash-test results out of their files. The front ends of most cars were no problem—with minor alterations they could stand the impact without losing fuel. "We were already working on the front end," Ford engineer Dick Kimble admitted. "We knew we could meet the test on the front end." But with the Pinto particularly, a 20-mph rear-end standard meant redesigning the entire rear end of the car. With the Pinto scheduled for production in August of 1970, and with $200 million worth of tools in place, adoption of this standard would have created a minor financial disaster. So Standard 301 was targeted for delay, and, with some assistance from its industry associates, Ford succeeded beyond its wildest expectations: the standard was not adopted until the 1977 model year.
context: Dowie traces Ford's deliberate eight-year strategy to block a safety standard that would have required rear-end design changes after tooling was already committed.

label: Ford used technical complexity and successive arguments to delay standard adoption
original_label: Ford used technical complexity and successive arguments to delay standard adoption
quote: There are several main techniques in the art of combating a government safety standard: a) make your arguments in succession, so the feds can be working on disproving only one at a time; b) claim that the real problem is not X but Y (we already saw one instance of this in "the problem is not cars but people"); c) no matter how ridiculous each argument is, accompany it with thousands of pages of highly technical assertions it will take the government months or, preferably, years to test. Ford's large and active Washington office brought these techniques to new heights and became the envy of the lobbyists' trade.
context: Dowie identifies Ford's organizational tactics for regulatory delay: systematic use of technical objections and successive reframing to exhaust regulators' capacity and time.

label: Ford initially argued fires were statistically minor problem
original_label: Ford initially argued fires were statistically minor problem
quote: The Ford people started arguing against Standard 301 way back in 1968 with a strong attack of technique b). Fire, they said, was not the real problem. Sure, cars catch fire and people burn occasionally. But statistically auto fires were such a minor problem that NHTSA should really concern itself with other matters.
context: Dowie documents Ford's first lobbying argument (claiming fires were not a significant hazard), which was refuted by independent research.

label: When fire data contradicted Ford, it shifted to rear-end collision rarity argument
original_label: When fire data contradicted Ford, it shifted to rear-end collision rarity argument
quote: Ford lobbyists then used technique a)—bringing up a new argument. Their line then became: yes, perhaps burn accidents do happen, but rear-end collisions are relatively rare (note the echo of technique b) here as well). Thus Standard 301 was not needed.
context: Dowie documents Ford's successive reframing of regulatory objections after its first claim (fires are rare) was contradicted by external research.

label: When rear-end collision data contradicted Ford, it shifted to impact-kills argument
original_label: When rear-end collision data contradicted Ford, it shifted to impact-kills argument
quote: Ford now had to enter its third round of battling the new regulations. On the "the problem is not X but Y" principle, the company had to look around for something new to get itself off the hook. One might have thought that, faced with all the latest statistics on the horrifying number of deaths in flaming accidents, Ford would find the task difficult. But the company's rhetoric was brilliant. The problem was not burns, but…impact! Most of the people killed in these fiery accidents, claimed Ford, would have died whether the car burned or not. They were killed by the kinetic force of the impact, not the fire.
context: Dowie traces Ford's third major reframing of lobbying arguments after independent research refuted the rear-end rarity claim.

label: When impact argument failed, Ford raised technical objections to test criteria
original_label: When impact argument failed, Ford raised technical objections to test criteria
quote: Waiting, as it normally does, until the last day allowed for response, Ford filed with NHTSA a gargantuan batch of letters, studies and charts now arguing that the federal testing criteria were unfair. Ford also argued that design changes required to meet the standard would take 43 months, which seemed like a rather long time in light of the fact that the entire Pinto was designed in about two years. Specifically, new complaints about the standard involved the weight of the test vehicle, whether or not the brakes should be engaged at the moment of impact and the claim that the standard should only apply to cars, not trucks or buses. Perhaps the most amusing argument was that the engine should not be idling during crash tests, the rationale being that an idling engine meant that the gas tank had to contain gasoline and that the hot lights needed to film the crash might ignite the gasoline and cause a fire.
context: Dowie documents Ford's fourth phase of regulatory delay: filing technical objections to test methodology that required additional NHTSA analysis.

label: Henry Ford II predicted regulatory compliance would destroy the industry
original_label: Henry Ford II predicted regulatory compliance would destroy the industry
quote: All Ford had to do was convince men like John Volpe, Claude Brinegar and William Coleman (successive Secretaries of Transportation during the Nixon-Ford years) that certain safety standards would add so much to the price of cars that fewer people would buy them. This could damage the auto industry, which was still believed to be the bulwark of the American economy. "Compliance to these standards," Henry Ford II prophesied at more than one press conference, "will shut down the industry."
context: Dowie documents Ford's public executive messaging to regulators, claiming that safety compliance would cause industry collapse.

label: 1977 Pinto passed federal rear-end test; Canadian-built car used in test
original_label: 1977 Pinto passed federal rear-end test; Canadian-built car used in test
quote: To everyone's surprise, the 1977 Pinto recently passed a rear-end crash test in Phoenix, Arizona, for NHTSA. The agency was so convinced the Pinto would fail that it was the first car tested. Amazingly, it did not burst into flame. How did it pass? Remember that one-dollar, one-pound plastic baffle that was on one of the three modified Pintos that passed the pre-production crash tests nearly ten years ago? Well, it is a standard feature on the 1977 Pinto. But was it? What Tom Grubbs and the Department of Transportation didn't know when they tested the car was that it was manufactured in St. Thomas, Ontario.
context: Dowie reveals that the 1977 Pinto test vehicle that passed was Canadian-built (subject to stricter standards) rather than American-built, suggesting selective test vehicle sourcing.

label: Regulator discovered Canadian Pintos in Arizona dealerships
original_label: Regulator discovered Canadian Pintos in Arizona dealerships
quote: Tom Irwin is the business manager of Charlie Rossi Ford, the Scottsdale, Arizona, dealership that sold the Pinto to Tom Grubbs. He refused to explain why he was selling Fords made in Canada when there is a huge Pinto assembly plant much closer by in California. "I know why you're asking that question, and I'm not going to answer it," he blurted out. "You'll have to ask the company." But Ford's regional office in Phoenix has "no explanation" for the presence of Canadian cars in their local dealerships. Farther up the line in Dearborn, Ford people claim there is absolutely no difference between American and Canadian Pintos. They say cars are shipped back and forth across the border as a matter of course.
context: Dowie documents how independent investigation revealed that Ford may have strategically placed Canadian-built vehicles (subject to stricter safety standards) for federal testing.

label: Pharmacist reports prescriber diversion concern
original_label: Pharmacist reports prescriber diversion concern
quote: On or about October 21, 2009, while PURDUE PHARMA was actively marketing to Prescriber-1, a PURDUE PHARMA sales representative submitted a written ROC to the ADD Program, informing PURDUE PHARMA that a local pharmacist had complained that Prescriber-1 was not prescribing OxyContin responsibly. The pharmacist complained that Prescriber-1's patients were selling their prescriptions written by Prescriber-1, but that Prescriber-1 refused to change prescribing habits after the pharmacist told Prescriber-1 of his concerns.
context: Description of first warning signal about Prescriber-1 through internal ROC submission process.

label: Sales rep reports prescriber as 'Candyman'
original_label: Sales rep reports prescriber as 'Candyman'
quote: On or about June 23, 2010, a PURDUE PHARMA sales representative submitted a second written ROC to the ADD Program about Prescriber-1's behavior, explaining that: [T]he pharmacy manager, says [Prescriber-1] is known as the "Candyman" . . . because [Prescriber-1] will immediately put every patient on the highest dose of narcotics [Prescriber-1] can, whether it's OxyContin or another product. He says when he goes to local pharmacist meetings, when [Prescriber-1's] name comes up everyone in the room cringes and moans because of [Prescriber-1's] practices. He says [Prescriber-1] is doing all kinds of wacky dosing and tablet strengths.
context: Sales representative submission of second ROC documenting field observations of prescriber abuse indicators.

label: Unauthorized nurse prescribing controlled substances
original_label: Unauthorized nurse prescribing controlled substances
quote: During a review following the ROC, senior-level PURDUE PHARMA employees within the ADD Program learned that a sales representative had visited Prescriber-1's office multiple times and witnessed a registered nurse who was not authorized to prescribe opioids writing such prescriptions on Prescriber-1's behalf in Prescriber-1's absence.
context: ADD Program internal review discovered unauthorized prescribing during sales representative office visits.
