original_label: ASI allegations of unqualified FSB members lacking training
quote: On March 28, 2019, the Committee corresponded with two FAA Aviation Safety Inspectors (ASI) from the Long Beach, California, Aircraft Evaluation Group (AEG) office. These ASIs disclosed concerns that members of the Flight Standardization Boards (FSB) formed in both Long Beach and Seattle for the Gulfstream VII and Boeing 737 MAX, respectively, had not completed the required training for job tasks such as issuing type ratings and conducting check rides. These whistleblowers stated that many ASIs had not completed FAA course number 21000138: 'Principles of Evaluation for Operations ASIs,' which serves as foundational training for all ASI.
context: Committee investigators documenting the initial disclosure by FAA inspectors about training deficiencies in the Aircraft Evaluation Group.

label: Historical GAO reports on inspector training deficiencies
original_label: Historical GAO reports on inspector training deficiencies
quote: Fundamental concerns about the quality of oversight, many of which are rooted in the inadequate level of training for key safety oversight positions within the FAA, go back as far as 1989. In that year, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) issued a report titled, FAA Aviation Safety Inspectors Are Not Receiving Needed Training. The report found that for a 6 month period in 1988, only 37 percent of active ASI's had received the required training. As a result of the GAO report, the FAA opened and staffed an office to oversee training.
context: Committee report documenting decades-long pattern of GAO warnings about FAA training deficiencies dating to 1989.

label: DOT OIG 2008 Southwest Airlines oversight findings
original_label: DOT OIG 2008 Southwest Airlines oversight findings
quote: In 2008, FAA whistleblower Bobby 'Charalambe' Boutris, alleged that Southwest Airlines had violated an FAA Airworthiness Directive (AD) requiring fuselage inspections that affected forty-six aircraft. According to a DOT OIG report, Southwest notified the FAA of the violation the day after it was discovered, but the FAA allowed the airline to continue operating the affected aircraft for 1,451 flights over eight days, carrying an estimated 145,000 passengers. DOT OIG estimated that, in total, the aircraft flew in violation of the AD for up to nine months, carrying over six million passengers. When inspectors finally inspected the aircraft, they found significant, dangerous fuselage cracks on five of the planes.
context: Committee report summarizing the DOT OIG's 2008 investigation findings about FAA's failure to ground Southwest Airlines aircraft despite known violations.

label: NTSB investigation revealing pilot reaction time assumptions unrealistic
original_label: NTSB investigation revealing pilot reaction time assumptions unrealistic
quote: On September 26, 2019, the NTSB issued seven safety recommendations that resulted from the NTSB's participation in the Lion Air and Ethiopian Airlines crash investigations. In its report, the NTSB raised concerns with the assumptions that Boeing used when designing the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS). Specifically, while Boeing based its design assumptions on FAA guidance, the NTSB concluded that Boeing did not 'adequately consider and account for the impact that multiple flight deck alerts and indications could have on pilots' responses to the hazard.' Essentially, when Boeing ran the flight test in which they tested the MCAS, they did not have any other alarms or alerts going off that could have theoretically been going off in a situation that led to an MCAS activation.
context: Committee report detailing NTSB safety recommendations identifying flawed assumptions in Boeing's MCAS design certification.

label: Whistleblower ad hoc simulator testing showing four-second assumption unrealistic
original_label: Whistleblower ad hoc simulator testing showing four-second assumption unrealistic
quote: The whistleblower's ad hoc testing was encouraged by the Aircraft Evaluation Group (AEG) officials, due to previous testing related to pilot reaction times to an MCAS induced runaway stabilizer in July 2019. According to the whistleblower and at least one other FAA official, the test was conducted utilizing one FAA Aircraft Certification Office (ACO) test pilot and one AEG test pilot who also participated on the 737 MAX Flight Standardization Board (FSB). The three flight crews presented with this scenario responded with reaction times to identify the problem in seven, nine, and eleven seconds. The time to complete the corrective action and correct the situation was forty-nine, fifty-three, and sixty-two seconds. The whistleblower emphasized these tests were completed in a 737-NG simulator and MCAS was not an available feature or factor in the test scenarios. The whistleblower contends that the result of these tests indicate Boeing's assumed reaction time of four seconds is unrealistic and found actual pilot reaction times were as much as four times the assumed time.
context: Committee investigators documenting whistleblower testing that demonstrated Boeing's pilot reaction time assumptions for MCAS were unrealistic.

At the time, an FAA inspector recommended an emergency revocation of the mechanic's FAA certificate. This recommendation was submitted in November 2019.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Enron confidentiality and ethics code requirements
original_label: Enron confidentiality and ethics code requirements
quote: Enron, like many other corporations, required its employees to sign a confidentiality agreement and acknowledge compliance with the company's code of ethics. Enron's confidentiality agreement required employees to disclose business activities outside Enron that could be considered a conflict of interest, among other things. Similarly, Enron's code of ethics prohibited employees from engaging in, among other activities, investments that could be considered to conflict with Enron's interests, without obtaining a waiver from Enron. FASTOW signed the confidentiality agreement and the certificate of compliance with Enron's code of ethics.
context: FBI affidavit describing the formal rules governing employee conduct and disclosure that FASTOW signed as CFO.

label: CFO authority over financial activities and SPE transactions
original_label: CFO authority over financial activities and SPE transactions
quote: FASTOW was Enron's Chief Financial Officer (CFO) from March 1998 until October 24, 2001. As CFO, FASTOW was responsible for overseeing many of Enron's financial activities. FASTOW reported directly to Enron's Chief Executive Officer (CEO). At times relevant to this Affidavit, Kopper reported directly to FASTOW. Kopper held various executive positions at Enron and also served in executive positions at certain special purpose entities (SPEs) created by Enron.
context: FBI affidavit establishing the chain of command and FASTOW's hierarchical position directing Kopper and overseeing financial operations.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Off-balance-sheet accounting rules and Wall Street metrics
original_label: Off-balance-sheet accounting rules and Wall Street metrics
quote: Enron management preferred the latter result, known as off-balance-sheet, because it enabled Enron to present itself more attractively as measured by criteria favored by Wall Street investment analysts, credit rating agencies, and others.
context: FBI affidavit explaining the structural incentive that drove Enron's accounting strategy and what metrics were valued by external stakeholders.

label: SPE equity requirements and control-independence violations
original_label: SPE equity requirements and control-independence violations
quote: Under applicable accounting rules, an SPE could receive off-balance-sheet treatment only if independent third-party investors contributed at least three-percent of the SPE's capital, and the third-party investment was genuinely at risk, among other requirements. If the third party was not truly independent, or its investment not truly at risk, consolidation of the SPE onto Enron's balance sheet was required.
context: FBI affidavit describing the regulatory red lines that FASTOW and Kopper systematically violated in structuring Friends of Enron and other SPEs.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Suppression of documentary evidence of buyback guarantees
original_label: Suppression of documentary evidence of buyback guarantees
quote: According to CS-1, there was an unwritten buyback agreement between FASTOW and Enron whereby if Enron could not find another purchaser for LJM's Cuiaba interest, Enron would buy back LJM's interest and guarantee LJM a profit. CS-1 stated that the original deal documents for Cuiaba made reference to such an agreement between LJM and Enron. Those documents were revised to remove such language out of concern that Andersen would not approve the transaction as a sale with such a provision in the transaction. Kopper also stated that reference to the buyback agreement between LJM and Enron was deleted because it would prohibit Enron from recognizing the sale to LJM and, therefore, Enron would have to consolidate Cuiaba. The parties circumvented these rules by orally agreeing to the buyback and entering into a written agreement that omitted the buyback language that would have alerted third parties to the scheme.
context: FBI affidavit detailing how FASTOW, Kopper and Enron deliberately removed written evidence of fraudulent buyback commitments to evade audit scrutiny.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Board misled about LJM purpose and control
original_label: Board misled about LJM purpose and control
quote: According to interviews of several Board members, the Board was led to believe by FASTOW, Enron's CEO, and others that LJM was a vehicle for Enron to sell assets, and did not contemplate that Enron would buy back assets from LJM. Board members described such buy-back transactions as antithetical to the business purpose for LJM that was presented to the Board at the time it approved FASTOW's involvement in LJM. Failing to inform the Board of such transactions hid the Enron-LJM fraudulent buy back activity.
context: FBI affidavit documenting how FASTOW and others deliberately misrepresented the purpose of LJM to the Board and concealed buyback transactions.

label: Board review committee for LJM transactions
original_label: Board review committee for LJM transactions
quote: According to interviews of Board members, and review of Board minutes and Board members' contemporaneous notes, in approving FASTOW's role at LJM the Board relied on false representations by FASTOW, Enron's Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Chief Accounting Officer (CAO), Treasurer, and others. Specifically, the Board understood that: (1) Enron's CAO and Chief Risk Officer would review transactions with LJM to ensure their fairness to Enron; (2) the Board would be informed of all Enron transactions with LJM; (3) the purpose of LJM was to buy assets from Enron; (4) Board approval would be required for any Enron employee to work at LJM; and (5) although FASTOW would be compensated by LJM, he would not be permitted to profit from any appreciation in the value of Enron stock held by LJM or its affiliates.
context: FBI affidavit describing the board-level oversight mechanisms that were supposed to control FASTOW's conflicts of interest but were undermined by false representations.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Hidden Global Galactic agreement guaranteeing LJM profits
original_label: Hidden Global Galactic agreement guaranteeing LJM profits
quote: According to Kopper and CS-1, far from reviewing transactions with LJM to ensure their fairness to Enron, Enron's CAO had an undisclosed agreement with FASTOW, which was referred to at LJM and Enron as the Global Galactic agreement. Under this agreement, LJM would not lose money in its dealings with Enron. Any Enron-LJM transaction that resulted in a loss to LJM would be made up later.
context: FBI affidavit revealing a secret side agreement that nullified the Board's purported oversight mechanism by guaranteeing LJM could not lose.

label: CAO conflict of interest in reviewing LJM transactions
original_label: CAO conflict of interest in reviewing LJM transactions
quote: Nor was the Board informed that FASTOW had arranged to have Kopper, while still Enron's Managing Director of Global Finance, serve as a managing director at LJM, or that FASTOW had staffed LJM with several other Enron employees. In late 2001, Board members confronted FASTOW and asked whether any current or former Enron employees other than FASTOW and Kopper had received remuneration from LJM. According to interviews of Board members and a review of contemporaneous notes, FASTOW responded by saying no. In fact, as FASTOW knew at the time, among other things, he personally had authorized several million dollars in LJM-derived payments to various Enron employees.
context: FBI affidavit showing how FASTOW staffed LJM with Enron employees and falsely denied this to the Board, blocking the Board from knowing it lacked independent review.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Earnings targets and balance sheet management dominate financial decisions
original_label: Earnings targets and balance sheet management dominate financial decisions
quote: This purported sale enabled Enron to recognize a total of approximately $65 million of income in the third and fourth quarter of 1999, when it was struggling to meet its projected financial results. From FASTOW's perspective, Enron's dealings with LJM ensured that: (1) as CFO, FASTOW readily could rid Enron of poorly performing assets and thereby improve Enron's reported financial results, which in turn would enable FASTOW to earn continued prestige, salary, bonuses, and other benefits from Enron.
context: FBI affidavit describing how quarterly earnings targets drove FASTOW's design of SPE transactions and his personal incentives.

label: Cuiaba project cost overruns and troubled status
original_label: Cuiaba project cost overruns and troubled status
quote: Enron, through a wholly-owned subsidiary, held approximately 65% of the equity in a company that was building a power plant in Cuiaba, Brazil (the Cuiaba project). The Cuiaba project was troubled from its inception. According to CS-6, an Enron employee who worked on the project, the Cuiaba project caused Enron to incur significant unexpected costs. By 2000, the Cuiaba project was approximately $120 million over budget. According to LJM documents, Enron sought to avoid consolidation of the project's debt on its balance sheet by selling its interest in the project. However, according to CS-7, the Cuiaba project was so problematic that no buyer would be interested in purchasing the project from Enron because there were too many serious risks and impediments to its being profitable in the time projected in the financial models.
context: FBI affidavit documenting that the Cuiaba project's problems were known internally and severe enough that no legitimate third party would buy it.

label: Cuiaba operational failures and financial impairments documented
original_label: Cuiaba operational failures and financial impairments documented
quote: For example, according to an E-mail from an LJM employee to FASTOW dated October 16, 2000: the Cuiaba plant was experiencing operational problems, did not have long term gas supply arrangements, and Conditions precedent for the permanent financing have not been satisfied, which is impairing returns. . . [t]he project has experienced cost overruns due to the delayed start and change orders of $148.4 MM on an original budget of $519 MM, which is impairing returns. Kopper, for instance, discovered that the rotors in the Cuiaba plant were cracking and that there were construction delays because the Brazilian government would not grant a permit for a pipeline to traverse a protected rainforest.
context: FBI affidavit citing internal LJM correspondence to FASTOW detailing severe Cuiaba failures that contradicted its financial viability.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Quarterly earnings goals drive asset sale decisions
original_label: Quarterly earnings goals drive asset sale decisions
quote: When Enron failed to sell the project by December 1999, Enron through FASTOW and its then Treasurer contacted, among other entities, the Financial Institution to pressure it to buy a $28 million interest in the project, with 75% of its purchase to be financed by Enron, so that Enron could book the sale by year end. Such a sale would allow Enron to record $12 million of earnings, and $28 million in funds flow, in the fourth quarter of 1999, which according to CS-3 was needed to meet Enron's earnings goals.
context: FBI affidavit showing how fourth-quarter earnings targets created pressure on FASTOW to force a sham transaction.

label: Financial institution documents flagging fraudulent earnings manipulation
original_label: Financial institution documents flagging fraudulent earnings manipulation
quote: In spite of some internal dissension, including a document expressing concern that it would be viewed as aiding and abetting Enron's fraudulent manipulation of its income statement, the Financial Institution ultimately agreed that it would invest $7 million in the project.
context: FBI affidavit citing internal Financial Institution warning that participation would constitute aiding fraud, but the institution proceeded anyway.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Oral side deal to hide takeout commitment
original_label: Oral side deal to hide takeout commitment
quote: According to Kopper, FASTOW told him that he had an undisclosed oral agreement with the Financial Institution whereby Enron promised to take the Financial Institution out of the deal within six months. FASTOW told Kopper that this agreement could not be put in writing because if the oral promise was memorialized Enron would not be able to recognize needed earnings on its fourth quarter 1999 financial statements. FASTOW also told Kopper that this transaction involved putting a lot of pressure on the Financial Institution, which FASTOW referred to as bear-hugging.
context: FBI affidavit documenting FASTOW's deliberate choice to keep the takeout guarantee oral to prevent audit detection and earnings reversal.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Client revenue importance driving investment bank accommodation
original_label: Client revenue importance driving investment bank accommodation
quote: According to the Financial Institution's own internal documents, it had a strong incentive to accommodate Enron because, Enron has paid [the Financial Institution] approximately $40 million in fees in 1999 and is expected to do so again in 2000, and it hoped to generate more Enron business. According to Kopper and others, FASTOW was also close personal friends with the Financial Institution's supervisory Enron relationship partner, who championed the deal within the Financial Institution.
context: FBI affidavit showing how Enron's fee revenue and personal relationships created incentives at the Financial Institution that overrode due diligence.

label: Financial institution failed to perform due diligence
original_label: Financial institution failed to perform due diligence
quote: According to CS-4, another Financial Institution employee, stated that it did no due diligence on the transaction, either before entering into the deal or afterward to monitor the supposed investment.
context: FBI affidavit documenting that Financial Institution deliberately skipped its normal risk controls on the Nigerian barge transaction.

label: Written documentation of guaranteed takeout and fixed return
original_label: Written documentation of guaranteed takeout and fixed return
quote: Documents also confirm that the sale of the Nigerian barges to the Financial Institution was a sham transaction. For example: Financial Institution documents reflect that its Chairman of Investment Banking scheduled a conference call with senior management of Enron to confirm Enron's commitment to guaranty the [Financial Institution] takeout within six month, and that the deal needed to close by December 31, 1999. According to an internal LJM document, Enron sold the barges to the Financial Institution, promising that the firm would be taken out by sale by June 2000. A December 23, 1999, draft engagement letter between Enron and the Financial Institution stated that the transaction would have a yield of approximately 15% and that the Financial Institution's interest would be sold to a third party or purchased by Enron. An e-mail dated May 11, 2000 from an Enron employee confirms that, ENE is obligated to get [the Financial Institution] out of the deal on or before June 30. Internal Financial Institution documents described the transaction as a relationship loan and reflected periodic interest calculations on the investment at a rate of 15%.
context: FBI affidavit citing multiple internal documents showing that Financial Institution and Enron both documented the fixed return and takeout commitment.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Unsent demand letter for guaranteed return
original_label: Unsent demand letter for guaranteed return
quote: With the end of June 2000, approaching without a buyer having been located by Enron, the Financial Institution drafted a letter to Enron dated June 14, 2000, which reiterated that Enron agreed to sell the Financial Institution's interest in the deal by June 30, 2000 and demanded payment from Enron of $7,510,976.65 [a figure that was the agreed-upon rate of return]. The letter was never sent because Enron arranged to park the barges with LJM.
context: FBI affidavit showing that Financial Institution drafted a demand letter but cancelled it when Enron arranged the re-parking scheme.

label: Enron restructured barge interest to hide liability
original_label: Enron restructured barge interest to hide liability
quote: With no true third-party purchaser available to buy the Financial Institution's interest, on June 29, 2000 – the day before Enron had promised to take out the Financial Institution – FASTOW arranged for LJM to purchase the Financial Institution's interest. Kopper stated that in May 2000 FASTOW instructed him to have LJM prepare to purchase the Financial Institution's interest, and that FASTOW agreed that Enron in turn would take out LJM by locating a third party buyer who would buy LJM's interest at a profit to LJM. CS-1 said he/she was told by a person who worked on the transaction that LJM purchased the Financial Institution's interest to fulfill Enron's commitment to the Financial Institution and because if Enron itself repurchased the interest it would have been required to reverse the earlier sale on its books.
context: FBI affidavit showing that FASTOW used LJM as an intermediary to fulfill the Financial Institution commitment while keeping it off Enron's balance sheet.

label: Raptor structured with inadequate outside equity
original_label: Raptor structured with inadequate outside equity
quote: Talon was funded mainly by Enron through a promissory note and Enron's own stock. The remainder of Talon's funding came from $30 million from LJM. This alleged third party funding served as the necessary three percent outside equity required for Talon not to be reflected on Enron's balance sheet. Talon, however, was not properly off balance sheet. In an undisclosed side deal with FASTOW, LJM was to receive its initial investment plus a substantial profit from Enron, all prior to Talon being allowed to engage in the hedging transactions for which it was created. Such a side deal, if disclosed, would have broken the SPE, that is, it would have required Talon to be consolidated on Enron's financial statements because the outside three percent equity was not at risk.
context: FBI affidavit documenting that Raptor's SPE structure violated the three-percent independent equity requirement by featuring a hidden side deal.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Side deal disguised as manufactured put option
original_label: Side deal disguised as manufactured put option
quote: In order to mask the side deal, FASTOW, Enron's CAO and others devised a scheme to manufacture a $41 million payment to LJM. To do so, Enron and Talon entered into a put, that is, a transaction that ostensibly served to hedge Enron against a decline in its own stock value. That put option was purchased by Enron for $41 million. The $41 million was paid to Talon and then transferred to LJM. Both Kopper and CS-1 said that the true purpose for the put option was to generate income to satisfy Enron's obligation to LJM under the undisclosed side agreement entered into by FASTOW.
context: FBI affidavit showing that FASTOW and the CAO deliberately disguised the side deal as a legitimate hedging transaction.

label: Document backdating to capture stock price peak
original_label: Document backdating to capture stock price peak
quote: Enron documents that I have reviewed note August 3, 2000, as the purported date of the Raptor hedges. At the close of business on that day, the price of the principal stock that Enron sought to hedge, approximately 1.09 million shares of AVICI, was at an all time high of $163.50. By entering into a hedge on that date Enron would have been able to lock in a substantial gain in the stock and avoid the risk of the stock declining. In fact, records reflect that within a month, AVICI stock had significantly declined.
context: FBI affidavit noting that Enron's chosen hedge date coincided exactly with AVICI's all-time high before the stock subsequently fell.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Backdating rationalized as LJM accommodation
original_label: Backdating rationalized as LJM accommodation
quote: Because the transaction made no economic sense from Talon's perspective if it were a legitimate transaction, when CS-1 learned of it, CS-1 questioned FASTOW about it. FASTOW told CS-1 that since LJM had already received its money and its profit from Enron, namely the $41 million discussed above, LJM was to accommodate Enron. FASTOW told CS-1 to have a hands-off approach with Enron in relation to future stock hedges entered into by Talon. According to CS-1, people at LJM and Enron were aware of the backdating and referred to it as the Enron time machine.
context: FBI affidavit showing that when CS-1 questioned the illogical backdating, FASTOW instructed hands-off oversight and used the side deal to justify the accommodation.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Board representation violated on Southampton stock appreciation
original_label: Board representation violated on Southampton stock appreciation
quote: FASTOW was prohibited by the Enron Board from having any direct pecuniary interest in Enron's stock held by LJM. Indeed, in his own presentation made to Enron's Board on June 28, 1999, FASTOW emphasized that he would not receive any current or future appreciated value of Enron's stock. Nevertheless, according to Kopper and various e-mail and other documents that I have reviewed, FASTOW decided that he, Kopper and three bankers employed by NatWest would defraud Enron and NatWest by capturing the increase in Swap Sub's value for themselves and others.
context: FBI affidavit showing that FASTOW violated his explicit Board representation regarding prohibition on profiting from Enron stock appreciation.

label: NatWest bankers in positions of trust with access to valuation information
original_label: NatWest bankers in positions of trust with access to valuation information
quote: NatWest E-mails reflect that by at least early 2000, three NatWest bankers working on matters relating to Enron and LJM, Gary Mulgrew, Giles Darby, and David Bermingham believed that the NatWest division where they worked was likely to be sold, affecting the security of their employment. E-mails reflect that around the same time, the bankers also became aware that while NatWest internally valued its Swap Sub interest at zero, it actually had significant value.
context: FBI affidavit documenting that the NatWest bankers gained knowledge of hidden value in Swap Sub and faced job insecurity, creating vulnerability to FASTOW's scheme.

label: Rhythms Net swap value increased despite LJM's illiquid hedge position
original_label: Rhythms Net swap value increased despite LJM's illiquid hedge position
quote: According to public records, Enron shares held by Swap Sub increased by 58% in January. Meanwhile, Swap Sub's only liability, the Rhythms Net put option, decreased because Rhythms Net shares climbed from $27.50 at the end of 1999 to reach high of $47.50 on February 17, 2000.
context: FBI affidavit noting that Swap Sub's value increased substantially in January 2000, creating the windfall that FASTOW and Kopper later captured.

label: Southampton restructuring presentation to NatWest
original_label: Southampton restructuring presentation to NatWest
quote: According to Kopper, as well as documents and travel records reviewed by the FBI, on February 22, 2000, the NatWest bankers traveled to Houston, Texas, to meet with FASTOW and others. During that meeting the bankers, purportedly representing NatWest, made a slide show presentation outlining their ideas for the restructuring of Swap Sub.
context: FBI affidavit documenting the meeting where the NatWest bankers and FASTOW discussed restructuring ideas, creating the opportunity for the scheme.

label: NatWest bankers breached duties to employer during restructuring
original_label: NatWest bankers breached duties to employer during restructuring
quote: Mulgrew and Darby, in violation of their duties to NatWest, recommended that it accept the $1 million offer. Subsequently, in violation of his duty to NatWest, Bermingham recommended to the Board of Directors of NatWest's Cayman Islands investment entity that it accept the offer.
context: FBI affidavit noting that the NatWest bankers deliberately violated their duties to NatWest by recommending acceptance of a vastly undervalued offer.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Board approval focus on FASTOW compensation disclosure
original_label: Board approval focus on FASTOW compensation disclosure
quote: By June 1999, in order to have an off-balance-sheet SPE to which Enron could readily turn, Enron's Board of Directors (the Board) agreed to permit FASTOW to create and serve as the managing partner of a new SPE named LJM1. The Board later approved FASTOW's participation in another even larger SPE, LJM2 (the LJM entities hereafter collectively will be referred to as LJM unless otherwise noted). LJM's business activity principally involved transactions with Enron and Enron affiliates.
context: FBI affidavit showing the Board focused on the convenience of having a ready SPE for transactions without scrutinizing how it would operate.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Kopper incentivized by promised lucrative future LJM transactions
original_label: Kopper incentivized by promised lucrative future LJM transactions
quote: The CAO explained that while FASTOW's continued involvement in LJM would require disclosure on Enron's financial statements, Kopper's would not. The CAO assured Kopper that LJM would be lucrative to Kopper because Enron would conduct significant future business with LJM to help Enron achieve its quarterly financial reporting goals. That Enron intended to continue its relationship with LJM also was reflected in a memorandum from Citigroup recommending that a loan to Kopper be approved because, among other things, many [Enron] transactions will continue to flow through LJM.
context: FBI affidavit showing how Enron explicitly assured Kopper that LJM would remain profitable because of planned future Enron transactions.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Parking poorly performing assets to improve reported results
original_label: Parking poorly performing assets to improve reported results
quote: According to Kopper and CS-1, various transactions between Enron and LJM were mere warehousing deals in which there was an understanding that LJM would hold Enron assets only for a short time, with Enron agreeing that LJM would make a profit on those assets. FASTOW and others caused LJM to purchase under-performing assets from Enron for prices that often bore no relation to the assets' true value. These assets were referred to as Enron's nuclear waste. In undocumented side deals, Enron agreed that LJM would not lose money even if the market value of an asset declined, because Enron would attempt to arrange a sale of the asset to a third party at a profit to LJM or, if no such third party could be found, Enron itself would repurchase the asset.
context: FBI affidavit describing the pattern of LJM transactions designed to move problem assets off Enron's books while guaranteeing profits.

label: FASTOW controlled nominee investors through Kopper
original_label: FASTOW controlled nominee investors through Kopper
quote: According to KOPPER, CS-9, CS-10, and CS-11, FASTOW initially proposed the formation of a partnership SPE to be known as Alpine Investors (Alpine), which would buy Enron's interest in the wind farms. The proposed investors in Alpine were all Friends of Enron, including relatives of FASTOW's wife, CS-9, and CS-10. Alpine did not complete the proposed transaction with Enron. Rather, according to Kopper and others, in May 1997, FASTOW and Kopper created two SPEs known as RADR ZWS LLC and RADR ZWS MM, LLC (collectively, RADR), which purchased a portion of Enron's interest in the wind farms. Because FASTOW knew that his participation as an equity investor in RADR would require Enron to make public disclosure, he and Kopper enlisted Friends of Enron to serve as the supposedly independent third party investors. Those investors included CS-9, CS-10, and CS-11.
context: FBI affidavit documenting FASTOW's use of nominees under his and Kopper's control to create the appearance of independent investment.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Gift program to disguise kickbacks as gifts
original_label: Gift program to disguise kickbacks as gifts
quote: According to Kopper, CS-9, and CS-11, RADR proved to be far more lucrative than initially expected, generating a windfall to the investors. According to Kopper and corroborated by bank records, FASTOW, who was aware of the windfall, obtained a share in the form of kickbacks from Kopper, CS-9, and CS-11. To disguise the nature of the payments, FASTOW instructed Kopper to establish a gifting program, whereby Kopper and CS-9 made annual gifts of $10,000 to individual FASTOW family members. The $10,000 amount was chosen because IRS rules exclude from taxable income and do not require reporting of gifts of $10,000 or less made to any one person in one year. FASTOW instructed Kopper that he and CS-9 should write checks not only to FASTOW but also to FASTOW's wife and two children. FASTOW cautioned that no gifts should come directly to him from CS-11 or RADR, as FASTOW wanted to conceal his link to the RADR deal and could think of no legitimate explanation why he would receive checks directly from CS-11. FASTOW told Kopper that, if ever asked, they could explain the checks from Kopper by saying that he and FASTOW were close friends and the checks were gifts.
context: FBI affidavit documenting FASTOW's deliberate structuring of payments to family members to exploit IRS gift tax thresholds and create a false explanation.

label: Loans to nominees never at risk from outset
original_label: Loans to nominees never at risk from outset
quote: CS-9 and CS-11 have admitted in FBI interviews that they were Kopper's nominees and lacked sufficient funds to invest in RADR. Indeed, bank and other documents reflect that their investments were funded by FASTOW, in the form of a $419,000 loan to Kopper, who in turn lent it to CS-9 and CS-11. CS-9, who never worked for Enron, received an additional $62,820 wire transfer from Enron, which CS-9 used as part of his RADR investment. According to Kopper, CS-9 and CS-11, it was understood from the outset that the loan to them would be repaid from RADR proceeds, and that Kopper would control any other RADR funds they received.
context: FBI affidavit showing that the supposed independent investors in RADR were actually funded by FASTOW, making their investment not at risk.

label: Chewco funding by Enron guarantee instead of true equity
original_label: Chewco funding by Enron guarantee instead of true equity
quote: According to Kopper and others, Enron was unable to meet the November 6, 1997, deadline imposed by CALPERS. Indeed, Chewco had no equity, much less the $383 million required to buy CALPERS' interest in JEDI. To meet CALPERS' deadline, FASTOW, Kopper, and others at Enron arranged to fund Chewco temporarily through $383 million in bridge loans from Barclays Bank PLC (Barclays) and Chase Manhattan Bank (Chase). Repayment of the loans was guaranteed by Enron.
context: FBI affidavit showing that Chewco was funded by Enron's loan guarantee rather than third-party equity, violating SPE requirements.

label: Chewco equity structure intentionally violated SPE requirements
original_label: Chewco equity structure intentionally violated SPE requirements
quote: According to public admissions by Enron and Andersen in the fall of 2001, Chewco's structure at the end of 1997 again violated SPE requirements. Its purported outside equity investment consisted of $11.49 million from Barclays. However, Enron structured the transaction so that more than $11 million of that supposed equity investment actually was a loan from Barclays to entities controlled by Kopper. Moreover, that loan was partially secured by Enron's interest in assets recently sold by JEDI, so that Barclays was not fully at risk. The only other equity investment consisted of $125,138 provided by entities under the control of Kopper, SONR#1 LP and SONR#1 LLC (collectively, SONR). Of that investment, $100,100 represented proceeds of the RADR scheme. Thus, as Enron and Andersen admitted in the fall of 2001, Chewco failed for several reasons to qualify as an SPE that could receive off-balance-sheet treatment.
context: FBI affidavit documenting that Chewco's structure was deliberately designed to appear to satisfy SPE rules while actually violating them.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: CAO authorized improper fee to Chewco despite counsel advice
original_label: CAO authorized improper fee to Chewco despite counsel advice
quote: For example, in December 1998, Kopper asked that Enron pay a $400,000 fee to Chewco to obtain its consent to an amendment of the JEDI partnership agreement. According to Kopper, although the amendment benefitted Chewco rather than Enron, FASTOW nevertheless authorized Enron to pay the fee, which was referred to within Enron as a nuisance/arrangement fee. According to Kopper, at FASTOW's direction, he subsequently transferred $67,224 of the nuisance/arrangement fee to FASTOW and members of FASTOW's family.
context: FBI affidavit showing that FASTOW authorized payment to an Enron-controlled entity and then took a personal share despite counsel opposition.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Board-approved FASTOW role created unmanaged conflict of interest
original_label: Board-approved FASTOW role created unmanaged conflict of interest
quote: FASTOW chose Kopper to serve as Chewco's managing partner only because FASTOW himself was told he could not do so without triggering disclosure on Enron's books. FASTOW's inability to serve in a formal role at Chewco, however, posed no impediment to his greed: he demanded a share of Chewco's profits, in violation of his duty to provide honest services to Enron and its shareholders.
context: FBI affidavit showing that FASTOW circumvented the formal disclosure requirement by using Kopper as a proxy while maintaining de facto control.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: FASTOW personal financial gain from LJM transactions
original_label: FASTOW personal financial gain from LJM transactions
quote: From FASTOW's perspective, Enron's dealings with LJM ensured that: (1) as CFO, FASTOW readily could rid Enron of poorly performing assets and thereby improve Enron's reported financial results, which in turn would enable FASTOW to earn continued prestige, salary, bonuses, and other benefits from Enron; (2) LJM would make money on all its dealings with Enron, since Enron management illegally and secretly guaranteed that LJM would not lose money and, if it did, would be made whole in future transactions; and (3) FASTOW and others at LJM personally reaped huge sums of money from such transactions, both in the form of management fees and skimmed deal profits.
context: FBI affidavit explaining the aligned incentives between FASTOW's ability to improve reported financials and his personal enrichment from LJM.

label: Watkins warns Lay of accounting irregularities
original_label: Watkins warns Lay of accounting irregularities
quote: EMAIL DATED OCTOBER 25, 2001 FROM: STEVEN KEAN TO: MARK PALMER SUBJECT: FW: ERRONEOUS PRESS (FORWARD OF EMAIL DATED OCTOBER 25, 2001 FROM: SHERRON WATKINS)
context: Email chain forwarding Sherron Watkins's concerns about Enron's accounting practices to senior management during October 2001 crisis.

label: Watkins raises internal concerns about disclosures
original_label: Watkins raises internal concerns about disclosures
quote: EMAIL DATED OCTOBER 30, 2001 FROM: SHERRON WATKINS TO ELIZABETH TILNEY, ET AL SUBJECT: PR FOR ENRON - WITH ATTACHMENT (DISCLOSURE STEPS TO REBUILD IN...) AND DISCLOSURE STEPS TO REBUILD INVESTOR CONFIDENCE (WITH HANDWRITING)
context: Sherron Watkins proposes disclosure steps to rebuild investor confidence, indicating concerns about what had not been disclosed.
