category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Level B training significantly less expensive for airlines than Level D

quote: As Boeing knew, "Level B" differences training was significantly less expensive for airlines to complete than "Level D." For example, a pilot could complete "Level B" differences training from anywhere in the world in a matter of hours using a computer or tablet. In contrast, a pilot could complete "Level D" differences training only by appearing in person wherever the pilot's airline operated a full-flight simulator. Apart from the cost of acquiring one or more multimillion-dollar simulators and other related expenses, airlines that were required by the FAA AEG to train pilots on a full-flight simulator could also lose revenue that the pilot might otherwise have generated from flying airline passengers during that time. Accordingly, if the FAA AEG required a less rigorous level—such as "Level B"—of differences training for the 737 MAX in the 737 MAX FSB Report, the 737 MAX would be a more attractive option for Boeing's airline customers already flying the 737 NG than switching to an entirely new airplane, such as the new version of Company-1's airplane, as such customers would save significant money in pilot-training costs by transitioning to the 737 MAX.
context: Statement of Facts explaining the commercial incentive structure that motivated Boeing's behavior.

quote: During this time period, Boeing was the subject of extensive negative media coverage over allegations that Boeing had withheld information from pilots, airlines, regulators and the general public regarding MCAS. Other articles raised concerns about MCAS being too powerful and/or relying on a single sensor, and about the integrity of the certification process for the 737 MAX.
context: Media reports after the Lion Air Crash raised concerns about Boeing's regulatory disclosures and certification process, which constituted external warning signals.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: NTSB complaints about omission and highlighting of facts in press release
original_label: NTSB complaints about omission and highlighting of facts in press release
quote: After the November 2018 Press Release was published, a senior official at the NTSB complained to Boeing, via email, that the November 2018 Press Release was not appropriate given Boeing's involvement in the crash investigation, and that "the omission of certain facts and the highlighting of other facts [in the November 2018 Press Release] leads the reader to Boeing's analytical conclusion."
context: The NTSB's regulatory complaint about selective disclosure in the press release was not acted upon by Boeing.

label: Boeing employees present MCAS as high-speed scenario to FAA-AEG
original_label: Boeing employees present MCAS as high-speed scenario to FAA-AEG
quote: In advocating for CBT only, Boeing employees responsible for communicating with the FAA-AEG as to differences training and manuals certification – including Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2, senior members of the 737 MAX Flight Technical Group – presented MCAS to the FAA-AEG as a feature that could only activate in a very specific, high-speed scenario that was outside the normal flight envelope and therefore unlikely to ever be encountered by a commercial pilot. They made these representations to FAA-AEG personnel beginning in or around June 2015.
context: Senior Boeing engineers who communicated with regulators made claims about MCAS's operational scope that were later contradicted by internal findings.

label: MCAS Expansion broadens operational scope after initial FAA presentations
original_label: MCAS Expansion broadens operational scope after initial FAA presentations
quote: In or around March 2016, Boeing introduced the MCAS Expansion, significantly broadening MCAS's operational scope. No longer limited to a specific, rare high-speed scenario, MCAS could now activate at abnormally high AoA throughout the entire speed range of the 737 MAX, including during the initial climb and the final descent, and its command authority was significantly increased to allow it to function effectively at lower speeds.
context: Boeing's technical change to MCAS in March 2016 significantly expanded its operating conditions, contradicting earlier regulatory representations.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Boeing stock price rises 4.8 percent on day of November 2018 press release
original_label: Boeing stock price rises 4.8 percent on day of November 2018 press release
quote: On November 28, 2018, the first trading day following the public release of the Lion Air Preliminary Report and Boeing's after-hours publication of the November 2018 Press Release, Boeing's stock closed at $333.5, up 4.8% from the prior day's close (compared to a 2% gain for the S&P 500).
context: Market reaction to the November 2018 Press Release suggests investors found the reassurance statement about aircraft safety significant.

label: Muilenburg approves November 2018 Press Release with safety assurance language
original_label: Muilenburg approves November 2018 Press Release with safety assurance language
quote: On the afternoon of November 27, 2018, Muilenburg approved the issuance of the November 2018 Press Release via email, writing, "Looks great – factual, and sticks to the report while making our key points. Good to go here …." The November 2018 Press Release was published on Boeing's website that evening, just after the public release of the Lion Air Preliminary Report by the Indonesian government.
context: CEO Muilenburg personally approved the press release that contained the safety assurance language, after having received briefing on the SRB's safety determination.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Muilenburg states no surprise or gap in certification process during earnings call
original_label: Muilenburg states no surprise or gap in certification process during earnings call
quote: But I can tell you with confidence that we understand our airplane, we understand how the design was accomplished, how the certification was accomplished, and remain fully confident in the product that we've put in the field. But we also know there are areas that we can improve, and that is the source of the software update here. But there was no surprise or gap or unknown here or something that somehow slipped through a certification process. Quite the opposite. We know exactly how the airplane was designed. We know exactly how it was certified. We have taken the time to understand that….
context: CEO Muilenburg's April 2019 response to analyst questions about the certification process after Boeing had discovered concerning documents about regulatory disclosures.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Questions raised by November 2016 Chat and compliance review omitted from April statements
original_label: Questions raised by November 2016 Chat and compliance review omitted from April statements
quote: The April 2019 Statements were misleading under the circumstances absent any discussion of the questions raised by the discovery of the November 15, 2016 Chat and the MCAS Certification Compliance Review concerning the adequacy of Boeing's disclosures to the FAA-AEG in connection with the FAA-AEG's review and approval of pilot training requirements and flight manuals for the 737 MAX. Accordingly, Boeing failed to exercise reasonable care in connection with the April 2019 Statements.
context: The SEC order identifies how Boeing's public statements omitted the serious concerns raised by internal investigations that Muilenburg had been briefed on.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Earnings growth targets as performance metric
original_label: Earnings growth targets as performance metric
quote: The scheme's objectives were, among other things, to produce reported earnings that steadily grew by approximately 15 to 20 percent every year; to meet or exceed, without fail, the published expectations of industry analysts forecasting Enron's reported earnings-per-share results; to avoid publicly reporting any large "write-downs" or losses; to persuade investors that Enron's future profitability would continue to grow; and to deceive lenders, rating agencies, and the investing public about the true magnitude of Enron's debt and other obligations and the true condition of Enron's cash flow.
context: DOJ indictment describing the fundamental performance metrics and targets that guided Enron executives' attention and decisions.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Budget targets derived from earnings goals, not business forecasts
original_label: Budget targets derived from earnings goals, not business forecasts
quote: In order to achieve their objectives, Enron's executives and senior managers, including defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY, imposed annual and quarterly earnings targets ("budget targets") on each of the company's business units. These budget targets were derived from earnings-per-share goals rather than on forecasts derived from the projected earnings likely to be generated by the company's various commercial operations.
context: Indictment establishing how Enron's target-setting system reversed normal causality, starting from financial goals rather than operational capacity.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Earnings levers and fraudulent devices as operational tools
original_label: Earnings levers and fraudulent devices as operational tools
quote: When the budget targets were not met through results from business operations, they were achieved through the use of various earnings "levers," many of which involved fraudulent devices, including but not limited to those described below. Enron's executives and senior managers frequently explained the use of these devices to Enron's outside auditors, and at times to the investing public, through misleading descriptions and justifications that were designed to dovetail with accounting and financial reporting requirements but which masked the true intent of Enron's executives and senior managers to present a false and misleading portrait of Enron's current and likely future financial condition.
context: Indictment describing how the target system normalized the use of accounting manipulations as standard operational tools and how they were explained to auditors.

label: Causey as principal architect and operator of earnings manipulation
original_label: Causey as principal architect and operator of earnings manipulation
quote: Defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY was a principal architect and operator of the scheme to manipulate Enron's reported earnings. He participated in the decisions about where budget targets were set and what demands were placed on each Enron's business unit both to meet each unit's own budget targets and to produce additional earnings to cover differences between the projected earnings of Enron's business units and the company's overall budget target. This difference, which at times constituted hundreds of millions of dollars, was referred to within Enron's variously as the "gap," "stretch" or "overview." From time to time, CAUSEY and others increased budget targets at or near the end of the quarter, and at times even after the close of the quarter, in order to achieve a revised earnings-per-share objective in comparison to the expectations of equity analysts.
context: Indictment establishing Causey's central role in designing and executing the target-setting system and its manipulation.

label: Causey's position as CAO managing accounting and disclosures
original_label: Causey's position as CAO managing accounting and disclosures
quote: As Enron's CAO, defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY was a principal manager of Enron's accounting practices. CAUSEY reported to Enron's Chairman/Chief Executive Officer ("CEO") and its Chief Operating Officer ("COO")/CEO. Enron's Chairman/CEO, its COO/CEO, its Chief Financial Officer ("CFO") Andrew S. Fastow, its Treasurer, and CAUSEY were the principal managers of Enron's finances. CAUSEY was also a principal manager of Enron's disclosures and representations to the investing public. He signed Enron's annual reports on Form 10-K and its quarterly reports on Form l0-Q as Executive Vice-President and CAO.
context: Indictment establishing Causey's institutional position controlling both accounting practices and public financial disclosures.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Stock price and analyst expectations as dominant focus
original_label: Stock price and analyst expectations as dominant focus
quote: The price of Enron's stock was influenced by factors such as Enron's reported revenue, earnings, debt, cash flow (sometimes categorized as "funds flow"), and credit rating, as well as its ability to meet revenue and earnings targets and forecasts. Enron's management, like that of many public companies, provided guidance to the investing public regarding anticipated revenue and earnings for upcoming reporting periods. Relying in part on the company's guidance, many professional securities analysts disseminated to the public their own estimates of the company's expected performance. These earnings estimates, or analysts' expectations, were closely followed by investors. Typically, if a company announced earnings that failed to meet or exceed analysts' expectations, the price of the company's securities declined. Quarter to quarter, industry analysts and the investing public evaluated Enron according to, among other things, reported revenue, net income, outstanding debt, cash flow, and earnings per share.
context: Indictment describing the metrics and forecasts that dominated investor and analyst attention, creating pressure on management to meet expectations.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Credit rating and debt as critical to operations and strategy
original_label: Credit rating and debt as critical to operations and strategy
quote: It was critical to Enron's ongoing business operations that it maintain an investment grade rating for its debt. An investment grade rating was essential to Enron's ability to enter into trading contracts with its counterparties and to maintain sufficient lines of credit with major banks. The credit rating agencies relied on, among other things, Enron's publicly filed financial statements in rating Enron's debt. In addition, members of Enron's senior management met regularly with, and provided financial and other information to, representatives of credit rating agencies. Two primary factors influencing Enron's credit rating and the willingness of banks to extend loans to Enron were Enron's total amount of debt and other obligations and its cash flow.
context: Indictment establishing that maintaining investment-grade ratings and concealing debt levels were core operational priorities for senior management.

label: Board approval of LJM SPE for off-balance-sheet transactions
original_label: Board approval of LJM SPE for off-balance-sheet transactions
quote: By 1999, Enron was increasingly dependent on transactions with SPEs to meet its financial reporting goals. In June 1999, in order to have an off-balance-sheet SPE to which Enron could readily and repeatedly turn to achieve its desired financial reporting results, Enron's Board of Directors (the "Board") agreed to permit CFO Fastow to create and serve as the managing partner of a new SPE named LJM. The Board later approved Fastow's participation in another even larger SPE named LJM2 (the LJM entities are collectively referred to as "LJM" unless otherwise noted). LJM's business activity principally involved transactions with Enron and Enron affiliates.
context: Indictment describing how the Board formally approved the SPE structures that became vehicles for financial reporting manipulation.

label: Undocumented side deals between Causey and Fastow
original_label: Undocumented side deals between Causey and Fastow
quote: Defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and Fastow had an oral side deal that LJM2 would receive its initial investment in Talon plus a profit of $11 million from Enron, all prior to Talon engaging in any of the hedging transactions for which it was created. As a quid pro quo for this payment to LJM2, Fastow agreed with CAUSEY that Enron employees could use Raptor I to manipulate Enron's balance sheet, including by allowing Enron employees, without negotiation or due diligence on behalf of LJM2, to select the values at which the Enron assets were hedged with Talon.
context: Indictment describing informal communication channels and agreements that bypassed formal documentation and controls.

label: Meetings to discuss LJM side agreement guarantees
original_label: Meetings to discuss LJM side agreement guarantees
quote: In or about August and September 2000, CAUSEY and others held a meeting to discuss Enron's and LJM's undocumented side agreement that LJM would be guaranteed against loss in certain of its transactions with Enron, and that other losses to LJM would be made up through other transactions with Enron.
context: Indictment indicating that senior managers held meetings to explicitly discuss and coordinate undisclosed side arrangements guaranteeing SPE returns.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Misleading descriptions masking true intent to auditors
original_label: Misleading descriptions masking true intent to auditors
quote: Enron's executives and senior managers frequently explained the use of these devices to Enron's outside auditors, and at times to the investing public, through misleading descriptions and justifications that were designed to dovetail with accounting and financial reporting requirements but which masked the true intent of Enron's executives and senior managers to present a false and misleading portrait of Enron's current and likely future financial condition.
context: Indictment describing how management deliberately reframed fraudulent accounting devices with misleading justifications when explaining them to auditors.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Raptor structure invalid under accounting rules but intentionally structured
original_label: Raptor structure invalid under accounting rules but intentionally structured
quote: The Raptor I structure, however, was invalid under applicable accounting rules because Talon was not independent from Enron, and LJM2's investment in Talon was not at risk. Defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and Fastow had an oral side deal that LJM2 would receive its initial investment in Talon plus a profit of $11 million from Enron, all prior to Talon engaging in any of the hedging transactions for which it was created.
context: Indictment establishing that Causey and Fastow knowingly violated accounting rules while putting protective side agreements in place.

label: Mariner Energy value manipulation to close budget gap
original_label: Mariner Energy value manipulation to close budget gap
quote: For example, in the fourth quarter of 2000, under the direction of CAUSEY and others, Enron personnel fraudulently increased the value of one of the largest of Enron's merchant assets, Mariner Energy, by $100 million in order to help close a budget gap.
context: Indictment describing management's direct action to manipulate asset values when operational earnings fell short of targets.

label: EES losses concealed through business segment reorganization
original_label: EES losses concealed through business segment reorganization
quote: Defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and others concealed massive losses in EES's business through fraudulently manipulating Enron's "business segment reporting." This was accomplished at the close of the first quarter of 2001 through a reorganization of Enron's business segments that Enron explained deceptively as solely meant to improve efficiency. In fact, the reorganization was designed to conceal EES's problems. Enron hid those problems from the investing public by moving large portions of EES's business where CAUSEY and others knew at the time of the change hundreds of millions of dollars in losses would have to be recorded - into Enron's Enron North American ("ENA") business segment. As CAUSEY and others knew, ENA would have ample earnings, including in the large reserve accounts described below, to ensure that ENA could book the huge losses that in fact were attributable to EES while at the same time continuing to meet Enron's budget targets.
context: Indictment describing how management reorganized business segments and shifted losses to hide failing units while maintaining earnings targets.

label: EBS one-time transactions to manufacture earnings appearance
original_label: EBS one-time transactions to manufacture earnings appearance
quote: However, Enron's executives and senior managers took steps to ensure that EBS's financial results did not publicly reveal its failure. For example, during late 2000, Enron structured a series of one-time financial transactions in EBS that were designed to manufacture earnings that Enron used to present the false impression that EBS was close to generating positive operating profits.
context: Indictment describing management's deliberate action to create one-time transactions to mask business unit failures.

label: EBS expense manipulation to avoid losses exceeding budget target
original_label: EBS expense manipulation to avoid losses exceeding budget target
quote: Even with these one-time earnings, EBS still was facing much larger than expected losses during the first quarter of 2001. In order to ensure that EBS did not record in the first quarter of 2001 losses that exceeded Enron's annual budget target for EBS, and in order to achieve the financial result dictated by defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and others for the first quarter 2001, CAUSEY and others fraudulently manipulated, and caused to be fraudulently manipulated, EBS's expenses for the first quarter of 2001.
context: Indictment describing how management manipulated expenses to prevent losses from exceeding budget targets.

label: Reserve accounts to mask trading profits and conceal losses
original_label: Reserve accounts to mask trading profits and conceal losses
quote: During 2000 and 2001, the profitability of Enron's wholesale energy trading business, primarily based in its ENA business unit, dramatically increased for reasons including rapidly rising energy prices in the western United States, especially in California. This sudden and large increase in trading profits, which exceeded $1 billion, threatened to undermine Enron's description and presentation of itself as the dominant "intermediator" in the energy markets, rather than as a speculative (and therefore risky) trading company whose stock would trade at a much lower price-to-earnings ratio. In order to mask these earnings and preserve them for later use, defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and others fraudulently created and used reserve accounts within ENA both to conceal the extent of ENA's trading profits and, as set forth above, to avoid reporting large losses in other areas of its business.
context: Indictment describing how management used reserve accounts as a tool to smooth earnings and hide both profits and losses from investors.

label: Raptor back-dating to capture asset high value
original_label: Raptor back-dating to capture asset high value
quote: CAUSEY and Fastow further used Raptor I fraudulently to promote Enron's financial position by back-dating a hedge to Enron's advantage, capturing the all-time high stock value of one of the Enron assets at a time when they knew that value already had declined.
context: Indictment describing how management manipulated transaction dates to capture advantageous valuations despite knowing assets had declined.

label: False and misleading statements to analysts about business performance
original_label: False and misleading statements to analysts about business performance
quote: In furtherance of the scheme to manipulate Enron's financial results and inflate its stock price, defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and others participated in presenting false and misleading statements about Enron's financial results, the performance of its businesses, and the manner in which its stock was and should be valued. These statements were disseminated to the investing public in conferences, conference calls, press releases, interviews, and statements to members of the media.
context: Indictment describing how management actively disseminated false representations through multiple public communication channels.

label: SEC filings with materially false financial statements
original_label: SEC filings with materially false financial statements
quote: In furtherance of the scheme to manipulate Enron's financial results and inflate its stock price, defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and others filed and caused to be filed with the SEC at least four false quarterly l0-Q and annual 10-K reports for the quarters ending September 30, 2000 through June 30, 2001 and the fiscal year ending December 31, 2000 that, among other things, contained materially false and misleading financial statements that overstated Enron's actual revenues and earnings and understated Enron's actual debt and expenses.
context: Indictment describing how management systematically filed false financial statements with the SEC.

label: COO resignation triggers stock price decline
original_label: COO resignation triggers stock price decline
quote: On August 14, 2001, Enron's COO/CEO unexpectedly resigned. Enron's stock price, which had been declining since January 2001, fell sharply.
context: Indictment describing an event that shifted market and investor attention, causing immediate consequences for stock price.

label: Third quarter loss announcement triggers sharp stock decline
original_label: Third quarter loss announcement triggers sharp stock decline
quote: On October 16, 2001, Enron announced a loss of $618 million for the third quarter of 2001. Enron's stock price again declined sharply.
context: Indictment describing how disclosure of losses reversed the financial narrative and caused market re-evaluation.

label: Credit rating downgrades trigger financial crisis
original_label: Credit rating downgrades trigger financial crisis
quote: On October 29 and November 1, 2001, the two leading credit rating agencies downgraded Enron's credit rating. On November 8, 2001, Enron announced its intention to restate its financial statements for 1997 through 2000 and the first and second quarters of 2001 to reduce previously reported net income by an aggregate of $586 million.
context: Indictment describing how rating agency downgrades and restated financials exposed the fraudulent scheme.

label: Bankruptcy filing renders stock worthless
original_label: Bankruptcy filing renders stock worthless
quote: On December 2, 2001, Enron filed for bankruptcy, making its stock, which less than a year earlier had been trading at over $80 per share, virtually worthless.
context: Indictment describing the final collapse when attention to solvency completely reversed the firm's valuation.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Personal enrichment through stock appreciation aligned with earnings targets
original_label: Personal enrichment through stock appreciation aligned with earnings targets
quote: At the same time, rising stock prices led to enrichment of defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY and Enron's other senior managers in the form of salary, bonuses, grants of artificially appreciating stock and stock options, and prestige within their professions and communities. For instance, between 1998 and 2001, defendant CAUSEY received more than $14 million from the sale of Enron stock and stock options, netting over $5 million in profit, and was paid more than $3 million in salary and bonuses.
context: Indictment establishing the personal financial incentives that aligned individual compensation with maintaining inflated stock prices.

label: Raptor structure designed with guaranteed return to LJM2
original_label: Raptor structure designed with guaranteed return to LJM2
quote: In or about the summer of 2000, in an undocumented side deal, CAUSEY and Fastow agreed that LJM2 would receive, without risk, a guaranteed return of its $30 million investment in the first Raptor structure, together with a profit of $11 million on that investment, in exchange for which Enron would be permitted unilaterally to determine the value of the assets hedged in Raptor without negotiation or due diligence by LJM2.
context: Indictment describing how senior managers structured side agreements that guaranteed SPE returns while eliminating independent verification.

label: Manufacturing Talon payment to satisfy LJM2 side deal
original_label: Manufacturing Talon payment to satisfy LJM2 side deal
quote: The defendant RICHARD A. CAUSEY, Fastow, Glisan, and others satisfied CAUSEY's and Fastow's side deal by manufacturing a transaction between Enron and Talon that generated a $41 million payment to LJM2 but had no business purpose for Enron.
context: Indictment describing how management created a transaction solely to fulfill the guarantees in the side deal.

label: Raptor hedges manipulated after value already declined
original_label: Raptor hedges manipulated after value already declined
quote: Enron employees manipulated the book values of Enron assets, many of which were expected to decline in value, before they were hedged, knowing that the Raptor I structure ensured that Eron would not suffer the financial reporting consequences of subsequent, and anticipated, declines in the value of those assets.
context: Indictment describing how management anticipated asset declines while inflating their values before hedging them.

label: LJM side agreements guaranteed against loss in transactions
original_label: LJM side agreements guaranteed against loss in transactions
quote: In numerous instances, these transactions were accomplished through another undisclosed side agreement between CAUSEY and Fastow that LJM would be guaranteed against loss in certain of its transactions with Enron, and that other losses to LJM would be made up through other transactions with Enron.
context: Indictment describing how senior managers created recurring side agreements guaranteeing SPE returns across multiple transactions.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Budget targets increased near end of quarter
original_label: Budget targets increased near end of quarter
quote: From time to time, CAUSEY and others increased budget targets at or near the end of the quarter, and at times even after the close of the quarter, in order to achieve a revised earnings-per-share objective in comparison to the expectations of equity analysts.
context: Indictment showing how the system allowed targets to be adjusted retroactively to match desired earnings outcomes.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: EBS and EES valued at half of total stock value
original_label: EBS and EES valued at half of total stock value
quote: In presentations to the investing public, Enron's executives and senior managers heavily emphasized the performance and potential of Enron Broadband Services ("EBS") together with Enron Energy Services ("EES") as major reasons for past and projected increases in the value of Enron's stock, attributing as much as half of Enron's total stock value to those two business units.
context: Indictment describing how management communications centered investor attention on two business units they knew were failing.

label: CFO and Kopper control SPE operations
original_label: CFO and Kopper control SPE operations
quote: Starting in at least early 1997, Enron's CFO, KOPPER, and others devised a scheme to defraud Enron and its shareholders by enriching themselves through the use of certain Enron SPEs. Some of these SPEs were not eligible for off-balance-sheet treatment because the supposedly independent third party investors were controlled by the CFO, KOPPER, and others and because the third party "investment" was not at risk, since Enron, the CFO, KOPPER, or others provided the funds to be invested or guaranteed the investment against risk of loss.
context: Charging document describes the organizational structure through which the scheme operated, establishing who held authority over the SPE decisions.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Off-balance-sheet treatment as preferred accounting outcome
original_label: Off-balance-sheet treatment as preferred accounting outcome
quote: Enron's treatment of the entities for financial statement purposes was subject to accounting rules that governed whether an entity should be consolidated in its entirety (including its assets and liabilities) onto Enron's balance sheet, or should be treated as an investment by Enron in a separate entity not under Enron's control. Enron management preferred the latter result – known as "off-balance-sheet"– because it enabled Enron to present itself more attractively as measured by criteria favored by Wall Street investment analysts and credit rating agencies.
context: Charging document identifies the metric and incentive structure that directed management attention toward off-balance-sheet treatment as a strategic objective.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Independent third-party equity requirement creates governance pressure
original_label: Independent third-party equity requirement creates governance pressure
quote: Under applicable accounting rules, an SPE could receive off-balance-sheet treatment only if independent third-party investors contributed at least 3-percent of the SPE's capital, and the third-party investment is genuinely at risk, among other things. If the third party was not truly independent, or its investment was not truly at risk, consolidation of the SPE onto Enron's balance sheet would be required.
context: Charging document establishes the formal accounting rule that should have created a governance check on SPE structure, defining the boundary between permitted and impermissible practice.

label: Kopper held multiple positions bridging Enron and SPEs
original_label: Kopper held multiple positions bridging Enron and SPEs
quote: The defendant MICHAEL J. KOPPER was a resident of Houston, Texas and held various positions at Enron from approximately 1994 through July 2001. For much of that time, KOPPER reported to Enron's Chief Financial Officer ("Enron's CFO"). Between January 2000 and July 2001, KOPPER also was a managing director of LJM2 Capital Management.
context: Charging document establishes Kopper's structural position as a bridge between Enron's core organization and the off-balance-sheet entities, reporting to the CFO while simultaneously managing the SPEs.

label: CFO substituted as general partner to avoid disclosure
original_label: CFO substituted as general partner to avoid disclosure
quote: In November 1997, Enron formed Chewco, an SPE, to buy out CALPERS' JEDI interest. Enron's CFO initially sought to become Chewco's general partner, but substituted KOPPER when it became clear that Enron otherwise would have to disclose publicly the CFO's participation.
context: Charging document describes how the CFO deliberately reassigned his position to Kopper specifically to circumvent disclosure requirements, demonstrating awareness of regulatory boundaries.

label: CFO granted conflict-of-interest waiver to run LJM Cayman
original_label: CFO granted conflict-of-interest waiver to run LJM Cayman
quote: Enron's CFO invested $1 million in LJM Cayman and was granted by Enron a limited waiver of Enron's conflict of interest rules so he could run LJM Cayman as its general partner.
context: Charging document indicates that Enron's formal governance process (conflict-of-interest rule enforcement) was deliberately suspended to permit the CFO to operate the SPE.

label: Fund flows routed through personal loans to friends
original_label: Fund flows routed through personal loans to friends
quote: As part of their scheme to enrich themselves through the use of Enron SPEs, Enron's CFO arranged to fund some of the friends' "investments" by making an unsecured personal loan to KOPPER, who in turn made unsecured loans to the friends so that they could "invest" in RADR. It was understood that the friends would repay KOPPER with distributions from their RADR "investments," and KOPPER would in turn repay Enron's CFO.
context: Charging document describes how the scheme used personal loans and informal repayment arrangements to route funds, bypassing standard corporate accounting and authorization procedures.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: False equity investment record created despite bank guarantee
original_label: False equity investment record created despite bank guarantee
quote: Chewco's structure at year-end again failed to meet SPE requirements. Its permanent financing structure consisted of a $240 million loan from Barclays guaranteed by Enron, a $132 million advance from JEDI to Chewco under a revolving credit agreement, and approximately $11.49 million as an apparent equity investment from Chewco's general and limited partners. However, Enron structured the transaction so that $11.03 million of the supposed outside equity was actually borrowed from Barclays by various entities controlled by KOPPER.
context: Charging document indicates that despite the SPE rules being in place and known, Enron structured the transaction to present false documentation of independent equity while actually using Barclays-guaranteed borrowing.

label: Enron CFO and Kopper contacted friends for equity facade
original_label: Enron CFO and Kopper contacted friends for equity facade
quote: Rather than seek independent third party equity investors, and to ensure that Enron effectively maintained control over the wind farms, Enron's CFO and KOPPER contacted several of their personal friends, including a friend of the Enron CFO's wife, KOPPER's domestic partner, and a Houston real estate broker.
context: Charging document describes how the CFO and Kopper deliberately substituted personal relationships for arm's-length investor relationships to maintain control while appearing to meet the 3% independent equity requirement.

label: Enron repurchased RADR at escalating prices
original_label: Enron repurchased RADR at escalating prices
quote: It was further understood that, at some time in the future, Enron would repurchase the RADR entities. The repurchase price would increase over time, so that the longer it took Enron to repurchase RADR, the higher the price it would have to pay.
context: Charging document establishes that Enron's management committed to repurchasing the SPE at terms structured to increase personal profit, demonstrating deliberate commitment to the scheme rather than arms-length dealing.

label: Payment redistribution scheme routed through selected investors
original_label: Payment redistribution scheme routed through selected investors
quote: In July 2000, Enron repurchased the RADR entities, resulting in an additional gain of approximately $1.8 million to the investors. Two of the investors were directed by KOPPER to transfer portions of their proceeds to various individuals. Among those who received money were Enron's CFO, KOPPER, several of their family members, and various Enron employees and their family members.
context: Charging document describes how Kopper used the investor distribution channel to redirect proceeds to participants including the CFO, creating a hidden distribution network outside normal Enron accounting.

label: NatWest bankers participated in scheme design
original_label: NatWest bankers participated in scheme design
quote: In approximately February 2000, Enron's CFO, KOPPER and three NatWest bankers devised and later executed a scheme to defraud Enron and others by: (i) causing Enron to pay $30 million to buy out, or "unwind", the banks' interests in Swap Sub; (ii) causing NatWest to accept only $1 million for its interest in Swap Sub while representing to Enron that NatWest was getting $20 million; and (iii) splitting the $19 million balance among themselves and certain Enron and LJM employees.
context: Charging document identifies NatWest bankers as structural participants in the scheme alongside Enron's CFO and Kopper, operating external to Enron's organization.

label: False pricing representation to justify Swap Sub payout
original_label: False pricing representation to justify Swap Sub payout
quote: To carry out the scheme, KOPPER, Enron's CFO, and others caused Enron to pay $30 million to unwind Swap Sub. That purchase price was based on Enron's CFO's false representation to Enron that NatWest and CSFB had agreed to sell their interests in Swap Sub for $20 million and $10 million, respectively. In fact, NatWest received only $1 million and had agreed to receive this sum based on misrepresentations and fraudulent conduct of its own employees, who sought to skim profits that should have gone to NatWest.
context: Charging document shows how the CFO used false pricing representations to internal Enron decision makers to justify the $30 million disbursement that funded the scheme.

label: Southampton entity created to distribute skimmed proceeds
original_label: Southampton entity created to distribute skimmed proceeds
quote: The balance of the funds went to investors in an entity called Southampton LP ("Southampton"), which KOPPER created. The Southampton "investors" were KOPPER, who contributed $25,000 and caused Chewco to loan another $750,000, and received approximately $4.5 million; a purported charitable foundation in the name of the CFO's family, which contributed $25,000 and received approximately $4.5 million; and five Enron and LJM employees chosen by KOPPER and the CFO, who contributed a total of less than $20,000 and received a total of approximately $3.3 million.
context: Charging document describes how Kopper created a separate distribution entity structured to hide the redistribution of $19 million in proceeds among participants while maintaining superficial legitimacy through minimal equity contributions.

label: Jury verdict as organizational accountability moment
original_label: Jury verdict as organizational accountability moment
quote: Today, a jury in Houston convicted former Enron executives Kenneth Lay and Jeffrey Skilling on multiple counts of fraud, conspiracy, and related offenses. The judge also convicted Lay of bank fraud and false statements in a separate case tried to the bench.
context: Deputy Attorney General Paul McNulty announcing the verdict on May 25, 2006, marking the culmination of the Enron Task Force investigation and a decisive external event that validated enforcement action.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Executive focus on misleading financial narrative
original_label: Executive focus on misleading financial narrative
quote: Lay, Skilling, and their numerous co-conspirators perpetrated an elaborate scheme to mislead analysts and investors about Enron's true financial picture. Their efforts to mislead the markets were protracted, deliberate and dishonest. At a time when the company was floundering, these defendants perpetrated a lie – that Enron was a robust and growing company in the strongest financial condition it had ever been in.
context: McNulty describing the defendants' deliberate attention to managing external perceptions through false messaging, revealing what executives prioritized in their decision-making.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Financial difficulties systematically masked by deceptive accounting
original_label: Financial difficulties systematically masked by deceptive accounting
quote: As they knew, the truth was something very different. Enron faced significant financial difficulties that had been systematically masked by a series of deceptive accounting tricks.
context: McNulty establishing that internal decision-makers were aware of true financial condition but structured responses through accounting manipulations to prevent that knowledge from reaching external stakeholders.

label: Multi-agency investigation spanning years and millions of documents
original_label: Multi-agency investigation spanning years and millions of documents
quote: The Enron Task Force was formed in late 2001. It involves multiple agencies, including the FBI, the SEC, and the IRS. And this task force that has worked on this Enron debacle has worked thousands and thousands of hours. They've gone over millions of pages of documents. They have devoted years of their professional life, sacrificing time from families, all in the effort to try to hold individuals accountable for corruption.
context: McNulty describing the external investigative response to Enron, indicating the scale of evidence reconstruction required after wrongdoing became visible.

label: Crash victims' families contact DOJ
original_label: Crash victims' families contact DOJ
quote: In February 2020, a representative of the Flight 302 crash victims' families contacted the Department, which told them that Boeing was not currently under criminal investigation.
context: The Fifth Circuit summarizes a communication from crash victims' families to DOJ, establishing an early signal from external parties about the incident.

label: DOJ failure to meet and confer with families
original_label: DOJ failure to meet and confer with families
quote: The Department later apologized for failing to meet and confer with the families, claiming it was caused by "a regrettable and inadvertent internal miscommunication."
context: The Fifth Circuit notes that DOJ's own internal procedures for victim notification broke down, with the Department itself acknowledging a communication failure.

label: Crash victims identified as crime victims under CVRA
original_label: Crash victims identified as crime victims under CVRA
quote: That error, the court explained, was the Department's mistaken belief that the crash victims were not "crime victims" under the CVRA. Ibid.; see 18 U.S.C. § 3771(e)(2)(A) (defining "crime victim" as "a person directly and proximately harmed as a result of the commission of a Federal offense or an offense in the District of Columbia").
context: The district court identified a structural gap: DOJ failed to recognize the families' position as crime victims with statutory rights, affecting their position in the decision-making process.

label: DOJ charges Boeing with conspiracy to defraud
original_label: DOJ charges Boeing with conspiracy to defraud
quote: In January 2021, the Department charged Boeing with conspiracy to defraud the United States under 18 U.S.C. § 371, alleging that two Boeing employees had intentionally misled the FAA regarding changes to the MCAS system. The same day, the Department filed a Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA) it had negotiated with Boeing, in which Boeing admitted responsibility for the acts charged.
context: The Fifth Circuit recounts DOJ's response to the investigation: simultaneous filing of criminal charges and a negotiated DPA, demonstrating DOJ's prosecutorial action and settlement strategy.

label: District court denies DPA challenge by families
original_label: District court denies DPA challenge by families
quote: In December 2021, victims' families moved to set aside the DPA under the CVRA. In February 2023, the district court denied their motion. It found that, although the Department had violated the CVRA by denying the families' right to confer prior to reaching an agreement with Boeing, see 18 U.S.C. § 3771(a), it had done so not out of bad faith but due to "legal error."
context: The Fifth Circuit describes the district court's procedural ruling, finding that DOJ violated the families' CVRA right to confer but excused the violation as legal error rather than bad faith.

label: Boeing breaches DPA compliance program requirement
original_label: Boeing breaches DPA compliance program requirement
quote: In May 2024, the Department notified the district court that Boeing had breached the DPA by "failing to design, implement, and enforce a compliance and ethics program to prevent and detect violations of the U.S. fraud laws throughout its operations."
context: The Fifth Circuit describes an event that redirected DOJ's prosecutorial attention: Boeing's breach of its DPA obligation, prompting DOJ to consider renewed prosecution.

label: DOJ holds video call with families about NPA
original_label: DOJ holds video call with families about NPA
quote: In May 2025, the Department held a video call with the victims' families about its renewed case against Boeing. The Department told the families it was considering resolving the case through a motion to dismiss and a non-prosecution agreement (NPA). It explained that an NPA meant it would agree not to prosecute Boeing, which would "require the Department to move to dismiss the charge pending against Boeing." In exchange, Boeing would agree to "various undertakings, such as paying a penalty, improving compliance, etc." The Department would agree not to revive the case unless it determined that Boeing had breached the NPA.
context: The Fifth Circuit describes DOJ's communication with victim families about the proposed NPA settlement terms, establishing a procedural channel through which victims could learn about and potentially influence the prosecution.

label: DOJ assures families of judicial review and refiling rights
original_label: DOJ assures families of judicial review and refiling rights
quote: The families had mixed opinions about the proposed NPA. In response to some concerns, the prosecution assured the families that their attorneys could "talk to [them] about the legal authority a judge has to deny the government's motion to dismiss." It also told the families that any NPA with Boeing would include a provision stating that if Boeing breached the NPA, "the Department could reﬁle the charge and prosecute the case, notwithstanding the passage of time." Finally, the prosecution stated it would "support the victims' families right to be heard in front of Judge O'Connor" while he was considering whether to grant the motion to dismiss.
context: The Fifth Circuit describes DOJ's procedural assurances to families about judicial authority, refiling rights, and rights to be heard, establishing the channels through which families could participate.

label: Boeing and DOJ sign NPA with refiling provision
original_label: Boeing and DOJ sign NPA with refiling provision
quote: About two weeks later, the prosecution and Boeing signed an NPA in line with the one it had discussed with the families. The ﬁnalized NPA and its attachments contained numerous references to the earlier DPA. One of the NPA's provisions required Boeing to agree that if it breached the NPA, it could be prosecuted for conduct "not time-barred by the applicable statute of limitations on the date of the signing of this [NPA]."
context: The Fifth Circuit describes the final settlement agreement between DOJ and Boeing, including provisions allowing future prosecution and references to prior settlement terms.

label: Families object to dismissal motion in district court
original_label: Families object to dismissal motion in district court
quote: The Department then ﬁled a motion to dismiss that included the in-eﬀect NPA. The families asked the district court to deny the motion, citing (1) their previous objections to the DPA, (2) the Department's alleged failure to meet and confer with them about the NPA, and (3) the NPA's alleged betrayal of the public interest.
context: The Fifth Circuit describes families' use of the district court procedure to object to the DOJ dismissal motion, establishing the procedural channel for victim input at the dismissal stage.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Court finds no misleading timing representation
original_label: Court finds no misleading timing representation
quote: The prosecution never suggested it would wait for a dismissal before entering the NPA. To the contrary, it suggested the opposite—namely, that "if the Department entered an NPA with Boeing, that would require the Department to move to dismiss the charge."
context: The Fifth Circuit evaluates families' claim that DOJ misled them about NPA timing, finding that DOJ's statements clearly indicated the NPA would be signed before dismissal, thus the families' interpretation was unfounded.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Court finds no misleading about refiling capability
original_label: Court finds no misleading about refiling capability
quote: The prosecution was also not misleading when it promised it could renew charges "notwithstanding the passage of time." Contrary to the families' argument, the NPA allows future charges against Boeing if Boeing violates the NPA. The NPA expressly permits prosecution for conduct that is "not time-barred by the applicable statute of limitations on the date of the signing of this Agreement." The NPA was signed in May 2025. As of that date, the pending section 371 charge was not time-barred because the prosecution tolled limitations by ﬁling an information in 2021.
context: The Fifth Circuit rejects families' argument that DOJ misrepresented its ability to refile charges, finding that the NPA's terms actually supported DOJ's representation because the statute of limitations had been tolled.

label: CVRA mandamus procedure limits appellate jurisdiction
original_label: CVRA mandamus procedure limits appellate jurisdiction
quote: The CVRA provides that victims' rights "shall be asserted in the district court," and "[i]f the district court denies the relief sought, the movant may petition the court of appeals for a writ of mandamus." 18 U.S.C. § 3771(d)(3). Because the CVRA mentions mandamus petitions only in the context of protecting the rights of crime victims, it confers no jurisdiction to review the underlying merits of a Rule 48 dismissal.
context: The Fifth Circuit describes the CVRA's procedural framework, which channels victim complaints to district court first with mandamus review in appeals courts, but limits appellate review to CVRA rights violations rather than dismissal merits.

label: Two crashes caused by MCAS design unfamiliarity
original_label: Two crashes caused by MCAS design unfamiliarity
quote: In October 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 crashed shortly after takeoﬀ in Indonesia, killing 189 passengers and crew. In March 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crashed shortly after takeoﬀ in Ethiopia, killing 157 passengers and crew. Both planes were Boeing 737 MAX airliners. The crashes were caused by pilots' unfamiliarity with Boeing's changes to the 737 MAX's Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS).
context: The Fifth Circuit summarizes the factual predicate for the entire case: two fatal crashes caused by Boeing's design changes that pilots were not familiarized with, prompting DOJ investigation.

label: DOJ launches two-year investigation into Boeing
original_label: DOJ launches two-year investigation into Boeing
quote: In response to the crashes, the Department of Justice launched a two-year investigation into Boeing.
context: The Fifth Circuit notes the DOJ's prosecutorial response to the crash incidents, marking the organization's move to investigate Boeing's conduct.

label: Two Boeing employees charged with misleading FAA
original_label: Two Boeing employees charged with misleading FAA
quote: the Department charged Boeing with conspiracy to defraud the United States under 18 U.S.C. § 371, alleging that two Boeing employees had intentionally misled the FAA regarding changes to the MCAS system.
context: The Fifth Circuit describes the criminal charges, identifying two Boeing employees as allegedly responsible for fraud against the FAA regarding MCAS changes.

label: First crash reveals MCAS activation
original_label: First crash reveals MCAS activation
quote: On October 29, 2018, a 737 MAX operating as Lion Air Flight 610 crashed shortly after taking off from Indonesia. None of the 189 passengers and crew survived. The AEG learned that MCAS had activated during the flight and began investigating the operation of MCAS in connection with pilot training.
context: The court's factual background describes the first crash that should have prompted attention to MCAS within the aviation system.

label: Second crash confirms MCAS problem
original_label: Second crash confirms MCAS problem
quote: On March 10, 2019, another 737 MAX, operating as Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, crashed shortly after taking off from Ethiopia. Reports reveal that MCAS also activated during that flight. Again, none of the 157 passengers and crew survived.
context: The court documents the second crash as a signal that MCAS was a systemic hazard, not an isolated incident.

label: Victim family seeks information about investigation
original_label: Victim family seeks information about investigation
quote: Around the time of the second crash, the U.S. Department of Justice began investigating Boeing. Initially, Boeing's response 'frustrated' the Justice Department's investigation. After a six-month delay, however, Boeing began cooperating with the investigation by identifying relevant documents and witnesses. In February 2020, Thomas Gallagher, a representative of the Flight 302 crash victims' families, reached out to the Justice Department seeking information about possible investigations.
context: The court recounts that victims' families tried to learn whether the crashes were being investigated criminally, indicating a potential warning signal that was being directed to authorities.

label: Victims' inquiry directed to Ombudsman and then dismissed
original_label: Victims' inquiry directed to Ombudsman and then dismissed
quote: The Justice Department's Victims' Rights Ombudsman informed Gallagher that the FBI had advised her that it was not investigating the crash, nor was it aware of any open cases at the Justice Department. She told Gallagher, 'If criminal charges are filed at some point, victims will be advised of that and notified of their rights under the [Crime Victims' Rights Act].' Gallagher then reached out to the FBI Victims' Witness Office, and a victim specialist informed Gallagher that she, too, was unaware of any FBI investigations.
context: The court documents how victim inquiries traveled through official channels but received responses that the crashes were not being investigated, suggesting that warning signals about potential criminal responsibility did not reach decision makers or were filtered out.

label: Chief technical pilots held authority over MCAS disclosure
original_label: Chief technical pilots held authority over MCAS disclosure
quote: The Government alleges that two Boeing employees hid MCAS's low-speed expansion from the AEG. Both employees held the position of chief technical pilot for the 737 MAX program at different times. Part of the chief technical pilot's duties were to work with the AEG on the differences training level determination. According to the Government, the chief technical pilots intentionally hid MCAS's low-speed expansion from the AEG so that they could secure the less rigorous—and less expensive—Level B training.
context: The court identifies that Boeing employees in specific positions with authority over FAA communications chose to conceal information about MCAS from regulators.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Level B training cost incentive drives Boeing's design goal
original_label: Level B training cost incentive drives Boeing's design goal
quote: One of Boeing's goals in designing the 737 MAX was to ensure the designated differences training would be no greater than Level B. Levels of training greater than Level B may require expensive, time-consuming flight-simulator training, while Level B training can be completed anywhere in a matter of hours using a computer or tablet. According to one of Boeing's chief technical pilots, differences training above Level B could have cost Boeing and its customers 'tens of millions of dollars.'
context: The court documents the economic incentive structure that directed Boeing's attention toward achieving low training certification levels, creating a pressure that motivated the fraudulent concealment.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: AEG reliance on Boeing's chief technical pilots
original_label: AEG reliance on Boeing's chief technical pilots
quote: The AEG principally relied on Boeing's chief technical pilots for information relevant to its 737 Max FSB Report, including for information necessary to determine the appropriate level of differences training the AEG would certify. Boeing's employees knew the agency relied on their input in making this certification decision but withheld from AEG the fact that MCAS could activate at low speeds, including during takeoffs and landings—a fact highly relevant for purposes of pilot training.
context: The court describes how the FAA's procedural reliance on Boeing as the primary information source created a structural vulnerability that Boeing employees exploited.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Boeing conceals MCAS low-speed expansion from AEG
original_label: Boeing conceals MCAS low-speed expansion from AEG
quote: The Government alleges that Boeing conspired to defraud the AEG in connection with the AEG's evaluation of MCAS, the 737 MAX differences-training determination, and the FSB Report. The AEG also removed all references to MCAS from its FSB Report based upon Boeing's misrepresentations about the system's low-speed capabilities. On multiple occasions, Boeing employees concealed their knowledge of MCAS's low-speed expansion from AEG and suggested the agency remove all reference to MCAS in its FSB Report based on the misrepresentation that the system would not activate during routine flight operating procedures.
context: The court documents the deliberate filtering and exclusion of information about MCAS from the FAA's certification process, preventing the warning signal from reaching decision makers.

label: Delayed investigation and initial non-cooperation
original_label: Delayed investigation and initial non-cooperation
quote: Around the time of the second crash, the U.S. Department of Justice began investigating Boeing. Initially, Boeing's response 'frustrated' the Justice Department's investigation. After a six-month delay, however, Boeing began cooperating with the investigation by identifying relevant documents and witnesses.
context: The court documents Boeing's initial resistance to cooperating with the DOJ investigation following the crashes, delaying the organizational response to the warning signal.

label: Continued MCAS deception during FAA investigation
original_label: Continued MCAS deception during FAA investigation
quote: Importantly, during the FAA's investigation in the months following the first crash, Boeing's employees continued to mislead the government about their knowledge of MCAS. It follows, then, that if the FAA still lacked all relevant information about the MCAS's low-expansion capabilities, by proxy, so did the broader aviation community.
context: The court finds that Boeing sustained its fraudulent withholding even after the first crash, demonstrating that the warning signal did not prompt corrective disclosure.

label: Presidential grounding order redirects attention after second crash
original_label: Presidential grounding order redirects attention after second crash
quote: Three days later, the President ordered the grounding of all 737 MAX aircraft in the United States.
context: The court notes the pivotal moment when executive action redirected organizational attention after the second crash exposed MCAS failures.

label: Emergency Airworthiness Directive issued after first crash
original_label: Emergency Airworthiness Directive issued after first crash
quote: Weeks after the first crash, and prior to the second, the AEG published an Emergency Airworthiness Directive that included some instruction about deactivating MCAS.
context: The court documents that the FAA responded to the first crash signal by issuing an emergency directive about MCAS, showing a shift in attention to the system's risks.

label: MCAS low-speed expansion scope change post-June 2015
original_label: MCAS low-speed expansion scope change post-June 2015
quote: As originally designed, MCAS operated only during a maneuver called a high-speed, wind-up turn, in which the airplane turns sharply in a corkscrew-like pattern at speeds of Mach 0.6 to 0.8. A high-speed, wind-up turn is a 'certification' maneuver that a pilot would never perform on a typical commercial passenger flight. But sometime after June 2015, MCAS's operational scope was expanded, allowing MCAS to activate at speeds as low as Mach 0.2. The low-speed expansion meant that MCAS could activate during takeoff and landing.
context: The court identifies a design change in MCAS functionality that substantially increased operational risk but was not disclosed to regulators.

label: Global aviation industry follows FAA guidance on training standards
original_label: Global aviation industry follows FAA guidance on training standards
quote: Because the FSB Report omitted material information related to MCAS, U.S.-based airplane manuals and pilot-training materials, relying on the report, did not include related information about the system. By extension, foreign entities did the same. As a matter of common aviation industry practice, it is well-known that foreign airlines and foreign civil aviation authorities rely on the FAA's guidance regarding airplane certification, training requirements, and other relevant information. 'The FAA is perceived to be the world's eminent aviation authority, the gold standard . . . and [] foreign carriers follow their lead.'
context: The court documents the procedural channel through which Boeing's fraudulent withholding from the FAA cascaded globally: foreign regulators adopted the FAA's guidance without independent verification.

label: Boeing representation to Ethiopian Airlines on training level
original_label: Boeing representation to Ethiopian Airlines on training level
quote: In fact, in 2014, Boeing directly represented to Ethiopian Airlines that it would not need differences training higher than Level B for operation of the 737 MAX.
context: The court documents that Boeing communicated the fraudulently obtained Level B training certification directly to foreign airlines, spreading the consequence of the deception.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Boeing prioritized cost reduction over MCAS disclosure
original_label: Boeing prioritized cost reduction over MCAS disclosure
quote: According to one of Boeing's chief technical pilots, differences training above Level B could have cost Boeing and its customers 'tens of millions of dollars.' One of Boeing's goals in designing the 737 MAX was to ensure the designated differences training would be no greater than Level B.
context: The court's factual findings reveal that Boeing's strategic agenda prioritized keeping training costs low, which drove the decision to conceal MCAS information from regulators.

label: FAA AEG certification process depends on Boeing information
original_label: FAA AEG certification process depends on Boeing information
quote: The Aircraft Evaluation Group ('AEG') is the sub-group that determines the minimum level of training required for U.S.-based airline pilots to fly a new version of an aircraft. The AEG does that by evaluating the differences between the new and old aircraft versions, then publishing a 'differences training' determination for the new version. Training levels range from Level A, the least intensive, to Level E, the most intensive. The AEG publishes its determination in a Flight Standardization Board Report ('FSB Report'). Airlines must train their pilots in accordance with the FSB Report, and more intensive training tends to be more expensive for the airlines.
context: The court describes the structural role of the FAA AEG as a procedural gatekeeper whose decisions cascade to global aviation training standards, creating both a pressure point for Boeing and a vulnerability to its deception.

label: Test pilots acknowledged MCAS risks in certification process
original_label: Test pilots acknowledged MCAS risks in certification process
quote: Both said the AEG certified the 737 MAX at a lower training differences level (Level B) than they otherwise would have (Level D) in reliance on Boeing's fraudulent withholding of relevant MCAS information.
context: The court's expert testimony establishes that qualified pilots knew Level D training would have been appropriate had they been told about MCAS's low-speed capabilities, indicating that the warning signal about MCAS risks existed within the certification community.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: AEG Level D training would have prevented crashes
original_label: AEG Level D training would have prevented crashes
quote: Lacking this knowledge and in reliance on Boeing's fraud, AEG certified the 737 MAX for Level B training, rather than the more rigorous, and far more costly, Level D training that AEG would have certified had it known of MCAS's low-speed expansion capabilities. And indeed, this projected course of conduct is affirmed by the fact that AEG ultimately did order Level D flight simulator training for the 737 MAX after obtaining all relevant information about MCAS's low-speed expansion.
context: The court establishes that the FAA possessed the capability to implement adequate safeguards had it not been denied the information Boeing concealed, demonstrating how filtering prevented corrective action.

label: Pilot training inadequacy would have been detected
original_label: Pilot training inadequacy would have been detected
quote: In Captain Norton's expert opinion, had the pilots been trained to respond when confronted with erroneous MCAS activation, as they were here, they could have safely landed those planes. Indeed, an adequately trained pilot could have quickly averted the crises by activating a series of stabilizer trim cutout switches to override MCAS as it was forcing the planes into a nosedive.
context: The court's expert evidence establishes that the warning signal of inadequate pilot training (had it been recognized) would have been actionable to prevent the crashes.

label: Adverse events reports to Sacklers
original_label: Adverse events reports to Sacklers
quote: In July 2007, staff told the Sacklers that more than 5,000 cases of adverse events had been reported to Purdue in just the first three months of 2007. Staff also told the Sacklers that Purdue received 572 Reports of Concern about abuse and diversion of Purdue opioids during Q2 2007 — including several reports in Massachusetts. Staff reported to the Sacklers that they completed only 21 field inquiries in response. Staff also told the Sacklers that they received more than 100 calls to Purdue's compliance hotline during the quarter, which was a "significant increase," but Purdue did not report any of the hotline calls or Reports of Concern to the FDA, DEA, Department of Justice, or state authorities.
context: The Complaint describes Purdue reporting to the Sacklers on adverse events and abuse/diversion reports in Q2 2007, showing board-level awareness of concerning signals.

label: Deaths reported in field
original_label: Deaths reported in field
quote: In December 2009, Purdue's sales rep noted that a patient of Malsky died from an overdose. Three months later, the Purdue representative recorded that Malsky "lost her affiliation with BCBS - however, 75% of those patients switched to other plans in order to stay in her practice; BCBS said she was writing too many opioids as an Internal Medicine doctor[.]"
context: A sales rep documents a patient death and loss of insurance affiliation due to excessive opioid prescribing by a Purdue target physician, demonstrating signals of harm reaching the field.

label: Emails about illegal pill mill
original_label: Emails about illegal pill mill
quote: In September 2009, a Purdue sales manager had emailed Crowley that Purdue was promoting opioids to an illegal pill mill: "I feel very certain this is an organized drug ring," and "Shouldn't the DEA be contacted about this?" Purdue sat on the information and did not report it to the authorities for more than two years, until after the pill mill doctor had already been arrested and the Sacklers had arranged for lawyers in case Crowley was questioned.
context: A Purdue employee raised concerns about drug diversion at a specific location, but the company suppressed the report for over two years, showing how warnings were filtered.

label: Regional Zero doctors with abuse flags
original_label: Regional Zero doctors with abuse flags
quote: At that same Board meeting in Bermuda, the Sacklers and other Board members asked staff about opioid sales generated by doctors who were suspected of diversion and abuse, which Purdue had collected on a list code-named Region Zero. Staff assured the Board that Purdue tracked prescriptions by Region Zero doctors, including the exact prescriptions, units, and dollars from each prescriber. Staff then sent the data on those prescriptions to the Board. Staff told the Board that Purdue had identified twelve prescribers in Massachusetts as likely involved in diversion and abuse. Staff gave the Board a list of the specific problem prescribers by name, along with the exact number of prescriptions and dollars of revenue each provided to Purdue.
context: Board members receive a detailed list of doctors suspected of illegal diversion and abuse, with revenue figures, demonstrating that the board-level decision makers were aware of suspicious prescribers.

label: Reports of dangerous prescribing with patient deaths
original_label: Reports of dangerous prescribing with patient deaths
quote: In 2012 and 2014, Purdue salespeople reported concerns about Choi's prescribing behavior. Both times, Purdue advised the sales reps they could continue promoting opioids to him. In 2017, the Massachusetts Board of Registration in Medicine suspended Choi's license after concluding he had committed negligence on multiple occasions, including in connection with two patients – a mother and son – who both overdosed on opioids and died.
context: Sales staff raised concerns about a prescriber's behavior twice, but Purdue directed them to continue promotion; later the doctor's license was suspended after patient deaths occurred.

label: Map of dangerous prescribers and poison control calls
original_label: Map of dangerous prescribers and poison control calls
quote: In February, staff told the Sacklers that Purdue received 284 Reports of Concern about abuse and diversion of Purdue's opioids in Q4 2007, and they conducted only 21 field inquiries in response. Staff also reported to the Sacklers that they received 39 tips to Purdue's compliance hotline during the quarter, but Purdue did not report any of them to the authorities. Staff also gave the Sacklers a map correlating dangerous prescribers in Massachusetts with reports of oxycodone poisonings, burglaries, and robberies.
context: Staff presented the Sacklers with a map showing geographic correlation between suspected diverter prescribers and overdose/poisoning incidents, making the connection between prescribing and harm visible.

label: DEA official warns about deaths
original_label: DEA official warns about deaths
quote: That spring, Purdue executives met with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency ("DEA"). A senior DEA official sat across from Richard Sackler. Before the meeting ended, she leaned over the table and told Richard: "People are dying. Do you understand that?"
context: A DEA official directly communicated to Richard Sackler that deaths were occurring from the company's opioids, constituting an external warning that reached top leadership.

label: Compliance violations reported to board
original_label: Compliance violations reported to board
quote: In May, staff told the Sacklers that Purdue had violated its Corporate Integrity Agreement with the U.S. government by failing to supervise its sales reps. Because sales reps lobbying doctors poses a high risk of misconduct (no witnesses, and the rep is paid to increase opioid sales), the United States required that Purdue managers supervise sales reps in person at least 5 days each year. Purdue management disregarded that obligation and did not even set up a system to track it.
context: Staff reported to the Sacklers that Purdue had violated a core requirement of its Corporate Integrity Agreement, revealing a structural breakdown in compliance supervision.

label: Weekly sales reports to Richard Sackler
original_label: Weekly sales reports to Richard Sackler
quote: What do I have to do to get a weekly report on Butrans sales without having to ask for it? One exasperated staff member begged another to respond. The CEO announced that, from then on, staff would send a sales report to the Sacklers every week. When staff sent the first weekly report, Richard responded immediately: "What else more can we do to energize the sales and grow at a faster rate?" The next week, Richard wrote to the sales staff to ask about the performance of a specific sales rep.
context: Richard Sackler demanded and received weekly sales reports, establishing a channel for very frequent monitoring of sales metrics that became routine.

label: Board minutes tracking sales visit quotas
original_label: Board minutes tracking sales visit quotas
quote: In February, Purdue's Sales and Marketing Department reported to Boer, Lewent, and Pickett that a key objective for 2010 was meeting a prescriber sales call quota of 545,000. Sales call quotas remained a priority over the next four years, and the Board tracked the sales force's performance on at least a quarterly basis as the quota rose from 545,000 prescriber visits in 2010, to 712,000 visits in 2011, 752,417 visits in 2012, and 744,777 visits in 2013.
context: The board formally tracked sales visit quotas as a key performance metric across multiple years, establishing prescriber visits as a central item of board-level attention.

label: Sacklers' controlling board majority
original_label: Sacklers' controlling board majority
quote: The Sackler family owns Purdue, and they always held a majority of the seats on its Board. Because they controlled their own privately held drug company, the Sacklers had the power to decide how addictive narcotics were sold. They hired hundreds of workers to carry out their wishes, and they fired those who didn't sell enough drugs.
context: The Complaint describes the structural position of the Sacklers as majority board members with full control over company strategy and personnel decisions.

label: Richard Sackler as CEO directing sales
original_label: Richard Sackler as CEO directing sales
