quote: From 2007 to 2018, the Sackler controlled Purdue's deceptive sales campaign. They directed the company to hire hundreds more sales reps to visit doctors thousands more times. They insisted that sales reps repeatedly visit the most prolific prescribers. They directed reps to encourage doctors to prescribe more of the highest doses of opioids. They studied unlawful tactics to keep patients on opioids longer and then ordered staff to use them. They asked for detailed reports about doctors suspected of misconduct, how much money Purdue made from them, and how few of them Purdue had reported to the authorities. They sometimes demanded more detail than anyone else in the entire company, so staff had to create special reports just for them. Richard Sackler even went into the field to promote opioids to doctors and supervise reps face to face.
context: The Complaint describes Richard Sackler's hands-on involvement in directing sales tactics, creating special information flows, and personally visiting the field.

label: Sackler micromanagement overwhelming VP of Sales
original_label: Sackler micromanagement overwhelming VP of Sales
quote: The Sacklers' micromanagement was so intrusive that staff begged for relief. The VP of Sales and Marketing wrote to the CEO: "Anything you can do to reduce the direct contact of Richard into the organization is appreciated."
context: The VP of Sales wrote to the CEO seeking relief from Richard Sackler's direct and frequent interventions into sales operations, showing the intensity of Sackler control over sales.

label: CEO Stewart reporting sales to Richard Sackler
original_label: CEO Stewart reporting sales to Richard Sackler
quote: Richard Sackler kept pushing for more sales. After one week of prescriptions doubled Purdue's forecast, Richard wrote to the sales staff: "I had hoped for better results." In a follow-up message, Richard asked staff to tell him the ratio of prescriptions per sales representative visit to a prescriber, divided out by the prescribers' specialties. He asked for a Board discussion of the barriers that sales reps were encountering during promotion. After trying to answer Richard's questions and getting another dissatisfied response, sales staff wrote to the CEO to ask him to intervene.
context: Richard Sackler directly pressured sales staff on sales metrics, and when they did not respond to his satisfaction, they escalated to the CEO, showing the hierarchical channel of attention.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Sales reps judged by opioid prescriptions
original_label: Sales reps judged by opioid prescriptions
quote: Purdue judged its sales reps by how many opioids they got doctors to prescribe. Sales reps who generated the most prescriptions won bonuses and prizes. Reps who failed to get enough Massachusetts patients on opioids were placed on probation, put on performance improvement plans, and fired.
context: The Complaint describes the formal performance metric and incentive system that made prescription volume the dominant measure of rep success.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Daily visit targets for sales reps
original_label: Daily visit targets for sales reps
quote: The Sacklers required each rep to visit an average of 7.5 prescribers per day. In April 2010, staff reported that they were falling short. During Q1 2010, reps had averaged only 7.0 visits per day. Staff promised to try harder. The Sacklers continued to set a target for daily sales visits for every sales rep, and they tracked the results, quarter by quarter, for at least the next four years. The results were always close to 7 visits per day.
context: The Sacklers set and monitored a specific daily visit target for each sales rep, making this a formal performance metric tracked by the board.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Quarterly sales visit quotas for entire force
original_label: Quarterly sales visit quotas for entire force
quote: The Sacklers also set targets for the total number of sales visits by the entire sales force per quarter — huge numbers that were always more than a hundred thousand visits. Meeting those targets was a top priority for the entire company. For Q1 2010, the target was to visit prescribers 127,376 times. Staff told the Sacklers that Purdue employed 489 sales reps and that, during Q1 2010, they achieved the goal.
context: The board set aggregate quarterly sales visit quotas as a top company priority and tracked achievement against them, making prescriber visits a central KPI.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Bonus compensation tied to opioid sales
original_label: Bonus compensation tied to opioid sales
quote: In March, the Sacklers voted to award bonuses and salary increases to executives, including those involved in marketing Purdue's opioids.
context: The Sacklers formally voted to provide bonus compensation to marketing executives, directly tying their pay to opioid sales efforts.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Employee scorecards weighted to opioid sales
original_label: Employee scorecards weighted to opioid sales
quote: That same month, the Sacklers voted to evaluate employees' 2014 performance on a scorecard that assigned the greatest value to the volume of Purdue opioid sales. Employees were expected to generate more than one-and-a-half billion dollars. The Sacklers also voted to establish the company's scorecard for 2015: once again, the biggest factor determining employees' payout would be the total amount of Purdue opioid sales.
context: The Sacklers established a formal performance evaluation system where the largest component of compensation and evaluation was opioid sales volume.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Board meetings focused on sales revenue
original_label: Board meetings focused on sales revenue
quote: In August, Richard Sackler convened a meeting of Board members and staff about "all the efforts Sales and Marketing is doing and planning to do to reverse the decline in OxyContin tablets market." He emphasized that $200,000,000 in profit was at stake. At the meeting, staff told the Sacklers that the 80mg OxyContin pill was far-and-away Purdue's best performing drug. Purdue sold many more kilograms of active ingredient in the 80mg dose than any other dose (about 1,000 kilograms: literally a ton of oxycodone).
context: Richard Sackler called a board meeting specifically to address declining OxyContin sales and hear about profit implications, showing sales revenue as the dominant agenda item.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Board meeting to reverse OxyContin decline
original_label: Board meeting to reverse OxyContin decline
quote: In July, Richard Sackler told staff that he was not satisfied with OxyContin sales and demanded a plan to "boost" them. He asked for the topic to be added to the agenda for the Board.
context: Richard Sackler directed that a declining opioid product become a priority board agenda item, showing sales volume as the core focus.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Board discussions of dose mix and tablet counts
original_label: Board discussions of dose mix and tablet counts
quote: Staff told the Sacklers that they were not achieving the goals of getting enough patients on higher doses of opioids and getting doctors to prescribe more pills in each prescription. Staff told them that "there is an 'unfavorable' mix of prescriptions across strengths," and Purdue was losing tens of millions of dollars in revenue because sales of the highest doses (60mg and 80mg) were too low. Staff told the Sacklers that there was also a second problem: "lower average tablet counts per prescription."
context: The board focused on two specific metrics: the mix of doses being prescribed and the average number of tablets per prescription, showing which metrics captured board attention.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Family dividend distributions tracked at board
original_label: Family dividend distributions tracked at board
quote: The Sacklers cared most of all about money. From 2007 to 2018, they voted to direct Purdue to pay their family billions of dollars, including tens of millions of dollars from opioids sold in Massachusetts. These payments show the total control that the Sacklers exercised over Purdue. The payments were the motivation for the Sacklers' misconduct. And the payments were deliberate decisions to benefit from deception in Massachusetts, at great cost to patients and families.
context: The Complaint notes that the Sacklers repeatedly voted to distribute billions to themselves, showing that family payments were a core board agenda item.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Reports of concern not reported to authorities
original_label: Reports of concern not reported to authorities
quote: Staff reported to the Sacklers that Purdue received 572 Reports of Concern about abuse and diversion of Purdue opioids during Q2 2007 — including several reports in Massachusetts. Staff reported to the Sacklers that they completed only 21 field inquiries in response. Staff also told the Sacklers that they received more than 100 calls to Purdue's compliance hotline during the quarter, but Purdue did not report any of the hotline calls or Reports of Concern to the FDA, DEA, Department of Justice, or state authorities.
context: Staff reported to the Sacklers that hundreds of abuse/diversion concerns were received but not investigated thoroughly and not reported to authorities, showing selective filtering.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Region Zero doctors not reported despite profit tracking
original_label: Region Zero doctors not reported despite profit tracking
quote: In March, staff reported to the Sacklers on OxyContin sales and again focused on revenue from doctors in Region Zero — prescribers that Purdue suspected of improper prescribing but that Purdue had not reported to the authorities. Staff told the Sacklers that if Region Zero doctors stopped prescribing opioids, Purdue would lose almost 10% of its sales.
context: Purdue tracked the financial contribution of Region Zero prescribers to the board but did not report them to authorities, showing profit interest overriding compliance duty.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Continued promotion despite reports of concern
original_label: Continued promotion despite reports of concern
quote: By 2012, Purdue knew or should have known that Benoit was engaged in problematic prescribing practices, keeping patients on opioids for extended periods without proper medical exams. Purdue's rep met with the doctor and recorded: "he said that he does just refill meds out of ease of refilling given challenge with time in exam." At the next sales visit two weeks later, Purdue encouraged the doctor to prescribe more refills of its opioids.
context: After a sales rep documented a doctor's problematic refilling practices, Purdue continued to promote opioids to the same doctor rather than acting on the report.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Sales continued after license suspension
original_label: Sales continued after license suspension
quote: In May 2016, Purdue's sales rep logged a "Report Of Concern" when a newspaper reported on Benoit's excessive opioid prescribing and police found a patient with 420 pills. Purdue kept promoting opioids to the doctor anyway. When the Board of Registration in Medicine suspended Benoit's medical license on May 5, 2016, Purdue was still urging him to prescribe its drugs. Purdue last attempted to promote opioids to Benoit on May 10, 2016, five days after his suspension.
context: After documented external warnings (police, board action) about a prescriber, Purdue continued promotion efforts, showing how warnings were disregarded.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: McKinsey advice to work around pharmacy safeguards
original_label: McKinsey advice to work around pharmacy safeguards
quote: McKinsey told Boer, Lewent, Pickett, Costa, and Snyderman that "deep examination of Purdue's available pharmacy purchasing data shows that Walgreens has reduced its units by 18%." Even worse for the Sacklers, the new safeguards were hurting sales of the highest doses: "the Walgreens data also shows a significant impact on higher OxyContin dosages" — specifically the 80mg dose. McKinsey urged Boer, Lewent, Pickett, Costa, and Snyderman to lobby Walgreens' leaders to loosen up. For the longer term, McKinsey advised the Board to develop a "direct-to-patient mail order" business for Purdue opioids, so they could sell the high doses without pharmacies getting in the way.
context: McKinsey recommended to the board that Purdue work around pharmacy compliance safeguards by shifting to channels outside pharmacy supervision, showing how warnings were reframed as obstacles to overcome.

label: Decision to not report hotline calls to authorities
original_label: Decision to not report hotline calls to authorities
quote: Staff reported to the Sacklers that Purdue received 284 Reports of Concern about abuse and diversion of Purdue's opioids in Q4 2007, and they conducted only 21 field inquiries in response. Staff also reported to the Sacklers that they received 39 tips to Purdue's compliance hotline during the quarter, but Purdue did not report any of them to the authorities.
context: The Sacklers were informed that hotline calls received were not being reported to authorities, and this policy was reported to the board as routine practice.

label: Sales force expansion ordered after abuse reports
original_label: Sales force expansion ordered after abuse reports
quote: In October, staff told the Sacklers that surveillance data monitored by Purdue indicated a "wide geographic dispersion" of abuse and diversion of OxyContin "throughout the United States." Staff told the Sacklers that "availability of the product" and "prescribing practices" were key factors driving abuse and diversion of OxyContin." On the same day, staff told the Sacklers that Purdue had begun a new "Toppers Club sales contest" for sales reps to win bonuses, based on how much a rep increased OxyContin use in her territory and how much the rep increased the broader prescribing of opioids — the same "availability of product" and "prescribing practices" factors that worsen the risk of diversion and abuse.
context: The board received a report that availability and prescribing practices were driving diversion, then simultaneously approved a sales contest designed to increase those same factors.

label: Settlement payments to individuals under investigation
original_label: Settlement payments to individuals under investigation
quote: In January 2011, the Sacklers voted to pay the legal expenses of specific individuals if they were defendants or witnesses in investigations of Purdue, including several sales executives and John Crowley, Executive Director of Controlled Substances Act Compliance.
context: The Sacklers voted to pay legal expenses for employees who might be questioned in investigations, showing a proactive step to protect potential witnesses.

label: Documents sent to field with anonymity instruction
original_label: Documents sent to field with anonymity instruction
quote: To make sure the Sacklers' involvement in marketing stayed secret, staff instructed: "Richard needs to be mum and be anonymous."
context: After Richard Sackler went into the field to promote opioids with sales reps, staff instructed him to remain unidentified, showing deliberate concealment.

label: Mitigation effort to counter Los Angeles Times
original_label: Mitigation effort to counter Los Angeles Times
quote: In June, staff sent the Sacklers an "Update on L.A. Times mitigation effort" about tactics to discourage scrutiny of Purdue's misconduct. Staff wrote to the Sacklers: "As you may recall, one of our efforts to mitigate the impact of a potential negative Los Angeles Times (LAT) story involved assisting a competing outlet in marginalizing the LAT's unbalanced coverage by reporting the facts before the LAT story ran."
context: Purdue's communications staff reported to the Sacklers on a strategy to plant favorable stories in competing outlets to pre-empt negative Times coverage.

label: Statement denying Sackler management roles
original_label: Statement denying Sackler management roles
quote: In November, staff prepared statements to the press denying the Sacklers' involvement in Purdue. Their draft claimed: "Sackler family members hold no leadership roles in the companies owned by the family trust." That was a lie. Sackler family members held the controlling majority of seats on the Board and, in fact, controlled the company.
context: Purdue communications staff drafted a false public statement denying Sackler board roles, showing deliberate misrepresentation to external audiences.

label: Compliance failures not reported despite requirement
original_label: Compliance failures not reported despite requirement
quote: Staff told the Sacklers that Purdue had violated its Corporate Integrity Agreement with the U.S. government by failing to supervise its sales reps. Because sales reps lobbying doctors poses a high risk of misconduct (no witnesses, and the rep is paid to increase opioid sales), the United States required that Purdue managers supervise sales reps in person at least 5 days each year. Purdue management disregarded that obligation and did not even set up a system to track it. Even though Purdue executives had ignored the requirement and not monitored it, they responded to the violation by firing three employees in the field and letting all the executives at headquarters keep their jobs.
context: Staff reported to the Sacklers that Purdue had failed to comply with a Corporate Integrity Agreement requirement, then fired field staff rather than executives.

label: FDA approval and early warnings ignored
original_label: FDA approval and early warnings ignored
quote: Purdue launched OxyContin in 1996. It became one of the deadliest drugs of all time. The FDA scientist who evaluated OxyContin wrote in his original review: "Care should be taken to limit competitive promotion." The Sacklers did not agree. From the beginning, the Sacklers viewed limits on opioids as an obstacle to greater profits.
context: An FDA scientist's warning about limiting promotion was issued at OxyContin's launch but did not alter Sackler strategy, showing early signals were overridden.

label: Criminal convictions in 2007 followed by continued misconduct
original_label: Criminal convictions in 2007 followed by continued misconduct
quote: In May 2007, the Sacklers voted again to have their company plead guilty and enter a series of agreements that Purdue would never deceive doctors and patients about opioids again. The Purdue Frederick Company confessed to a felony and effectively went out of business. The Sacklers continued their opioid business in two other companies: Purdue Pharma Inc. and Purdue Pharma L.P.
context: After Purdue's guilty plea and commitment not to engage in deceptive marketing, the Sacklers immediately continued similar conduct under different corporate entities.

label: Chicago subpoena for internal documents
original_label: Chicago subpoena for internal documents
quote: After Q4 2013, Purdue abolished the detailed Quarterly Reports that had created a paper trail of targets for sales visits and been emailed among the Board and staff. In 2013, the City of Chicago served Purdue with a subpoena seeking internal documents about Purdue's marketing of opioids. That provoked a flurry of activity, including discussion among the Sacklers. Purdue fought the subpoena, and it was withdrawn. For 2014, Purdue decided to limit many of its official Board reports to numbers and graphs, and relay other information orally.
context: After a government subpoena for internal documents, Purdue changed its record-keeping practices to limit the paper trail, shifting to oral communication of sensitive information.

label: Massachusetts becomes focus after legislation introduced
original_label: Massachusetts becomes focus after legislation introduced
quote: Later that month, Stewart met with Gasdia, Landau, and others to discuss legislation that had been introduced in Massachusetts to ban extended-release oxycodone, including Purdue's OxyContin.
context: After Massachusetts legislation threatened Purdue's product, it became a topic of executive attention and response planning.

label: New Yorker article about family published
original_label: New Yorker article about family published
quote: A week later, the New Yorker published an article entitled "The Family That Built an Empire of Pain." The story quoted a former FDA Commissioner: "the goal should have been to sell the least dose of the drug to the smallest number of patients." The reporter concluded: "Purdue set out to do exactly the opposite."
context: A high-profile media exposé directly attributed the opioid strategy to the Sackler family, marking a major triggering event for external scrutiny.

label: Sacklers begin resigning from board after lawsuit
original_label: Sacklers begin resigning from board after lawsuit
quote: On June 12, 2018, the Massachusetts Attorney General filed this suit to hold the Sacklers as well as Purdue accountable. Just as their employees predicted, the Sacklers tried to run. Richard Sackler was the first to go: he resigned from the Board in July. David Sackler quit in August. Theresa Sackler served her last day in September.
context: The filing of the Massachusetts AG lawsuit triggered immediate resignations by Sackler family members from the board, marking a shift to defensive posture.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: McKinsey analysis of Massachusetts high-dose revenue at risk
original_label: McKinsey analysis of Massachusetts high-dose revenue at risk
quote: In April, the Sacklers considered exactly how much money was riding on their strategy of pushing higher doses of opioids. The month before, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control announced guidelines to try to slow the epidemic of opioid overdose and death. The CDC urged prescribers to avoid doses higher than 30mg of Purdue's OxyContin twice per day. The CDC discouraged twice-a-day prescriptions of all three of Purdue's most profitable strengths — 40mg, 60mg, and 80mg. Staff studied how much money Purdue was making from its high dose strategy and told the Sacklers that $23,964,122 was at risk in Massachusetts each year.
context: After CDC guidelines against high doses, Purdue calculated and reported to the board the exact dollar amount at risk in Massachusetts, showing financial exposure became a board-level agenda item.

label: Richard Sackler demanding spreadsheets for analysis
original_label: Richard Sackler demanding spreadsheets for analysis
quote: In preparation for an upcoming Board meeting, Richard Sackler instructed staff to give him the spreadsheets underlying their sales analysis, so that he could do his own calculations. The spreadsheets showed that, in 2007, Purdue expected to collect more than half its total revenue from sales of 80mg OxyContin — its most powerful, most profitable, and most dangerous pill.
context: Richard Sackler demanded raw sales data and spreadsheets to conduct personal calculations, creating a direct information channel from operations to the controlling shareholder.

label: Sales VP Gasdia caught between Richard and CEO
original_label: Sales VP Gasdia caught between Richard and CEO
quote: Sales VP Russell Gasdia was struggling to handle the pressure. When Richard Sackler sent Gasdia a list of seven sales questions to answer on a Saturday (and copied Ilene, Jonathan, Kathe, Mortimer, and Theresa Sackler), Gasdia wrote to John Stewart: "John, I know it is tricky, but Dr. Richard has to back off somewhat. He is pulling people in all directions, creating a lot of extra work and increasing pressure and stress. I will draft a response but he is not realistic in his expectations and it is very difficult to get him to understand."
context: The VP of Sales was caught between Richard Sackler's direct demands and his role under the CEO, and appealed to the CEO for relief from the pressure.

label: Staff warned about federal investigation of four Massachusetts prescribers
original_label: Staff warned about federal investigation of four Massachusetts prescribers
quote: In 2002, staff sent Gasdia an email identifying four Massachusetts OxyContin prescribers believed to be the subjects of a federal investigation. The urgency of the message was explicit: 'This is most urgent.'
context: The complaint describes how Gasdia received a warning about prescribers under federal investigation in Massachusetts but did not act to restrict sales targeting to them.

label: Gasdia as vice president controlled sales targeting and performance
original_label: Gasdia as vice president controlled sales targeting and performance
quote: From 2007 until 2014, Gasdia was Purdue's Vice President of Sales and Marketing. He was responsible for getting more patients on opioids, at higher doses, for longer periods of time. Gasdia had his hands on every part of Purdue's deceptive sales campaign: from the fundamentals of getting more patients on opioids at higher doses for longer periods; to the targeting of prolific opioid prescribers; to paying doctors to promote Purdue opioids; to concealing Purdue's list of problem doctors codenamed Region Zero; to deciding what would get a sales rep hired or fired.
context: Gasdia's position and scope of authority over the sales scheme are outlined in the complaint, showing his central role in directing attention toward sales volume.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Sales force targets measured by prescriber visit frequency
original_label: Sales force targets measured by prescriber visit frequency
quote: Managing down, Gasdia tracked his subordinates' adherence to his targets and assigned them grades that determined their pay. Gasdia understood that sending sales reps to promote opioids would get more patients on opioids. A detailed analysis he ordered showed Purdue opioid prescriptions by each doctor increasing from less than one per month to more than forty per month as sales reps visited doctors more often.
context: Gasdia's management system tied compensation to sales rep performance measured by prescriber visits, directing attention to sales volume as the key metric.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Board reports focused on increasing prescriptions and sales
original_label: Board reports focused on increasing prescriptions and sales
quote: Staff explained to Stewart and the Board that in the fourth quarter of 2013, sales reps would increase the number of visits to prescribers. In Massachusetts, during those three months, sales visits increased by 30%. Staff also reported to Stewart that a key initiative in 2013 was to train sales reps to keep patients on Butrans longer. They told Stewart that, at exactly the same time as the initiative to keep patients on opioids longer, Purdue launched a new high dose of its Butrans opioid. Sales reps began promoting the new high dose to physicians and initial orders were double the company's forecasts. Staff also reported to Stewart that marketing and sales activities generated 266,842 additional prescriptions and opioid savings cards generated especially 'high returns' by keeping patients on opioids longer.
context: Board reports in 2013 focused CEO Stewart's attention on sales metrics and prescription volume increases, showing the dominant agenda was commercial growth.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Compensation system paid reps for higher doses of opioids
original_label: Compensation system paid reps for higher doses of opioids
quote: In 2014, Gasdia proposed revising Purdue's compensation system to pay sales reps more when the doctors they targeted prescribed higher doses of opioids. Gasdia noted that, for many years, Purdue paid sales reps 'based on 20mg equivalents,' so a sales rep who convinced a doctor to move a patient from 40mg to 80mg OxyContin would double his credit. But recently Purdue was treating all prescriptions the same: 'right now, an Rx has the same value on the incentive plan, when each Rx has different values to the company.' Gasdia admitted (in private, in his email to his colleagues) that Purdue's tradition of paying reps more for higher doses posed an inherent risk of 'reps inappropriately promoting the higher doses.' But he recommended that Purdue consider it anyway.
context: Gasdia's proposal shows how compensation rules directed attention and incentive toward higher-dose prescribing, with explicit acknowledgment of the risk this created.

label: Gasdia prohibited email communication on sensitive topics
original_label: Gasdia prohibited email communication on sensitive topics
quote: To limit the evidence of its misconduct, Purdue tried to discourage email. When staff emailed Gasdia a detailed report of illegal OxyContin trafficking, he responded: 'These should not be on email. Tell [District Managers] and Reps to use fax.' When the Northeast Regional Manager emailed Gasdia about the arrest of a profitable 'core physician' in Massachusetts, Gasdia ordered: 'Discontinue use of email on this subject.' When sales staff emailed each other about how to 'push' doctors, Gasdia instructed: 'Please take this off line. I would prefer a face to face discussion on this.'
context: Gasdia used procedural control over communication channels to prevent documentation of misconduct, blocking email as a channel for sensitive topics.

label: Gasdia fired sales rep for sending email to doctor about opioids
original_label: Gasdia fired sales rep for sending email to doctor about opioids
quote: Purdue's most severe policy against email prohibited sales reps from writing down in emails their sales pitches to doctors. By insisting that sales reps discuss opioids only in face-to-face oral conversations, Purdue tried to avoid discoverable evidence of its misconduct. As the top sales and marketing executive in the company, Gasdia personally enforced that rule with a vengeance. When Gasdia learned that a sales rep had sent a doctor email about Purdue opioids, he ordered: 'Fire her now! We can't afford this.'
context: Gasdia's enforcement action against documentation of sales pitches shows how procedures designed to avoid evidence were backed up with severe discipline.

label: Staff suggested reporting Region Zero doctors to insurance companies
original_label: Staff suggested reporting Region Zero doctors to insurance companies
quote: In 2012, as more patients got addicted and died, a staff member made a plea to Gasdia that Purdue should tell insurance companies the names of doctors in Region Zero so that insurance companies could double-check their prescriptions for signs of illegal prescribing. In language that stands out from many of the other Purdue emails, the employee wrote that 'it just seems like the right and ethical thing to do.' He wrote: 'it seems to make sense for a number of reasons for us to share the information on Region 0 doctors with payers. At a basic level, it just seems like the right and ethical thing to do. Doing so could help those companies identify those physicians that may be of a concern, not just with respect to our products, but also other CII and CIII therapies. As a result, if it reduces abuse and diversion of opioids then it seems like something we should be doing.' Gasdia rejected the suggestion, and Region Zero remained secret.
context: A staff member raised a warning signal and ethical concern about concealment of problem prescribers, but Gasdia blocked this corrective action.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Sales rep bonuses tied to prescriptions from Core and Super Core doctors
original_label: Sales rep bonuses tied to prescriptions from Core and Super Core doctors
quote: To enforce focus on the prolific prescribers, Gasdia changed the compensation plan to pay larger bonuses for increased prescribing by Core and Super Core prescribers. For example, the First Quarter 2014 Incentive Program provided a quarterly bonus of up to $11,655 for OxyContin prescriptions by 'Selected Prescribers' — Cores and Super Cores — and up to $4,995 for OxyContin prescriptions by 'All Other Prescribers.' The memo announcing the incentive program explained: '[t]his incentive gives you the opportunity to earn a greater bonus for the Selected Prescribers with whom you have the greatest ability to appropriately influence prescribing patterns.'
context: Gasdia's incentive structure focused sales force attention on the highest-volume prescribers, many of whom were targeted because they were known to prescribe dangerously.

label: Purdue maintained secret list of problem prescribers without reporting them
original_label: Purdue maintained secret list of problem prescribers without reporting them
quote: Gasdia also kept track of another list of profitable prescribers who were as dangerous as the Super Cores — Purdue's secret Region Zero. Purdue did not want to be blamed for those doctors' prescriptions, so it did not send sales reps to visit them. But Purdue still tracked dollar-by-dollar its profits from their prescriptions, and those profits were large, and Purdue did not report the doctors to the authorities.
context: Purdue's response to identifying problem prescribers was to segregate them from overt sales visits while continuing to profit from them and concealing them from authorities.

label: Gasdia prepared Region Zero reports for Board meetings
original_label: Gasdia prepared Region Zero reports for Board meetings
quote: In 2010, the Board asked for an update on opioid sales generated by Region Zero prescribers. Together with three other executives, Gasdia prepared a report that told the Board exactly which doctors were suspected of illegitimate opioid prescribing, and each one's prescriptions, by units and dollars. That list included Massachusetts prescribers in Brookfield, Buzzards Bay, Holyoke, Lawrence, Leominster, New Bedford, Northampton, Orleans, Springfield, Stoneham, Waltham, and Worcester.
context: Gasdia's position allowed him to funnel information about problem prescribers directly to the Board while keeping this list secret from outside authorities.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Performance reviews tied to opioid sales targets
original_label: Performance reviews tied to opioid sales targets
quote: In March 2012, Gasdia wrote to Purdue's top sales staff that they would be paid at 69% of target because they did not sell enough drugs. For the lowest-level sales reps, the consequences were more severe: Gasdia wrote that his staff was 'addressing poor performance with PEP [performance enhancement plans], probations, and terminations.' He wrote that many sales rep resignations were firings in disguise. Gasdia wrote that employees' jobs depended on meeting the Sacklers' expectations for opioid sales: 'We must achieve forecast for Butrans and OxyContin.'
context: Gasdia's management system created incentives and discipline tied directly to opioid sales volume, making this the dominant measure of success.

label: Gasdia placed sales reps on performance improvement plans to increase prescriptions
original_label: Gasdia placed sales reps on performance improvement plans to increase prescriptions
quote: Although they did not fire all the Boston reps, Gasdia saw to it that sales reps who failed to meet their sales objectives were placed on probation or on performance improvement plans ('PIPs'). As explained in paragraph 350 above, one sales rep was put on a performance improvement plan and ordered to visit 10 specific prescribers twice every week and increase prescriptions by 43%. Another rep was ordered to increase prescriptions by 62%. Purdue issued a performance enhancement plan to another sales rep that said: 'Anticipated Challenges: Dr. trying to cut down on opioid prescribing due to abuse.' 'Action Steps: Sell for patients they are willing to Rx opioids …(elderly).' Purdue also ordered the rep to do a better job using gifts ('coffee, lunch') to buy time with prescribers and reminded her that Purdue had a budget for that purpose.
context: Gasdia used performance management procedures as a mechanism to enforce sales targets, even when aware that prescribers were trying to reduce opioid prescribing.

label: Sales staff warned that prescriber was dangerous but targeting continued
original_label: Sales staff warned that prescriber was dangerous but targeting continued
quote: Seventeen patients who were prescribed Purdue opioids by Mashali died of opioid overdoses. Purdue's sales reps visited Mashali and Jayma more than 195 times, and Purdue management ordered the reps to keep promoting opioids to them, even after reps warned Purdue that they were dangerous prescribers.
context: Sales reps raised warnings to management about dangerous prescribers, but Gasdia's response was to order continued promotion of opioids to these doctors.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: CEO Stewart received reports on sales strategy and revenue impacts
original_label: CEO Stewart received reports on sales strategy and revenue impacts
quote: In December, Stewart informed Kathe Sackler and Gasdia that Evolve 2 Excellence — the aggressive sales strategy — was already increasing prescriptions and revenue. Stewart knew and intended that these changes in sales practices would drive increased prescriptions, including in Massachusetts.

label: Stewart as CEO responsible for sales and marketing strategy
original_label: Stewart as CEO responsible for sales and marketing strategy
quote: Stewart resigned from Purdue at the end of 2013. Stewart has collected substantial revenue from the sale of Purdue opioids in Massachusetts, as detailed in Exhibit 2. While Stewart was Purdue's chief executive, at least 247 Massachusetts patients died of opioid-related overdoses after taking the drugs he sold.
context: Stewart's position as CEO gave him responsibility for sales strategy and direct financial benefit from opioid sales, establishing his structural role in the scheme.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Gasdia measured sales rep performance by prescriber visit frequency
original_label: Gasdia measured sales rep performance by prescriber visit frequency
quote: Gasdia understood that sending sales reps to promote opioids would get more patients on opioids. A detailed analysis he ordered showed Purdue opioid prescriptions by each doctor increasing from less than one per month to more than forty per month as sales reps visited doctors more often. Accordingly, Gasdia worked to expand the sales force, over and over, from around 300 sales reps in 2007 to more than 600 sales reps in 2014.
context: Gasdia's analysis linked visit frequency to prescriptions, which became the metric used to direct attention and allocate resources in sales force expansion.

label: Gasdia reported to board on sales rep presentation metrics
original_label: Gasdia reported to board on sales rep presentation metrics
quote: Managing up, Gasdia told the Sacklers how many times sales reps would visit prescribers each day, each quarter, and each year. Managing down, Gasdia tracked his subordinates' adherence to his targets and assigned them grades that determined their pay.
context: Gasdia's reporting to the board and management of subordinates created a communication channel that made prescriber visit frequency the dominant metric flowing upward.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Gasdia reported board concern about OxyContin sales trends
original_label: Gasdia reported board concern about OxyContin sales trends
quote: When sales rep presentations to doctors and nurses fell, Gasdia ordered reps to visit prescribers more often to increase opioid use: 'We are nowhere near the number of [sales] presentations required to meet our objective … which is unacceptable and a significant concern. I can't impress upon you enough the significant concerns at the Board level as well as senior management with regards to the OxyContin sales trends. We have assured the BOD that with an increase in [sales] presentations, we should see a lift in Rxs.'
context: Gasdia's communication shows how the board's attention was focused on sales presentation frequency and its linkage to prescriptions, which was the dominant agenda.

label: Data showed higher doses keep patients on therapy longer
original_label: Data showed higher doses keep patients on therapy longer
quote: Gasdia knew that higher doses put patients in danger. The same presentation that explained Gasdia's sales plan listed public health efforts that Gasdia believed were responsible for the drop in high-dose, high-profit sales. Indeed, Purdue knew more about the dangers than the authorities did. Purdue had studied confidential prescription data and determined that higher doses kept patients on opioids longer: 'There is a direct relationship between OxyContin LoT [length of therapy] and dose.'
context: Gasdia and the company had internal data showing the risks of higher doses in relation to length of therapy, yet proceeded with promotion of higher doses.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Opioid savings cards featured as high-return marketing tool
original_label: Opioid savings cards featured as high-return marketing tool
quote: Staff told the Board that keeping patients on opioids longer was so profitable that the Return On Investment for the marketing was 4.28 — Purdue collected an extra $4,280,000 for every $1,000,000 it spent. That analysis did not take into account the cost to patients and families from addiction, overdose, and death.
context: The board was presented with financial metrics showing the profitability of keeping patients on therapy longer, directing attention toward this outcome.

label: Gasdia targeted doctors under federal investigation as Super Core
original_label: Gasdia targeted doctors under federal investigation as Super Core
quote: Gasdia did not steer Purdue reps away from the doctors. Instead, he did the opposite and ordered reps to focus on them as highly-profitable 'Super Core' targets. Under Gasdia's direction, sales reps visited those specific doctors hundreds of times.
context: Gasdia's response to learning about federal investigation of four prescribers was to intensify sales targeting of them rather than restrict contact.

label: Purdue paid investigated prescriber to promote opioids
original_label: Purdue paid investigated prescriber to promote opioids
quote: For one of the four doctors on the 'urgent' investigation list, Gasdia went further. Sales staff had selected Dr. Walter Jacobs in North Andover, Massachusetts, as a 'thought leader' and paid Purdue spokesperson, and Gasdia signed and renewed contracts to pay Jacobs tens of thousands of dollars. Weeks earlier, Jacobs had admitted in disciplinary proceedings before the Massachusetts Board of Registration in Medicine that he continuously prescribed narcotics to patients, ignored the risk of addiction, and kept prescribing narcotics even after his patients overdosed.
context: Gasdia's action was to formalize payments to a prescriber known to be under investigation and disciplined for dangerous prescribing, rather than restrict the relationship.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Gasdia refused to restrict targeting of fired prescriber without license loss
original_label: Gasdia refused to restrict targeting of fired prescriber without license loss
quote: For years, Gasdia helped to decide which doctors went into Region Zero. For example, in 2003, Gasdia refused a request from staff to place in Region Zero a profitable Massachusetts prescriber who had been fired by his practice. Gasdia did not want to take a doctor off the sales target list unless he had lost his license or was already under investigation by the authorities. Gasdia directed the staff member: 'Let's discuss one-on-one.' Eleven years and many prescriptions later, the Massachusetts Board of Registration in Medicine suspended the doctor's license in 2014 — after he prescribed Purdue opioids to a patient who overdosed and died.
context: Gasdia's criteria for restricting sales targeting to a prescriber were highly restrictive (license loss or federal investigation only), filtering out concerns about practice termination or other warning signs.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Gasdia tracked Core and Super Core prescriber targeting metrics
original_label: Gasdia tracked Core and Super Core prescriber targeting metrics
quote: Gasdia tracked the implementation and effect of his targeting and reported on them to the other individual defendants. In 2011, Gasdia wrote to CEO John Stewart that 'Core and Super Core have combined for just under 90% of all Rxs the past few weeks … I am digging deeper to see how many [Super Cores] have been seen 6 times in first three months as well as those seen more and those seen less.'
context: Gasdia's communication to the CEO shows that attention was focused on the metric of prescriber targeting by visit frequency, with 90% of prescriptions coming from targeted doctors.

label: Gasdia demanded explanation for missed Core and Super Core targeting
original_label: Gasdia demanded explanation for missed Core and Super Core targeting
quote: In 2013, Gasdia sent staff a series of emails raising 'serious concern[s]' about sales reps' failure to call on the most prolific prescribers. He demanded an explanation for why some prescribers that sales reps had targeted were 'off list,' noting 'we have 46% of reps who didn't follow direction and don't have the correct # of COREs/SUPER COREs.' Gasdia reproached his team, noting: 'Our management team needs to get on this ASAP. We are not getting the job done and when sales targets aren't hit, this first step is to have the right targets. It appears as if the reps have missed the boat.'
context: Gasdia's enforcement action focused on ensuring adherence to targeting strategy for prolific prescribers, treating deviation from this targeting as a management failure.

label: Timney became CEO in January 2014
original_label: Timney became CEO in January 2014
quote: In January 2014, just a few months before Massachusetts declared the opioid epidemic a public health emergency, Timney picked up as CEO where John Stewart left off, directing and overseeing the sale and marketing of Purdue's opioids and the expansion of the sales force, including in Massachusetts. Timney directed Purdue sales reps to target Massachusetts doctors to prescribe opioids to more patients, at higher doses, for longer periods of time.
context: Timney assumed the CEO position and continued the sales strategy as his structural role in the company.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Timney received daily reports on opioid-related abuse and overdoses
original_label: Timney received daily reports on opioid-related abuse and overdoses
quote: Starting in January and continuing for his entire time at Purdue, Timney regularly received internal reports — sometimes multiple times a day — that summarized media coverage of opioid-related issues. The reports included articles about doctors over-prescribing opioids, stories of people overdosing, drug abuse chatroom chatter, and more. After receiving these reports, Timney often followed up with requests to his staff to dig deeper on an item in that day's summary.
context: Timney's attention was directed to receive regular reports about opioid-related harms, but his follow-up involved investigating media coverage rather than changing company conduct.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: McKinsey advised focusing on high-volume and high-value prescribers
original_label: McKinsey advised focusing on high-volume and high-value prescribers
quote: As CEO, Timney continued John Stewart's aggressive sales strategy known as Evolve 2 Excellence or E2E. In an updated presentation to Timney, consultants from McKinsey emphasized that to increase profits, Purdue must increase the number of visits to high-volume and 'high-value' prescribers. Timney knew and intended that Purdue sales reps aggressively target prolific prescribers.
context: External consultants reinforced the company's strategic focus on targeting high-volume prescribers, directing Timney's attention toward continued aggressive sales strategy.

label: Timney created call center to reach restricted-access prescribers
original_label: Timney created call center to reach restricted-access prescribers
quote: At the same time, Timney created a new way to reach physicians who did not allow sales reps in their clinics (no- and limited-access prescribers). Timney directed staff to set up a call center, where sales reps would call restricted-access prescribers and promote Purdue's opioids over the phone. Timney oversaw this and other initiatives to reach those prescribers, including email and digital marketing.
context: Timney's response to restricted-access policies was to develop alternative channels to continue sales targeting of these prescribers.

label: Timney requested regular updates on Evolve 2 Excellence progress
original_label: Timney requested regular updates on Evolve 2 Excellence progress
quote: In March, Timney received updates from sales staff about the Evolve 2 Excellence sales strategy. Sales staff wrote among themselves that Timney had 'requested regular updates' on the E2E project and that '[t]here will continue to be a great deal of focus on the activity of the Sales Force as a measurement of whether we are making the necessary progress during 2014.'
context: Timney's request for regular updates established a reporting channel focused on sales force activity as the measure of progress toward company goals.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Timney touted Massachusetts pro-abuse-deterrent legislation
original_label: Timney touted Massachusetts pro-abuse-deterrent legislation
quote: In May, Timney reported to the Board about how, under his direction, Purdue had successfully lobbied for legislation in Massachusetts that prohibited a non-abuse deterrent formulation from being dispensed if an abuse deterrent formulation of that drug was available. Timney touted this as a 'positive development' 'in a state from which we've seen significant anti-opioid activity in recent months' and 'closely aligned with our commercial strategy.'
context: Timney's board reports highlighted favorable legislation as aligned with commercial strategy, showing political advocacy was part of the dominant agenda.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Timney acknowledged but minimized risks of abuse-deterrent ineffectiveness
original_label: Timney acknowledged but minimized risks of abuse-deterrent ineffectiveness
quote: In February 2015, Timney gave an internal presentation about Purdue's strategy for continuing to profit from the sale of opioids. Timney acknowledged that the abuse deterrent properties of OxyContin do 'not address overconsumption' orally —i.e., the most common mode of abuse—and that 'abusers are likely to find a way around the ADP technology.' At the same time, Timney directed Purdue's sales reps to promote OxyContin's abuse deterrent properties—without disclosing these critical facts.
context: Timney acknowledged in internal presentations that abuse-deterrent claims did not address the most common abuse route, but this awareness did not prevent sales force promotion of these claims.

label: Mother of addict asked Purdue to fund treatment center
original_label: Mother of addict asked Purdue to fund treatment center
quote: In March, Timney received an email from a mother whose daughter was in treatment for opioid addiction. The mother asked Purdue to fund a recovery treatment center. Timney forwarded the email to his colleagues and the mother received a form letter in response, listing various things Purdue had done to 'help solve' the opioid crisis.
context: Timney received a direct warning signal about harm from a family member affected by opioid addiction, which was handled with a form letter response.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Timney demanded strategies to mitigate business risks from opioid pressure
original_label: Timney demanded strategies to mitigate business risks from opioid pressure
quote: In April, as public pressure against opioids grew, Timney sent an email to staff titled, 'Urgency and Intensity.' Expressing serious concern about the future of the business, Timney demanded staff calculate Purdue's potential losses, develop strategies to mitigate them, and focus on improving the effectiveness of the sales force.
context: Timney's communication shows his attention was focused on business risks from the growing opioid crisis, with a response focused on sales force effectiveness rather than product safety.

label: Consultant recommended humanizing company and shifting focus from OxyContin
original_label: Consultant recommended humanizing company and shifting focus from OxyContin
quote: In September, Purdue received recommendations from a consultant on how to '[c]ontain and mitigate the reputational harm to Purdue Pharma and the Sackler family as a result of multiple investigations and litigation.' Rather than working on actual solutions to the opioid epidemic, the report recommended that Purdue 'shift attention [from OxyContin] to fentanyl and other opioids.' The report recommended that Timney be deployed 'to humanize the Company.' Timney's focus continued to be Purdue's profits and reputation, not the health and welfare of patients, including in Massachusetts, who continued to overdose and die due to Purdue's dangerous drugs.
context: A consultant's recommendations and Timney's response show how the company addressed reputational harm through messaging rather than substantive changes to sales practices.

label: Landau joined Purdue in 1999 as Chief Medical Officer from 2007-2013
original_label: Landau joined Purdue in 1999 as Chief Medical Officer from 2007-2013
quote: Craig Landau has been selling Purdue opioids for nearly twenty years. He joined Purdue in 1999, was Chief Medical Officer from 2007 to 2013, and has been CEO since 2017. Landau participated in and directed a significant part of Purdue's misconduct from the 2007 convictions until today. In each of his positions, Landau worked to get more Massachusetts patients on opioids at higher doses for longer periods of time.
context: Landau's structural positions gave him authority over medical and regulatory strategy, linking sales goals to clinical claims.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Landau placed commercial reps on every research team
original_label: Landau placed commercial reps on every research team
quote: In January 2008, Landau addressed the entire sales force at the National Sales Meeting. He explained that he put a commercial representative on every research team, to orient research in ways that will sell more opioids.
context: Landau's structural innovation of placing commercial reps on research teams directed the attention of research toward sales-relevant outcomes.

label: Landau reviewed doctor-shopping data showing higher oxycodone misuse in Massachusetts
original_label: Landau reviewed doctor-shopping data showing higher oxycodone misuse in Massachusetts
quote: Landau knew there was a high rate of oxycodone misuse in Massachusetts. Indeed, in April 2010, Landau edited and approved a presentation to the Board showing that the rate of 'doctor shopping' in Massachusetts was far higher for oxycodone products than for other opioids. He reiterated this information in August.
context: Landau received and presented to the board data showing elevated risk of misuse in Massachusetts, but this did not result in restricted marketing to that market.

label: Landau received reports of abuse-deterrent formulation being defeated
original_label: Landau received reports of abuse-deterrent formulation being defeated
quote: In October, Landau received reports from internet chat rooms where abusers shared how to defeat OxyContin's new formulation. Landau passed this information on to John Stewart and Russell Gasdia.
context: Landau received warning signals about the ineffectiveness of abuse-deterrent formulations but passed them up the chain rather than acting on them.

label: Landau approved plan to target military healthcare convention with opioid promotion
original_label: Landau approved plan to target military healthcare convention with opioid promotion
quote: In March, Landau approved a plan to send sales reps to the Military Healthcare Convention & Conference to promote Purdue's opioids as part of Purdue's strategy to target vulnerable patient population such as veterans.
context: Landau's approval directed sales targeting toward vulnerable populations as part of commercial strategy.

label: Landau noted publications questioning opioid therapy efficacy
original_label: Landau noted publications questioning opioid therapy efficacy
quote: In July, Landau emailed a staff member, flagging 'publications calling into question the benefit of opioid therapy for chronic non/malignant pain,' including a publication from Massachusetts General Hospital. These publications were funded, in part, by Purdue, and Landau wanted to make sure they in turn were supporting Purdue's opioids.
context: Landau identified warning signals in published research questioning opioid therapy, but his response was to ensure that Purdue-funded researchers would support company marketing.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Landau compiled meta-analysis showing limited efficacy of long-term opioid use
original_label: Landau compiled meta-analysis showing limited efficacy of long-term opioid use
quote: In March, Landau compiled a meta-analysis of studies of chronic opioid use, writing that most studies showed only 'mild to moderate improvement' in function, that some studies suggested that 'long-term opioid therapy is associated with negative outcomes,' and noting that there is a 'critical need for additional studies to determine the long-term safety and efficacy of chronic opioid therapy for durations longer than 1 year.'
context: Landau compiled a meta-analysis showing limitations and risks of chronic opioid use, which did not prevent continued promotion of long-term therapy.

label: Landau wrote plan proposing opioid consolidation strategy
original_label: Landau wrote plan proposing opioid consolidation strategy
quote: Landau proposed that Purdue should take advantage of the public concern about opioids to become an even more dominant opioid seller 'as other companies abandon the space.' Purdue would pursue an 'opioid consolidation strategy' and be the last one standing.
context: Landau's response to the emerging opioid crisis and public pressure was to propose a strategy to consolidate market dominance as competitors exited.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Landau's notes identified key problems in opioid prescribing
original_label: Landau's notes identified key problems in opioid prescribing
quote: As Purdue's scheme unraveled, in the fall of 2017, Purdue CEO Landau wrote down notes about the opioid crisis. He wrote: 'There are: Too many Rxs being written Too high a dose For too long For conditions that often don't require them By doctors who lack the requisite training in how to use them appropriately.'
context: Landau's notes show he identified and articulated the core problems created by the scheme he was leading, but did not act to stop it.

label: Purdue's own testing revealed abuse risk
original_label: Purdue's own testing revealed abuse risk
quote: Purdue's own testing in 1995 had demonstrated that 68% of the oxycodone could be extracted from an OxyContin tablet when crushed.
context: Van Zee cites Purdue's internal pharmacology review showing the company knew the controlled-release formulation could be compromised before OxyContin was marketed.

label: MS Contin abuse precedent within Purdue
original_label: MS Contin abuse precedent within Purdue
quote: There had been some precedence for the diversion and abuse of controlled-release opioid preparations. Purdue's own MS Contin had been abused in the late 1980s in a fashion similar to how OxyContin was later to be; by 1990, MS Contin had become the most abused prescription opioid in one major metropolitan area.
context: Van Zee documents that Purdue had direct experience with abuse of its own prior controlled-release opioid product before launching OxyContin.

label: Geographic clustering of early abuse reports
original_label: Geographic clustering of early abuse reports
quote: Opioid prescribing has had significant geographical variations. In some areas, such as Maine, West Virginia, eastern Kentucky, southwestern Virginia, and Alabama, from 1998 through 2000, hydrocodone and (non-OxyContin) oxycodone were being prescribed 2.5 to 5.0 times more than the national average. By 2000, these same areas had become high OxyContin-prescribing areas—up to 5 to 6 times higher than the national average in some counties. These areas, in which OxyContin was highly available, were the first in the nation to witness increasing OxyContin abuse and diversion, which began surfacing in 1999 and 2000.
context: Van Zee presents evidence showing that OxyContin abuse appeared earliest and most intensely in regions where Purdue targeted high-prescribing physicians.

label: Rapid escalation of treatment admissions for opioid dependence
original_label: Rapid escalation of treatment admissions for opioid dependence
quote: In eastern Kentucky from 1995 to 2001, there was a 500% increase in the number of patients entering methadone maintenance treatment programs, about 75% of whom were OxyContin dependent. In West Virginia, the first methadone maintenance treatment program opened in August 2000, largely in response to the increasing number of people with OxyContin dependence. By October 2003, West Virginia had 7 methadone maintenance treatment clinics with 3040 patients in treatment.
context: Van Zee documents dramatic increases in opioid-dependent patients in specific regions where OxyContin was highly prescribed, indicating observable public health signals.

label: Sharp rise in opioid-related deaths in high-prescribing region
original_label: Sharp rise in opioid-related deaths in high-prescribing region
quote: In southwest Virginia, the number of deaths related to opioid prescriptions increased 830%, from 23 in 1997 to 215 in 2003.
context: Van Zee cites mortality data from a region with the highest OxyContin prescribing, documenting escalating drug-related deaths coinciding with market availability.

label: Studies show high addiction rates in chronic pain patients
original_label: Studies show high addiction rates in chronic pain patients
quote: There are a number of studies, however, that demonstrate that in the treatment of chronic non-cancer-related pain with opioids, there is a high incidence of prescription drug abuse. Prescription drug abuse in a substantial minority of chronic-pain patients has been demonstrated in studies by Fishbain et al. (3%–18% of patients), Hoffman et al. (23%), Kouyanou et al. (12%), Chabal et al. (34%), Katz et al. (43%), Reid et al. (24%–31%), and Michna et al. (45%). A recent literature review showed that the prevalence of addiction in patients with long-term opioid treatment for chronic non-cancer-related pain varied from 0% to 50%, depending on the criteria used and the subpopulation studied.
context: Van Zee reviews published research documenting high rates of abuse and dependence that contradicted Purdue's promotion of extremely low addiction risk.

label: FDA medical reviewer found no advantage over existing drugs
original_label: FDA medical reviewer found no advantage over existing drugs
quote: The FDA's medical review officer, in evaluating the efficacy of OxyContin in Purdue's 1995 new drug application, concluded that OxyContin had not been shown to have a significant advantage over conventional, immediate-release oxycodone taken 4 times daily other than a reduction in frequency of dosing.
context: Van Zee cites the FDA's own internal evaluation from the new drug approval process showing OxyContin lacked superior efficacy.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Sales compensation tied to volume targets
original_label: Sales compensation tied to volume targets
quote: A lucrative bonus system encouraged sales representatives to increase sales of OxyContin in their territories, resulting in a large number of visits to physicians with high rates of opioid prescriptions, as well as a multifaceted information campaign aimed at them. In 2001, in addition to the average sales representative's annual salary of $55 000, annual bonuses averaged $71500, with a range of $15 000 to nearly $240 000. Purdue paid $40 million in sales incentive bonuses to its sales representatives that year.
context: Van Zee documents Purdue's incentive structure that directed sales effort toward high-volume prescribers regardless of medical appropriateness.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Prescriber profiling identifies and targets high prescribers
original_label: Prescriber profiling identifies and targets high prescribers
quote: One of the cornerstones of Purdue's marketing plan was the use of sophisticated marketing data to influence physicians' prescribing. Drug companies compile prescriber profiles on individual physicians—detailing the prescribing patterns of physicians nationwide—in an effort to influence doctors' prescribing habits. Through these profiles, a drug company can identify the highest and lowest prescribers of particular drugs in a single zip code, county, state, or the entire country. One of the critical foundations of Purdue's marketing plan for OxyContin was to target the physicians who were the highest prescribers for opioids across the country. The resulting database would help identify physicians with large numbers of chronic-pain patients. Unfortunately, this same database would also identify which physicians were simply the most frequent prescribers of opioids and, in some cases, the least discriminate prescribers.
context: Van Zee explains how Purdue's marketing infrastructure systematically identified and targeted high-volume opioid prescribers, creating a channel that made indiscriminate prescribers salient to the sales organization.

category: Rules of the game and attention-directing incentives
label: Expansion of sales force directed to increase physician reach
original_label: Expansion of sales force directed to increase physician reach
quote: From 1996 to 2000, Purdue increased its internal sales force from 318 sales representatives to 671, and its total physician call list from approximately 33 400 to 44 500 to approximately 70 500 to 94 000 physicians.
context: Van Zee documents how Purdue's organizational structure was explicitly redesigned to expand contact with and influence over prescribers.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Marketing expenditure targeting non-cancer pain market
original_label: Marketing expenditure targeting non-cancer pain market
quote: Purdue pursued an 'aggressive' campaign to promote the use of opioids in general and OxyContin in particular. In 2001 alone, the company spent $200 million in an array of approaches to market and promote OxyContin. Purdue 'aggressively' promoted the use of opioids for use in the 'non-malignant pain market.' A much larger market than that for cancer-related pain, the non–cancer-related pain market constituted 86% of the total opioid market in 1999.
context: Van Zee documents Purdue's strategic focus and resource allocation toward expanding opioid use in a much larger, less medically established market segment.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Aggressive symposia recruitment and speaker training
original_label: Aggressive symposia recruitment and speaker training
quote: From 1996 to 2001, Purdue conducted more than 40 national pain-management and speaker-training conferences at resorts in Florida, Arizona, and California. More than 5000 physicians, pharmacists, and nurses attended these all-expenses-paid symposia, where they were recruited and trained for Purdue's national speaker bureau.
context: Van Zee describes Purdue's large-scale, structured program to train and deploy physicians as advocates for OxyContin, indicating this was a core organizational focus.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Patient starter coupon program distributed nationally
original_label: Patient starter coupon program distributed nationally
quote: Through the sales representatives, Purdue used a patient starter coupon program for OxyContin that provided patients with a free limited-time prescription for a 7- to 30-day supply. By 2001, when the program was ended, approximately 34 000 coupons had been redeemed nationally.
context: Van Zee documents a consumer-focused promotional program coordinated nationally to drive trial and uptake.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Branded merchandise for controlled-schedule drug unprecedented
original_label: Branded merchandise for controlled-schedule drug unprecedented
quote: The distribution to health care professionals of branded promotional items such as OxyContin fishing hats, stuffed plush toys, and music compact discs ('Get in the Swing With OxyContin') was unprecedented for a schedule II opioid, according to the Drug Enforcement Administration.
context: Van Zee cites DEA testimony noting that Purdue's consumer-marketing approach to a controlled substance was novel in scope and nature.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Primary care physician recruitment as strategic target
original_label: Primary care physician recruitment as strategic target
quote: Purdue promoted among primary care physicians a more liberal use of opioids, particularly sustained-release opioids. Primary care physicians began to use more of the increasingly popular OxyContin; by 2003, nearly half of all physicians prescribing OxyContin were primary care physicians.
context: Van Zee documents that Purdue's marketing strategy deliberately targeted a physician population with limited addiction expertise.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: Low addiction risk claims despite contrary evidence
original_label: Low addiction risk claims despite contrary evidence
quote: In much of its promotional campaign—in literature and audiotapes for physicians, brochures and videotapes for patients, and its 'Partners Against Pain' Web site—Purdue claimed that the risk of addiction from OxyContin was extremely small. Purdue trained its sales representatives to carry the message that the risk of addiction was 'less than one percent.' The company cited studies by Porter and Jick, who found iatrogenic addiction in only 4 of 11882 patients using opioids and by Perry and Heidrich, who found no addiction among 10 000 burn patients treated with opioids. Both of these studies, although shedding some light on the risk of addiction for acute pain, do not help establish the risk of iatrogenic addiction when opioids are used daily for a prolonged time in treating chronic pain.
context: Van Zee analyzes how Purdue selectively cited acute-pain studies while systematically ignoring published research on chronic-pain addiction to support an unjustified low-risk narrative.

category: Filtering, discounting and neglect of warnings
label: FDA approval labeling stated addiction very rare
original_label: FDA approval labeling stated addiction very rare
quote: When OxyContin entered the market in 1996, the FDA approved its original label, which stated that iatrogenic addiction was 'very rare' if opioids were legitimately used in the management of pain.
context: Van Zee notes that the initial FDA-approved label contained an unsubstantiated claim about addiction risk, setting a framing that persisted in marketing.

label: OxyContin video distributed without FDA pre-review
original_label: OxyContin video distributed without FDA pre-review
quote: In 1998, Purdue distributed 15 000 copies of an OxyContin video to physicians without submitting it to the FDA for review, an oversight later acknowledged by Purdue. In 2001, Purdue submitted to the FDA a second version of the video, which the FDA did not review until October 2002—after the General Accounting Office inquired about its content. After its review, the FDA concluded that the video minimized the risks from OxyContin and made unsubstantiated claims regarding its benefits to patients.
context: Van Zee documents that Purdue distributed promotional materials through direct physician channels outside FDA oversight, and the FDA's limited capacity meant delayed review of corrected materials.

label: FDA capacity to monitor promotional materials severely limited
original_label: FDA capacity to monitor promotional materials severely limited
quote: The FDA has a limited number of staff for overseeing the enormous amount of promotional materials. In 2002, for example, 39 FDA staff members were responsible for reviewing roughly 34 000 pieces of promotional materials.
context: Van Zee identifies a structural constraint in the regulatory channel: the FDA's review function was understaffed relative to the volume of promotional output.

label: FDA label revised to reflect scientific evidence
original_label: FDA label revised to reflect scientific evidence
quote: In July 2001, to reflect the available scientific evidence, the label was modified to state that data were not available for establishing the true incidence of addiction in chronic-pain patients. The 2001 labeling also deleted the original statement that the delayed absorption of OxyContin was believed to reduce the abuse liability of the drug.
context: Van Zee notes that the FDA required label modifications in 2001, more than five years after market approval and years after abuse had begun to surface regionally.

label: Purdue pleads guilty to misbranding charges
original_label: Purdue pleads guilty to misbranding charges
quote: Misrepresenting the risk of addiction proved costly for Purdue. On May 10, 2007, Purdue Frederick Company Inc, an affiliate of Purdue Pharma, along with 3 company executives, pled guilty to criminal charges of misbranding OxyContin by claiming that it was less addictive and less subject to abuse and diversion than other opioids, and will pay $634 million in fines.
context: Van Zee documents Purdue's legal resolution of charges arising from its marketing claims, occurring well after the abuse crisis had become national.

label: OxyContin abuse surfaces regionally 1999-2000
original_label: OxyContin abuse surfaces regionally 1999-2000
quote: These areas, in which OxyContin was highly available, were the first in the nation to witness increasing OxyContin abuse and diversion, which began surfacing in 1999 and 2000.
context: Van Zee marks the emergence of observable abuse as a potential triggering event in specific geographic markets.

label: Maine opioid abuse admissions spike 460 percent
original_label: Maine opioid abuse admissions spike 460 percent
quote: From 1995 to 2001, the number of patients treated for opioid abuse in Maine increased 460%, and from 1997 to 1999 the state had a 400% increase in the number of chronic hepatitis C cases reported.
context: Van Zee documents dramatic public health indicators in Maine that should have drawn regulatory and industry attention to the OxyContin-opioid problem.

label: Primary care physicians lacked addiction training
original_label: Primary care physicians lacked addiction training
quote: Some experts were concerned that primary care physicians were not sufficiently trained in pain management or addiction issues. Primary care physicians, particularly in a managed care environment of time constraints, also had the least amount of time for evaluation and follow-up of patients with complicated chronic pain.
context: Van Zee notes that Purdue's targeting of primary care physicians placed prescription authority with doctors structurally positioned to miss addiction risk.

label: Medical research showed oxycodone no better than alternatives
original_label: Medical research showed oxycodone no better than alternatives
quote: The Medical Letter on Drugs and Therapeutics concluded in 2001 that oxycodone offered no advantage over appropriate doses of other potent opioids. Randomized double-blind studies comparing OxyContin given every 12 hours with immediate-release oxycodone given 4 times daily showed comparable efficacy and safety for use with chronic back pain and cancer-related pain. Randomized double-blind studies that compared OxyContin with controlled-release morphine for cancer-related pain also found comparable efficacy and safety.
context: Van Zee cites published clinical trials showing OxyContin offered only a dosing frequency advantage, not superior therapeutic efficacy, undermining the basis for aggressive promotion.

category: Focus of attention and dominant agendas
label: Sales growth from 48 million to 1.1 billion in four years
original_label: Sales growth from 48 million to 1.1 billion in four years
quote: When Purdue Pharma introduced OxyContin in 1996, it was aggressively marketed and highly promoted. Sales grew from $48 million in 1996 to almost $1.1 billion in 2000.
context: Van Zee documents the rapid commercial scaling of OxyContin as evidence that market expansion was the dominant organizational agenda.

label: OxyContin became leading abused drug by 2004
original_label: OxyContin became leading abused drug by 2004
quote: The high availability of OxyContin correlated with increased abuse, diversion, and addiction, and by 2004 OxyContin had become a leading drug of abuse in the United States.
context: Van Zee establishes that by 2004, OxyContin's status as a leading drug of abuse represented a public health signal of marketing-driven harm.

label: Nonmedical users grew from 1.9 to 3.1 million in two years
original_label: Nonmedical users grew from 1.9 to 3.1 million in two years
quote: Lifetime nonmedical use of OxyContin increased from 1.9 million to 3.1 million people between 2002 and 2004, and in 2004 there were 615000 new nonmedical users of OxyContin.
context: Van Zee cites epidemiological data showing explosive growth in non-prescription OxyContin use by 2002-2004, a public health signal.

label: Oxycodone prescribing increased 402 percent nationally
original_label: Oxycodone prescribing increased 402 percent nationally
quote: Nationwide, from 1997 to 2002, there was a 226%, 73%, and 402% increase in fentanyl, morphine, and oxycodone prescribing, respectively (in grams per 100 000 population).
